Immunological Targets for Immunotherapy: Inhibitory T Cell Receptors 49 combination are ongoing in other indications including PD-1 naïve melanoma (NCT03743766), and advanced chordoma (NCT03623854). Similar to BMS-986016 (relatlimab), MK-4280 is an IgG4 mAb that binds to LAG-3 on CD8 T cells and T regs with high affinity. MK-4280 is being studied both singly and in combination with pembrolizumab in a phase I dose-escalation study in solid tumors (NCT02720068). In the dose-escalation portion of the study which included 33 patients, 18 patients received MK-4280 monotherapy (7–700 mg every 3 weeks), while 15 were treated with MK-4280/pembrolizumab combination. No adverse safety signals were seen in either monotherapy or combination therapy arms (grade 3/4 adverse events: MK-4280 6%; MK-4280/pembrolizumab 20%). Responses were seen in both monotherapy and combination therapy arms (ORR: MK-4280 6%; MK-4280/pembrolizumab 27%) [159]. LAG525 was also studied singly and in combination with PD-1 inhibitor spartalizumab in a dose-escalation study (NCT03365791). LAG525 was dosed at 15 dose-levels (0.3 mg/ kg up to 1000 mg) either every 2 weeks or either every 4 weeks in combination with spartalizumab (1 mg/kg every 2 weeks or 400 mg every 4 weeks) in the phase I dose-escalation trial. No adverse safety signals were seen with either LAG525 or LAG525/ spartalizumab combination (grade 3/4 adverse events: LAG525 8%; MK- LAG525/spartalizumab 8%). Durable responses were seen with LAG525/spartalizumab combination (10%) including 11 partial and 1 complete response [160]. OMP-313M32 (etigilimab) is an investigational LAG-3 inhibitor that is currently being evaluated in advanced cancer patients. Eighteen patients with advanced solid organ cancer were treated in the dose-escalation study with single-agent OMP-313M32 (etigilimab) at doses ranging from 0.3 to 20 mg/kg every 2 weeks (NCT03119428). As no dose-limiting toxicities were observed, 20 mg/kg was picked as the recommended phase 2 dose. Adverse events were typical for the class. No responses were seen, although four patients (22%) had prolonged stable disease lasting >200 days [161]. Phase I studies of EOS8844488, TJT6, AB154 (NCT03628677), TSR-033 (NCT03250832) and IMP321 (NCT03252938) are planned or ongoing. 1.6 Other Inhibitory B- and T-lymphocyte attenuator (BTLA) is a member of the immu- T Cell Receptors: BTLA noglobulin superfamily of receptors which includes coinhibitory and VISTA (CTLA-4, PD-1, and BTLA) and costimulatory [CD28 and inducible T cell costimulator (ICOS)] molecules. BTLA has an 1.6.1 BTLA and VISTA: intermediate type Ig fold in ectodomain and an ITIM inhibitory Structure and Ligands signaling domain in the cytosolic portion of the receptor. Unlike the other members of this family which interact with ligands of the

50 Diwakar Davar and Hassane M. Zarour B7 family, BTLA interacts with a member of the TNF receptor superfamily (TNFRSF) termed herpes virus entry mediator (HVEM, also known as TNFRSF14) [162]. However, besides binding to BTLA, HVEM binds for other ligands including two members of TNFRSF including LIGHT (TNFSF14) and lymphotoxin α (LTα), herpes simplex virus glycoprotein D (HSV-1 gD), and CD160. The BTLA binding site on HVEM overlaps but is distinct from the LIGHT binding site, although glycoprotein D inhibits the binding of both ligands [163]. The BTLA binding site on HVEM overlaps with the binding site for HSV-1 gD but is distinct from where LIGHT binds [163]. V-domain Ig suppressor of T cell activation (VISTA) is a type I transmembrane protein that contains a signal peptide, extracellular Ig-V domain, stalk, transmembrane domain linked to a cytoplasmic tail [164]. VISTA’s cytoplasmic domain does not contain ITAM, ITIM, or ITSM motifs [165]. VISTA has structural homology with PD-L1 and like PD-L1, potently suppresses T cell activation [164]. In healthy patients, VISTA is abundantly expressed in placental tissue; however, in the context of cancer VISTA is predominately expressed on T regs and MDSCs, which are upregulated in the TME [166, 167]. The receptor that VISTA binds to on human immune cells is unknown at this time. 1.6.2 BTLA and VISTA: BTLA is expressed on Th1 but not Th2 cells, B cells and to a lesser Signaling and Function extent on macrophages, DCs and natural killer cells [168, 169]. In humans, BTLA expression on T cells is associated with poor prognosis in multiple cancers including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) [170] and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [171]. Similar to PD-1, BTLA signaling has been shown to exert an inhibitory effect upon antigen-specific T cells; blockade of which enhances the expansion, proliferation, and cytokine production of TA–specific CD8+ T cells [172]. However, other data suggests that BTLA signaling plays crucial roles in sustaining activated T cells in multiple models including murine models of graft versus host disease (GVHD) [173], CD4+ CD45RBhigh T cell transfer induced colitis in recombination activating gene (Rag) knockout mice [174] and bacterial infection [175]. Concordantly, in advanced melanoma patients treated with adoptive cell therapy, BTLA expression on TIL correlated with response to therapy [176, 177]. The ubiquitous expression of HVEM and BTLA, coupled with broad ligand interaction of HVEM and the ability of HVEM/ BTLA to interact in cis or trans configurations suggest that the BTLA-HVEM pathway is capable of bidirectional signaling with context dependent outcomes. In syngeneic murine models, VISTA blockade enhanced infiltration, proliferation, and effector function of CD8 T cells in TME [167]. Combination VISTA/PD-L1 blockade produced greater antitumor effects than either agent alone, suggesting that VISTA

Immunological Targets for Immunotherapy: Inhibitory T Cell Receptors 51 and PD-1/PD-L1 signaling have overlapping but nonredundant inhibitory effects on CD8 T cells [178]. The effects of VISTA blockade appears to be mediated by IL-23/IL-17 axis, although how IL-17 regulates TA-specific adaptive immunity remains to be clarified [179]. 1.6.3 BTLA and VISTA: At this time, no BTLA development programs have been Preclinical and Clinical disclosed. Data VISTA development programs have been disclosed by Curis (CA-170), and Janssen (onvatilimab, JNJ-61610588). CA-170 is an oral small molecule inhibitor of PD-L1, PD-L2, and VISTA. Target specificity was inferred through functional studies. Preclinically, CA-170 administration demonstrated antitumor activity in syngeneic models of MC38 colorectal carcinoma, CT26 colon carcinoma, and B16 melanoma at a level comparable to PD-1 blockade. A dose-escalation trial of CA-170 in advanced solid tumors and lymphoma patients is ongoing (NCT02812875). Fifty nine patients have been treated across 9 dose levels (50– 800 mg daily and 600–1200 mg twice daily). Interestingly, neither dose-limiting toxicities nor immune related adverse events were noted. In 51 evaluable patients, no responses were observed, although 25 patients had stable disease, several of whom had prolonged stable disease [180]. Although a phase I trial of JNJ-61610588 was launched in solid tumors (NCT02671955), this study was subsequently terminated and no results are available at this time. 2 Conclusions The use of mAb targeting PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 has produced durable responses in a multitude of advanced malignancies hitherto considered terminal. The CTLA-4 inhibitor ipilimumab received regulatory approval for the treatment of metastatic melanoma in 2011. Following this, 6 PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors (cemiplimab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab, avelumab, and durvalumab) and the PD-1/CTLA-4 inhibitor combination (ipilimumab/nivolumab) have been approved to treat advanced cancers in 13 indications, including the first-ever tissue agnostic approval to treat a broad class of cancers defined by a biomarker (pembrolizumab and ipilimumab/nivolumab for DNA mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability—high (MSI- H) tumors). The use of PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 inhibitors is characterized by several features including: unusual patterns of response requiring novel radiographic response criteria [immune related response criteria (irRC)] and unique spectrum of toxicities [immune related adverse events (irAE)]. However, adaptive immune resistance is an issue of increasing concern.

52 Diwakar Davar and Hassane M. Zarour LAG-3, TIM-3, and TIGIT comprise the next generation of inhibitory receptor targets that are being explored in clinical trials. Our current understanding indicates that these receptors provide an overlapping and nonredundant mechanism of regulating immune responses with PD-1; suggesting that coblockade with anti-PD-1 mAbs will improve antitumor immune responses over PD-1 therapy alone. This hypothesis is borne out by early data in dose-escalation trials hinting at responses to LAG-3, TIM-3, and TIGIT blockade at least in small subset of patients. However, the rational evaluation of these agents requires an increased understanding of both the specialized functions of these receptors and their ligands and their effects on TME components besides effector T cells including Tregs, TAMs and MDSC. This will permit the rational design of combinatorial clinical trials particularly in combination with existing therapies; and the determination of biomarkers of response to these novel immune checkpoints. Notably, these studies showed that cancers associated with high exposure to mutagens, such as melanoma (UV exposure) and NSCLC (exposure to tobacco smoke) have higher median TMB than most other cancer types [1–3]. ICI therapy has been remarkably successful in the treatment of these and other malignancies ([4–9], reviewed in [10]). Studies by several groups showed that melanoma, NSCLC and urothelial carcinoma patients with high TMB have higher response rates to ICI therapy than patients with low TMB [8, 11–15]. These studies also showed that the mutational burden determined from WES is highly concordant with the mutational burden determined from WGS. WES has a faster and less computationally intensive data analysis pipeline than WGS, and the coding fraction of the genome (which is directly related to neoantigen production [16]) can be sequenced at a greater depth at lower cost allowing the detection of both clonal and subclonal variants. For these reasons WES is currently the standard approach for TMB measurement. 1.1 Selection The bioinformatics analysis methods described in this chapter of Mutation Types involve the calculation of TMB from nonsynonymous SNV and and Whole-Exome indel mutations only. Some studies have reported that there is a Sequencing high consistency in between TMB measurement from all SNVs of Matched Germline (including synonymous) and TMB from nonsynonymous muta- Samples tions only [17]. However, TMB determined from nonsynonymous mutations may be a more accurate predictor of response to immunotherapy, considering that neoantigens are generated from nonsynonymous mutations only. To obtain an accurate measure of TMB, it is important to remove germline (nontumor and benign) variants from the mutation count. While commonly occurring germline variants can be filtered using data from population sequence databases such as gnomAD [18], ESP (Exome Variant Server, NHLBI GO Exome Sequencing Project), ExAc [18] dbSNP [19], or The 1000 Genomes Project [20], patient-specific single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) that are not present in population databases would be captured in the TMB count, resulting in overestimated TMB (Fig. 1). This is an especially important consideration for patients from ethnic groups that are not well represented in SNP databases. For these reasons, the best practice approach is to sequence a patient-matched germline sample using WES and to use the germline sequencing data to filter out nontumor variants unique to each patient. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) are commonly used as a source of germline material as blood collection is noninvasive and can be readily included in clinical protocols. Normal tissue adjacent to tumors in biopsy specimens can be used as an alternative source of germline, but it is important to ensure

65 80 70 slope = 1.05 60 R2 = 0.9852 50 40 30 20 10 0 0 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 that such specimens are not contaminated by malignant cells. Sequencing of a matched germline sample may also aid in the assessment of other genomic biomarkers, including the detection of MSI and the evaluation of copy number variation (CNV). 1.2 TMB Data Output TMB values are best expressed as the number of mutations per and Clinical Reporting megabase of sequenced genome, as normalization to the fraction of sequenced genome enables the comparison of TMB measurement between different exome capture assays (and even more so between targeted sequencing panels). A crucial challenge for the field of immune-oncology is how to best define a threshold for high TMB. This is not a trivial consideration as there is considerable overlap in TMB between patients who respond to ICI therapy and those who do not respond. This is further complicated by differences in TMB distribution in different cancers [1, 2], and it remains to be determined whether a common TMB threshold will be appropriate for predicting ICI treatment response in multiple cancer types or whether distinct TMB thresholds will be defined for different histologies and different biological contexts (e.g., PD-1/PD-L1 expression, extent of inflammation and T cell infiltration, and defects in antigen presentation). High TMB thresholds have been defined differently in different studies: as a set value (20 mutations per Mb [21, 22]), as a value best associated with the responding patient population (10 mutations per Mb [23]), as median +2 × interquartile range (13.8 mutations per Mb [24]), and as a value derived from a receiver operating characteristic curve,gniretlif PNS enilmreg tuohtiw BMT bM rep snoitatum Measuring Tumor Mutational Burden Using Whole-Exome Sequencing TMB after germline SNP filtering, mutations per Mb Fig. 1 Comparison of TMB determined with and without germline SNP filtering in patient-derived xenograft samples from the NCI Patient Derived Model Repository (https://pdmr.cancer.gov)

66 Tomas Vilimas (23.1 mutations per Mb [3]). Thus, there is currently no consensus on a single method for setting the TMB threshold for predicting response to ICI therapy and different thresholds may be appropriate for different indications and ICI therapies. 1.3 Factors Although TMB is currently one of the most-promising biomarkers for Influencing predicting response to ICI therapy, it is important to note that the the Association specificity and sensitivity of TMB measurement is imperfect. Based on of TMB with ICI analyses of TCGA and published ICI response data, it was shown that Response the best-case estimate of performance TMB had a 74% sensitivity and 59.3% specificity for predicting clinical benefit to ICI therapy [25]. It is becoming clear that the association of TMB and neoantigen load with response to ICI therapy is influenced by intrinsic biological differences between tumor types. Several studies have shown that the association of TMB with survival is influenced by the frequency of subclonal vs clonal mutations [17, 26]. These studies suggest that the burden of clonal mutations (i.e., those that are present in all tumor cells) is more predictive of clinical benefit to ICI therapy than the burden of subclonal mutations, likely because an immune response mounted against subclonal neoantigens is not effective against tumor subclones lacking these neoantigens. 1.4 Relationship High TMB has been shown to be associated with exposure to UV of TMB to Disease and tobacco smoke [1, 27], with DNA mismatch repair (MMR) Features and Other deficiency and microsatellite instability (MSI; [28]), and with Biomarkers mutations in POLE and POLD1 genes, which encode proofreadof Immunotherapy ing DNA Polymerases Epsilon and Delta 1, respectively [29, 30]. Response MMR deficiency drives high TMB and MSI but the overlap between these genomic features is imperfect (Fig. 2; [28]). Interestingly, there is only a marginal correlation between PD-L1 IHC positive score and TMB/MMR/MSI measurement (Fig. 2; [28]), indicating that PD-L1 IHC expression is largely independent from the genomic biomarkers. As alluded earlier in the chapter, TMB likely relates to the abundance of neoepitopes, and several groups showed that neoantigen load correlates with TMB and with ICI treatment response [12, 13, 16, 31]. Neoantigen presentation (and thus the immune response) is also dependent on the function of the antigen presentation machinery. Unlike NSCLC, the neoantigen burden in lung squamous cell carcinoma was found to have no association with survival, possibly due to lower expression of HLA genes and B2M in this disease [26]. Although neoantigen load may be a more direct predictor of immune response than TMB, neoantigen prediction is more difficult to implement as it requires HLA typing for each patient as well as in vitro validation of candidate neoantigens, and these techniques and algorithms have not yet been validated in clinical practice.

Some studies using commercial gene panels showed that TMB can be measured with reasonable concordance to WES and that targeted panel-derived TMB is associated with higher frequency of

68 Tomas Vilimas response to ICI therapy [3, 21, 22, 32, 33], while others reported a correlation of gene panel-equivalent TMB with response in NSCLC but not in melanoma patients [34]. Commercial sequencing panels enable higher-depth sequencing than WES and include optimized data analysis pipelines. However, there are several important considerations for implementing targeted sequencing panels for TMB measurement. One is that the accuracy of TMB calling is inversely proportional to panel size, as reducing panel size (in terms of the number of covered genes and coding sequence capture) results in increasing variance. Chalmers and colleagues modeled the accuracy of TMB calling as a factor of panel size and showed that the variance becomes excessively high when a panel covers less than 0.5 Mb of coding sequence [21]. Another consideration is that TMB calling from targeted panels may require a different selection of mutation types than TMB calling from WES. Synonymous mutations may need to be included in the TMB calculation for some panels [3, 21] as the count of nonsynonymous mutations alone may not provide sufficient power to accurately measure TMB. However, other studies have reported a strong correlation of TMB measurement between WES and targeted panel based on the nonsynonymous mutation count only [22, 33]. Some algorithms also exclude mutations in the most common driver genes to avoid the potential bias that may be inherent in cancer diagnosis-f ocused sequencing panels [21]. Some targeted panel sequencing assays enable TMB measurement without matched germline samples using custom algorithms to predict and filter likely germline alterations [21, 35]. Furthermore, targeted panels are not suitable for comprehensive neoantigen prediction as they are limited to finding mutations only in defined gene sets. The differences in gene content and data analysis between different gene panels highlight the importance of standardizing TMB calling to enable consistent and reproducible use of TMB as a biomarker in clinical practice. An effort to standardize TMB calling is being spearheaded by a working group led by Friends of Cancer Research (FOCR), with the aim to develop a WES-based benchmark for the evaluation of TMB reporting from commercial NGS assays and to define best practices for TMB measurement. In this chapter I describe standardized DNA preparation, whole-exome library construction, sequencing, and bioinformatics analysis protocols for the measurement of TMB using whole-exome sequencing. The protocol described here involves the use of dual index adapters for sequencing using Illumina NovaSeq 6000 sequencers.

7. Concentration calculations.
(a) C alculation example: A library at the 106 dilution yielded 2000 copies/μL in the ddPCR mixture. Multiply 2000 by 106 and by 5 to account for the dilution in the reaction mixture (2000 × 106 × 5 = 1010 copies/μL of original stock library). To obtain nM: (1010 copies/μL × 106 μL)/ (6.023 × 1023 copies/mole) = 1.66 × 10−8 M or 16.6 nM. (b) U se the ddPCR data from the least diluted reactions that yielded concentration information between 100 and 5000 copies per reaction. For most samples this means the 106 data will be used. 2. MTC for whole-exome sequencing of germline samples: ≥50×

3. Minimal acceptable MTC: 120× mean per-base coverage.
Nonsynonymous Somatic Variants for TMB 4. Minimal acceptable Phred quality score: at least 80% of bases with Q ≥ 30.
5. Minimal acceptable uniformity of coverage: least 80% of tar-
geted exome regions should have target coverage above 20% of the MTC.
6. Minimal acceptable variant allele frequency (VAF) for SNV
and insertion/deletion mutations (indels): at least 50% of called variants with ≥5% VAF and a minimum of 3 reads.
7. When sequencing germline samples, all variants are considered
germline except those with 1–3 reads, as variants with very low read counts are likely to be from low-abundance cell-free DNA shed by tumor cells. 3.3.2 Standardized The pipeline summarized below and in Fig. 6 is a standardized Pipeline pipeline that was developed at the Molecular Characterization Lab at Frederick National Lab for Cancer Research for WES data analysis and TMB determination from patient samples. The pipeline is implemented as an integrated algorithm series and includes modules for the measurement of TMB and other genomic biomarkers. As described below, we incorporated two unique pipeline paths depending on the availability of matched germline WES data.

7. Variant calling and TMB determination if germline WES data

Measuring Tumor Mutational Burden Using Whole-Exome Sequencing 89 (c) ( Optional) HLA typing: HLAminer [40], Seq2HLA [41]. (d) ( Optional) Mutational signatures: deconstructSigs [1], https://github.com/raerose01/deconstructSigs). 4 Notes
1. For measuring TMB, it is important to consider is specimen
type, tumor content, tissue processing method and specimen age. Resected tissue, core needle biopsies and FNA specimens of tumor tissue are acceptable, as long as there is sufficient material to determine tumor content—which is an important criterion for sample processing for WES. In our workflow we attempt to enrich tumor tissue specimens to at least 70% tumor content via hand macro dissection or laser capture microdissection (LCM). If tumor tissue enrichment is not feasible, it is important to define the minimum acceptable tumor content. We recommend at least 20% tumor content when sequencing to 200× mean target coverage (MTC) and at least 10% tumor content when sequencing to 400× MTC, as the sensitivity of variant allele detection declines sharply for samples with low tumor content. Similar tissue requirements have been described with other assays reporting TMB—for example, a minimum of 20% tumor cell content is required for the FoundationOne assay [21].
2. Both FFPE (formalin fixation–paraffin embedding) and flash-
frozen tissue samples are suitable for TMB determination using WES. FFPE processing introduces sequence artifacts such as C to T transitions [44, 45] which tend to increase with storage time [46], but the frequency of FFPE artifacts is usually below the minimal allele frequency cutoff in variant-calling pipelines (even when sequencing archival specimens) and has minimal or no influence on the accuracy of TMB calling. If necessary, flash- frozen tissue sample collection can be implemented in prospective studies, as frozen specimens do not exhibit the artifacts seen in FFPE tissue.
3. The pellet will be used for DNA purification. Depending on
the amount and nature of the FFPE sample, the pellet may be very small or difficult to see. If the pellet is aspirated with the supernatant, allow the pellet to drop slowly to the bottom of the tube and use the pipette tip to reattach the pellet to the tube. Alternatively, centrifuge the supernatant again. The DNA- containing pellet can be stored for 2 h at room temperature, for up to 1 day at 2–8 °C, or for longer periods at −20 °C if not processed immediately. The pellet should be equilibrated to room temperature (15–25 °C) prior to resuspension if it has been previously stored at low temperature.

## Chapter 4


94 Tomas Kirchhoff and Robert Ferguson efficacy, toxicity and survival. Host immune homeostasis proves to be critical in determination of ICI success, involving key biological mechanisms controlling host immunity. An emerging determinant of host immune homeostasis is the underlying germline genetic component, which has been shown to impact host immunity; genetic factors explain a large variance in the abundance and activation state of multiple immune cell types, including CD4+ and CD8+ T cells [11–13], immunomodulatory molecules [14, 15], and genes [16, 17], likely translating to distinct immune states. Prior studies have demonstrated that inherited genetic variation affects expression of a substantial number of immune-related genes [18–20]. Hundreds of genetic risk loci for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases have been identified in genome-wide association studies (GWASs) [21], further underscoring the heritable nature of immune variability. Data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and other repositories of extensive genetic data from large populations triggered the hypothesis-driven approaches in identification of germline factors controlling cancer immune responsiveness [22]. These efforts revealed specific germline/immune signatures, some associated with T-cell tumor infiltrates. Altogether, this clearly outlines a possibility that germline genetic repertoire may be a modulating factor in immune-based therapies or prognostic outcomes. However, the concept of germline genetics as a novel surrogate of immune responsiveness has yet to be comprehensively explored in immuno-oncology (IO). Historically, prior studies have focused on candidate designs, assessing a handful of genetic variants with the most plausible biological relevance for their association with clinical IO outcomes such as ICI response or survival [23, 24]. Small-scale variant focus (e.g., variants in cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), PD-1 ligand (PD-L1)), clinical heterogeneity, a lack of independent validation or consideration for other biological immune or tumor surrogates (immunophenotyping, cytokine profiles, TILs, tumor mutation burden, and others), and most importantly a limited power of sample cohorts, were among the major drawbacks preventing the reproducibility of these findings. Some of these impediments are addressed by implementing genome-wide approaches (such as GWAS and next-generation sequencing technologies [NGS]), or by including other layers of “omics” or immunological information generated from tumor microenvironment (TME), peripheral blood, and other host factors (e.g., microbiome). While it is generally expected that the germline genetic host factors associated with IO outcomes may exert only moderate-tolow penetrant effects, these analyses need to be performed in a large collaborative framework, with harmonized clinical information on ICI efficacy, toxicity, or survival. Following the successful identification of these novel germline biomarkers, the development of a clinical assay will need to be complemented with other relevant

Germline Variants as Biomarkers of Immunotherapy 95 biomarkers of ICI, as recently introduced in proposed personalized “immunograms” [25–27]. 1.1 Hereditability The idea that germline genetics affects host immunity has been of Baseline Host promoted by intriguing observations suggesting that the immune Immunity: the Lessons specific traits in humans are under influence of germline genetics. from Immunopheno Methodological approaches have primarily focused on the heredityping tability of different subclasses of peripheral blood cells, cytokine levels, and/or serum protein diversity [11, 15, 22]. With technological advancements, in particular high-resolution deep immunophenotyping flow cytometry, and implementation of twin populations, more comprehensive strategies for the assessment of hereditability of immune cell profiles became feasible. Adopting these techniques, many studies [11, 13, 28–30] reported that immune cell subsets, including the phenotypes of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells are under strong genetic influence [31]. In a seminal report, 497 adult female twins (TwinsUK) were profiled by high- resolution deep immunophenotyping flow cytometry for >23,000 robust blood immune cell phenotypes. More than 75% of these traits showed a predominantly heritable influence; most notably, the immune homeostasis of B2, CD4+ and CD8+ cells was largely attributed to the effects of inherited genetics [32]. This study demonstrated that the germline genetics has a strong effect on adaptive immune traits, a finding that may have important implications for the genetic susceptibilities to autoimmunity (discussed in subsequent sections) and IO. The implementation of GWAS and genome-wide single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays technology, coupled with large scale immune phenotyping, helped to identify common genetic variation associated with specific categorical or quantitative representation of blood cell phenotypes on a large population-based scale. This is exemplified in a large effort [13], analyzing 78,000 immune traits in 669 female twins and identifying 300 SNPs (representing 11 genetic loci) that control the phenotypes of 19 functionally important immune subsets in the blood. The most heritable trait among these was the frequency of CD39+ cells within the CD4+ compartment, which is consistent with the previous studies showing that CD4+ phenotypes are strongly controlled by germline genetic factors [11]. As CD39+CD4+ T cells are functional T regulatory cells (Tregs) [33], a key subset in the modulation of immune responses in tumorigenesis [34], these findings may be highly relevant for IO; the balance between CD4+ cells and T-reg/CD8+ T cells is an important marker of favorable ICI outcomes [35]. This is important evidence to support studying germline genetic factors in the context of IO, including tumor-host interactions and immune-based therapies.

96 Tomas Kirchhoff and Robert Ferguson 1.2 Germline Genetic Large pan-cancer “omics” information has been accumulated Interaction with Tumor through TCGA, including GWAS SNP array data, NGS data on Microenvironment germline and tumor tissues, corresponding tumor RNA-sequencing (TME): a Role (RNA-seq), and other phenotype information such as total tumor of Germline Genetic lymphocytic infiltrate (TILs) (from genomic and H&E image data) Variation in Cancer [36]. Along with the outcome information available, the utilization of these resources allowed for pivotal exploration of the host Immune genetics interacting with putative somatic phenotypes across can- Responsiveness cer types. A straightforward approach tested the germline genetic variation that impact the gene expression in tumor—that is, expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs)—the variants associated with the expression of genes in their vicinity (cis) or genes mapping in different loci of the genome (trans). Studies have shown that the single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) reproducibly associated with complex disorders [37] as well as certain pharmacologic phenotypes [38] are significantly enriched for eQTLs, relative to frequency- matched control SNPs. Using the integration of TCGA datasets across 24 different human cancers, >64,000 eQTLs were recently identified as associated with the tumor expression of 18,210 genes (eGenes) [22]. Notably, these genes were enriched for involvement in immune processes, suggesting that tumor expression of immune genes may be shaped by hereditary genetics. Inferring on the abundance of immune cells in TCGA tumor samples using a cellularity deconvolution method [39], the study identified 103 germline genetic variants that were significantly associated with the immune gene signatures of specific immune cell infiltration (31 lymphoid and 72 myeloid signatures). These included T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and dendritic cells, suggesting the widespread impact of germline genetics on immune cellularity within the TME [22]. Finally, the two most significant eQTLs consistently expressed across all 24 cancer types were in ERAP2 and ICOSLG genes, the expression of which predicted overall survival in patients treated with anti-PD1 ICI. These findings clearly provide insight into possible stratification of patients receiving anti–PD-L1 therapy, by integrating germline genetic data with TME phenotypes. As the inflammation of tumors is an important factor associated with sensitivity to anti-PD1/anti– PD-L1 therapies [40, 41], the germline genetic factors driving the presence of immune cell infiltrations may be an important personalized biomarker in IO. Currently, as part of collaborative efforts in the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer (SITC), an ongoing TCGA analysis is underway for a comprehensive assessment of TME immunophenotypes impacted by germline genetic variation, following a seminal recent work on pan-cancer TME-associated immune signatures [42].

Germline Variants as Biomarkers of Immunotherapy 97 1.3 Inherited Host With the strong evidence that germline genetic factors affect Immunity and ICI immune propensity of TME, parallel efforts have tested whether Outcomes inherited factors also associate with outcomes of immune-based therapies. Methodologically, the early investigations examined the 1.3.1 The Candidate most plausible biological candidates for their association with can- Studies cer survival or therapy response. These include associations of genetic variants in TLR4, P2RX7, and FPR1 with differential outcome in breast and colon cancer patients treated with adjuvant chemotherapy, likely through the modulation of antitumor immune response [43, 44]. Several studies have assessed the contribution of CTLA-4 polymorphisms in the context of anti- CTLA-4 ICI [24, 45, 46]. Although some significant associations have been reported, these lacked independent validation. Recently, an NGS scan revealed that the germline heterozygous state of the human leukocyte antigen class I (HLA-I) loci associate with anti- PD1 response and post-treatment survival of melanoma and lung cancer patients [47]. This effect was enhanced by, but not dependent on, the tumor mutation burden (TMB). Furthermore, efficacy of ICI was diminished by somatic loss of HLA-I heterozygosity in the tumor cells. Importantly, molecular dynamics simulations of HLA super-types associated with poor prognosis revealed unique elements that might affect neoantigen recognition by cytotoxic T cells [47]. These results may have important implications not only for predicting response to ICI based on germline status of HLA-I, but the stratification by HLA-I germline states may predict specific and perhaps personalized neoantigen presentation patterns. This may provide important insight into “outlier” tumors: for example, a resistance to ICI observed in tumors with high TMB, versus the ICI sensitivity in less mutated “cold” tumors. This may also be essential for the design of more effective and personalized neoantigen-based therapeutic vaccines [48]. 1.3.2 Autoimmune Recent GWASs performed in large consortia collaborations identi- Genetic Risk as a Germline fied >1000 SNPs associated with >60 different autoimmune condi- Genetic Marker of ICI tions [49, 50]. Interestingly, the association patterns showed Outcomes considerable genetic pleiotropy—the enrichment of autoimmunity risk variants often overlapped between different autoimmune traits, and vice versa, suggesting the complex nature of genetic susceptibility to these diseases [49, 51–54]. Remarkably, among the genetic variants associated with specific immune-cell phenotypes, such as Th cells [55] and CD4+ or CD8+ T-cells [56, 57], there was consistent enrichment for autoimmunity risk variants. In fact, a comprehensive analysis estimated that >75% of T-cell-specific phenotypic variation is explained by cis-acting eQTLs, significantly enriched for autoimmune risk loci [58]. This may have an important implication in IO as the activity and balance of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells is instrumental in the success of ICI [35]. If the

98 Tomas Kirchhoff and Robert Ferguson process of regulation of these cells is controlled by underlying autoimmune variants, it is highly plausible that the germline status of these variants in patients treated by ICI would modulate the treatment outcome. Also, the autoimmunity is most prevalent among adverse immune-related side effects (irAEs) associated with ICI, including autoimmune manifestations in GI, endocrine and other sites. It is possible that the germline susceptibility to these autoimmune conditions may stratify patients by risk to the same autoimmune irAEs before the ICI treatment is administered. Of note, while the autoimmune risk alleles confer only a small-risk effect (relative risk ranging between 1.1 and 1.5), these effects will likely be substantially enhanced upon ICI, with possible actionable clinical applicability as predictive biomarkers (a concept described in Subheading 1.4). This is exemplified in our recent study, in which we tested 25 risk variants, each associated with multiple autoimmune conditions in recent GWAS, for their effect on ICI efficacy. We found that genetic variation in the IL2/IL21 region— a risk locus for allergy, colitis and type 1 diabetes—was associated with increased anti-PD-1 response, with significance surpassing multiple testing adjustments (OR = 0.26; 95% CI = 0.12–0.53; p = 0.0002). Pending further validation, our study provides the first evidence that autoimmune genetic susceptibility may modulate ICI efficacy, suggesting that systematic testing of autoimmune risk loci can reveal personalized biomarkers of ICI outcome [59]. We have recently found a significant association of an eQTL in IL10/BATF3 locus on 1q32 with better melanoma survival, with an effect size suggesting a clinical implication complementing other established clinicopathological prognostic markers [60]. This is a well-established risk variant associated in recent GWASs with multiple autoimmune conditions [61], strongly suggesting that the germline autoimmunity risk may be an advantage favoring longer overall survival in immunogenic tumors. 1.3.3 Genome-Wide The genome-wide DNA microarray technologies used in GWAS Approaches: Genetic offer an affordable solution for linking the common genetic varia- Variation in Coding tion across the genome with the phenotypes of interest. In IO, the Versus Regulatory Genome use of germline GWAS design has been most apparent in linking the germline genetics with TME immune-component [22], as described in previous sections. Currently, no large GWAS effort has been reported for ICI outcomes, despite an urgent need for such an analysis. The lessons learned from GWAS studies of disease risk revealed the associated common genetic variants conferring only moderate-to-low penetrant risk effects. A simple calculation of statistical power estimates that >2500 cases and equal number of controls are needed to achieve statistical power of 80% for the discovery of low-penetrant loci, ranging in effect size between 1.1 and 1.5. Thus, a large collaborative effort, pooling the ICI-treated patient resources across the world, is necessary to overcome the

Germline Variants as Biomarkers of Immunotherapy 99 power limitations. Recently, we have established an international consortium for conducting the first comprehensive GWAS on metastatic melanoma ICI efficacy, autoimmune toxicity and ICIassociated survival, pooling >10,000 patients treated across different ICI modalities. While still in the initial phase, some data have already been generated, in particular on anti-CTLA-4 treatment response. Not surprisingly, significant associations have been noted for anti-CTLA4 resistance with established autoimmune risk loci (unpublished data), reaching statistical threshold of GWAS level of significance (p < 10−8). Remarkably, however, while these loci showed only low-penetrant association effects in autoimmunity GWAS, the observed effect size for these variants in ICI study are much larger (relative risk of 4–5), which are the effects with “actionable” clinical potential. While SNP array design comprehensively captures genetic variation across the genome, including regulatory regions, these arrays contain mainly common variants. As the cost of NGS is gradually dropping, the possibility emerges of a parallel assessment of both common and rare variants contributing to ICI outcomes. However, the data complexity is among the major hurdles of NGS technologies and the standard single SNP tests may not be the most feasible in NGS. The use of geneburden tests, such as Sequence Kernel Association Test (SKAT) [62, 63] may reduce these problems by simultaneous analysis of both common and rare variants in regions of interest. Also, the cost of these technologies is still prohibitive to allow for testing a large number of patients on a population scale. Whole-exome sequencing (WXS) offers a relatively cost-effective alternative, however it targets only exonic regions (representing about 1% of genome). Nevertheless, the expectation that coding genetic variation may exert causal biological effects with imminent clinical applicability is another notable advantage in favor of WXS. Recently, we performed WXS germline analysis as part of a multi-i nstitutional collaboration on peripheral blood lymphocytes from >250 metastatic melanoma patients treated by anti-CTLA-4 ICI. Using geneburden SKAT analysis we discovered significant associations of anti-CTLA-4 resistance with genetic variants in chemokine-related locus (CCR2, CCRL2, CCR5) on chromosome 3p21. Several coding variants in this locus show individual associations with IPI resistance across a ~23-kb region and the pathway analysis of the most significant associations implicated molecular networks of dendritic chemotaxis (p < 0.00001) and chemokine receptors (p < 0.0002). This provides evidence that the germline genetic variation modulates chemokine pathways in anti-CTLA4 response, possibly by altering dendritic cell migration during ICI-mediated T-helper cell stimulation [64]. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) offers the most comprehensive platform for the discovery of germline genomic determinants of ICI. However, WGS use in large populations is

100 Tomas Kirchhoff and Robert Ferguson still challenging due to the cost and analytical complexity, in particular for assessing the variants in noncoding regulatory regions (>99% of genome data form WGS) with unknown biological relevance. To maximize the discovery success in WGS it is critical to integrate other layers of biological, genomic, transcriptomic and other “omics” data from TME, immune cell infiltrates, peripheral blood immune cells to narrow down the genomic regions of interests for analytical prioritization in WGS. In our preliminary data, we have recently initiated a large WGS scan on the identification of germline genetic determinants of host immunity that will modulate ICI outcomes in metastatic melanoma patients treated in clinical trials by ICI. The analysis combines genomic, epigenetic and transcriptomic layers of information in the target T-cell population to narrow down the regions in the genome that are under control of germline genetic variants. These types of integrative NGS analyses will provide the ultimate discovery strategy to encompass the complete immunogenetic landscape of ICI treated patients on an individual level. 1.4 Inherited Genetic The germline genetic variants in IO represent putative predictive Factors as Clinically biomarkers with personalized potential; the genetic variation may Relevant be polymorphic or private (rare in the population) hence can rep- Biomarkers of ICI resent a predictive “fingerprint” specific to individual patients. Moreover, it can be assessed in a noninvasive test from the blood 1.4.1 Clinical by a low-cost genotyping assay, and can therefore be feasibly Applicability applied in clinical stratification of large number of patients prior to treatment in a robust high-throughput setting. An excellent example of germline ICI biomarkers in current clinical practice is the status of mismatch repair deficiency in colon cancer [65, 66]; the germline mutations in mismatch repair pathways result in high TMB, hence increased neoepitope presentation and better immune tumor recognition upon ICI, in particular in anti-PD1 treatments. Testing the mismatch repair deficiency before treatment may stratify the patients who are most likely to benefit from ICI therapies. However, this test benefits only a small fraction of CRC patients who are the carriers of mismatch repair high-risk germline mutations (~5% of CRC populations). In the proposed germline designs discussed in this chapter, the benefit of predictive stratification of patients undergoing ICI is expected to expand to the patient population- level due to the comprehensive discovery and assessment of both common and rare variants. From the preliminary scans described above, it is likely that numerous loci would be associated with ICI efficacy, toxicity or survival, showing similar genetic pleiotropy as observed in autoimmune risk susceptibilities; for example, many different loci likely in distinct pathways would contribute to the same treatment regimen efficacy, same toxicity site or survival. Nevertheless, unlike germline design of disease risk, it is also highly possible that the associations of common genetic

Germline Variants as Biomarkers of Immunotherapy 101 variants on ICI outcomes will exert substantially higher penetrant effect. This is due to the fact that the germline factors associated with ICI will not be under the selection pressure observed for disease risk variants in case/control designs. This is exemplified in our preliminary GWAS data, described in previous sections, showing that the associations with ICI efficacy confer strong effects of relative risk >4, an effect size with imminent clinical applicability. Additional support comes from our recent biomarker study showing that the specific, functionally relevant, common SNPs in interleukin pathways may associate with improved melanoma survival, with the effect size reaching the clinical applicability, independent of the current prognostic melanoma predictors [67]. Standardization in terms of platforms, experimental conditions, and bioinformatics pipelines is critical for the success of this kind of investigation. As such, the putative biomarkers discovered in the genome-wide designs, (that include training and validation phase), will need to be further tested in the setting of a prospective clinical trial (metastatic or adjuvant) before developing clinical tests (see diagram design in Fig. 1). For these analyses, a suitable genotyping platform allowing for testing dozens of variants simultaneously in a robust and reproducible fashion needs to be implemented. 1.4.2 Targeted As part of our preclinical validation of putative germline biomark- Genotyping Assay ers predictive of ICI efficacy, we have established a robust low-cost for Experimental genotyping assay that may be applied for this purpose, utilizing and Clinical Validation MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (MassARRAY®). This targeted of ICI Germline Loci genotyping platform allows for testing panels of common or rare (MassARRAY®) SNPs as well as small structural insertions/deletion (indels) in a scalable fashion. Up to 45 variants can be simultaneously tested in a single reaction and up to 15 reactions (45 × 15 = 675 variants) can be processed in parallel using automated pipelines on this platform. As part of the optimization test, we have compared the genotyping performance of 21 autoimmune SNP panel, developed in our recent study [59] and tested in 286 ICI-treated metastatic melanoma patients, using MassARRAY®, Infinium Global Screening Array v2.0 (GSA), and WGS. MassARRAY® showed 100% concordance with both alternative platforms; the genotypes were consistently classified for all three methods. With 0% discordance, the sensitivity and specificity of MassARRAY® was 100%, positioning MassARRAY® among platforms with high reproducibility and accuracy. While the genotyping failure rate of MassARRAY® was <0.5%, it was comparable with GSA, yet both platforms had call rates superior to WGS. Regardless, the failure rate per each multiplex SNP assay can be significantly and feasibly improved by “replexing” using the SNP assay design tool, as part MassARRAY® protocols, described in Methods section. Importantly, another significant advantage of MassARRAY® is the short turnaround time, which is superior to most targeted or

Germline Variants as Biomarkers of Immunotherapy 103 genome-wide high-throughput platforms. The clinical applicability of MassARRAY® has been demonstrated in various cancer panels [68–72], some already routinely used under Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) certified setting. Recently the specific application of this technology (IMPACT-Dx) has been approved by Food and Drug Administration agency (FDA) for clinical germline genotyping assays of Mendelian disorders. We strongly suggest that this technology, while surpassing the cost and high-throughput compared to NGS targeted platforms, may be an optimal solution for clinical validation of ICI-associated biomarker potential of germline genetic variants. 1.4.3 Current Despite the accumulating evidence supporting germline genetic Methodological contribution to host immunity, there is currently only a limited Impediments and Solutions knowledge of host genetic factors as predictive biomarkers of in Germline Genetic ICI. Few reported associations with ICI efficacy or survival have Studies of ICI not been independently cross-validated or moved forward to clinical utilization. Also, to date, no systematic scan has been reported on genetic variation as a surrogate of IO outcomes on the genome-wide level. The main reason for these research gaps is a lack of sufficiently powered ICI patient cohorts. We estimate that >5000 patients will be needed to achieve the statistical power of ~80%, for the discovery of low-penetrant germline loci associated with ICI outcomes. This clearly indicates the need for a large international collaboration pooling patient resources. While an ICI-focused germline consortium is currently being formed, an important component will be the harmonization of clinical data, in particular for patients outside of clinical trials, due to expected clinical heterogeneity of this information (in particular for ICI toxicity, heterogeneity of ICI treatments) across centers. Subtle differences in adjustments for clinical factors will have a contributing effect on germline genetic association tests in this context; hence, appropriate considerations must be put in place to address these confounding factors. The genome-wide approaches will be instrumental in the comprehensive discoveries of germline contributions to ICI. In a standardized way, the collaborative consortia should follow the pattern of GWAS design, eventually complemented by NGS technologies, which are still relatively costly for the scope of larger populations. A solution to this will be the prioritization of genomic Fig.1 (continued) patient cohorts. The validated host germline genetic markers can be subsequently integrated with other ICI biomarkers to generate personalized ICI prediction models (cancer immunograms). Further clinical tests in prospective populations can be designed (likely in the framework of a prospective clinical trial) to translate the germline genetic biomarkers of IO outcomes into routine clinical practice, following the established biomarker development pipelines established previously

104 Tomas Kirchhoff and Robert Ferguson regions for more targeted assessment, based on other layers of genetic, epigenetic, proteomic or immune-based evidence. This will also address the functional impact of identified genetic variants, as many will map in noncoding regions, and understanding how they affect gene regulation and immune function will otherwise be challenging. With a more comprehensive picture of germline genetics associated with ICI it is also difficult to disentangle the causal relationships between SNPs, intermediate immune phenotypes, other candidate biomarker surrogates (e.g., TMB, cytokine levels), and outcomes (toxicity, efficacy, survival). Computational methods relying on Mendelian randomization are being developed to address this problem [73, 74], and while this will require a large sample size, it will be possible within large collaborations such as the newly established international ICI germline consortium. It is unlikely that the effects of novel putative germline host factors in ICI will be independent of other biomarkers already established. Combining the different layers of biomarker discoveries from ICI designs in machine-learning modalities, as applied recently [75, 76], will be essential for the discovery of complex transcriptional and immunological networks that may be controlled by underlying genetic variation. These approaches, once clinically relevant assays are developed, may pave a path to more integrative personalized “immunograms” as clinical platforms for personalized prediction of ICI, currently proposed for a growing number of immunogenic cancers [25–27]. The immunograms will likely be substantially improved with the inclusion of other relevant host factors that are currently not considered, including germline genetic information. 2 Materials 2.1 Genomic DNA 1. For further specifications refer to the manual at agenacx.com. 3.3.2 Preparing The primers for the multiplex assays for the PCR and extension the Multiplexed PCR reactions should be prepared as defined by the primer design softand Extension Primer ware previously. Assays

108 Tomas Kirchhoff and Robert Ferguson The PCR primer multiplex assays are prepared as below:
1. Add 2.5 μl of each PCR primer to a tube.
2. Add H
2 O to obtain a final volume of 500 μl. The Extension primer assays are prepared as follows:
3. Divide the primers into three groups containing approximately
equal numbers of primers, the high mass group containing the highest mass primers, the low mass group containing the lowest mass primers, and a medium mass group containing the remaining primers. If the numbers of primers are not evenly divided by 3, add 1 extra primer to the high mass and medium mass groups as required.
4. Transfer 6.25 μl of each primer in the high mass primer group,
12.5 μl of each primer in the medium mass group and 18.75 μl of each primer in the low mass group to the multiplexed assay.
5. Add H
2 O to a final volume of 500 μl. To ensure that the primers are at an appropriate concentration in the assay, the samples must be run on the primer optimization program on MassARRAY®.
6. Add 24 μl of H
2 O and 1 μl of the primer mix from step 4 to a well of a 384-well sample plate.
7. Place the sample plate in the plate holder in the Nano dispenser
and place a SpectroCHIP II-G384 in the chip holder.
8. Set the Nano dispenser following the manufacturer’s protocols
(Agena) to spot the prepared primer mix(s) to the SpectorCHIP in triplicate.
9. Transfer the SpectroCHIP to MassARRAY® after spotting.
10. Follow the manufacturer’s protocols (Agena) and program
MassARRAY® for the primer optimization protocol. Run MassARRAY®. The primer optimization protocol checks the total mass of each primer in the multiplexed assay and provides an estimate of the percentage of the original primers’ volumes to add (column name “percent to add”). Average the “percent to add” across the triplicates for each primer; if it is within 50% for all primers in the assay then the assay is properly optimized. For primers with an average of “percent to add” above 50% then add: the original volume of primer multiplied by (the average percentage to add/100) to the multiplexed assay and repeat the primer optimization steps above to ensure the primers are now within the acceptable threshold. 3.3.3 Initial PCR 1. PCR master mixes are prepared for each multiplex primer assay separately according to Table 1.
2. Add 1 μl of the DNA to be tested at approximately 10 ng/μl
per each specific well.

2. Set the Nano dispenser following the manufacturer’s protocols
(Agena) and spot the prepared samples to the SpectorCHIP.
3. Transfer the SpectroCHIP to MassARRAY®.
4. Follow the manufacturer’s protocols (Agena) program for
analysis of the samples.
5. Perform basic QC steps below before proceeding.
(a) C heck the output to ensure that no contamination is present (no-template control wells should show no extension signal). (b) C heck the overall quality of the analysis. MassARRAY® uses a color system to indicate the number of SNPs successfully tested for each well of the plate. In the high quality experiment, the wells on the sample layout should be green-colored: this indicates the high call rate per sample (most SNPs were called successfully). (c) E nsure that the genotype clustering is well-defined for each SNP tested (refer to the manufactures protocols for examples). Manually inspect any samples where the genotype was not automatically called to determine if the genotype call can be improved manually.
6. Export the results for the subsequent analyses.
3.3.8 From MassARRAY® 1. The exported file from MassARRAY® is in Excel format. For Genotype Calls to PLINK the subsequent genetic analysis, the genotype Excel file needs File Format to be converted to PLINK file format. Before doing so, make sure to perform basic quality control of the genotype calls: (a) C onfirm the negative controls have minimal or no genotype signal. Otherwise this suggests potential contamination in the experiment or nonspecific amplification of the extension primers due to hairpins and nonspecific dimers. (b) C heck the genotype concordance between paired duplicates. In case of a discrepancy (not 100% concordance), investigate further.
2. Convert the genotype calls into PLINK format (ped/map
files). The column format of the ped file: Family ID/Within-

Germline Variants as Biomarkers of Immunotherapy 113 family ID/Within-family ID of father/Within-family ID of mother/Sex code/Phenotype value followed by genotype information (MassARRAY®). The ped file is accompanied by the map file providing SNP ID information. The file contains one SNP per line ordered by corresponding columns in the ped file. There are four columns in the map file: chromosome code, variant ID, position in morgans, and base-pair coordinate, which can be obtained from UCSC genome browser. Please see more detailed description of these two files format on PLINK online manual. 3.3.9 QC in PLINK 1. Convert ped/map to binary files with –make-bed.
2. Filter samples with missing call rates >10% (--mind 0.10).
3. Filter variants with missing call rates >5% (--geno 0.05).
4. Drop variants significantly departing Hardy–Weinberg
Equilibrium (--hwe 0.00001). Since HWE is performed only in controls, make sure to have cases/controls assigned prior to this step using –make-pheno flag. Please note that the above cutoff values for QC are suggestive thresholds. Please modify as required for the study samples and the design.
5. The genotype files are now ready for downstream statistical
analyses of association. 4 Notes
1. The design software will attempt to select an extension primer
that does not contain any other reported SNPs. The default design parameters are stringent, preventing the selection of a primer that contains any variant previously reported (both common and rare). Changing the parameters to only restrict the design of primers containing rare SNPs (MAF <0.005) often helps to increase the primer design yield of extension primers that were “undesignable” using standard default settings.
2. Extension primers that create stable Hairpins/Dimers are also
penalized and lowering the levels of this penalization may allow for further assays to be designed. Lowering this threshold leads to a greater chance that the primers will self-extend leading to an increased potential for false positives.
3. The ability of extension primers to bind to other off-target
areas of the genome is also penalized. Lowering this threshold can increase the design yield.

## Chapter 5


120 Russell Bonneville et al. 1.1 MSI In normal cells, microsatellites are 10–60 base pair (bp) regions in as a Biomarker the genome containing a defined number of repetitive DNA for PD-1 Inhibition sequences ranging from 1 to 5 bp (Fig. 1). Germline (inherited) or

somatic (acquired) mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) proteins characteristically lead to unorganized expansion and/or contraction of these repetitive DNA sequences termed MSI-H+ (high levels of microsatellite instability). Defective mismatch repair results in high tumor mutation burden and abundant neoantigen formation, which can be recognized by the host immune system. Cancer cells with high expression of PD-L1, a ligand of PD-1, evade detection and killing by the body’s adaptive immune system. Blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 interaction reprimes a patient’s immune system to attack previously “invisible” cancer cells [1]. Multiple studies have reported positive correlations between MSI- H+ status and increased PD-1/PD-L1 expression, as well as between MSI-H+ status and overall tumor mutational burden [2]. For example, in MSI-positive colorectal cancer, elevated PD-L1 expression was detected on tumor-infiltrating immune (lymphoid and myeloid) cells [3]. For these reasons, the use of pembrolizumab and nivolumab in patients with MSI-H cancers has proved to be efficacious. The observation of deep, durable responses in these patients has demonstrated the utility and validity of MSI as a predictive marker for response to immunotherapy with PD-1 blockade [1, 2]. 1.2 New Assays Up until approximately 2 years ago, the detection of MSI from and Methods for MSI tumor specimens has relied on the immunohistochemical detec- Detection tion (MSI-IHC) of the following four MMR proteins: MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. One main disadvantage of MSI-IHC is the inability to detect MSI caused by point mutations or small insertion/deletion mutations in MMR proteins that can still produce a positive IHC result. A second standard method for MSI detection has been a PCR-based assay of five (Bethesda panel) or eight (Promega® panel) standardized microsatellite loci Fig. 1 Schematic of microsatellite instability due to deficient mismatch repair (MMR). Loss of MMR prevents a cell from repairing random mismatches between antiparallel strands that arise at repetitive regions during DNA replication, leading to propagation of random insertions/deletions (indels) in microsatellites

Detection of Microsatellite Instability Biomarkers via Next-Generation Sequencing 121 (MSI- PCR). The main disadvantage of MSI-PCR is the severely limited number [5–8] of MSI loci that are evaluated by the assay. Both of these assays were originally designed for the diagnosis of inherited mismatch repair deficiency, or Lynch syndrome. Since Lynch syndrome predominantly includes colorectal and uterine cancers, these assays may be biased for these cancer types. To overcome the limitations of traditional methods of MSI- IHC and MSI-PCR, integrated next generation sequencing (NGS) assays and novel computational methods have been developed to detect MSI-H+ [4]. Some examples of NGS gene panels for MSI- H+ detection include MSIPlus [5] and ColoSeq [6]. MSIPlus is an assay that has been optimized for colorectal cancer and evaluates 16 microsatellite loci along with mutational hotspots in oncogenes (KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF). ColoSeq is an alternative NGS assay that is designed to detect mutations, deletions or complex structural rearrangements in seven DNA repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM, APC, and MUTYH) that can lead to MSI. New bioinformatics approaches developed for MSI detection include mSINGS [7], MSISensor [8], MOSAIC [9], MANTIS [10, 11], and others (Table 1). Most of these computational algorithms compare the length distribution of a selection of microsatellite loci by determining the read counts of all alleles. Their development has enabled the assessment of thousands of microsatellite loci located predominantly in the protein-coding region of the genome (compared with just 5–8 loci using MSI-PCR) across many cancer types through analysis of publically available and previously annotated datasets. 122 Russell Bonneville et al. MOSAIC, Hause et al. evaluated MSI-H+ status in n = 5930 cases spanning 18 cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) [9]. Adding to this knowledge, Bonneville et al. assessed MSI-H+ status with the program MANTIS in n = 11,139 cases spanning 39 distinct cancer types from the TCGA and Therapeutically Applicable Research to Generate Effective Treatments (TARGET) [10]. In a third study, Middha et al. evaluated MSI-H+ with MSISensor in n = 12,288 advanced solid cancers profiled with the NGS assay, Memorial Sloan Kettering-Integrated Mutation Profiling of Actionable Cancer Targets (MSK-IMPACT) [8]. Finally, methods that assess MSI-H+ based on mutation burden in microsatellites are available [12–14]. An example of this is MSIseq Index [12], which is the only MSI-H+ detection method that utilizes RNA sequencing data to determine proportion of insertion/deletions in microsatellites relative to all insertion/deletions in RNA transcripts. In summary, numerous studies that have applied novel computational approaches have revealed an unexpectedly high incidence of MSI-H+ in a diverse range of human cancers. Importantly, these studies identify patients with non-Lynch cancer types affected by MMR deficiencies leading to MSI-H+ who may benefit from immunotherapy. Given the validity of MSI-H+ as a predictive biomarker of response to PD-1 inhibition, it is likely that standardized clinical MSI-H+ testing will become incorporated into the routine care of cancer patients in the near future. In Subheading 3, we provide detailed protocols of DNA extraction from tissue, sequencing library generation, targeted hybridization/capture and bioinformatics methods (i.e., MANTIS) for computational MSI detection. It is important to note that the target region for hybridization and capture is dependent on the end user’s needs and resources, and therefore the size may vary accordingly. Our laboratory targets 99 top performing microsatellite loci for determination of MSI status. Due to the small amount of genomic space occupied by these loci, we have chosen to use this design in combination with a larger panel (~1 megabase) for the detection of single nucleotide variants (SNV) and copy number variation (CNV). The methodologies described below are applicable across a variety of capture region sizes, however some optimization may be required. 1.3 Concluding Microsatellite instability has proven to be a clinically important bio- Remarks marker for predicting response to immunotherapy. MSI has been observed across a wide variety of cancer types, and this requires a pan-cancer scope of testing. Next-generation sequencing and new analytical software have permitted expanded testing for MSI-H+ detection. NGS-based methods demonstrate superior performance to previous technologies, and MSI-H+ testing can be easily integrated into other sequencing assays for more comprehensive genomic analysis.
