Detection of Microsatellite Instability Biomarkers via Next-Generation Sequencing 125 3 Methods For general notes pertaining to the entire workflow (see Notes 1–5). 3.1 GenExtraction Genomic DNA is extracted from whole blood using the Qiagen of DNA from Blood QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit, following the manufacturer’s protocol. For points to be considered with respect to the protocol (see Notes 6–10). 3.2 Extraction Genomic DNA is extracted from FFPE tissue using the Qiagen of DNA from FFPE QIAamp DNA FFPE Tissue Kit, following the manufacturer’s pro- Tissues tocol. For points to be considered with respect to the protocol (see Notes 11–15). 3.3 Nucleic Acid Extracted DNA needs to be quantified and its quality should be Quality Control (QC) assessed. Three methods that are readily available and recommended for use include Agilent TapeStation, Thermo Scientific NanoDrop, and Thermo Scientific Qubit. After determining the quantity and quality of DNA extracted with one of the r ecommended methods, one can proceed to the library preparation, hybridization, and sequencing of samples for MSI detection. 3.3.1 TapeStation Genomic DNA should be run on the TapeStation using Genomic DNA Reagents and ScreenTapes according to the manufacturer’s protocol. After the run is complete, examine the electropherogram traces and note the quality of genomic DNA. General guidelines are that if more than 75% of the DNA sample is 10,000 bp or larger the sample is considered “intact.” If between 50% and 75% of the DNA sample is 10,000 bp or larger the sample is considered “partially degraded.” If less than 50% of the DNA sample is 10,000 bp the sample is considered “degraded.” Adjustments to these guidelines can be made in individual circumstances. 3.3.2 NanoDrop Genomic DNA should be assessed by the NanoDrop according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Instrument blanking should be performed with the buffer used in genomic DNA elution. To ensure proper blanking, the blanking solution should also be measured and this value recorded. Additionally, the A and A val-260/280 260/230 ues and provided concentration should be recorded (although this is not the concentration that will be used for calculating input volume for subsequent steps). 3.3.3 Qubit Genomic DNA should be quantified using the double stranded DNA (dsDNA) quantification assay (either high sensitivity (HS) or broad range (BR) based on sample concentrations) by the Qubit. This assay should be used according to the manufacturer’s

126 Russell Bonneville et al. protocol, including use of the provided standards. The dsDNA concentration reported by the Qubit will be used for calculating the input volume for subsequent steps. 3.4 Fragmentation Fragmentation of DNA is completed using a Covaris S220 of DNA Focused-ultrasonicator. The following protocol is recommended:
1. Prior to fragmentation of DNA, fill Covaris S220 water tank
with deionized water to lower marker 15. Turn on unit and pump, and open sonification software. Allow 1 h for system to initialize.
2. Dilute 200 ng of each gDNA sample from above steps
(Extraction of DNA from Blood and Extraction of DNA from FFPE Tissues) in 10 mM Tris–HCl pH 8.0 to a total volume of 55 μL. Ensure that the same input is used for all samples that will be combined into the same hybridization reaction.
3. Transfer 55 μL of diluted gDNA to a Covaris microTUBE,
place in tube holder, and fragment the DNA using the following settings which are optimized for creating library inserts of 200–400 bp: Duty factor 10% Cycles per burst 200 Duration 120 s Peak power 175.0 Mode Frequency sweeping Temperature 7 °C
4. Label 0.2 mL strip tubes for each sample and transfer 50 μL
fragmented dsDNA sample from microTUBE to corresponding strip tube. 3.5 Library The KAPA Hyper Prep Kit is used for the rapid preparation of Preparation and QC libraries from fragmented, double-stranded DNA for sequencing on the Illumina platform. The KAPA Hyper Prep Kit contains all of the necessary reagents for the three steps to generate libraries: end repair and A-tailing, adapter ligation, and library amplification. For points to be considered with respect to the protocol (see Notes 16–19). 3.6 Hybridization Hybridization and capture of the above DNA libraries is completed and Final Library QC using IDT xGEN® Lockdown Probes and Reagents. The protocol should be followed according to manufacturer’s recommendations. For recommendations to best optimize the protocol (see Notes 20–26).

Detection of Microsatellite Instability Biomarkers via Next-Generation Sequencing 127 3.7 Sequencing Prior to sequencing on the MiSeq, final capture libraries must be denatured and diluted to an appropriate concentration for optimal cluster generation. Additionally, commercially available PhiX library should be denatured and diluted for use as a sequencing control. This should be done according to the MiSeq System Denature and Dilute Libraries Guide from Illumina. For recommendations to best optimize the protocol (see Notes 27 and 28). 3.8 Data File These steps only need to be performed once. Preparation The reference genome FASTA file at /path/to/hg19.fa must be indexed with samtools: samtools faidx /path/to/hg19.fa A BED file of targeted microsatellite regions must be generated. First, in the tools directory of MANTIS, run: make to build the RepeatFinder utility. To extract microsatellite regions from the reference genome, run:./RepeatFinder -i /path/to/hg19.fa -o hg19_microsatellites.bed Using bedtools, filter this file for microsatellites within your genomic capture region or other desired regions to identify microsatellites: bedtools intersect -a hg19_microsatellites.bed -b / path/to/targets.bed -wa > hg19_microsatellites_in_ target.bed For additional comments on the bioinformatics workflow outlined in this chapter (see Notes 29–32). 3.9 QC Beginning with gzipped FASTQ files 123456_T_R1.fastq.gz and 123456_T_R2.fastq.gz from the tumor sample, initial QC is performed with fastqc as follows: fastqc -o. 123456_T_R1.fastq.gz 123456_T_R2.fastq.gz 3.10 Alignment Alignment will be performed by bwa using the MEM algorithm as follows: bwa mem -M -t <number of threads> -R "@RG\ tID:123456_T\tLB:123456_T\tSM:123456_T\tPL:ILLUMINA" /path/to/hg19.fa 123456_T_R1.fastq.gz 123456_T_ R2.fastq.gz | samtools view -s -b -o 123456_T.bam - The resulting BAM file must now be sorted and indexed using samtools: samtools sort -o 123456_T_sorted.bam 123456_T.bam samtools index 123456_T_sorted.bam

128 Russell Bonneville et al. 3.11 Deduplication PCR duplicates are removed using Picard tools: gatk --java-options "-Xmx20g" MarkDuplicates --INPUT 123456_T_rmdup.bam --OUTPUT 123456_T_rmdup.bam --METRICS_FILE 123456_T_rmdup_metrics.txt --VALIDATION_STRINGENCY LENIENT --ASSUME_SORTED true --REMOVE_DUPLICATES true This BAM file must also be indexed: samtools index 123456_T_rmdup.bam 3.12 Base Quality Several post-alignment processing steps are recommended to Recalibration improve alignment accuracy around indels and reduce quality score bias. These will be performed with the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK), using the dbSNP VCF listed in Subheading 2.4: gatk --java-options "-Xmx20g" BaseRecalibrator -R / path/to/hg19.fa -O 123456_T_recal.data.grp -I 123456_T_rmdup.bam --known-sites /path/to/dbsnp.vcf gatk --java-options "-Xmx20g" ApplyBQSR -R /path/to/ hg19.fa -O 123456_T_recal.bam -I 123456_T_rmdup.bam -bqsr 123456_T_recal.data.grp samtools index 123456_T_recal.bam Important: Repeat Subheadings 3.9–3.12 for the matched normal sample, beginning with 123456_N_R1.fastq.gz and 123456_N_ R2.fastq.gz and ending with 123456_N_recal.bam. 3.13 MSI Calling With the aligned and processed BAM files, along with the BED file of in-target microsatellite regions, we can now detect microsatellite instability in this sample. Run: python /path/to/mantis.py -t 123456_T_recal.bam -n 123456_N_recal.bam -b hg19_microsatellites_in_target. bed -o 123456.mantis.txt --genome /path/to/hg19.fa This will output several files, including 123456.mantis.txt.status. View this using cat: cat 123456.mantis.txt.status In the table, there will be a value listed for “Step-Wise Difference (DIF).” This is the MSI score for this tumor. There will also be a status, either “Stable” for MSS or “Unstable” for MSI-H. 4 Notes General Notes
1. Laboratory personnel must wear gloves and laboratory coat at
all times during extraction of DNA from blood samples.
2. Pipettes should be calibrated every 6 months and decontami-
nated with Sporicidin® Disinfectant Solution daily prior to and after each use.

Detection of Microsatellite Instability Biomarkers via Next-Generation Sequencing 129
3. Should blood not be available to be used as a normal control,
DNA from buccal swabs or adjacent normal tissue from FFPE block can also be used.
4. This protocol can also be completed on fresh frozen tissues.
To extract DNA from these tissues or buccal swabs use the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit.
5. In regard to the three options indicated for quantity and qual-
ity control of DNA, NanoDrop will quantify single and double stranded DNA, whereas Qubit only quantifies dsDNA. It is recommended to use the Qubit concentration for input calculations. However, the more degraded the sample, the bigger of a difference will be observed between NanoDrop and Qubit concentration values. NanoDrop also provides 260/280 and 260/230 ratios which are helpful to assess quality and can help determine protein or RNA contamination. Additionally, the Agilent Bioanalyzer can be used instead of the TapeStation. Extraction of DNA from Blood
6. DNA must be extracted from whole blood samples stored at
4 °C within 1 week (7 days). Whole blood samples can be stored at −80 °C for months to years and then can subsequently be used for DNA extraction.
7. Prior to starting the protocol, allow samples to equilibrate to
room temperature (15–25 °C).
8. It is recommended to add RNase A stock solution (100 mg/
mL) to the sample prior to the addition of Buffer AL in order to yield RNA-free genomic DNA as the presence of RNA may inhibit downstream enzymatic reactions.
9. A second elution step with Buffer AE or distilled water may
increase yields up to 15%.
10. DNA can be stored at 4 °C for short-term storage but should
be stored at −80 °C for long-term storage. Extraction of DNA from FFPE Tissues
11. DNA should be extracted from FFPE tissue as soon as possible
upon receipt.
12. Depending on tissue size, 1–8 sections should be cut at a
10 μm thickness and placed on a slide. If the tissue block is large enough to be macro dissected, scrape off the area of interest (enriched with tumor cells) using a scalpel and place in a 1.5 mL eppendorf tube, avoiding excess paraffin in the process. Alternatively, if using the entire tissue from the block, scrolls can be cut and placed directly into 1.5 mL eppendorf tubes.

130 Russell Bonneville et al.
13. If using only one heating block, leave the sample at room
temperature after the 56 °C incubation until the heating block has reached 90 °C.
14. Incubating the QIAamp MinElute column with Buffer ATE
on center of the membrane for 1–5 min prior to centrifugation can increase yields.
15. DNA can be stored at 4 °C for short-term storage but should
be stored at −80 °C for long-term storage. Library Preparation and QC
16. Ensure that the same input is used for all samples that will be
combined into the same hybridization reaction.
17. Adapters must be purchased separately and are available from
several commercial companies. The adapter stock concentration needs to be adjusted depending on the amount of DNA input used for library preparation. Recommended adapter concentrations for DNA inputs ranging from 1 ng to 1 μg are found in the Technical Data Sheet for the KAPA Hyper Prep Kit.
18. The number of PCR cycles used for library amplification needs
to be modified depending on the amount of DNA input used for library preparation. It is recommended to use 5 PCR cycles for an input of 200 ng. Recommended PCR cycle numbers to generate either 100 ng or 1 μg of amplified library from 1 ng to 1 μg of input DNA are found in the Technical Data Sheet for the KAPA Hyper Prep Kit.
19. After generation of the libraries, the Qubit and TapeStation
(D1000) should be used to check library concentration and size. Hybridization and Final Library QC
20. Inspect the tube of 2× Hybridization Buffer for crystallization
of salts. If crystals are present, heat the tube at 65 °C, shaking intermittently, until the buffer is completely solubilized (may require heating for several hours).
21. The recommended protocol uses a 4-h incubation for the
hybridization, however the protocol can be modified for an overnight hybridization (16–18 h).
22. DynaBeads® M-270 Streptavidin Beads should be prepared
immediately before use. Do not allow beads to dry out.
23. Hybridization/capture reactions have been optimized to
include a total of 4 samples (matched normal and tumor libraries from two patients) based on the size of our capture region and sequencing capacity on the MiSeq instrument. To bias sequencing in favor of the tumor samples, we input a greater quantity of tumor library (200 ng) compared to normal

Detection of Microsatellite Instability Biomarkers via Next-Generation Sequencing 131 library (50 ng). Based on these inputs we are able to achieve sequencing depths of ~150× for normal samples and 500× for tumor samples.
24. It is recommended to use 12 cycles of PCR for the post- capture
amplification step. The number of PCR cycles should be optimized based on the panel size and total amount of library in the hybridization reaction to ensure sufficient material for sequencing. Recommended PCR cycles based on these parameters can be found in the xGen® Hybridization Capture of DNA Libraries for NGS Target Enrichment protocol handbook available through IDT’s website.
25. After hybridization, Qubit and TapeStation (D1000) should
be used to check final library concentration and size. Alternatively, library quantification can be carried out using a qPCR kit.
26. To calculate the final nM concentration of your library, use the
formula listed below:  ng  106µL 1nmol 1 Finallibraryconc. × × × =Finallibraryconc.(nM) µL 1L 660ng Fragmentsizzeinbp Sequencing
27. Prepare a fresh dilution of NaOH for each run and use within
12 h.
28. Denatured 20 pM PhiX library can be stored at −15 °C to
−25 °C for up to 3 weeks. Bioinformatics
29. This workflow can be adapted to hg38 (or future human
genome builds) by substituting the appropriate genome FASTA file and a targeted capture BED in hg38 coordinates.
30. RepeatFinder has several options to fine tune the microsatellites
considered for analysis. Of particular interest is -L to determine the maximum length of the microsatellite repeat unit (k-mer), along with -m and -M to control the minimum and maximum length of microsatellites respectively. The default settings are appropriate in most use cases.
31. If either your target BED or microsatellites BED files are very
large, bedtools may fail due to excessive memory usage. In this case, position-sort both BED files by bedtools sort -i in.bed > out.bed, then run bedtools with the -sorted flag [19].
32. The flag "-Xmx20g" allocates 20 gigabytes of memory for
Java. If you encounter an out of memory error, consider increasing this threshold.

Since the number of repeat units varies from one individual to another, they represent excellent tools as “polymorphic markers.” Variations of the repeat copy numbers are also recognized as “dynamic mutations” [4, 5]. When such modifications occur in or near a gene, they can determine a change (gain or loss) of the function of that gene product, acting as regulators of gene expression. Microsatellites have acquired an important interest from the oncological point of view because they represent the main sign of the existence of a generalized genetic instability condition, which is detected as expansion or contraction of microsatellite sequences in tumor DNA with respect to the normal DNA from the same patient [6]. MSI has been associated with increased load of nonsynonymous single-nucleotide variants (ns-SNVs; that are mutations which determine changes in gene products), hypermethylation status, mutated BRAF gene, activated RAS-dependent pathways, and prevalent immune infiltrates [6]. Conversely, tumors with aneuploidy are more heterogeneous for the involvement of specific candidate genes (mostly, by changes at expression level), with activation of a wider spectrum of molecular and metabolic pathways, intermediate levels of either mutation or methylation events, and poorly immunogenic microenvironment [7]. An inverse relationship between MSI and aneuploidy has been described: cancers showing MSI are, in general, diploid and exhibit normal rates of gross chromosomal changes, whereas stable tumors are usually aneuploid and exhibit increased rates of chromosomal abnormalities [8, 9]. While alterations affecting the molecular machinery that monitors the proper progression of the cell cycle seem responsible for the presence of recurrent chromosome changes [8, 10, 11], deficit in mismatch repair with a subsequent increase of replication error rates and a sequential accumulation of genetic mutations represents the causative mechanism in tumors with high rates of MSI (MSI+; see below) [3, 9, 12, 13]. From the pathogenic point of view, one could speculate that near-diploid karyotypes with few or single structural or numerical anomalies may be present as a specific feature in an initial stage of the neoplasia (in contrast to the complex karyotype anomalies with deeply heterogeneous structural and numerical alterations, which may be possibly related to advanced stages of the disease) [12, 14, 15], whereas the genome-wide microsatellite instability may be correlated to the existence of pathogenic mechanisms inducing progressive accumulation of sequence errors and providing a selective advantage during malignant evolution [16]. The MSI tumors are characteristically hypermutated and express abundant peptides that serve as neoantigens to elicit an immune response within a context of a favorable tumor microenvironment

MSI Detection Tests 135 characterized by abundant tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes [16–19]. Moreover, the MSI cancers have been demonstrated to express high level of checkpoint proteins, including PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4, LAG-3, and IDO [19, 20]. Therefore, patients with MSI tumors have the highest probability of responding to anti-PD-1 antibodies, though exceptional responses to PD-1 blockade have also been observed in patients with tumors carrying high rates of mutations not associated with the MSI [21]. Overall, the presence of the hypermutated status—either with or without the MSI phenotype— makes the difference in eliciting the proper immune response [21]. Highly mutated tumors are markedly infiltrated by T lymphocytes, particularly by cytotoxic T cells that express immune-checkpoint molecules, such as CTLA-4, PD-1, and LAG3 [22]. While the chromosomal instability determining a condition of aneuploidy is described in another chapter, here we report methodologies to assess MSI by evaluating changes at the nucleotide level with altered microsatellite sequences. The MSI is caused by defective DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes—MLH1, MSH2, PMS1, PMS2, MSH6, or MSH3; such defects can be inherited (i.e., germline mutations in MLH1 gene) or sporadic (e.g., inactivation of MLH1 through hypermethylation of its promoter) [16]. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is commonly used to identify the loss of the MMR proteins, which are widely expressed in normal tissues and show positive nuclear staining [23]. Indeed, the lack of specific staining of one or more of the main array of MMR proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2) represents a strong indication of an underlying inactivation of the correspondent genes [23, 24]. In a wider view, the genes involved in controlling the DNA mismatch repair mechanisms may be inactive due to the occurrence of mutations affecting their functional domains with normal expression rates [16]. Therefore, it is widely recognized that the most appropriate approach to assess the existence of the MSI status is represented by the detection of the instability effects on tumor genomic DNA. At genomic level, MSI is indeed characterized by small insertion or deletion within short tandem repeats in tumor DNA when compared with the corresponding normal DNA; these DNA shifts between the two sample types—as determined by modifications into the length of such tandem repeat stretches—can be thus revealed by application of the PCR technique in DNA testing [25–27]. From the practical point of view, molecular testing for MSI is performed through a PCR amplification of DNA regions containing microsatellite repeats followed by evaluation of the size of the PCR fragments or, alternatively, through a real-time PCR-based high-resolution melting curve analysis on a panel of seven monomorphic homopolymer biomarkers, using specific assays.

136 Giuseppe Palmieri et al. Some considerations need to be inferred: – Tumors displaying unstable multiple genomic loci are classified as high-frequency MSI (MSI-H) whereas those presenting with one unstable marker are referred to as low-frequency MSI (MSI-L); microsatellite stable (MSS) status is established when none of the analyzed markers shows instability; – Tumors displaying absence of at least one of the four MMR proteins can be appropriately considered to belong to the MSI-H group, whereas those with intact MMR protein expression cannot be discriminated for their inclusion in either the MSS or the MSI-L subgroups. Assuming that IHC- and PCR-based analyses indeed act as complementary tests, both with proper sensitivity and specificity for MMR deficiency assessment, performing synergistically them is expected to increase the detection rates of MSI [23, 24] when adequately prepared tissue specimens are used. In other words, the assessment of the MMR protein expression at tumor tissue level by IHC stain should be combined with the PCR-based analysis on genomic DNA in order to achieve a comprehensive classification of the MSI status. 2 Materials 2.1 Immunohisto­ The VENTANA MMR IHC Panel includes the following primary chemistry for MMR antibodies: anti-MLH1, anti-MSH2, anti-MSH6, and anti-PMS2 Deficiency Detection (Table 1). 2.2 Isolation The GeneRead DNA FFPE Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany; cataof Genomic DNA log no. 180134) is intended for 50 sample analyses and includes from Tissue Sections QIAamp MinElute Columns, Collection Tubes, Deparaffinization Solution, Uracil N-glycosylase, RNase-free Water, RNase A, and Buffers (FTB, AL, AW1, AW2). 2. Tumor tissue samples are taken from the patients, fixed in 10%
neutral buffered formalin for 6–24 h, and embedded in paraffin according to standard laboratory practice. Sections of 5 μm of thickness are mounted on positively charged glass microscope slides; one of them is then stained with H&E. When morphologic evaluation confirms that the H&E slide is acceptable (≥50% viable tumor cells) and before proceeding with the IHC staining protocol, the slides with tissue sections must be deparaffinized and rehydrated (incomplete removal of paraffin can lead to poor staining of the section).
3. For this purposes, the slides must be placed in a rack, and the
following washes be performed using a Coplin jar: (a) T wo washes of 3 min each with xylene. (b) O ne wash of 3 min with 1:1 xylene–100% ethanol. (c) T wo washes of 3 min each with 100% ethanol. (d) O ne wash of 3 min with 95% ethanol. (e) O ne wash of 3 min with 70% ethanol. (f) O ne wash of 3 min with 50% ethanol. Once the slides have been washed in the above sequence, they must be placed in running cold tap water to rinse off ethanol.

MSI Detection Tests 141
4. Slides are then incubated with each of the antibodies constitut-
ing the VENTANA MMR IHC Panel, usually employing automated DABMap system (Ventana) for hMSH6 detection and UltraMap system (Ventana) to detect hMLH1, hMSH2, and hPMS2 proteins. In particular, cells labeled with the IHC assays for the four MMR proteins are evaluated for the presence or loss of the diaminobenzidine (DAB) signals. The DABMap system consists of cell conditioning, followed by addition of primary antibody and incubation at room temperature for 1 h. After washing with PBS, slides are incubated with biotinylated secondary antibody, before counter staining with hematoxylin and dehydration in serial ethanol alcohol dilutions. The standard UltraMap protocol is used to detect hMSH2 and again consists of cell conditioning followed by incubation of the tissue section with primary antibody for 12 h at 37 °C. No secondary antibody is added, but tissue section undergoes counter staining and slides dehydration. The extended UltraMap protocol is used to determine the expression of hMLH1 and hPMS2. It was different from the standard one in the extension of the cell conditioning to three cycles of incubation with medium cell conditioner as compared to the two cycles in standard UltraMap protocol.
5. For IHC assessment, changes in protein expression within
tumor tissues are observed in stained cells using Olympus BX60 microscope and image analySIS software. Two pathologists at each site independently evaluated the reading set for the MMR IHC panel to determine the expression status for each case: (a) P ositive (intact) signal is characterized by tumor cells that exhibit unequivocal nuclear staining of any intensity above background; (b) N egative (loss) signal intensity is characterized by an absence of any detectable signal or pale grey or tan nuclear discoloration in tumor cells.
6. The DAB signal may be distributed homogeneously, having a
uniform level of intensity throughout the neoplastic portions of the tumor or distributed heterogeneously having more than one intensity level. A species-matched negative control antibody is used to evaluate the presence of background in test samples and establish a staining intensity baseline. Each assay requires three serial tissue sections from each tissue specimen, one section for H&E staining, a second section for negative reagent control antibody staining, and a third section for staining with one of the MMR antibodies. Unequivocal nuclear staining in lymphocytes, fibroblasts or normal epithelium in the vicinity of the tumor will serve as internal positive controls (see Note 1).

142 Giuseppe Palmieri et al. 3.2 PCR­ The quality of the specimen undergoing evaluations through PCR Based Assays arrays represents a variable that can profoundly influence MSI classification. Crucial preanalytic requirements are represented by 3.2.1 Preanalytical either the identification of the right tissue areas (adequate fraction Requirements for PCRof neoplastic and/or normal cell content, exclusion of the necrotic Based Analysis parts) either the selection of specimens able to provide the sufficient quantity and quality of genomic DNA for microsatellite instability analysis. The first steps are thus the morphologic diagnosis and accurate analysis of the tissue biopsy sections through microscopic imaging techniques. In this sense, a genomic DNA obtained from a quality-assessed tissue sample may markedly increase the sensitivity of the MSI testing, especially in nonsurgical cases, considering the intrinsic difficulties of less invasive approaches (core needle biopsy, fine-needle aspiration smears or cell blocks, or exfoliative cytology) in providing sufficient tissue quantities. An additional factor affecting the quality of the tissue samples (and, thus, of the genomic DNA isolated from them) is the modality of the direct preservation of the biopsy materials, including the time elapsed from the initial surgical removal to the final embedding in paraffin. In our experience, a statistically significant difference in results of mutation analysis was found between samples with at least 50% of neoplastic cells and those with less than 50% of neoplastic cells, with proportion of malignant cells significantly higher in samples obtained by biopsy and those obtained by surgery [28]. To avoid any acquisition of artificial adducts or abnormal crosslinks into the DNA double-strands for the successive isolation of an undamaged genomic DNA, the modality of the formalin fixation is indeed critical [29–31]. For this purpose, the following variables play an important role: the adequate volume of buffered formalin where biopsy specimens must be placed and the duration of the fixation time which is tightly depending on the total volume of the biopsy specimen. 3.2.2 Isolation This represent a very crucial step toward a successful analysis result of Genomic DNA in downstream PCR-based arrays (see Note 2). from Tissue Sections
1. Starting material for DNA isolation should be a freshly cut
section of FFPE tissue, with a thickness of up to 10 μm. Roughly, DNA yields from this amount of material exceed 500 ng, which is a quantity highly sufficient for PCR-based downstream applications. However, DNA yield from FFPE samples varies greatly, depending on the tissue type, as well as fixation and embedding conditions. In this sense, a more precise verification of yields should be taken more precisely (i.e., using NanoDrop™ 2000/2000c Spectrophotometer) before proceeding.
2. The most used protocol for the purification of genomic DNA
from FFPE tissues ready for reliable screening analysis is that

MSI Detection Tests 143 based on the GeneRead DNA FFPE Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany); it does not require too much starting material, since this severely affects the performance of the kit.
3. The GeneRead DNA FFPE protocol reckons on the combina-
tion of different types of buffers and includes the following sequential procedures: (a) Using a scalpel, excess of paraffin must be trimmed off the sample block. (b) In cutting the tissue section up to 10 μm thick, it is better discarding the first 2–3 sections from the sample surface which has been exposed to air (if there is sufficient tissue material. (c) Sections must be immediately placed in a 1.5–2 ml microcentrifuge tube. (d) An adequate volume (160 μl) of Deparaffinization Solution is then added; tube is vortexed vigorously for 10 s, then centrifuged briefly to bring the sample to the bottom of the tube, incubated at 56 °C for 3 min, and then allowed to cool at room temperature. If too little Deparaffinization Solution is used or if too much paraffin is carried over with the sample, it may become waxy or solid after cooling. If this occurs, additional Deparaffinization Solution must be added and incubation at 56 °C repeated. (e) A mixture comprising RNase-free water, Buffer FTB, and proteinase K is then added, and the sample is then vortexed and briefly centrifuged (the Deparaffinization Solution form a layer above Buffer FTB with the addition of proteinase K), before incubation at 56 °C for 1 h. (f) The sample is finally incubated at 90 °C for 1 h, which partially reverses formaldehyde modification of nucleic acids. Longer incubation times or higher incubation temperatures may result in more fragmented DNA. (g) After a brief centrifugation of the tube (to remove drops from inside the lid), the lower, clear phase is then transferred into a new microcentrifuge tube, 115 μl RNase-free water is added and solution is mixed. (h) After the previous steps aimed at removing cross-links, the DNA is accessible for the specific removal of deaminated cytosine residues by the enzyme uracil N-glycosylase (UNG), which can specifically remove artificially induced uracils from the DNA obtained from the FFPE sample. Therefore, 35 μl UNG is added to the sample; solution is vortexed and incubated at 50 °C for 1 h in a thermomixer or heating block.

144 Giuseppe Palmieri et al. (i) After brief tube centrifugation, 2 μl RNase A (100 mg/ ml), is added, mixed, and incubated for 2 min at room temperature. (j) In sequence, 250 μl Buffer AL and 250 μl ethanol (96– 100%) are added to the sample and mixed thoroughly by vortexing. (k) After brief tube centrifugation, the complete lysate is transferred to the QIAamp MinElute column (in a 2 ml collection tube), which is centrifuged at maximum speed for 1 min. The flow-through is discarded and the collection tube reused. If the lysate has not completely passed through the membrane, centrifugation is repeated at a higher speed until the QIAamp MinElute column is empty. (l) Sequentially, the following solutions are added to the spin column, centrifuged at maximum speed for 1 min, always discarding the flow-through between one step and another: 500 μl Buffer AW1, 500 μl Buffer AW2 and 250 μl ethanol (96–100%). (m) The spin column is placed into a new 2 ml collection tube and centrifuged at maximum speed for 1 min to remove any residual liquid. (n) Finally, the QIAamp MinElute column is placed in a clean 1.5 ml microcentrifuge tube and 20–40 μl Buffer ATE is applied to the center of the membrane (to ensure complete elution of bound DNA). IMPORTANT: the Buffer ATE needs to be equilibrated at room temperature. The volume of eluate will be up to 5 μl less than the volume of elution solution applied to the column. (o) After incubation for 5 min at room temperature, the QIAamp MinElute column loaded with Buffer ATE is centrifuged at maximum speed (20,000 × g or 14,000 rpm) for 1 min. 3.2.3 PCR-Based MSI The most common molecular test for MSI classification is usually Detection performed using PCR amplification of DNA regions containing microsatellite repeats followed by electrophoretic separation of the Bethesda Panel Assay PCR fragments. Genomic DNA is isolated from normal and tumor tissue of each patient by GeneRead DNA FFPE Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Isolated DNA is separately amplified by PCR with fluorescent-labeled primers. The National Cancer Institute guidelines for MSI testing recommend a panel of five microsatellite loci, including three dinucleotide repeat markers (D2S123, D5S346, and D17S250) and two mononucleotide repeat markers (BAT 25 and BAT 26). This panel is known as the Bethesda panel. The five microsatellite loci are amplified in a single multiplex PCR reaction, using the Type-it Microsatellite PCR Kit from Qiagen (Hilden, Germany) that is a ready-to-use master mix based

MSI Detection Tests 145 on proven QIAGEN Multiplex Technology, and contains optimized concentrations of HotStarTaq Plus DNA Polymerase, MgCl, and dNTPs, and an innovative PCR buffer, specially devel-2 oped for multiplex PCR-based detection of microsatellites and minisatellites. The combination of all components provided in the master mix and the specialized formulation result in highly specific amplification of all loci in parallel. Primers used to amplify simple sequence repeat markers are listed in Table 2.
1. Multiplex PCR is usually performed in a total 25 μl reaction
volume using: (a) 2 × Type-it Multiplex PCR Master Mix (12.5 μl; final concentration 1×); (b) 1 0× primer mix, 2 μM each primer (2.5 μl; final concentration 0.2 μM). The 10× primer mix may contain up to 12 primer pairs with a concentration of primer stock of 50 μM (50 pmol/μl); (c) ≤ 200 ng template DNA; (d) R Nase-free water (variable, up to the final volume of 25 μl).
2. The reaction mix typically contains all the components required
for multiplex PCR except the template DNA. Therefore, one should prepare a volume of reaction mix 10% greater than that required for the total number of reactions to be performed. For reaction volumes less than 25 μl, the 1:1 ratio of Type-it Multiplex PCR Master Mix to primer mix and template should be maintained.
3. The reaction must be mixed gently by pipetting the reaction
mix up and down a few times, before dispensing appropriate volumes into PCR tubes or plates. Due to the hot start, it is not necessary to keep samples on ice during reaction setup. Then, template DNA (200 ng/reaction) is added to the individual PCR tubes or wells containing the reaction mix.
4. The PCR tubes or plate are finally placed in the thermal cycler
(usually, all runs are processed in a Veriti 96-Well Thermal Cycler) according to the following cycling program: (a) I nitial heat-activation step at 95 °C for 5 min (to activate HotStarTaq Plus DNA Polymerase); (b) T hree-step cycling with the following conditions: denaturation at 95 °C for 30 s, annealing at 60 °C for 90 s, and extension at 72 °C for 30 s. The annealing temperature of 60 °C is suitable for most PCR systems; if the lowest melting temperature/T (as determined according to the form mula: T = 2 °C × (number of [A + T]) + 4 °C × (number m of [G + C]) of the primer mixture is below 60 °C, the starting annealing temperature may start from 57 °C.

146 Giuseppe Palmieri et al. (c) T he total number of cycles is usually 28 (which gives good results in most cases). However, the number of cycles is strictly dependent on the amount of template DNA and the sensitivity of the detection methods. Using a capillary sequencer instrument, the following number of cycles are recommended according to the template DNA amount per PCR reaction: 20–24 cycles/50–200 ng DNA, 24–28 cycles/10–50 ng DNA, 28–32 cycles/0.1–10 ng DNA; (d) F inal extension at 60 °C for 30 min (optimal for amplicons up to 500 base pairs in length; for targets longer than 0.5 kb, the extension time should be increased by 30 s per 0.5 kb). (e) A fter amplification, samples can be stored overnight at 2–8 °C or at −20 °C for long-term storage.
5. A dilution of 1:10 to 1:50 of the PCR product (1:10 is suffi-
cient in most cases) must be prepared before injecting it into a capillary sequencer, by diluting the PCR product using deionized formamide or water. An internal lane size standard is added to the amplified samples to assure accurate sizing of alleles and adjust for run-to-run variation; in Fig. 1 the electropherogram of the GeneScan 500 LIZ—one of the most used size standard—is represented. In summary, 1 μl of diluted sample is added to 9 μl of the dye mix per reaction.
6. After denaturation of the sample by heating it at 90 °C for
5 min, electrophoretic separation of the PCR products is carried out on a capillary-based electrophoresis DNA sequencer with automation capabilities (i.e., Applied Biosystems 3130 Genetic Analyzers; Life ThermoFisher, Foster City, CA). The output data are analyzed with the GeneMapper (Applied Biosystems/Life ThermoFisher, Foster City, CA) or similar software to determine the microsatellite status of analyzed samples. Patterns of amplified alleles among normal and tumor tissues are compared to identify insertions or deletions of repetitive units in the tumor sample as compared to the normal counterpart. In other words, instability at microsatellite loci is defined by the comparison of the amplified DNA samples between tumor and corresponding normal tissue that allows the identification of contraction or expansion of microsatellite repeats with consequent change in microsatellite length in analyzed sample (Fig. 2).
7. Using the Bethesda panel, MSI-H is defined when two or more
of the five markers are unstable (different sizes in microsatellite lengths between tumor and normal samples), whereas MSI-L is defined when instability is detected in one locus marker. The MSS status is established when none of the markers shows instability.

The presence of new alleles in the test sample (indicated by arrows) that were not present in the normal sample indicates MSI Alternative to Bethesda Classification of MSI is also useful for selecting candidate cancer Panel Test patients who might carry an MMR gene mutation. On this regard, although the Bethesda panel is still considered the standard, its sensitivity may vary according to which MMR gene is mutated (from 85% in patients with MLH1 mutations to only 60% for patients with MSH6 mutations) [32]. To increase the sensitivity in detecting a defective MMR mechanism, an extended Bethesda panel—consisting of eight microsatellite and two homopolymer markers (BAT25, BAT26, D5S346, D17S250, D2S123, TGFB, BAT40, D18S58, D17S787, and D18S69)—has been proposed to diagnostically assess MSI [33]. For the same purpose, a recent PCR protocol based on the use of ten microsatellites (BAT25, BAT26, BAT40, D2s123, D10s197, D13s153, D17s250, D18s58, D5s346, and MycI) has been established on the QiaXcel Advanced system (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) [34]. In both cases, the PCR assays are conducted using the same procedures as for the Bethesda panel test (through the fluorescent detection of PCR products in a capillary sequencing device) and the primer set includes the five recommend Bethesda protocol primers plus five additional marker useful for detection of the MSI status not caused by common mutations in the MMR genes. Again, according to the Bethesda agreement samples are considered as MSI-H if two or more markers of the Bethesda panel are mutated.

Fig. 3 Microsatellite instability assays using the MSI Analysis System. Matching normal sample (top panel) and MSI-positive test sample (bottom panel) were analyzed using the MSI Analysis System. The presence of new alleles in the test sample (indicated by arrows) that were not present in the normal sample indicates MSI MSI Analysis System Alternatively, the PCR-based MSI detection can be also carried out using the MSI Analysis System, which consists of five nearly monomorphic mononucleotide markers (BAT-25, BAT-26, NR-21, NR-24, and MONO-27) for MSI determination and two polymorphic pentanucleotide markers (Penta C and Penta D) for sample identification (Table 3). The mononucleotide markers are used for MSI determination, since their monomorphism implies that nearly all individuals are homozygous for the same common allele for a given marker. This simplifies data interpretation of any contraction or expansion of the nucleotide amount at these loci in samples containing mismatch repair defects. The pentanucleotide repeat markers are characterized for their high level of polymorphism and low degree of MSI, confirming that the test sample and the paired normal samples are from the same individual. After combining the MSI 10× Primer Pair Mix, the AmpliTaq Gold 10× buffer, AmpliTaq Gold DNA polymerase (Life Thermofisher, Foster City, CA), and nuclease-free water to a reaction volume of 8 μl in a sterile 1.5 ml tube, 2 μl of template DNA (1–2 ng) is added and solution is mixed. Amplification is usually carried out on the GeneAmp PCR System 9700 Thermal Cycler, with the following program: 95 °C for 11 min, followed by 30 cycles at 94 °C for 30 s, 58 °C for 30 s, and 70 °C for 1 min, and completed with an extension cycle at 60 °C for 30 minutes.

150 Giuseppe Palmieri et al. Running the electrophoresis on Applied Biosystems 3130 Genetic Analyzer, the PCR products are separated using a POP-4 polymer and a 36-cm capillary. Using this capillary sequencer instrument, the output data are analyzed with GeneMapper software (Applied Biosystems/Life ThermoFisher, Foster City, CA) to determine the MSI status of the tested samples. Again, microsatellite instability at ≥2 mononucleotide loci is defining as MSI-H, instability at a single mononucleotide locus as MSI-L, and no instability at any of the loci tested as MSS. Detection of MSI is based on comparing allelic profiles generated by amplifying matching normal and tumor DNA samples. The appearance of novel alleles in the test sample indicates MSI as shown in Fig. 3. Idylla™ MSI Test The Idylla™ MSI Test (Biocartis, Bruxelles, Belgium) has been developed using a unique set of novel biomarkers (Zhao et al. 2014; eLife) capable of faster detection with greater specificity and selectivity compared to current methods. It allows qualitative detection of mutations called indels, where short fragments of DNA are inserted or deleted into longer DNA sequences, within a panel of seven monomorphic homopolymer biomarkers located in the ACVR2A, BTBD7, DIDO1, MRE11, RYR3, SEC31A, and SULF2 genes (Table 3). MMR-deficient tumors commonly contain indel mutations; Zhao et al. have found 59 indels that can be used to detect MMRdeficient tumors, where each indel had been identified in several tumors taken from different tissues [35]. Indels in microsatellites from noncoding regions are more reliable markers of MSI across cancer types since they are subjected to less selection pressure than indels in coding regions. In fact, over 50% of the indels from noncoding regions occurs in MMR-deficient tumors with proven MSI [35]. When focusing on the clinical relevance of indel mutation patterns to diagnose MSI, it has been observed that indels specifically affected homopolymer stretches, which is more relevant even after comparison with the extended Bethesda panel consisting of eight microsatellite and only two homopolymer markers [36]. According to the indel rates, MSI status can be characterized as follows: if 20% or more of the studied microsatellite regions contains an indel, the tumor is MSI-H, if between 2% and 20% of the microsatellite regions contains an indel, the tumor is MSI-L, and if less than 2% of the microsatellite regions contains an indel, the tumor is microsatellite stable (MSS). The main advantage of the Idylla™ MSI assay is to identify specimens with MSI in a fully automated manner, with no need for paired tumor and normal tissues. Indeed, since the Idylla™ MSI biomarkers are tumor specific and genes included into the assay are frequently mutated in MSI-H cancers, there is no need to make comparison with normal tissues as controls; the occurrence of mutations into the candidate genes into the panel is considered to reflect the existence of a MSI status. The assay is conducted on

MSI Detection Tests 151 DNA extracted from FFPE cancer tissue sections and utilizes a real-time PCR assay followed by high-resolution melting curve analysis. Fully automated software interpretation and reporting is also integrated, providing a result in less than 3 h. Using the Idylla™ system with the seven given makers, the MSI results can be classified adopting three possible options: MSI-H, when ≥2 markers are mutant; MSS, when <2 markers are mutated, and Invalid if >2 markers are invalid. The MSI specific software will automatically check the validity of the measured fluorescence profiles: the presence of specific PCR amplicons will result in biomarker-specific fluorescence profiles, which eliminates the need for an additional sample processing control in the cartridge. For each individual biomarker, the assay simply reports if it is mutated, not mutated, or invalid. 4 Notes
1. Some cases analyzed by IHC may be particularly challenging
due to the following issues: (a) Nonspecific background. Some specimens may exhibit nonspecific background staining for reasons that are not well understood. Therefore, evaluation of an MMR IHC slide must include a comparison of the slide to the negative reagent control slide to determine the level of nonspecific background staining. Cytoplasmic staining, if present, should be disregarded in MMR IHC interpretation. (b) F ocal staining. Some specimens may exhibit focal staining in the tumor cells and staining intensity may vary from weak to strong. Based on the MMR IHC scoring algorithm, focal weak equivocal nuclear staining in the viable tumor cells in the presence of internal positive controls should be categorized as negative (loss) signal. (c) Punctate staining. Some specimens may exhibit discrete punctate staining within a few nuclei of the tumor; the staining intensity may vary from weak to strong. This staining pattern should be ignored and if a case has only this type of staining pattern, with a good internal positive control, it should be categorized as negative (loss) signal. (d) Tissue or staining artifact. Histologic artifacts originating from the sample processing and microtomy processes can also complicate the determination of MMR IHC classification. These artifacts may include, but are not limited to, fixation gradients and edge effects, DAB trapping, nuclear bubbling, lack of staining in some regions of the tissue, tearing or folding of the tissue, and loss of the tissue section. In some instances, repeat staining of new sections or acquisition of a new specimen may be required.

152 Giuseppe Palmieri et al.
2. Standard formalin-fixation and paraffin-embedding procedures
always result in significant fragmentation of nucleic acids. To limit the extent of DNA fragmentation, the following precaution measures should be taken: (a) T issue samples must be fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin as quickly as possible after surgical removal; (b) F ixation time of 6–24 h, according to the thickness of the tissue sample (longer fixation times lead to severe DNA fragmentation, resulting in poor performance in PCR assays); (c) D ehydration in serial ethanol alcohol dilutions must be highly accurate and homogeneously performed in all tissue areas prior to embedding (residual formalin can inhibit proteinase K digestion for DNA purification). 5 Concluding Remarks Considering the ever-increasing advances in the knowledge of the molecular mechanisms underlying the genetic instability at the chromosome and nucleotide levels as well as the recognized ascertainment of their clinical impact on cancer management, selection of the subgroups of patients according to the type of instability present (aneuploidy+, aneuploidy−, MSI+, MSI−) is becoming mandatory. Further advancements will be, however, achieved by increasing correlations between such molecular features—through a continuous dissemination of the methodologies to be used for their assessment into the clinical practice—and all disease-related and therapy-dependent parameters. These efforts should facilitate the development of innovative diagnostic, predictive, and/or prognostic tools for a better molecular classification of cancer patients. Syeda et al. dynamic range of several logs [6], and its short in vivo half-life of approximately 2 h can offer physicians a direct snapshot of the tumor status at the time of blood draw [7]. ctDNA has been detected at varying frequencies across tumor types, including up to 80% of melanoma patients enrolled in BRAF targeted therapy clinical trials [8, 9]. cfDNA concentrations typically range from 7 ng/mL in healthy donors [10] to as high as 1125 ng/mL in metastatic melanoma patients [11]. 1.1 Rationale Since 2011 there have been ten new therapies approved for use in to Develop ctDNA patients with unresectable, regionally recurrent (stage III) and Assays to Detect metastatic (stage IV) melanoma (hereafter collectively referred to Metastatic Melanoma as “metastatic”), as well as the application of several of those treatments to the adjuvant setting for resectable metastatic melanoma [12, 13]. With multiple treatment choices, there is a need for sensitive and specific, quantitative blood-based biomarkers of disease activity that could assist in optimizing patient management. For example, several studies have shown that metastatic melanoma patients with lower tumor burdens at the initiation of systemic therapies have superior survival rates compared with those who initiate treatment with higher disease burdens [14–17]. This was true for patients receiving either immune checkpoint blockade or MAPK pathway inhibitors. Tumor burden was assessed in these studies using pretreatment radiographic measurements (i.e., RECIST), serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), or cell-free circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) levels [14, 15, 17, 18]. Although not yet proven in melanoma, it is conceivable that switching to secondline therapy when tumor burden is low, but signs of treatment failure are detectable, could result in more durable responses and longer survivals. Likewise, the early detection of melanoma relapse in the adjuvant setting and the initiation of a new treatment could potentially increase a patient’s survival. Unfortunately, there are no validated, clinically useful blood-based markers to monitor disease relapse in patients who fail systemic therapies. Serum LDH is part of the melanoma staging system [19] and is the only serologic marker used in the United States to monitor advanced melanoma [20]; however, its sensitivity and specificity to detect disease progression are low [21, 22]. Given the limited utility of serial LDH measurements as a melanoma biomarker, radiologic imaging studies are needed every 2–3 months to define disease progression in patients with metastatic disease [20]. These scans are costly, timeconsuming, and not always definitive in their assessment of disease activity, especially in patients on immunotherapy drugs who may exhibit pseudo progression [23]. The prevalence of single base substitutions and the availability of several highly sensitive technologies for the detection of mutational hot spots make melanoma an ideal tumor for liquid biopsy. Mutations in BRAFV600 occur in approximately 40% to 50% of

Validation of Melanoma ctDNA Assays 157 melanomas, with VE and VK substitutions comprising nearly 90% of those mutations. NRASQ61 mutations (mainly QR, QK, QL) have been identified in approximately 25% of melanomas, mutually exclusive to BRAF mutations [24]. Most recently C/T mutations in the TERT promoter at −124 and −146 have been identified in 30–85% of melanomas depending upon the stage of disease [25–27]. The common BRAF, NRAS and TERT mutations are encoded by single or tandem base-pair substitutions that can be detected using the primer/probe based strategies that underlie the PCR- based approaches discussed below. 1.2 ctDNA Detection There are various methods to analyze ctDNA including mutation- Methods specific methods such as qPCR [28], BEAMing [6, 29] and digital PCR [30]. Broader investigations into a tumor’s genomic characteristics are possible using next-generation sequencing (NGS)based methods such as whole-genome [31], whole-exome [32], and targeted sequencing panels [33–35]. NGS has the advantage of being able to scan each cfDNA fragment for alterations using genomic library constructs [33]; however, NGS methods typically have lengthy and complex workflows [34, 36] The sensitivity of NGS varies with each sequencing method and generally ranges between 0.2% and 1% mutant allele frequency [33, 34, 37]. Given the potential limited sensitivity, complex workflows and high cost of NGS-based methods [38] they may not be the optimal method for ctDNA detection for clinical applications such as disease monitoring due to the need for frequent, repeated testing. Conversely, specialized PCR methods have greater sensitivities and lower costs, but are more restricted in the information they generate. In contrast to NGS-based approaches, the high-sensitivity methods—including qPCR, “BEAMing” and digital PCR—are focused on detection and/or quantification of one or a few specific mutations. qPCR is employed in the FDA-approved non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ctDNA diagnostic test to detect epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations in plasma to determine patient eligibility for erlotinib therapy [39]. When testing samples with low DNA concentrations, such as plasma-derived cfDNA, qPCR becomes less reliable and may yield variable results [40]. One approach to overcome this limitation is BEAMing (beads, emulsion, amplification, and magnetics) which uses magnetic beads coated with specific primers to capture predetermined ctDNA fragments prior to amplification. This approach yields a higher sensitivity for detecting the gene of interest compared to routine qPCR [41]. In studies performed on colorectal cancer patients, Diehl and colleagues tested plasma samples for four commonly mutated genes and obtained limits of detection (LoDs) ranging from 0.01% to 0.18% [6, 29]. This method has also been employed in melanoma [42, 43].

158 Mahrukh M. Syeda et al. Digital PCR is another approach for maximizing the detection of ctDNA when present at low concentrations. There are several different digital PCR systems available which use either preformed microchambers on a chip or dynamically formed droplet partitions [30, 44]; for the purpose of this chapter we will only focus on the latter approach, referred to as droplet digital™ PCR (ddPCR™) technology. In the ddPCR workflow, the 20 μL reaction mixture is partitioned into ~20,000 equally sized droplets in a water-oil emulsion [45]. Each droplet will contain either the target molecule(s), nontarget molecule(s), both or neither. The reaction is amplified to endpoint in a thermocycler and the fluorescence of each droplet is measured in a flow-cytometer-like specialized droplet reader. By dividing the sample into partitions (i.e., droplets) and analyzing them individually, the probability of detecting rare target molecules increases. ddPCR also enables absolute DNA quantification without the use of a standard curve by employing Poisson statistics to the end-point PCR amplification data [46]. The use of Poisson statistics is based on the assumption that all molecules are randomly distributed among equally sized droplets resulting in a coefficient of variation of 1.5% in 10,000 droplets [45]. ddPCR can accurately detect single nucleotide alterations with LoDs of ~0.005% for EGFR [47], 0.005% for BRAF [48], and 0.05% for TERT promoter mutations [49]. As we discuss below, ctDNA LoDs (i.e., assay sensitivity) are related to the total amount of input DNA as well as the mutant fraction of the sample. Despite its high sensitivity, ddPCR assays generally require a priori knowledge of the tumor mutational genotype to choose the appropriate assay. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach referred to as a “drop-off assay” has recently emerged, where all mutations pertaining to a specific locus are detected using a high affinity wild-type probe that is destabilized or “drops-off” in the presence of a single nucleotide change in the sequence [50–52]. With this technique, Decraene et al. were able to identify patients with any mutation for KRAS or EGFR using wild-type drop-off probes covering known mutational hot spots in exons 2 and 19, respectively, achieving LoDs of <0.1% [53]. Finally, it is important to remember that cfDNA is derived from many different sources, including hematopoietic cells. The presence of clonal hematopoiesis, in which “normal” cells carry a single somatic mutation in a proto-oncogene or tumor suppressor such as DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, JAK2, TP53, and KRAS [54, 55], may lead to a false-positive clinical assessment based on the detection of these mutations in cfDNA [56]. If these mutant alleles are being analyzed as ctDNA, the potential for clonal hematopoiesis must be considered by evaluating peripheral blood mononuclear cells along with cfDNA and the tumor under study [56].

Validation of Melanoma ctDNA Assays 159 1.3 Assay Validation Assays intended for patient care should be analytically and clinically validated, and ideally demonstrate clinical utility. Analytical validation entails demonstrating accurate and reliable measurement of the analyte of interest in the intended-use patient sample type (e.g., plasma), along with specified limits of detection, and background levels in healthy individuals. Clinical validation involves demonstrating that detection and/or quantification of the analyte associates with clinical parameters such as clinical stage, tumor burden, and survival outcomes. Clinical utility means that the use of the experimental assay could improve patient management/outcomes compared to existing paradigms [57, 58]. In the absence of a prospective study in which the assay result (e.g., “molecular relapse”) is used to determine patient management compared to the standard of care (e.g., radiographic disease progression), clinical utility can be demonstrated using clinical trial samples if the retrospective analysis demonstrates that optimal patient management could have been achieved based on the assay result (e.g., identifying a tumor mutation in ctDNA and starting appropriate targeted therapy) as was done to approve the EGFR ctDNA test for NSCLC [39]. Preanalytical validation addresses variations in assay measurement that may be due to factors affecting the recovery or stability of the analyte prior to being measured. With respect to ctDNA measurement, the major preanalytical issues involve blood collection and plasma purification methods. For an excellent review of this topic see [57, 59]. In the sections below we review an approach to assay validation for ctDNA measurements in metastatic melanoma patients. 1.3.1 Preanalytical There are several important preanalytical factors to consider in Validation: Purification measuring ctDNA. These include the volume of blood collected, of ctDNA from Blood the choice of blood collection tube, and the method of ctDNA Samples purification. To maximize the potential to detect low abundance ctDNA, efforts should be made to collect as large a volume of blood as is feasible for analysis. Plasma volumes of 3–5 mL should be used to extract cfDNA, as these volumes will achieve a higher DNA yield than 1 or 2 mL of plasma, increasing the probability of detecting the mutation(s) of interest [60, 61]. In particular, patients with a low tumor burden will have lower amounts of ctDNA so it is essential to maximize their plasma volume collection to increase the probability of detecting a tumor-associated mutation(s). During the process of blood collection it is critical to minimize the release of DNA derived from intact leukocytes as this would result in the dilution of ctDNA with cellular genomic DNA, reducing the mutant allele fraction, and potentially reducing mutation-detection when methods reporting mutant fraction are utilized.

160 Mahrukh M. Syeda et al. For this reason, ctDNA is preferentially extracted from plasma rather than whole blood [62], or serum, which can be variably contaminated by cellular DNA released into the liquid fraction as a result of lysis of white blood cells in the collection tube during clot formation [63]. EDTA-coated blood collection tubes are most commonly used for cfDNA extraction. EDTA not only serves as an anticoagulant minimizing the lysis of mononuclear cells but also inhibits DNase enzymes found in the blood, protecting cfDNA from degradation [64]. Other common anticoagulants such as heparin or citrate have been associated with lower cfDNA yields, perhaps because they do not inhibit DNases [65]. One limitation of EDTA-coated blood collection tubes is the commonly accepted need to process them quickly, generally within 6 h. After 6 h hematopoietic cells will begin to lyse releasing their DNA and RNA in the sample [66]. The potential for the release of hematopoietic cell DNA into plasma samples prior to processing spawned the commercial development of specialized collection tubes from several companies. These tubes employ additives that inhibit cell lysis and maintain DNA stability for several days at room temperature, facilitating transport between clinics and labs [63, 67–70]. While these tubes can simplify the specimen collection and processing workflow, the cost of these tubes can be prohibitive, in some cases almost 37 times more expensive than EDTA blood collection tubes. Centrifugation of blood samples is also a critical factor during the cfDNA extraction process. Plasma isolation from EDTA-coated tubes traditionally involves a single 10-min spin at approximately 1600 × g, which eliminates most cells and platelets from the sample. However, this method is ineffective at eliminating all residual cells in plasma, and DNA from the remaining cells may significantly dilute the tumor DNA with cellular DNA [71]. Therefore, blood samples collected in EDTA tubes need to be processed by a double spin, 10-min at 1600 × g, with the supernatant transferred to a second tube for a 10-min microcentrifugation at 16,000 × g [71]. Importantly, the centrifugation protocols of specialized collection tubes may differ from EDTA tubes, so users are urged to follow the specific instructions provided by the manufacturer. After plasma separation, cfDNA is extracted from each sample. Several cfDNA extraction kits with different chemical compositions have been compared side by side demonstrating different characteristics [70, 72]. Newer kits have also been developed recently, so users may wish to test various kits before committing to one for their work. The final step in cfDNA purification is sample elution. To maximize assay sensitivity, we suggest using elution methods that will allow the greatest yield and concentration of cfDNA, and a volume that will allow the entire sample to be analyzed by the downstream method. In general, maximizing the total

Validation of Melanoma ctDNA Assays 161 amount of cfDNA used as input for the assay will improve the detection rate of rare events, although each platform will have its own limitations to assay sensitivity. 1.3.2 Creation To create standardized, renewable calibrator sample sets for anaof Calibrator Samples lytical validation studies and for inter laboratory harmonization for Quality Control Testing experiments, known amounts of reference DNA can be spiked into pooled healthy donor plasma. Reference DNA should mimic the biological matrix being tested. For example, if a plasma sample is being tested then small fragmented DNA like nucleosomal DNA or sheared DNA should be used to mimic the fragment size of cell-free DNA. Larger fragments typically obtained from routine cell line DNA extraction may not be recovered as efficiently as smaller DNAs when using specialized cell-free DNA extraction kits [73] leading to undercounting of target copies in the sample; conversely, when assays generating larger amplicons (e.g., >100 bp) are used on the small fragments in cfDNA, they may not efficiently detect all copies present if both primer sequences are not present on any given fragment. The calibrator samples should be created with a range of analyte concentrations expected to be identified in the intended use patient samples, and include an unspiked normal plasma (i.e., negative control). Separate aliquots of pooled healthy donor plasma and reference DNA samples at different concentrations can be frozen and subsequently thawed to create freshly spiked controls for each run. 1.3.3 Analytical The accuracy of an experimental assay is the closeness of its results Validation to the true value of the analyte tested. Ideally, accuracy is determined by comparing the results of the experimental assay to that Accuracy obtained with a standard assay using a reference sample (e.g., validated source of mutated DNA). In cases where there is no available reference standard, a nonstandard analyte can be used (e.g., cell line-derived DNA or patient sample) as long as its true value is determined by a validated orthogonal method. With respect to mutation detection and ctDNA analysis, accuracy can include concordance between two methods analyzing the same plasma cfDNA sample. Concordance may be measured by agreement in mutation detection (i.e., present/absent), or agreement in quantification. In addition, accuracy assessments in the ctDNA field are often reported as comparisons between mutations detected in paired tumor and plasma samples from the same patient. In multiple ctDNA studies (especially in larger studies), the rate of concordance is generally less than 100% even when the most sensitive ctDNA detection approaches are employed. There are multiple factors contributing to this discordance including tumor type, tumor burden, and tumor location and its degree of vascularization. Some tumor types generally yield lower ctDNA levels than others

162 Mahrukh M. Syeda et al. (e.g., brain tumors), and patients with lower tumor burdens generally possess lower amounts of ctDNA in their circulation, decreasing the odds of detecting their tumor-associated mutations reviewed in [74]. For quantitative assays, the accuracy of quantification should also be considered. For the assay itself, the linearity of the relationship between estimated and actual concentrations can be measured using a dilution series of a purified analyte. The dilution range needs to include the range of analyte concentrations expected to be encountered in clinical practice. Quantification of clinical samples also includes preanalytical factors affecting analyte recovery. During assay development, percent recovery is typically measured with spike-in experiments. For example, a known amount of DNA is added to a normal plasma sample prior to extraction. Recovery is expressed as the percentage of the spiked-in DNA that was measured by the assay before and after extraction ((assay measurement/spiked-in amount) × 100%). The recovery of the analyte should be optimized in order to maximize the sensitivity of the assay for clinical samples. Recovery need not be 100 percent, but it needs to be reproducible (see Precision—below). Ultimately, the variability in quantification of a known amount of analyte should be defined as a range, so that variations beyond the range can be attributed to real differences in analyte concentration rather than variability in the assay method. The accepted range of accuracy within runs and between runs according to FDA guidelines is ±20% coefficient of variation (CV) of the nominal concentrations [75]. Inhibition of Assay When a compound affects the accuracy of measuring an analyte, it is referred as an “interfering substance.” In every assay there will be substances that are found in trace or even large quantities in the samples analyzed that can potentially affect the ability of the assay to perform adequately. Identifying these substances (aka “interferents”) and evaluating what levels can cause an inhibition of the assay is necessary for validation. Interferents can be endogenous or exogenous. To evaluate the effect of interferents in plasma, first spike a known concentration of reference analyte (e.g., mutated DNA) into a plasma sample, and divide it into two aliquots. Then add the interferent to one aliquot and compare the accuracy of detection and/or quantification between those samples. Endogenous interferents relevant to plasma samples include hemoglobin, albumin, bilirubin and triglycerides; exogenous interferents include therapeutic drugs and excess EDTA. Performing serial dilutions with interferents will provide information on the concentration level at which these substances interfere. In case of interference, measures should be taken to eliminate or minimize the interference [76]. It should be noted that these endogenous or exogenous substances may interfere with the preanalytical steps in

Validation of Melanoma ctDNA Assays 163 analyte purification, or the analyte measurement technique, or both. One of the advantages of ddPCR as a measurement technique is that it is tolerant to inhibitors because the reactions are run to endpoint and thus do not need to have 100% amplification efficiency to produce a positive droplet [77]. Precision Precision is a measure of the variability in assay results between replicate experiments measuring the same samples under normal assay conditions. Precision includes repeatability and reproducibility. Repeatability is a measure of within-run variability (i.e., the variation between technical replicates in a single experiment). Repeatability experiments include multiple individual measurements of the same sample using a single lot of reagents and the same equipment (e.g., thermocycler) on the same day. Reproducibility measures the variability between experimental results using the same sample on different days, or with different lots of reagents, or with different operators using a single lot of reagents. Ideally, one would run different concentrations of the analyte in each experiment to determine reproducibility across a range of concentrations expected for the intended use clinical samples. For example, when determining the reproducibility of a ddPCR assay, the template DNA dilutions should be prepared at different concentrations for a minimum of three runs. Aliquot the template DNA into a minimum of 3 vials (1 vial per run) and freeze them to avoid possible DNA degradation. Run 1 DNA aliquot each day on 3 different days to determine the reproducibility of the assay. One measure of precision is the coefficient of variation, which is calculated as: CV = σ/μ where σ is the standard deviation and μ is the mean. This measures the extent of variability in relation to the mean. The FDA defines the acceptable range for within-day and between-days precision with different operators as ±20% CV [75]. Specificity Analytical specificity is the ability of an assay to exclusively identify a target analyte in the presence of other components expected to be present in the intended use clinical sample. For PCR-based mutation-detection assays the other components of greatest interest are the wild-type allele, and closely related mutant alleles that may cross react with assay primers/probes due to sequence similarities. The ability to discriminate between closely related mutations may (or may not) have clinical relevance. For example, patients with BRAF V600E vs. V600K mutant melanoma had comparable survival rates in a randomized phase III clinical trial of the BRAF V600 inhibitor vemurafenib [78]. A recent retrospective study of BRAFmutant patients treated with anti-PD-1 immunotherapy, however, suggested possible differences exist in response and survival between patients with V600E vs. V600K mutations. Currently, it is not critical to distinguish these mutations for initial

164 Mahrukh M. Syeda et al. treatment decisions. However, for monitoring applications, the optimal performance characteristics are likely to be achieved by ctDNA assays that are specific for a single mutation. In general, specificity can be confirmed by obtaining positive results from reference materials containing known amounts of the analyte, coupled with negative results from samples which do not contain the analyte, including samples with a different mutation from the one targeted by a mutation-specific assay. Sensitivity Analytical sensitivity is generally measured as the limit of detection (LoD) of the experimental assay. For ctDNA studies, LoDs are typically expressed as the lowest fractional abundance of mutant alleles detected (i.e., mutant fraction), or the lowest number of mutant copies/mL of plasma detected. The first step in determining sensitivity is to calculate the background signal of the assay (i.e., the Limit of Blank (LoB)). The LoB is the amount of signal reported by your assay when analyzing a sample lacking the desired analyte. The assay conditions (e.g., number of replicates per sample that are analyzed) should be identical to those for the clinical samples so the results are representative of standard assay conditions. LoB can be calculated using the average and standard deviation (SD) of a series of blank samples [79]. As shown below: LoB=mean(blank)+1.645×SD(blank) The recommended minimum number of blank samples to be tested for calculating LoB is 10, but increasing the number of blanks to 20–30 samples can improve precision by reducing the standard deviation, which results in a lower LoB. The type of blank sample analyzed should be based on the intended use of the assay as background levels may differ depending upon the sample type analyzed (e.g., FFPE tissue vs. plasma). For mutation detection in FFPE tumor samples, normal DNA extracted from FFPE normal tissues (e.g., tonsil, lymph node) can be used. For ctDNA assays, patient plasma samples lacking the mutation(s) of interest should be used. It is important to use cfDNA samples from multiple individuals and not simply replicate cfDNAs extracted from a single patient for the LoB determination. The point of the measurement is to determine the background level among patients overall, so samples from multiple individuals need to be tested. Once the LoB is determined, the Limit of Detection (LoD) can be measured. To calculate the LoD, samples with known quantities of analyte are diluted to the minimum level of analyte that is sufficient for consistent differentiation from the background level, and run using the standard assay conditions. Generally, a minimum of 20 replicate samples of this dilution are run to determine the

Validation of Melanoma ctDNA Assays 165 LoD. The LoD can then be calculated by taking 1.65 times the standard deviation of the results of that analyte level and adding it to the already determined LoB, as shown below: LoD=LoB+1.645×SD(lowconcentrationanalyte) It is important to understand that ctDNA assay sensitivity is related to the total amount of input DNA as well as the mutant fraction of the sample. To achieve high LoDs (i.e., low mutant fractions, low copies/mL), one must analyze a sufficient amount of cfDNA. As shown in Table 1, if an assay has a reported 1% sensitivity to detect a mutant allele, it could theoretically detect three mutant alleles in a 1 ng sample. However, given the expected losses in DNA purification from plasma, the random variations in the distribution of three alleles in a solution, and the potential for amplification inefficiencies, the probability of detecting even one copy is likely to be less than 100%. If a 10 ng sample is analyzed, there will be 33 mutant alleles available, so the probability of detection is likely to be 100% and quantification is likely to be more precise due to the larger number of copies measured. Understanding and defining these relationships will determine the amount of sample required to obtain a reliable result. Inter laboratory If the assay will eventually be used in more than one laboratory, it Harmonization is important to demonstrate that comparable results are obtained for a sample regardless of the laboratory in which it is analyzed. Inter laboratory harmonization studies should be conducted after the repeatability/reproducibility studies have been completed in the laboratory that initially validated the assay (the reference lab). This is important as the degree of variability between laboratories will be evaluated against the expected degree of variability encountered in multiple runs from the reference laboratory.
