166 Mahrukh M. Syeda et al. To harmonize ddPCR-based cfDNA assays between laboratories, a first step is to establish that the sensitivity obtained in the test lab is comparable to that in the reference lab. The reference lab can prepare a dilution series of a known positive control samples sufficient for multiple runs to be used by both labs. The use of a d ilution series ensures that the expected linearity of the assay across a range of concentrations is reproducible between labs. The purified reference samples are run by both labs and the variability in results between the labs is compared using measures such as coefficient of variation. Once sensitivity is established, preanalytical factors (e.g., plasma extraction) should be tested for reproducibility. Calibrator plasma samples can be created by the reference lab by spiking a known amount of analyte into healthy donor plasma, freezing the sample and shipping it to the test lab. Both labs independently perform cfDNA extraction from plasma and run the assay to confirm the recovery and reproducibility of extraction method. If the intended use of the assay involves blood collection in specialized tubes that do not require prompt plasma separation and freezing, a final step in interlab harmonization would ideally involve the reference and test laboratories conducting independent analyses of duplicate samples from a series of patient blood draws. Two blood tubes are collected from each patient and transported to the reference and test labs. This real-world study design also allows the potential assessment of sample stability during shipment. Both labs carry out the entire sample analysis process including plasma separation, cfDNA extraction, and ddPCR analysis. Analysis of real-world patient samples between labs is an excellent measure of the robustness of the entire assay system from sample collection to reporting of results. 1.3.4 Clinical Validation To demonstrate the clinical validity of a ctDNA biomarker in melanoma the marker should associate with meaningful patient/disease characteristics (tumor-associated mutation, clinical/pathological stage, overall disease burden as assessed radio graphically, etc.) and/or survival outcomes. As in the development of therapeutics, the strongest level of evidence will come from the analysis of prospectively collected samples and clinical data from a clinical trial, where patient characteristics and their survival outcomes are strictly defined. In melanoma, several studies have demonstrated associations between ctDNA measurements and the various clinical characteristics listed above (reviewed in [80]). In particular, Santiago- Walker reviewed the utility of pretreatment BRAFV600 ctDNA detection using BEAMing in four BRAF-targeted therapeutic clinical trials enrolling 836 unresectable metastatic patients. They found BRAFV600 mutant ctDNA in 76% of samples, and statisti-

Validation of Melanoma ctDNA Assays 167 cally significant associations between the detection of ctDNA and survival outcomes. In addition, more recent studies have examined the potential for baseline ctDNA measurements to be used as predictive markers for therapies not targeting BRAFV600. One study used ddPCR to examine baseline and follow up BRAF, NRAS or cKIT ctDNA samples in patients with unresectable stage IV melanoma treated with immunotherapy. They found that detection of on- treatment ctDNA was independently associated with poor survival in more than one patient cohort [81]. Another study used ddPCR to examine plasma samples from 161 patients with resected metastatic melanoma enrolled in the AVAST-M trial of adjuvant bevacizumab vs. placebo. They found that detection of ctDNA in patients rendered radio graphically disease-free by surgery was independently associated with markedly decreased survival [82]. Overall, these studies illustrate the types of endpoints needed to demonstrate clinical validity of a biomarker in cancer medicine, which is required to advance the marker to the next step in development, clinical utility. Clinical utility is based on a demonstration that the use of the biomarker in managing patients results in equal or improved outcomes compared to the standard management without the biomarker. Further details can be found in Dobbin et al. [59]. 1.4 Concluding As multiple therapies are currently available for the treatment of Remarks metastatic melanoma, and the development of new, more effective agents and combination treatments proceeds apace, there is an increasing need for blood-based tools to support clinical decision-making that can potentially improve patient outcomes. Currently, there are no validated blood-based biomarkers for monitoring melanoma treatment response and disease progression. The high prevalence of hot spot mutations makes melanoma an ideal candidate for evaluating ctDNA as a disease biomarker. Despite the preliminary evidence from multiple groups showing the clinical validity of ctDNA as a melanoma biomarker, analytical validation of specific assays are needed, and further studies establishing the clinical utility of ctDNA measurements are required before these assays can be properly integrated into clinical practice. 1.5 Overview The remainder of the chapter describes the analysis of plasma samof Workflow for ctDNA ples using ddPCR assays to quantify mutant alleles in cfDNA. This Detection Using approach relies on knowledge of the tumor genotype in order to Droplet Digital PCR choose the appropriate ctDNA assay. In cutaneous melanoma patients the BRAF mutation status is commonly available from clinical molecular pathology studies, and other mutations (e.g., NRAS, TERT promoter) may also be reported. Alternatively, tumor mutation status can be determined in the research lab if a representative tissue sample is available.

168 Mahrukh M. Syeda et al. Following blood collection, patient plasma is separated (generally within 6 h) and can be immediately processed for cfDNA extraction or frozen for later use. To control for contamination that may occur during extraction, the workflow should include a blank sample/process control (e.g., water) that will be carried through the entire procedure [60]. Generally, mutation-specific ddPCR assays that are run in the Bio-Rad QX200 ddPCR system can tolerate up to 132 ng per well of digested or fragmented DNA per 20 μL reaction. The cfDNA concentration in plasma samples from metastatic melanoma patients is eluted at relatively low concentrations (average 1.14 ng/μL) [83]. Since only 8–10 μL of this eluate can be assayed per 20 μL ddPCR reaction, the nanogram input per well is typically well below the maximum tolerated amount. We utilize 8 to 12 replicate wells (20 μL reactions/well) to measure the total mutant copies in the entirety of the eluted sample. We also quantify the total cfDNA amount based on the sum of ddPCR copies/μL for mutant and wild-type copies. This strategy streamlines the workflow and maximizes the sensitivity of the ddPCR assays by analyzing all the available cfDNA in the sample. The standard duplex ddPCR assay uses two fluorescently labeled hydrolysis probes designed to selectively detect the mutant or the WT target sequences present in short length amplicons (70–115 bp). The ddPCR reaction is prepared in a Master Mix solution and then aliquoted into PCR tube strips as illustrated in Fig. 1. Each tube in the strip will contain the required volume for 4 replicate wells corresponding to 4 columns of the 96-well plate (see Methods). In order to maintain standardization in the field, the ddPCR assay should include run controls for the wild-type (WT) and mutant DNA, as well as a no-template control (NTC) [60]. Prior to transferring the reaction mixtures to the 96-well plate for thermocyling, each replicate mixture is partitioned into ~20,000 equally sized droplets in a water-oil emulsion using the microfluidic Droplet Generation system. After end-point PCR amplification, fluorescence is measured using the QX200® Droplet Reader. Data analysis is conducted using the QuantaSoft™ Analysis Pro software. Data can be exported as a.csv file for additional analyses). As mentioned above, one feature of the ddPCR workflow is that dilute samples can be analyzed in multiple replicate wells. This is particularly useful in samples where mutant copies/mL or fractional abundance is very close to the assay LoD. We generally use 8–12 replicate wells per sample. In the data analysis, all replicate wells are merged into a single “meta-well” which allows for a more accurate estimation of the true fractional abundance or copies/ mL, and yields tighter error bars expressed as 95% confidence intervals as shown in Fig. 2, or as standard deviations.

## Chapter 8


182 Shayna Sharma and Carlos Salomon disease is diagnosed also influences the survival rates. Patients that are diagnosed in the early stages, that is, Stages I and II have a survival rate of approximately 90%, compared to patients that are diagnosed at an advanced stage, that is Stages III and IV, where the survival rates drop to approximately 20% [3]. This marked decrease in the survival rates is due to the disease metastasizing to distant organs, at which stage, current treatments are no longer useful. Therefore, it is imperative that patients are recognized before the cancer has metastasized to distant locations to improve patient outcomes [4]. However, there are no routine screening tests currently available and diagnostic tests that are used, have limited sensitivity and specificity [5]. Therefore, recent research has turned its attention to other sources to identify novel biomarkers, and a burgeoning field has been extracellular vesicles. Extracellular vesicles are released by multiple cell types and have either a plasma membrane origin (apoptotic bodies and microvesicles) or endosomal origin (exosomes) [6]. They encapsulate genetic information in the form of proteins and miRNAs, which can be transferred from the cell of origin to recipient cells. This ability of exosomes to capture a snapshot of the cellular environment is highly appealing, thus establishing them as a potential biomarker for multiple diseases including ovarian cancer. Thus, this chapter will identify the current issues associated with biomarker development for ovarian cancer, discuss the proposed biomarkers and highlight the potential of exosomes to overcome the challenges associated with biomarker development (Fig. 1). 2 Ovarian Cancer and the Potential of Exosomes The lack of an early detection technique for ovarian cancer is evident through the percentage of patients that are diagnosed at an advanced stage-over 70% [7].The current tests that are used for detection include circulating cancer antigen-125 (CA-125) levels and transvaginal ultrasounds [8]. Furthermore, radiological imaging is also used to identify masses and to discriminate between benign and malignant lesions. However, this is also limited as tumors which are less than 2 cm in size are not easily detectable. Additionally, the continuous use of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and Computed Tomography (CT) are not feasible due to the radiation exposure to patients. Since there are currently no highly sensitive and specific diagnostic tests available, protective salpingo-oophorectomy is recommended [9]. Salpingo- oophorectomy is the removal of either one or both ovaries and therefore, it is often not accepted by women of reproductive age. Hence, it is essential that other potential diagnostic avenues be explored. Duffy (2013) proposed the following criteria for ideal tumor markers including clinical validation, inexpensive and standardized

Techniques Associated with Exosome Isolation for Biomarker Development: Liquid… 183

Fig. 1 Exosomes as potential biomarkers for ovarian cancer detection. Exosomes are released from the ovarian cancer microenvironment into the circulation, leading to disease progression. Blood samples obtained from a patient can be used to isolate these exosomes, through the use of multiple methods such as differential centrifugation, immunoisolation and size exclusion chromatography (discussed in this review). These exosomes can provide a fingerprint of the metabolic state of the cells in the tumor microenvironment, thus providing a minimally invasive biomarker assays, high positive and negative predictive values, and acceptable to patients that are being administered the test [8, 10]. Furthermore, markers should be highly sensitive while avoiding false positive results. Therefore, plasma proteins and miRNA that have been proposed as potential biomarkers [11–13] have a major setback, as they may be masked in circulation by high abundance proteins. Additionally, the use of tissue biopsies for proteomics and miRNA sequencing is also difficult as the procedure is invasive and the tumors may be in locations that are inaccessible. Therefore, recent research has proposed the use of circulating extracellular vesicles in aiding biomarker discovery [14–20]. However, extracellular vesicles are a broad term for a heterogeneous population of ectosomes, apoptotic bodies, and the vesicles of interest, exosomes [21]. There are two broad categories: plasma membrane derived vesicles, which encompasses ectosomes and microvesicles and endosomal vesicles which include exosomes. Microvesicles bud from the plasma membrane of a cell and have a

184 Shayna Sharma and Carlos Salomon varied size range of approximately 100–1000 nm [22]. Contrarily, exosomes are secreted from the endosomal compartments of a cell and are more homogenous in size (~100 nm) [23]. 3 Exosomes Exosomes are membranous vesicles derived from within the endosomal compartments of a cell [24]. Therefore, exosomes do not contain proteins from other intracellular organelles such as the nucleus or mitochondria [25]. However, the endosomal origin of exosomes is advantageous as it captures the intracellular cytoplasmic environment thus giving an opportunity to understand what is happening inside a cell. Exosome biogenesis begins with an engulfment of the intracellular environment leading to the formation of a small vesicle known as an early endosome [26]. The early endosome than progresses to a late endosomal stage and the late endosome can be distinguished through a change in shape toward a more spherical appearance. Furthermore, the late endosome transitions to a multivesicular body (MVB) phase which can be identified through the presence of vesicles known as intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) [26]. The ILVs are representations of an inward growth of the once endosomal membrane. The MVB can then undertake one of two pathways leading to either degradation or the release of the ILVs. Degradation occurs when the MVB fuses with lysosomes whereas exosome secretion occurs when the MVB fuses with the plasma membrane and releases the ILVs through exocytosis [26]. The secreted ILVs are now termed exosomes. Exosomes vary in size with a diameter of approximately 100 nm and have a flotation density between ~1.12 g/mL and 1.19 g/mL in a sucrose gradient [27, 28]. It has also been reported that environmental conditions such as oxygen tension and glucose concentration can influence exosome release [29]. There are several proteins which are found in abundance within exosomes or on the exosomal membrane such as TSG101, Alix, tetraspanins (CD9, CD63), and heat shock proteins (HSP90) [28]. Exosomes have been shown to have several roles including, but not limited to, facilitating cell–cell communication, transporting molecules such as proteins and miRNA and influencing target cells [30]. However, the ability of exosomes to transport a variety of molecules also indicates that they may be involved in transforming healthy cells in to cancerous cells resulting in the formation of a premetastatic niche [30]. Therefore, in addition to their involvement in biological processes, exosomes are also involved in pathological conditions such as infectious diseases and cancer. Exosomes have been implicated in several types of cancers, including ovarian, prostate and breast cancer. The majority of research has shown that exosomes are involved in metastasis and

Techniques Associated with Exosome Isolation for Biomarker Development: Liquid… 185 cancer progression by influencing the Epithelial to Mesenchymal Transition (EMT). Established literature has shown that the miRNA profile of exosomes derived from tumors varies, compared to exosomes isolated from healthy controls. Therefore, exosomes and their content are being investigated as potential diagnostic tools. Taylor and Gercel-Taylor (2008) proposed that the miRNA profile of tumor-derived exosomes could be used as a substitute for tumor biopsy profiling, thus minimizing the need for invasive biopsies [31]. Furthermore, it has also been shown that different ovarian cancer cell lines release varying amounts of exosomes with more invasive cell lines releasing greater amounts of exosomes [32]. There are several processes that have been proposed for exosome secretion and regulation including the activity of Rabs proteins. The Rab GTPases are involved in several mechanisms such as the ability of exosomes to be transported throughout a cell via communication with the cytoskeleton [30]. Additionally, they have been associated with an exosomes ability to adhere to the target cell to transfer contents and induce a biological reaction. Moreover, calcium (Ca2+) ionophores are also able to upregulate the release of exosomes [24]. It has also been shown by Riches and colleagues that exosomes present in the microenvironment of a cell are able to regulate the release of exosomes by that cell [33]. They showed that when exosomes are added to the growth medium of cells, the number of exosomes that are secreted decreases greatly. In addition to metastasis, exosomes have a role in several cancer hallmarks such as angiogenesis, extracellular matrix degradation, immune system suppression and the induction of tumor drug resistance [34]. It has also been noted that exosomes derived from patients with later stages of ovarian cancer contain higher amounts of proteins when compared to exosomes isolated from patients with early stage disease. In addition, it has been noted that under acidic conditions (such as the tumor microenvironment), the fusion between exosomes and target cells occurs at a greater rate than in less acidic areas [35]. Due to their ability to encapsulate molecules such as proteins and miRNAs, exosomes and their content have been proposed as biomarkers by several groups [18, 36, 37], however, a consensus on the exosome isolation technique has to be reached before further investigations. Thus, it is vital that standardization of an isolation procedure in addition to the characterization of the isolated vesicles be performed, if exosomes are to be used in a clinical setting. 4 Exosome Isolation Techniques There have been several methods proposed for the isolation of extracellular vesicles; specifically, exosomes (refer to Table 1). Techniques Associated with Exosome Isolation for Biomarker Development: Liquid… 193 ultracentrifugation, filtration, ultra filtration and separation using a density gradient [38]. Attempts have been made to compare these methods, where the exosomal yield is compared using techniques such as Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis (NTA) to establish size distribution, Western Blotting for markers found in abundance in exosomes such as Alix, TSG101, and CD63 as well as the use of electron microscopy to determine the morphology [38, 44]. Isolation generally involves differential centrifugation to remove contaminants such as cells, cell debris, and other large vesicles when purifying exosomes from samples such as cell- conditioned media (CCM), plasma, serum, urine, saliva and other bodily fluids [42, 46]. The number and speed of centrifugations varies depending on the starting sample. In cases where bodily fluids such as blood are used, the sample is centrifuged several times at high speeds, as there are an increasing number of contaminating factors (red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets etc.). In comparison, CCM may only be contaminated with one cell type as well as cell debris. After preparation of the sample, the sequential centrifugation steps begin with centrifugation at a low speed, up to 10,000 × g, following which, the supernatant is collected and further centrifuged at a greater speed, around 20,000 × g [41]. Upon completion, the supernatant is ultra centrifuged at speeds ranging around 100,000 × g. The exosomal yield using the centrifugation and ultracentrifugation methods is generally lower compared to other methods (e.g., ultra filtration and separation according to a density gradient) as it has been suggested that exosomes may form aggregates which interfere with separation using size [59]. Nonetheless, the pellet could also contain nonexosomal vesicles that may be larger than exosomes but are not removed during the centrifugation steps. To further enrich exosomes obtained after centrifugation, filtration and ultra filtration can also be used. The process of filtration is based on the separation of vesicles depending on their size. Commercially available syringe filters are used to allow particles smaller than a particular size to be passed into an ultra filtration tube. 0.22 μm filters are used to allow exosomes (and other particles that are less than 220 nm in size) to pass while excluding larger vesicles [48, 57]. The sample is then separated according to molecular weight, through the use of an ultra filtration tube, which is centrifuged at a low speed [51]. The residue is then collected and stored as this is the concentrated exosomal pellet. The ultra filtration procedure for isolation of exosomes from CCM is described in detail in Lobb et al. [57]. Briefly, the CCM is centrifuged at 300 × g for 10 min to discard dead cells and the supernatant is collected. This supernatant is then filtered through a 0.22 μm filter to remove other microvesicles and apoptotic bodies. The purified CCM is then ultra centrifuged at 100,000 × g for 90 min to pellet the exosomes.

194 Shayna Sharma and Carlos Salomon Additionally, the exosome pellet can be further clarified using ultra filtration devices such as the Amicon® Ultra-15,100 kDa tube which has a molecular weight cutoff (MWCO) of 100 kDa [51, 57]. Therefore, the particles present in the filtered residue should ultimately have a maximum diameter of 220 nm (0.22 μm) and a molecular weight of 100 kDa. Additionally, the filtration devices have a maximum size cut-off of 10 nm which results in the residue having particles greater than 10 nm in size. In addition to filtration, or apart from filtration, the density gradient method is also used (Table 1). Literature has reported the use of sucrose and iodixanol gradients as well as sucrose cushions [38, 46, 57]. The density gradients can be both continuous and discontinuous although discontinuous gradients are traditionally used due to ease of preparation [57]. A continuous gradient can be prepared by layering a low percentage solution (e.g., 5%) on top of a high percentage solution (e.g., 30%) and placing the tube in a magnetic holder [46]. The magnetic platform is used to create the continuous gradient from the step gradient. A discontinuous density gradient is prepared by layering different percentages of weight/volume (w/v) of a solution with the highest percentage at the bottom and the lowest at the top of the tube [57]. The sample is then placed on the top and the tube is centrifuged at a high speed. After centrifugation, fractions are collected and washed. This method is used to increase the purity of the sample although the yield may be similar to the other methods. Immunoisolation has also been used to obtain exosomes that are positive for MHC II molecules from samples. This process involves the use of magnetic beads that are coated with antibodies against proteins found on exosomal membranes. Immunoisolation is considered to be appropriate for repetitive isolations as the process is rapid. Furthermore, the binding of the antibody-coated beads to specific proteins allows for evidence that the isolated vesicles are exosomes rather than other extracellular vesicles or protein aggregates within the sample [38]. However, there are limitations to this procedure as exosomes cannot be isolated from cells that are MHC class II negative. Nonetheless, the use of members of the tetraspanin family such as CD63 has been proposed. However, when exosome-associated antigens such as CD63 are used, other extracellular vesicles which also present the antigens are isolated in addition to exosomes [60]. Tauro and colleagues (2012) used the epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM) (CD326) to coat magnetic microbeads. Following the coating, they centrifuged the samples at 100,000 × g for 1 h to allow for the exosome bound microbeads to pellet. The exosomes were then eluted from the beads and further analyzed. Other isolation techniques have been introduced although they have been considered less. Chen et al. [40] used a Microfluidic

Techniques Associated with Exosome Isolation for Biomarker Development: Liquid… 195 device to separate exosomes from serum using microchannels. The slanted grooves present within the microchannels were used to capture and separate particles. There have been a significant number of papers published, which have attempted to compare the different methods that are available for exosome isolation [38, 45, 57]. An early paper published by Thery et al. [38] attempted to compare differential centrifugation, filtration, sucrose gradient density separation and Immunoisolation. They found that the average amount of released exosomes was 0.1 μg per 106 cells. In addition, they noted that exosomes appeared cup-shaped when viewed under an electron microscope with an average diameter between 50 and 100 nm. However, papers published later stated varying size and morphology of the vesicles with no current agreement. Nonetheless, characterization of the obtained vesicles using several methods is essential as cells release a multitude of vesicles in addition to exosomes [47]. Nevertheless, Mathias et al. [39] published an isolation protocol using ultracentrifugation and filtration, however, the following year, Chen and colleagues [40] presented a new approach. They concluded that the use of a microfluidic device was cheaper, faster and required only a small amount of starting sample thus confirming its benefits for clinical use. Additionally, the device prevented the formation of aggregates. They used serum samples with optimized flow rates to demonstrate the use of the microfluidic device, although the flow rate would have to be adjusted depending on the starting sample, and this would be difficult due to the several different types of samples from which exosomes are isolated, for example, bovine colostrum and milk. Hata and colleagues (2010) revealed that there are microvesicles present within bovine milk samples and that these vesicles contain mRNAs and miRNAs. Furthermore, Michael et al. [42] demonstrated the presence of exosomes in saliva and stated that exosomal content was representative of the releasing cells thus hypothesizing a biomarker role for exosomal miRNA. This was also stated by Wei et al. [49] as they suggested that tumor-derived exosomes provide a source of tumor mRNA and miRNA. However, to establish exosomes as biomarkers, it is essential that the isolation technique eliminates the isolation of soluble proteins, thus increasing sensitivity [57]. A major contaminant when using urine samples is the Tamm–Horsfall Protein (THP) and different techniques such as the use of DTT, nylon mesh filters and Size Exclusion Chromatography have been used to eliminate this contaminant [46, 55]. It was shown that ultracentrifugation followed by SEC was efficient in eliminating soluble proteins such as albumin and THP [57]. Kosanovic and Jankovic [51] also examined the role of THP in contaminating the obtained exosomes and proposed a method involving centrifugation and filtration which eliminated the requirement for washing steps thus decreasing the amount of time required.

196 Shayna Sharma and Carlos Salomon While the above papers focused mainly on centrifugation and filtration, there were other papers that examined the use of EpCAM immunoaffinity capture. Tauro and colleagues [45] found this to be the best isolation method in comparison to ultracentrifugation and density gradient separation as the isolated vesicles had a greater amount of exosomal markers and proteins. This was also reported by Greening et al. [54] as they performed a proteomic analysis to compare the different isolation methods. There was a twofold increase in the amount of exosomal proteins within the sample isolated using EpCAM compared to filtration. Nonetheless, they also noted that density gradient separation was advantageous compared to EpCAM due to the lack of suitable exosomal markers [54]. Another method which had a similar concept to immunoaffinity capture was the ExoChip device, proposed by Kanwar et al. [50]. The ExoChip device has channels coated with anti-CD63 which can capture exosomes positive for CD63. However, a limitation to this method is that it is not able to isolate exosomes or other extracellular vesicles that are not positive for CD63. In addition to lab based methods, commercial preparations to isolate exosomes have also been proposed. The ExoSpin Exosome Purification Kit, Invitrogen Total Exosome Purification Kit, and PureExo Exosome Isolation Kit were compared to ultracentrifugation and each other. The ExoSpin and Invitrogen kits were able to recover a greater amount of exosomes when compared to ultracentrifugation or PureExo (measured using dynamic light scattering and tunable resistive pulse sensing) [56]. However, Tang and colleagues showed that although ultracentrifugation recovered a smaller number of vesicles compared to the kits, the samples had greater purity whereas exosomes isolated using the commercial kits had higher amounts of contaminating proteins [61]. Therefore, density gradient separation remains the gold-standard method for exosome isolation. However, a recent method that has been described in literature, may have the potential to replace density gradient separation. The method, known as size exclusion chromatography, utilizes a resinbased technique, to collect a purified fraction of extracellular vesicles from which RNA can be easily isolated [53]. Gámez-Valero and colleagues showed that the use of size exclusion chromatography maintained the structural integrity of the vesicles while removing contaminating proteins, making it the ideal methodology for biomarker studies involving exosomes [62]. Another recent study also reported that size exclusion chromatography is a superior method when compared to commercial kits [58]. Although the number of studies utilizing size exclusion chromatography is limited, the results from these studies suggest that it is a useful method for the isolation of pure exosome samples, with minimal contamination. Therefore, it is essential to consider the advantages and disadvantages of multiple methods for exosome isolation, depending on: the starting sample material, the endpoint analysis and the time and labor associated with sample preparation.

Techniques Associated with Exosome Isolation for Biomarker Development: Liquid… 197 5 Conclusions In conclusion, exosome present an attractive avenue for the detection of molecules present in the tumor microenvironment. Exosomes can be isolated in a minimally invasive manner, and through encapsulation, protect molecules such as miRNAs and proteins, from degradation. Furthermore, exosomes allow the detection of molecules that could be potentially masked by other abundant proteins when examining plasma samples or tissue biopsies. In the context of ovarian cancer, a disease with limited detection techniques (associated with late diagnosis) and the presence of tumors in areas that are difficult to access, exosomes may provide a solution to the several challenges associated with the disease. # Part III

Epigenetic Profiling

## Chapter 9


204 Joanne B. Weidhaas Non-coding RNA DNA
- transcription
transcription
- processing
mRNA ORF Non-coding RNAs, microRNA 18-24 nucleotide translation non-protein-coding negative regulators protein AGO c. 1996-today 78% of our DNA c. 1953-1965 2% of our DNA (all other biomarkers) Fig. 1 The new understanding of human DNA. A great amount of effort has been spent on searching for biomarkers in what was thought to be the only functional part of the DNA, the protein coding regions (left) which are produced from messenger RNA (mRNA) templates. However, it is now known that the majority of our DNA is actively transcribed and produces noncoding RNA, with microRNAs being the first class to be discovered (right). MicroRNAs work primarily through binding to the 3′ untranslated region of mRNAs. MicroRNA and other noncoding RNA species and their binding regions have been largely ignored in discovery efforts biology with the discovery of noncoding RNAs [1](Fig. 1). Since the discovery of the first human miRNA, let-7, in 2000 [2], miR- NAs have led the charge in the noncoding RNA revolution [2]. miRNAs appear to provide a powerful new avenue to the discovery of functional genetic markers in cancer, as they are altered in all cancers studied [3, 4]. Due to the importance of miRNA functions in development and growth, miRNAs are highly conserved—a recent study of reported single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in miRNAs found a relatively low level of sequence variation in functional regions of miRNAs [5]. Several such polymorphisms have now been identified and appear to be deleterious in cancer, making them likely candidates for causal variants [6–9]. It has also been shown that there are genetic variations within the 3′ untranslated regions (3′-UTR) of cancer genes and in some cases, the variations specifically alter miRNA binding sites [7]. MiRNAs are also critical players in the response to cancer therapy, including radiation therapy, which partly involves an immune-mediated systemic stress response [10]. The strongest evidence for miRNA involvement in the radiation response is for the let-7 and miR-34 families [10, 11], which appear to play key roles in DNA repair, apoptosis [12], and immunity, as misexpression of let-7 [13] and/or miR-34 [14] directly impacts and alters immune function. Recently it was found by us that miR-34 is uniquely activated in a posttranscriptional manner postirradiation by the central DNA

Identifying MicroRNA Pathway Variants as Biomarkers of Patient Selection for Immune… 205 repair regulator, ATM [15], supporting its critical and central importance in the radioresponse. Furthermore, others have found that miR-34 regulates PD-L1 after cancer treatment, including radiation and checkpoint therapy, changing the visibility of tumors to the immune system [14]. Based on our understanding of miRNA biology and the mechanisms of key miRNA target regulation, we investigated miRNA circuitry to look for germline biomarkers which may impact the response to cancer therapy. Through this initial investigation we identified the first miRNA binding site mutation in cancer, a functional, deleterious variant in a let-7 binding site in the KRAS 3′-UTR [7], referred to as the KRAS variant. The KRAS-variant is a predictive biomarker that identifies treatment response regardless of cancer type [16–20], that is, response or nonresponse is based on the patient being a “KRAS-variant patient,” not on what type of tumor they have. For example, KRAS-variant patients with ovarian cancer or HNSCC are resistance to cisplatin [16, 21], and KRASvariant patients with colon cancer or HNSCC are sensitive to cetuximab [19, 22]. Most recently, we found that the KRAS- variant is predictive of response to radiation therapy through an altered radiation-immune response—in a Phase III clinical trial of radiation and cisplatin plus or minus cetuximab in HNSCC patients, KRASvariant patients had higher rates of systemic failure. Our work suggested that KRAS-variant patients have a weak systemic immune response to radiation with elevated TGFB [23]. Given the impact of the KRAS-variant, and the existence of relatively rare, functional variants in miRNAs and their binding sites in target genes, as well as their critical role in the response to cancer therapy, we chose to systematically sequence germline genomic DNA obtained from cancer patients to discover additional functional variants in the miRNA regions and 3′-UTRs of cancer-related genes. We have now extensively mined this data to identify and apply functional mutations most likely to disrupt miRNA circuitry in genes and miRNAs known to be most important in the stress response mediated through the immune and DNA damage repair system and applied them to cohorts of patients treated with checkpoint therapy. We describe these procedures in this chapter. 2 Materials 2.1 Patients For variant discovery, we chose to interrogate a cohort of women for Discovery with ovarian cancer. We identified patients through the GYN (See Note 1) Oncology Clinic at Yale University for these studies. All had a confirmed pathological diagnosis of ovarian cancer. In all cases germline DNA was studied (see below).

206 Joanne B. Weidhaas 2.2 Patient Cohort One hundred and sixty-one cancer patients treated with single for Analysis agent anti-PD1 or anti-PDL1 therapy were identified and included of Checkpoint Therapy in our first study. For our collection, all patients were consented on Response and Toxicity one of three HIC approved protocols. Cycle number, toxicity sta- (See Note 2) tus, and in some cases cancer response rates were collected directly from the patient charts by physicians with access rights. Only patients who had received equal to or more than 4 cycles of therapy, unless they stopped due to toxicity before cycle 4, who were not on steroids for other reasons, who had their anti-PD1/PDL1 therapy every 2 or 3 weeks, and who did not have a preexisting diagnosis of an autoimmune disease prior to treatment, were included in the analysis. We chose to limit patients by these guidelines to exclude other associated causes of toxicity to checkpoint therapy. 3 Methods 3.1 Variant Our original workflow consisted of capturing these regions using Discovery in Cancer NimbleGen’s sequence capture technology using a custom devel- Patients (Full Details oped hybridization array followed by high throughput paired end as Published [24]) sequencing to identify genetic variations using individual genomic DNA samples from ovarian cancer patients (described in Subheading 2) and is detailed below (see Note 3). We next used a network-wide analysis to focus on those genes with variation in their sequence and their expression in ovarian tumors.
1. Target enrichment and high throughput sequencing of miRNA
genes and 3′-UTRs of cancer genes: At the time of this study, whole genome sequencing was not standard. We utilized a target gene capture procedure to obtain sequences enriched in all 718 of the known human miRNA genes in miRBase 14, and 3′-UTRs of cancer-associated genes. (a) F irst, genomic DNA was sheared to fragments compatible with Illumina/Solexa sequencing systems. (b) S econd, the individual genomic DNA was denatured and hybridized to a custom DNA NimbleGen array [25–27] carrying sequences complementary to the 718 known miRNA genes (miRBase 14) and 3′-UTRs of 5424 genes (obtained from the list of cancer genes in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) http://cancergenome.nih.gov/). (c) F inally, the captured DNA was eluted and processed through standard Solexa sequencing [28]. We successfully performed gene capture, and large scale paired end sequencing with ~500× coverage per sample, and most of the sequencing reads were mapped to the target regions by aligner BWA [29].

Identifying MicroRNA Pathway Variants as Biomarkers of Patient Selection for Immune… 207
2. Identification of known and novel genetic variants: Variations to
the consensus genotype were called with Samtools (version 0.1.11) [30]. To increase the quality of variant calls, the read depth threshold was set to 10. With this, each sample contained approximately 9000 SNPs passing the threshold compared to the reference genome hg18 downloaded from UCSC (http:// genome.ucsc.edu/). Most samples had approximately 300 SNPs in pre-miRNA regions and 8500 other SNPs with the chosen read depth. To determine how many novel SNPs were discovered in our sequencing data, the SNPs were compared with the dbSNP database (ver. 135) [31] and the 1000 Genomes Project (1KG) (SNP calls are based on 1092 individuals from the 20,101,123 sequence and alignment release of the 1000 genomes project; 379 individuals from European population.) [32]. We defined “novel SNPs” as those not reported in dbSNP or 1KG. We found approximately 50 novel SNPs in pre-miRNA regions and 900 novel SNPs in 3′-UTRs per sample, which constitutes almost 5–10% of total SNPs identified from each patient, consistent with the identification rate of novel SNPs in other studies [33]. For known SNPs, we compared the allele frequency of SNPs with the frequency in 1KG or dbSNP, and the vast majority of SNPs had a very similar frequency between our patients and the “normal” people from 1KG, either all populations or European descent only.
3. MiRNA target site prediction: We predicted the targets of all
human miRNAs in miRBase v14 (including 5p, 3p, and star miRNAs) by miRanda [34] and TargetScan [35], and then compared targets with SNPs called from our samples. Of 24834 distinct, known SNPs, 14084 of them were within predicted miRNA binding sites; of 13030 distinct, novel SNPs, 7023 of them were within miRNA complementary sites. Almost half of SNPs are at putative miRNA complementary sites. 3.2 Selection Identification of variants to apply to immune therapy cohorts was of Biomarkers determined through bioinformatic approaches and is detailed for Testing for Immune below. Performing follow-up genotyping has been performed Therapy using Sequenome or direct Taqman genotyping per standard protocols (see Note 4). We chose to focus on checkpoint inhibitors and wanted to evaluate the impact of single-agent therapy and thus felt that anti-PD1 or anti-PDL1 was reasonable candidates.
1. Identification of variants important for response or toxicity to
immune therapy: Our goal was to identify functional variants in key players in the immune response. We focused on two significant groups of genes: DNA damage repair and response genes and immune response genes, as well as the promoter regions and key targets of miRNAs known to be most critical in these stress response pathways. We cross-referenced these lists against

208 Joanne B. Weidhaas any 3′-UTR variant (SNPs or indels) from our DNA sequencing data as described above, and variants were confirmed that they were predicted to occur within a miRNA target site using several predictive algorithms (Miranda, TargetScan, PicTar, etc.). Additionally, we compiled a list of candidate variants found in the genes on our list using multiple free-access software programs that predict miRNA target site variants by aggregating information from the dbSNP and HapMap databases and running it against their own miRNA target site prediction algorithms (e.g., PolymiRTS, MirSNP, miRNASNP, and MicroSNiPer). We hand-checked every single variant on our list using RNA Hybrid, a software program that anneals RNA sequences in trans [36]. 3′-UTR variants were assessed for their ability to (negatively or positively) disrupt miRNA binding according to the “old” and “new rules” for miRNA-target site recognition [35, 37–40]. We additionally included promoter region variants in any of the miRNAs known to be important in DNA repair or immune responses. As a final step in our evaluation for candidate variants to test, we limited our lists to variants predicted to be found in at least 5% of the population, as we are looking for biomarkers that would be present in a reasonable number of patients. Our search filtered 2540 total variants, which we brought down to a final list of ~350 variants fitting the above defined priority parameters for evaluation (Fig. 2).
2. Preparation of samples and scoring for analysis of response and tox-
icity to anti-PD1/PDL1 immune therapy: DNA was isolated from blood or saliva for all patients using standard techniques. iRAEs were recorded by the treating physician and graded per ASCO guidelines as Grade 1–4 [41]. Response was recorded for the melanoma patients by treating physicians categorizing them using immune-RECIST (iRECIST) criteria [42] using best overall response as follows: progressive disease (PD), stable disease (SD), partial response (PR), and complete response (CR).
3. Statistical analysis approach: Four classifiers were trained on a set
of 62 melanoma patients evaluated for toxicity. Subjects were classified as experiencing high toxicity (≥Grade 2) versus low toxicity (≤Grade 2). Performance of the classifiers was tested on a validation set of 99 patients with other types of cancer. Markers were treated either as categorical variables (i.e., wild type, heterozygous mutant, or homozygous mutant) or continuous variables by assigning a value of 0 to wild type, 1 to heterozygous mutants, and 2 to homozygous mutants. Classifiers were built for each treatment of marker data (i.e., categorical or continuous) comparing classification trees (CT) [43], LASSO-regularized logistic regression (LASSO-LR) [44], boosted trees (BT) [45], and random forests (RF) [46]. Two sets of CT were tuned separately on minimum split and minimum node size, LASSO models were

209 From master pool (16,000 genes) generate list of relevant genes and biomarkers (currently ~250) 3’UTR-seq data In silico database 9140 mining mining Cross-check with RNA Hybrid 7824 Targeting miRNA implicated 2540 in response of interest Minor allele frequency between 5-790 20% Screen samples of interest 350 Evaluate for significance using 21 simple and complex models tuned on the regularization parameter lambda, BT were tuned on the learning parameter eta, tree depth, and the number of rounds, and RF were tuned on number of trees and variables considered at each split. Due to the class imbalance in observed toxicity, subjects with toxicity were up-weighted in the training data and tuning parameters were selected to minimize the F1 score (defined as the harmonic mean of sensitivity and positive predictive value) using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). The final performance measures, accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, negative predictive value, positive predictive value, area under the curve (AUC), and F1 score were reported on the training data using LOOCV and on the validation data not used in training. CT, LASSO-LR, BT, and RF classifiers were fit in R (version 3.5.1) [47] with mlr (version 2.1.1) calling rpart (version 4.1-11), glmnet (version 2.0-10), xgboost (version 0.71.2), and ranger (version 0.10.1), respectively. Missing marker values were imputed five times via chained equations [48] with markers treated as categorical variables. 210 Joanne B. Weidhaas 4 Notes
1. The greatest challenge in all of these discovery efforts it to find
excellent data sets that are carefully cleaned by the appropriate people with access and clinical insight to confirm they are appropriate to be included. While the discovery work was done on a small cohort, it yielded numerous mutations to pursue. Although the trend with approaches like GWAS has been to get very large collections to study, this often dilutes the purity of the input and likely leads to loss of meaningful findings.
2. The example of the cohort used in this review is just to repre-
sent considerations that should be made when choosing a collection of patients to study. Involvement of clinicians familiar with the agents to help guide selection as well as to confirm that all patients have accurate and complete clinical annotation cannot be stressed enough.
3. Sequencing technology has advanced significantly since the
original discoveries and approach to discover them described in this chapter. The challenge in finding variants is not currently the technology but instead the work to determine that they are functional as well as the need to find the appropriate clinically annotated patient data set.
4. We do feel it is important to validate calls carefully with the
most sensitive technologies, even those from sequencing. Taqman genotyping is likely the gold standard for evaluation. Using imputed SNPs is rarely fully accurate and can lead to error, which is problematic in small carefully annotated data sets. References

## Chapter 10


214 Erin M. Taylor et al. modulate chromatin compaction, allowing or denying the transcriptional machinery access to the regulatory regions of genes. Regions of highly compacted chromatin, also known as heterochromatin, are generally associated with genes that are not being transcribed, while less compacted regions of chromatin, or euchromatin, are associated with regions that are being actively transcribed. The amino acid site and chemical makeup of the histone PTMs determine the level of chromatin compaction, which effectively turns gene transcription on or off. Histone PTMs play roles in DNA damage repair [1, 2], DNA replication [3, 4], cell cycle regulation [4, 5], and apoptosis [6]. Dysregulation of the enzymes that add or remove epigenetic marks, called epigenetic modifiers, are known to contribute to multiple diseases, one of the most prevalent being cancer. Epigenetic dysregulation in cancer is a key area of diagnostic and therapeutic cancer research [7–14]. Since histone proteins are highly abundant in cells and have dysregulated PTMs in various cancers, there is an interest in using histone PTMs as cancer biomarkers [9, 15–17]. One area of interest for using histone PTMs as cancer biomarkers is determining responsiveness to immunotherapy. In recent years, the use of immunotherapy, like immune checkpoint blockade, has redefined how we treat certain cancers. Some patients show a durable response to these immunotherapies, while others show little response or develop secondary resistance. Defining biomarkers of responsiveness to immunotherapy would help oncologists determine what immunotherapy regimen would be most effective for a given patient and thereby positively impact outcome and survival. Here, we review the current knowledge on identification of histone PTMs as biomarkers for immunotherapy responsiveness, and how they have been identified in both tumor and immune cells. 1.1 Histone PTMs Cancer formation stems from a set of biological processes generally as Biomarkers known as the hallmarks of cancer that govern transformation of for Immunotherapy normal cells into cancer cells. The hallmarks of cancer encompass a of Cancer: Cancer variety of mechanisms from sustained angiogenesis to insensitivity Cells to antigrowth signals [18]. Three of the hallmarks that are particularly important in the context of immune function are the ability for cancer to evade induced apoptosis, escape immune surveillance, and the production of tumor-promoting inflammation. Under normal circumstances, aberrant cell growth or behavior is recognized and eliminated by the immune system. However, in the context of cancer, abnormal cell growth has managed to escape immune regulation and avoid elimination. Mechanisms of immune escape can be broadly classified into two groups. One group is altered tumor–immune cell interactions and includes tumor cell changes in antigen expression, decreased expression of FAS receptor, and altered expression of immune checkpoint components that inhibit T-cell responses [19, 20]. The other group is altered

Histone Modifications as Biomarkers for Immunotherapy 215 tumor microenvironment and includes production of proinflammatory and immunosuppressive cytokines and changes in immune trafficking [19]. Acquisition of characteristics that allows cancer cells to develop and survive depends largely on genomic instability [18]. There are multiple mechanisms in which genomic instability can arise including telomere damage, DNA damage, centrosome amplification, and epigenetic modifications [21]. Epigenetic mechanisms that contribute to genomic instability largely depend on chromatin remodeling through DNA methylation and histone PTMs [22]. Changes in histone PTMs in tumor cells can influence immune system trafficking and response to cancer. These changes typically result in suppression of a normal immune response by decreasing expression of tumor-associated antigens, antitumor chemokines, and the Fas receptor on tumor cells [23–27]. The ability for histone modifications to alter immune response to cancer cells indicates that it may also play an important role in predicting response to immunotherapy and serve as suitable biomarkers. 1.2 Elevated Histone 3 Lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) is a histone H3K27me3 Inhibits mark that is predominately added by the methyltransferase EZH2 Antigen Presentation [28]. EZH2 is the functional enzymatic subunit of the polycomb and Chemokine repressive complex 2 (PRC2) [28]. H3K27me3 is a transcription- Production ally repressive mark that downregulates gene expression through the formation of heterochromatin [29]. Altered levels of H3K27me3 have been associated with several cancers such as ovarian cancer, multiple forms of lymphoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, lung cancer, malignant pleural mesothelioma, breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma [30–37]. Increased levels of H3K27me3 have been shown to reduce antigen processing and presentation via MHC class I molecules [23]. MHC class I molecules present endogenously synthesized antigens which then interact with CD8+ T cells and are important in the removal of virally infected cells and cancer cells [38, 39]. The immunoproteasome processes proteins from the cell into antigenic peptides which can then bind to MHC class molecules [40]. Once bound to an antigenic peptide, the MHC class molecule is then stably expressed on the cell surface where it can interact with the T cell receptor on T lymphocytes [40]. A study by Zingg et al. found that treatment with an immune checkpoint inhibitor in a mouse melanoma model resulted in tumors with elevated EZH2 levels and subsequently increased H3K27me3 [23]. When compared to the control, tumors from treated mice demonstrated decreased levels of genes related to MHC class I molecules, antigen processing, and immunoproteasome. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) for H3K27me3 showed enrichment at the promoter region of a large number of these genes involved in antigen processing and presentation.

216 Erin M. Taylor et al. Elevated levels of H3K27me3 have also been observed to decrease chemokine production and alter immune trafficking [24, 25, 41, 42]. Chemokines are a type of cell signaling molecule known as a cytokine. They are secreted from cells and act as chemoattractant dictating cell migration [43]. Chemokines play an important role in immune trafficking under normal and inflammatory conditions [44]. Altered chemokine signaling has been implicated in a variety of cancers including melanoma, breast cancer, lung cancer, prostate cancer, glioblastoma [45]. In cancer, the role of chemokines can be divided into four main categories: tumor growth and progression, angiogenesis, metastasis, and tumor immunology [45]. Chemokines involved in promoting an antitumor immune response include CCL3, CCL5, CCL20, CXCL9, and CXCL10 [46–49]. CXCL9 and CXCL10 are important in generating a form of effector CD4+ T cell response designated type-1 helper (Th1) response [50]. Th1 cells are thought to play a role in initiating a cytotoxic T cell immune response [51]. The study by Zingg et al. found that the treatment of mouse melanoma with immune checkpoint inhibitors resulted in increased H3K27me3 and decreased levels of the chemokines CXCL9 and CXCL10 [23]. ChIP for H3K27me3 showed enrichment at the promoter region of these two chemokines. EZH2 knockdown with short hairpin RNA (shRNA) rescued expression of CXCL9 and CXCL10 and treatment with an EZH2 inhibitor (GSK503) and immunotherapy improved CD8+ T cell accumulation into mouse tumors. In the studies by Peng et al. and Nagarsheth et al., it was found that elevated H3K27me3 plays a role in immune regulation by repressing expression of CXCL9 and CXCL10 in ovarian and colon cancer [24, 25]. Knockdown of EZH2 function with shRNA targeting EZH2 or SUZ12 demonstrated a global decrease in H3K27me3 in human primary ovarian cancer and colon cancer cells. ChIP revealed significantly reduced abundance of H3K27me3 at the promoter regions of CXCL9 and CXCL10 and lead to an increase in abundance of the chemokines. In addition, ovarian and colon cancer patients with higher levels of EZH2 had decreased overall survival and had a slight inverse correlation between EZH2 abundance and the number of intratumoral CD8+ T cells. The studies by Zingg, Peng, and Nagarsheth show that elevated levels of H3K27me3 cause downregulation of antigen presentation and decrease the production of antitumor chemokine. These results suggest that H3K27me3 could play an important role in dictating response to immunotherapies and could serve as a potential biomarker.

Histone Modifications as Biomarkers for Immunotherapy 217 1.3 Elevated Histone 3 Lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) is a posttransla- H3K4me3 Increases tional modification that is added by the histone methyltransferase Complement Factors SET1A, SET1B, KMT2A, KMT2B, KMT2C, or KMT2D [52]. and Chemokine H3K4me3 generally functions a transcriptionally active mark that Production upregulates gene expression [52]. Chromatin remodeling factors CHD1 and BPTF target H3K4me3 and modify chromatin structure, thereby enhancing transcriptional activity [53, 54]. While H3K4me3 generally functions as a transcriptionally active mark, it can also occur along with a repressive mark such as H3K27me3 on bivalent chromatin which has little or no transcriptional activity but is poised for activation [55, 56]. KDM5B is a histone demethylase that is capable of demethylating trimethylated, dimethylated, and monomethylated lysine 4 of histone 3 [57]. KDM5B plays a role in transcriptional repression through the demethylation of H3K4 and has been found to be elevated in breast cancer, lung cancer, bladder cancer, and prostate cancer [58, 59]. Increased levels of H3K4me3 have been found to directly correlate with complement factor abundance and chemokine production [26]. The complement system is part of the innate immune response and is comprised of a set of proteins that are activated in a cascading manner [60]. The complement system has many functions including destruction of bacteria and viruses, promoting antibody formation and effectiveness, formation of memory immune cells, and attracting macrophages and neutrophils [60]. Chemokines, as discussed above, and the complement system both play a potential role in immune trafficking to the tumor microenvironment. A study by Klein et al. found that knockdown of KDM5B led to global increase of H3K4me3 levels and increased expression of immune response genes [26]. The genes found to be most significantly increased were chemokines and complement factors. Chemokines and the complement system are both important in initiating an immune response and immune trafficking indicating that H3K4me3 levels could serve as a potential biomarker for responsiveness to immunotherapy. 1.4 Elevated Histone 3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) is posttranslational H3K9me3 Inhibits Fas modification that can be catalyzed by several different SET-domain Expression containing methyltransferases which include SETB1, SETB2, SUV39H1, and SUV39H2 (reference for SETB2) [61]. H3K9me3 is a transcriptionally repressive mark and changes in abundance are associated with multiple forms of cancer including acute myeloid leukemia, melanoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, prostate cancer, gastric adenocarcinoma, and colon cancer [62–67]. Increased H3K9me3 has been found to be elevated at the promoter region of the Fas gene and thereby decreased Fas expression [27, 68]. Fas is a member of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF)

218 Erin M. Taylor et al. receptor superfamily and can be expressed on the cell surface of both immune and nonimmune cells including tumor cells [20]. It has been shown to play a vital role in the regulation of programmed cell death [20]. Fas ligand (FasL) is the physiological ligand of Fas and is a transmembrane TNF family protein expressed on activated cytotoxic T cells [69]. The Fas-FasL pathway results in apoptotic cell death and is essential in immune system regulation [27]. Interaction of Fas with the corresponding ligand results in the formation of the death inducing signaling complex (DISC) through the recruitment of the Fas-associated death domain protein (FADD), procaspase-8 and procaspase-10 [70]. FasL mediated immune attack has been found to be an important regulator of early tumor growth [71]. Inhibition of Fas-mediated apoptosis is one of the general hallmarks of cancer and its expression has found to be altered in the progression of numerous cancers such as melanoma, breast cancer, epithelial ovarian cancer, non-small cell lung carcinoma, and colon cancer [72–78]. In the study by Paschall et al., it was found that H3K9me3 plays an important role in immune escape by silencing Fas expression in colon cancer [27]. ChIP-sequencing analysis of a human metastatic colorectal carcinoma (CRC) cell line revealed H3K9me3 in two locations of the Fas promoter. However, global H3K9me3 levels were not found to be different. Treatment with Verticillin A, a selective inhibitor of SUV39H1 and SUV39H2 was able to decrease H3K9me3 and restored Fas expression. In a mouse model, differences in tumor growth were mediated by FasL expression on tumor-infiltrating cytotoxic T cells. These results suggest that the Fas-FasL pathway is important in cancer immune surveillance and H3K9me3 at the Fas promoter could serve as a potential biomarker for responsiveness in immunotherapy. 1.5 H3K27me3 While histone PTMs of tumor cells play a surprisingly strong role in as a Biomarker regulating immune cell infiltration and function, immune cells for Immunotherapy themselves are highly dependent on their histone landscape for their of Cancer: Immune differentiation, survival and function [79–81]. Arguably the histones Cells PTMs of specific lymphocyte populations will serve as stronger, more direct biomarkers for immunotherapy effectiveness [82, 83]. While there are many immune cell types that have been implicated in the success/resistance to cancer immunotherapy, we will focus on H3K27me3 in tumor infiltrating effector (T ) and regulatory T cell eff (T ) populations. T exhaustion/dysfunction is a hallmark of reg eff cancer and immunotherapy responsiveness [84]. Exhausted T cells show a distinct chromatin landscape, in which histone modifications play a large role in defining [85, 86]. These modifications support the dynamic nature of T cells, allowing for rapid control of gene expression. The specific modifications and the genes they regulate is becoming clearer, paving the way for the use of these modifications as biomarkers for immunotherapy of cancer.

Histone Modifications as Biomarkers for Immunotherapy 219 Upon stimulation, the adaptive immune system displays remarkable plasticity. The ability of these cells to generate diverse phenotypes is in part due to histone PTMs. Histones modifications have been shown to play a vital role in the rapid and extensive chromatin changes required to support the differentiation, cell cycle and metabolism of these naïve T cells. While the functional and phenotypic changes during T cell differentiation/activation are well characterized, the epigenetic contributions are a fairly new addition to the story and still incompletely understood. This highly regulated processes of gene expression control involves many epigenetic modifications and combinations, making it a challenging area to fully define. However, the role H3K27me3 plays in the immune response to cancer has become clearer in the last 5 years [87]. Preventing or reversing T cell exhaustion is the goal of many cancer immunotherapies, effective prevention or reversal of this induced dysfunction have been very effective. Exhausted T cells in chronic infection and in cancer express distinct gene expression patterns. The regulation of gene expression in exhausted T cells is poorly understood, however H3K27me3 has been shown to play an important role in early exhaustion of T cell populations [88, 89]. 1.6 Elevated During T activation the levels of EZH2 and H3K27me3 are rapeff H3K27me3 Enhances idly induced. EZH2, through the placement of the repressive Cytotoxic T Cell H3K27me3 PTM has been shown to control T polyfunctionality eff Survival and Function (IFN-γ+, TNF+ and granzyme B+), promote memory and enhance survival [88]. This is consistent with the use of EZH2 inhibitors to treat autoimmune and graft vs. host conditions [90]. Similarly to EZH2 in cancer cells, T cell EZH2 primarily acts as a gene silencer. In ovarian cancer EZH2+CD8+ TILs did not express exhaustion markers and produced effector cytokines. The attributing mechanism is thought to be through promotion of Notch signaling which leads to increased survival and effector function of T cells. eff Infiltration into the tumor microenvironment has been shown to interfere with T EZH2 expression through glucose-withdrawal eff induced microRNAs (miRNA101 & miRNA26a) [88]. It is clear that EZH2 expression can enhance the survival and function within the tumor microenvironment, this is consistent with prognosis in patients. A study by He et al. demonstrated the contribution of EZH2 in the development and maintenance to T cell memory precursors which correlated with enhanced tumor control. They showed that phosphorylation of EZH2 by Akt altered transcriptional programing and ability to control tumor growth. This could be attenuated by introducing an Akt-insensitive EZH2 in T cells [89]. These studies suggest that like cancer cells, EZH2 and its histone PTM, H3K27me3, are crucial for an effective T cell responses to cancer. Therefore, the number of H3K27me3, CD8+ T cells would seem to predict patient responsiveness to cancer immunotherapy.

Small molecule inhibitors for EZH2 are being used in clinical trials with immune checkpoint inhibitors (NCT03525795), in an effort to disrupt regulatory T cell repression [93]. This approach disregards the role EZH2 in T, though eff there appears to be a therapeutic window for this combinatorial strategy to work. Taken together T require H3K27me3 for gene regs suppression and maintenance and loss of H3K27me3 specifically in T cells would indicate a more immunotherapeutic responsive reg cancer. 1.8 Conclusions Identification of biomarkers indicating responsiveness to immunoand Future Directions therapy treatment of cancer will have profound impacts on patient outcome and survival. First, defining biomarkers of responsiveness will help clinicians make decisions on what immunotherapies to use for a given patient, or whether immunotherapy is a viable treatment option. Knowledge of which personalized treatment strategy to take will provide the optimal regimen of drugs delivered in a timely manner, which are both key factors influencing outcome and survival. Second, uncovering biomarkers of responsiveness will allow secondary studies to better understand the molecular mechanisms and pathways of responsiveness. These dysregulated molecular markers and associated pathways will provide targets for new therapeutic development to increase the effectiveness of immunotherapy. Histone PTMs have the potential to be used as sensitive biomarkers to determine responsiveness to immunotherapy treatment of cancer. However, utilizing histone PTMs as biomarkers of immunotherapy responsiveness is currently an evolving field. One of the obstacles to overcome is the initial identification and detection of histone PTMs that are dysregulated in tumor or immune cells. Discovery phase workflows for identification of dysregulated histone PTMs typically utilize antibodies or mass spectrometry. Antibody-based workflows are limited by antibody availability, quality, and specificity. Furthermore, histone PTM specific antibodies are generally available for only single histone PTMs, while combinations of histone PTMs on single histone molecules cannot readily be measured. Mass spectrometry provides an unbiased and quantitative method for the discovery of dysregulated histone PTMs. Discovery-based proteomic approaches have been used to

Histone Modifications as Biomarkers for Immunotherapy 221 identify histone PTMs dysregulated in melanomas from immunotherapy nonresponders [37]. As these discovery phase proteomic platforms evolve, there will be a tremendous expansion in the identification of dysregulated histone PTMs that are potential biomarkers for immunotherapy responsiveness. These histone PTMs will help define how cancer patients are treated with current and future immunotherapies. In the following sections, we outline a methodological workflow for using mass spectrometry to identify dysregulated histone PTMs in cancer relevant specimen. 2 Materials 2.1 Acid Extraction 1. Acid extraction reagents: hypotonic lysis buffer (10 mM Tris– HCl pH 8.0, 1 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.4 mM 2 PMSF, Complete Protease Inhibitor (Roche)), sulfuric acid, trichloroacetic acid (TCA), and acetone.
2. Microcentrifuge.
3. Tube rotator (1.5 mL tube adaptor).
4. Vacuum concentrator (Thermo Scientific SpeedVac).
5. Gel electrophoresis: NuPAGE LDS Sample Buffer (4×),
NuPAGE 4–12% Bis Tris Gel, SeeBlue Plus2 Pre-stained Protein Standard, Mini Gel Tank (Invitrogen), power supply, and Coomassie Blue. 2.2 Mass 1. Mass spectrometry reagents: Windex, Ammonium bicarbon- Spectrometric Sample ate, methanol (UHPLC, for mass spectrometry), water Preparation (UHPLC, for mass spectrometry), acetonitrile (ACN; UHPLC, for mass spectrometry), D6-acetic anhydride, sequencing grade modified trypsin, and formic acid.
2. Vortex mixer (1.5 mL tube adaptor).
3. Incubator (37 °C).
3 Methods 3.1 Acid Extraction 1. Resuspend ~5 million cells in hypotonic lysis buffer (10 mM of Histones Tris–HCl pH 8.0, 1 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl, 1 mM DTT, 2 0.4 mM PMSF, Complete Protease Inhibitor) to rupture cell membranes for 20 min, then spin for 10 min at 15,600 × g at 4 °C to pellet cell debris.
2. To extract histones, resuspend the pellet in 200 μL sulfuric
acid (H SO ) and incubate rotating at 4 °C overnight. Next 2 4 day, spin for 10 min at 15,600 × g at 4 °C to pellet cell debris.

222 Erin M. Taylor et al.
3. To precipitate histones, harvest supernatant (~200 μL) to fresh
1.5 mL tube and add 66 μL 100% Trichloroacetic acid (TCA), incubate for 30 min on ice. Spin for 10 min at 15,600 × g at 4 °C to pellet histones and aspirate supernatant.
4. For final resuspension, first wash the pellet with ice-cold acetone
twice and dry the pellet (speed vac or air dry). Then resuspend histones in deionized water (20–50 μL). Resolve 5–10 μg purified histones on SDS-Page gel and stain with Coomassie Blue (see Note 1). Cut histones bands (~15–17 kDa) out of the gel and place in fresh 1.5 mL tube for proteomic preparation. 3.2 Mass 1. To destain gel slices, wash with 1 mL 50% ammonium bicar- Spectrometric Sample bonate/50% methanol for 1 h at 4 °C, repeat three times (see Preparation Note 2). Dehydrate bands using 100 μL ACN. Gels band will turn opaque.
2. To chemically modify nonmethylated and monomethylated
lysine residues, add 20 μL of 30% D6-acetic anhydride in 100 μL of 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate to the dehydrated gel bands and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. Aspirate excess D6-acetic anhydride solution.
3. Wash away D6-acetic anhydride three times with 500 μL of
100 mM ammonium bicarbonate for 5 min (see Note 3). Dehydrated gel pieces with 100 μL ACN until opaque.
4. For trypsin digestion add 125 ng of trypsin in 40 μL of
100 mM ammonium bicarbonate to each band and incubated overnight at 37 °C. Next day, 0.5% formic acid is added to a final concentration of 0.1%. Samples are then ready for submission to a proteomic core facility. 3.3 Mass Mass spectrometric analysis of histone peptides is performed in a Spectrometric Proteomics Core Facility (see Note 4). Each Proteomics Core Analysis Facility has specific workflows and instrumentation. Prior to preparing samples, users should contact their local core for specific guidance to ensure that prepared samples are appropriate for available mass spectrometers. An example of how histone mass spectrometry can be performed and analyzed is below:
1. Tryptic peptides can be separated by reverse phase Jupiter
Proteo resin (Phenomenex) on a 100 × 0.075 mm column using a nanoAcquity UPLC system (Waters). Peptides can be eluted using a 40 min gradient from 97:3 to 35:65 buffer A:B ratio. [Buffer A = 0.1% formic acid, 0.5% acetonitrile; buffer B = 0.1% formic acid, 75% acetonitrile.]
2. Eluted peptides can be ionized by electrospray (1.9 kV) fol-
lowed by MS/MS analysis using collision induced dissociation on an LC-MS/MS on a Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific). MS data can be acquired using the FTMS analyzer

Histone Modifications as Biomarkers for Immunotherapy 223 in profile mode at a resolution of 60,000 over a range of 375 to 1500 m/z. MS/MS data can be acquired for the top 15 peaks from each MS scan using the ion trap analyzer in centroid mode and normal mass range with a normalized collision energy of 35.0.
3. Proteins from human samples can be identified by searching
the UniProtKB database (2015_06 release; restricted to Homo sapiens; 20,207 entries) using an in-house Mascot Sever (v 2.4; Matrix Science). Peak lists can be generated from raw data files by MSFileReader (v2.2; Thermo Scientific) and ExtractMSn (January 2011 release; Thermo Scientific). Mascot search parameters can be as follows: trypsin digestion with up to two missed cleavages; fixed carbamidomethyl modification of cysteine; variable methyl, dimethyl, trimethyl, acetyl, acetyl:2H 3 and methyl+acetyl:2H modification of lysine; variable phos-3 phorylation of serine and threonine; 2.0 ppm precursor ion tolerance; 0.50 Da fragment ion tolerance. Other histone PTMs can be searched as desired. A reverse-sequence decoy search can also be performed. Peptide and protein identifications can be validated using Scaffold (v4.4; Proteome Software). Peptide identifications could be accepted at >50.0% probability as determined by the Scaffold Local FDR algorithm. Protein identifications could be accepted at >95.0% probability and a minimum of two identified peptides. Protein probabilities could be assigned by the Protein Prophet algorithm. Histone H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 peptide precursor intensity values can be manually extracted from the raw files using Qual Browser (Thermo Xcalibur 2.2 SP1.48). The intensity values for all histone peptides can be log normalized, centered based on the 2 median value, scaled based on the standard deviation, and the median of each technical triplicate value used to calculate the Student t-test for the biological replicate samples. 4 Notes
1. All handling of the gel should be done with powder-free gloves
and clean labware. Cleaning items with a commercial glass cleaner such as Windex is good for minimizing keratin contamination, which is the major source of contamination during processing.
2. Care should be taken when aspirating solutions away from gel
pieces. In particular, ACN dehydrated gel pieces stick to gel loading tips during aspiration and can furthermore be easily lost from tubes.
3. It is critical to thoroughly wash the D6-acetic anhydride solu-
tion away following chemical modification of lysine residues.
