# Part IV

Functional Genomic Profiling

## Chapter 11


232 Ena Wang et al. TIL Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes TIS Tumor inflammation signature TME Tumor microenvironment 1 Introduction In the year 2000, we proposed the use of serially obtained minimally invasive tumor biopsies for the study of the biology determining CIR. The foremost goals was to identify predictors (pretreatment samples) of immune responsiveness, document MOAs of therapeutics (on treatment samples), and understand the cause of recurrence and the underlying mechanisms adopted by cancer cells to escape from immune recognition (posttreatment biopsies) [1, 2]. This approach led to several seminal observations [3] including the identification in 2002 [4] of a transcriptional signature predicting responsiveness of melanoma metastases to a melanoma differentiation antigen-based vaccine administered in combination with human recombinant interleukin-2. Ranking of gene expression data from pretreatment samples identified approximately 30 genes predictive of clinical response (P < 0.001). “Analysis of their annotations denoted that approximately half of them were related to T-cell regulation, suggesting that immune responsiveness might be predetermined by a tumor microenvironment conducive to immune recognition,” a conclusion that has been corroborated by several subsequent studies [5, 6]. Classifications range from a measure of cytolytic activity by mean expression of GZMA and PRF1 genes (Rooney et al. [79]), to reflections of immune cell infiltration by distinctive transcriptional profiles [7, 8], or gene signatures reflecting multiple components of an antitumor immune response, including Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC), costimulatory or immunomodulatory molecules [6, 9]. This strategy also allowed us to define the mechanisms of cancer immune rejection [10], demonstrating that the mechanism responsible for the clearance of neoplastic tissue is merely a facet of the broader phenomenon of immune-mediated tissue-specific destruction: a conserved mechanism that we termed the immunologic constant of rejection (ICR) [11]. Indeed, the ICR biology pertains also to flares of destructive autoimmunity, clearance of pathogen-infected cells during acute infections, graft-versus-host disease and rejection of transplanted organs [12]. More recently, this strategy has been extended to the use of serial biopsies for protein profiling of remainders of fine needle aspirate material for the classification of cancer subtypes [13]. Transcriptional profiling of serial tumor biopsies lead also to the observation that lack of response to immune therapy is most often associated with peripheral ignorance and/or to lack of persistence of the anticipated MOA of a given immune therapeutic modality [4]

Functional Genome Profiling to Understand Cancer Immune Responsiveness 233 rather than with the escape of tumor cells from cognate recognition by an immunologically active immune effector process. Immune escape phenotypes, on the other hand, result most often from the immune pressure exercised on cancer cells during successful treatment and are, therefore, observed most frequently in recurring lesions after an initial response [14]. Thus, immune editing depends on a fine balance between the strength of the immune pressure exercised by the host in response to immunogenic stimuli and the cancer cell need to adapt to it for survival [15]. Several studies followed these original observations demonstrating that the ICR accuracy of prediction is independent of model system tested [16, 17], treatment applied and type of cancer targeted. Even though it is well accepted that cancer is an eclectic entity endowed with magnificent creativity, its growth is evolutionarily challenged by a highly conserved ancestral bottleneck orchestrated by innate and adaptive immune surveillance processes [18]. Thus, as for several phenomena in nature, although potential permutations are countless, the observable reality responsible for CIR demonstrates a relatively limited range of possibilities: a concept recently summarized as “the theory of everything” [18]. Extensive analysis of transcriptional patterns deposited in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), demonstrated that cancer immune phenotypes are conserved among distinct etiologies and are shaped according to a two option evolutionary choice: either they are genetically unstable, endowed with a high mutational burden that leads to immunogenicity through the processing and presentation of neoantigens, or they are silent and are less likely to be subjected to immune surveillance [19]. In the former case, cancer can survive only in the presence of complex compensatory mechanisms of immune regulation against the immune effector forces fighting against its growth while in the latter very little or no immune recognition is observed and, consequently, no immune suppression is necessary. In addition, it has become evident that the ICR model applies to a continuum of immune surveillance with prognostic [20–23], predictive [24], and mechanistic [25] implications several of which are discussed in this and other chapters of this book. 2 Understanding CIR in the Clinical Settings To better address CIR, it is important to frame the semantics of a multifaceted biology determined by interrelated but distinct factors. Broadly, CIR depends upon the genetic background of the host, the somatic evolution of the cancer genome and epigenome and other circumstantial environmental and behavioral d eterminants [26] such as dietary habits [27] that may influence the immune status of the host and its microbiome [28].

234 Ena Wang et al. Improvements in the clinical effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy, has facilitated the study of CIR in humans for various reasons. The increasing number of patients studied, the consistency and rigor of later phase clinical trials and the enhanced frequency of observable clinical responses enhanced the power of investigations looking for associations and potential determinants of CIR [29]. For instance, immune-checkpoint inhibitor therapy (ICT) has received considerable attention in the last decade since it improves overall survival and it is effective in a wide range of tumor types resulting in the development of several experimental or standard of therapy clinical trials addressing this approach as monotherapy or in combination [29, 30]. However, responsiveness is limited to a few indications and within each indication to a limited fraction of patients. The reasons for this heterogeneous responsiveness are still poorly understood. It is becoming increasingly apparent that the immune landscape of individual cancers is roughly linked to CIR [6, 18]. Yet cancer patients often do not benefit from ICT even when their tumors display favorable immune characteristics [6]. These discrepancies cannot be directly dissected using experimental animal models because the latter follow an evolutionary selection quite different form the one shaping the growth of human cancers in the immune competent host; the former are primarily selected by “human selection” according to experimental requirements rather than carefully valued according to their biological relevance to a specific clinical context [18]. This statement is not meant to detract from the fundamental value of experimental animal models to study mechanistically hypotheses derived from human observation. It is meant to emphasize the need to frame animal experimentation within the context of the heterogeneous reality of human disease that can be addressed only by correlative studies matching clinical outcome with human biology. Clinical observation in patients undergoing ICT have generated multiple and often contrasting explanation for CIR [18, 19]. However, some conserved patterns can be observed across cancers of different histology. It is evident that cancers can be roughly separated into two opposite immune categories according to their transcriptional profile: immune “active” and immune “silent.” This separation is discernible by using as guide the expression of genes included in the ICR signature [11, 20] determining the continuum of cancer immune surveillance within their tumor microenvironment (TME) [25]. The ICR signature comprises the coordinate expression of approximately 500 genes related primarily to interferon (IFN)-γ signaling. In several studies, we applied a limited set of 20 representative ICR genes to demarcate cancer immune phenotypes [18–20, 24, 31]. Similarly, Ayers et al. [6] segregated tumor types according to an IFN-γ-related gene signature termed the tumor inflammation signature (TIS) that largely

Functional Genome Profiling to Understand Cancer Immune Responsiveness 235 overlaps with the ICR [18] and observed that TIS was predictive of response to ICT. The ICR was also applied to categorize one thousand breast cancers from TCGA: samples were subdivided into separate immune phenotypes called ICR-1 to ICR-4 according to the incremental level of expression of ICR genes. This segregation proved to be predictive of overall survival that was significantly longer in patients bearing cancers with the ICR-4 phenotype. The prognostic and predictive role of ICR in breast cancer was validated in a meta-analysis including almost 9000 breast cancer transcriptomes [24]. Importantly, the ICR classification was able to refine the prognostic value provided by clinical-grade molecular classifiers such as the ones implemented by MammaPrint®, Oncotype DX®, and Prosigna® assays. The expression of transcriptional signatures that have been associated in various studies with immune regulatory properties supposed to dampen CIR was then matched to the immune phenotypes [18]. These phenotypes were selected from published data sets and were representative of distinct immune regulatory mechanisms. These included the immune-checkpoint cluster [32], regulatory T cells [33], IL-23/IL-17 axis [34], myeloid suppressor cells [35], IDO [36], immunogenic cell death (ICD) [37], TAM tyrosine kinase receptors [38], hypoxia [39], cancer-associated fibroblasts [40], and barrier molecules [41]. Selforganizing clustering distributed according to the ICR-1 to ICR-4 classes of immune landscapes demonstrated that immune regulatory functions pertained almost exclusively to immune active cancers (ICR-4 ) and to a lower extent to the functionally adjacent ICR-3 immune landscape [18]. This observation suggests that resistance to ICT therapy may be determined by different biological phenomena. In the context of immunogenic ICR-3 and ICR-4 tumors, resistance to ICT is probably due to the coexistence of alternate regulatory mechanisms that overrule a single blockade in the context of CIT. This distinct biology that could be termed compensatory immune resistance should be distinguished from that of tumors in the ICR-1 and ICR-2 categories that are not inflamed, not immunogenic and that are not affected by immune regulatory mechanisms including the checkpoint cluster. While the biology of the “cancer immunity cycle” described by Chen and Mellman [42] may pertain particularly, and perhaps exclusively, to the immunogenic tumors, it is likely that there is no such cycle in silent tumors and their resistance to ICT could be referred to as primary immune resistance or primary immune ignorance. In addition, immune responsive tumors may become resistant under the selective pressure induced by therapy that molds escape mechanisms. This biology could be, therefore, defined as acquired immune resistance.

236 Ena Wang et al. Finally, a type of resistance to therapy that is not directly related to the cancer or the host’s genetics and somatic adaptations may modify immune responsiveness according circumstances dictated by the environment, individual patients’ habits and comorbidities that may alter the immune status including nutritional patterns that may modify the microbiome [27]. This can be referred to it as circumstantial immune resistance. Similarly, other factors may modulate CIR that are extrinsic to the biology of individual tumors such as variations in quality of products delivered during ACT [43]. Moreover, immunodeficiency deficiencies limiting the ability to mount an effective immune response may affect CIR independent of favorable predictors at the tumor side [44]. In summary, it is important to segregate distinct biological phenomena before deepening the efforts to understand CIR to improve the strategies for sample collection and facilitate the interpretation of the generated corresponding data sets. 3 Genetics Determining Cancer Immune Landscapes The segregation of tumors according to immune phenotypes frames the context in which cancer genetics should be queried to understand CIR. It has been observed for instance that cancer characterized by high mutational burden display an immune active phenotype [20, 45]. This association is commonly attributed to a stochastic propensity of these tumors to express mutated protein domains that can originate adaptive nonself-recognition frequently referred to as development of immunity against neoantigens or neoepitopes [46, 47]. However, several mutations disrupt the function of cancer driver genes [48] creating a “messier” cancer cell biology quite different by a more orderly process displayed by the nonimmunogenic cancers [18, 19]. It is conceivable that the evolutionary process molding cancer adaptation in the immune competent host presents cancer cells with a binary choice: the first is to follow an orderly succession of genetic alterations that engender essential growth advantages following a developmental path reminiscent of that followed by stem cells during the formation of normal tissues [49]. As soon as deviations occur from this orderly process the second path for the successful growth of cancer is triggered. As cancer growth becomes dependent predominantly on genetic instability, a “trial-and-error” reshuffling of genetic traits selects for a proliferative advantage over normal cell growth. At this point, the intrinsic biology of the cancer cell orchestrates its surroundings [50] by releasing factors that stimulate stromal and vascular architecture in the developing new tissue as per Virchow’s “healing wound” model [11, 51]. The cross talk with host cells may result in chemoattraction of innate and adaptive immune cells turning cancer into a chronically inflamed tissue [51]. In addition,

Functional Genome Profiling to Understand Cancer Immune Responsiveness 237 it is possible that genetic instability may result in a disorderly cell cycle prone to ICD [52]. Indeed, the expression of the ICD signature is tightly associated with the immune active landscape [18, 53] characterized in turn by genetic instability [54]. Thus, the destabilization of the cellular life cycle resulting in ICD may represent the primary trigger of immunogenic reactions in line with Polly Matzinger’s danger model [55]. 4 Current Understanding of the Transcriptional Footprints of Cancer Determining CIR CIR is determined by the summative effects of the genetic background of the host, somatic alterations related to the oncogenic process, and environmental modifiers [56]. Several of them are discussed in other chapters of this book, while here we summarize the role that transcriptional changes play in determining CIR. CIR can be determined by transcriptional alterations within the TME, and transcriptional patterns can therefore be used to categorize it. There is a general association between the presence of activated, tumor-specific CD8+ T cells and sensitivity toward immunotherapy [4–6, 57, 58]. Indeed, most of the characterization of cancer has focused on transcriptional patters associated with cytotoxic CD8+ T cell function [6, 56, 57, 59–61]. Single-cell sequencing might increase the granularity of these observations. For instance, a recent study in melanoma patients treated with checkpoint blockade showed that CD8 T cells in responding lesions express genes linked to memory, activation and cell survival, while the ones in progressing lesions display a functional orientation consistent with T-cell exhaustion [59]. Moreover, tissue-resident memory signatures developed from single-cell sequencing analysis have been associated with increased overall survival in triple-negative breast cancer [60]. Yet, the factor that determines the accumulation of effector/memory cells must be dissected within the context of the complexity of the TME [7, 61]. Transcriptional analysis of bulk tumor tissue to include also transcriptional changes related to cancer or stroma cells and a better segregation of individual contributions will be important in future studies. This could be partly obtained by antibody-guided single cell sequencing. The antibodies bind to the cell surface marker and introduce a unique molecular barcode into the cell that will then be marked by single cell transcriptional analysis allowing paired analysis of TCR repertoire and transcriptional profiles associated with specific TCR clones. Identification of TCR-α and TCR-β chain pairs in concert with elucidation of neoantigens or tumor-a ssociated antigens might allow us to decipher the i mmune- dominant T cell responses across multiple patients [62], which in turn may inform about clonal expansion requirements and CIR [59, 60].

238 Ena Wang et al. However, single cell analyses depend on tissue disassociation to separate individual cells disrupting the critical information about spatial relationship among different cell types in distinct locations. Novel approaches such as digital spatial profiling [63] may obviate this problem. The integrated analysis of digital spatial profiling which characterize cellular phenotype and their neighboring structure with single cell sequencing analysis may overcome the aforementioned hurdle and provide 3D insight of molecular and cellular compartments and their relationship to CIR. 5 Intrinsic Cancer Cell Biology and Stromal Contributions to CIR Intrinsic cancer cell biology can directly orchestrate the immune environment of tumors [50, 64, 65]. Beta-catenin, epidermal growth factor receptor, anaplastic lymphoma kinase, RAS/RAF/ MEK, PTEN/PI3K [66], and pathways associated with epithelial to mesenchymal transition have been implicated in determining immune landscapes and consequently CIR [18, 19, 48, 64, 65, 67–71]. This in turn can be related to distinct mutational or epigenetic patterns responsible for the disruption of these pathways creating an integrated model to explain CIR from the genetic code all the way to transcriptional and translational and posttranslational behaviors [72–74]. Aside from the disruption of intrinsic cancer cell biology, other deficiencies affecting for instance the antigen-processing and presentation machinery or the IFN-γ response pathway can disrupt several aspects of innate and adaptive immune cross talk [75–80] and associate with resistance to CIT [75, 76, 81]. Among nonneoplastic contributors to the immune landscapes of tumors, cancer-associated fibroblasts and other by-stander cells have been shown to play several immune regulatory roles more or less linked to the primary role played by cancer cells in orchestrating their behavior [40, 82]. These contributions are discussed in detail in the respective chapters of this book. 6 Immunogenic Cell Death (ICD) and CIR ICD is a type of cell death accompanied by the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that enhance the immunogenic potential of dying cells [37, 83] and it is, consequently, defined by its functional consequence—the generation of antigen-specific protective immunity. ICD consists of two main components: (1) tumor cells that die in a way that promotes immunity, and (2) immune cells recruited to the TME that respond and generate protective immunologic memory. A broad range of biological phenomena related to cancer cell death including even

Functional Genome Profiling to Understand Cancer Immune Responsiveness 239 some types of apoptosis can induce ICD according to a specific spatiotemporal sequences of DAMP and tumor-associated antigen release [37, 84–86]. The mechanism of cell death is shaped by factors intrinsic to the cancer cells, the TME, and infiltrating immune cells. Chemotherapy and targeted therapy may induce variable quality and quantity of ICD depending upon the underlying mechanism of cytotoxicity, dose of the agent used and sensitivity of the host’s immune status. Often and especially mild chemotherapy or low dose, fractionated radiation induce more potent immune responses than higher doses, with the added benefit of fewer side effects [87–90]. Oncolytic viruses selectively kill cancer cells and induce high rates of antigen and DAMP release while simultaneously triggering type 1 IFN production [91]. Autophagy, a cellular response to stress that causes recycling of internal organelles for energy, may alter release of DAMPs or other immune stimulatory molecules and impact the efficacy of ICD-inducing treatments inducing resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy [92]. Consequently, therapeutics modulating autophagy pathways combined with CIT may increase its effectiveness [93]. ICD can be monitored in experimental settings in vivo [94] by a the vaccination model in which a given cancer cell line is treated in vitro with an ICD-inducing agent and inoculated into immunocompetent hosts, followed by a challenge with viable tumor cells. In addition, the occurrence of ICD can be proven by an abscopal model where tumors are implanted in vivo into bilateral flanks, and a potentially ICD-inducing therapy is delivered to one of the tumors. Elimination of the untreated tumor is evidence for the generation of systemic productive immunity. A significant challenge in the monitoring of ICD in vivo is the occurrence of efferocytosis, the process whereby phagocytes quickly remove dead cells and promote immunosuppression, which makes cell death difficult to confirm directly [89]. Thus, for clinical purposes other biomarkers need to be considered. These biomarkers should measure the type of cell death, the release of DAMPs, and the abundance, identity, and location of immune cells that contribute to a functional adaptive immune response. Specifically, biomarkers should distinguish between bona fide ICD and direct immune modulatory effects of the therapeutic drugs by focusing on cell types that are immediate sensors of DAMPs. As the end stage of ICD is a protective T cell response, T cell populations also should be measured to assess success of these strategies. Proposed clinical biomarkers of ICD include direct measurements of DAMPs such as HMGB1, ATP, calreticulin, type I IFNs, histones, heat shock proteins, markers of immunological fitness (LDH release, soluble serum markers), and specific immune cell populations (T cell repertoire and phenotype) and their cell surface markers. One promising biomarker strategy is the systemic immune inflammation index,

240 Ena Wang et al. which measures ratios of specific immune cell types to monitor shifts in the balance of immune populations accumulating within the TME and peripheral circulation [95, 96]. 7 Conclusions In summary, big progress has been made in the last two decades in the understanding of the biology of CIR for several reasons that revolve predominantly around to preeminent factors: improved technologies and higher response rate to immunotherapy agents, particularly those used for CIT, that balance the number of responder vs. nonresponder cases historically heavily skewed toward the latter category. These achievements have pointed with increasing accuracy to predictors of immune responsiveness and mechanisms of response and escape. Most importantly, the definition of ICD and a key component of the initiation of CIR that combines innate to adaptive immune activation is a major step in providing a goal for future therapeutics particularly in the context of true primary/genuine immune resistance. This chapter addresses more specifically some aspects of functional profiling that illustrate forward looking strategies for a evermore refined understanding of CIR and the respective identification of useful biomarkers to select and stratify patients and monitor their immunotherapies. 246 C. C. Smith et al. sequencing datasets such as those of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). Immunogenomics is largely focused on the immune response in the context of malignancy, within which the complex tumor-immune microenvironment can be dissected with the use of transcriptomic analysis of tumor and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. The initial evaluation of the tumor microenvironment was performed using cDNA microarray technology. However, microarray technology is limited by (1) transcript-specific probes that do not allow novel transcripts to be queried, (2) limited range for the detection of low abundant transcripts, and (3) inability to alter the process to improve this detection. The use of microarray technologies has largely been replaced by whole transcriptome RNA-seq methods, which circumvent many of the issues associated with microarray analysis. Using RNA-seq, investigators are able to identify tens of thousands of genes within a single tumor-derived sample. The use of RNA-seq to characterize tumors has allowed investigators to reconstruct the cellular heterogeneity of the tumor microenvironment from archival tissues [1, 2]. Additionally, RNAseq can be used in combination with or lieu of pathological approaches to subtype cancers [3]. Among immunogenomic advancements aided through the use of RNA-seq include correlative analyses of responders versus nonresponders to immunotherapy [4], design of biomarkers for predicting patient prognosis and response to therapies [5, 6], and characterization of the antigen spectrum of a tumor and subsequent targeting of these antigens (neoantigens [7, 8], cancer testes antigens [9], tumor associated antigens [10], etc.). These analyses have allowed for a greater understanding of the tumor-immune microenvironment, with recent advancement in single-cell sequencing technologies providing even further granularity in deconstructing the complicated cellular immune microenvironment. Evaluation of the tumor-immune microenvironment with RNA-seq can frequently provide data orders of magnitude larger than conventional immunological techniques such as flow cytometry (which require fresh sample processing) or other assays that are not accessible from FFPE material. As a result, consistency and automation of the RNA-seq workflow is necessary. In this chapter, we will provide a summary of our RNA-seq workflow, which is broken down into the following steps: (1) tissue collection and isolation of RNA, (2) library preparation and sequencing, (3) data processing and quality control, (4) alignment and quantitation, and (5) analysis of data. Lastly, it should be noted that the field of RNA-seq analysis is rapidly progressing, with more accurate methods constantly in development. While we have provided examples and recommendations for analysis software in the chapter, the fluid nature of this field may mean that some of these methods may be

Using RNA Sequencing to Characterize the Tumor Microenvironment 247 replaced in the near future by newer technologies. As such, the reader should examine recent developments in the field and make adaptations as these newer technologies are made available. 2 Materials 2.1 Tissue 1. However, if greater computational power is required and a com-2.3.1 Computer puting cluster is not available, we recommend the use of Google Compute Engine, which we have historically used for certain highrequirement jobs. 2.3.2 Workspace If running analyses on multiple computing clusters or outside computing engines, we recommend consultation with a data scientist and use of a containerization method such as Docker (https:// www.docker.com) for convenience and stability. 3 Methods 3.1 Isolation of Total RNA isolation is critical to the success of RNA sequencing and as RNA and QC a result maximizing yield and purity of RNA is crucial. The time needed for tissue collection needs to be minimized to prevent 3.1.1 General RNA degradation. The collection of tissue in this protocol is opti- Considerations mized for a specific amount of RNA; the addition of a greater amount of tissue may paradoxically reduce the yield of RNA. Please remember to perform all isolations with an extraction agent in a fume hood with gloves and eye protection. RNA may be extracted from fresh or flash frozen samples or FFPE material. A number of extraction methods exist and an isolation strategy should be chosen based on the starting material and RNA subpopulation of choice [43, 44]. Beta-mercaptoethanol (2-ME) is commonly added to guanidium-based lysis buffers to improve RNA isolation from whole tissues samples abundant in RNases [45], and should be added in the manufacturer’s recommended amount when using commercially available kits. When freezing RNA or material for subsequent RNA extraction, nuclease free, tight-closure tubes such as Eppendorf DNA LoBind tubes are recommended to prevent contamination from RNases. The volume of lysis buffer needed per sample should be determined empirically based on cell type and number or tissue type and mass, using the manufacturer’s recommendations as a general guideline. For total RNA isolation, we routinely use the Qiagen RNeasy Mini kit when processing tissue or when starting with larger cell numbers and the RNeasy Micro Kit when starting with fewer than 500,000 cells. Given that RNA is easily degradable and potentially prone to contamination, certain workspace precautions should be taken [46]:
1. Optimally, an RNA-only workspace with a molecular biology
hood to prevent contamination from debris in the air should be used during extraction and reverse transcription, with a separate workspace for DNA-related molecular biology. Additionally, having a separate space for different species may prevent cross- contamination between different experiments.
2. To further prevent cross-contamination, reagents used for
handling RNA should remain in the RNA-only workspace and

252 C. C. Smith et al. used exclusively for handling RNA. Ensure all reagents are RNase free and/or molecular biology grade.
3. Use disposable, sterile RNase-free plasticware that does not
require pretreatment and barrier pipette tips.
4. The workspace should be cleaned with an RNAse removing
material, such as Sigma RNaseZap RNase decontamination solution.
5. RNase-free gloves and gowns should be work to prevent con-
tamination from skin cells during handling of RNA.
6. As a general rule, RNA and DNA should be kept on ice while
handling (unless otherwise stated by a protocol), working as quickly as possible. Keep UV-light sources away from nucleic acids to prevent degradation. For FFPE slides, it is recommended to have a pathologist score the slides to ensure the material taken for RNA extraction is the tissue of choice (ex. tumor), and to control for estimated cellular heterogeneity when comparing experimental groups [47]. Numerous commercially available FFPE extraction kits have been compared [48–50] or modified [51] and should be chosen based on down-stream applications. We routinely use the Roche High Pure RNA Paraffin Kit for manual RNA extraction or the Maxwell 16 LEV RNA FFPE Purification Kit for automated extraction (see Note 1). 3.1.2 Collection/ 1. When starting with fresh tissue, the material should be sec- Suspension/Lysis Using tioned into small pieces (<20 mg). If starting with a single cell Qiagen Reagents suspension, the cells should first be washed in PBS, pelleted, and the supernatant removed.
2. RLT lysis buffer supplemented with 1% (v/v) beta-
mercaptoethanol is then added to each cell pellet or 20 mg piece of tissue and vortexed. The sample resuspended in RLT can then be flash frozen with either liquid nitrogen or an ice bath using dry ice and 70–100% ethanol. If no lysis buffer is available, the tissue or cell pellet can be frozen dry and lysis buffer added upon thawing.
3. Fresh tissue in RLT or thawed tissue in RLT can be homoge-
nized with a tissue disrupter according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We typically homogenize tissue in a nuclease free 50 mL conical using the Qiagen TissueRuptor II at full speed for 30 s.
4. Homogenized tissue should then be transferred to a
QIAshredder before proceeding to the RNeasy Mini Kit. If the starting material is a single cell suspension, the cells in RLT can be transferred directly to a QIAshredder for homogenization prior to using the RNeasy Mini Kit for large cell numbers or RNeasy Micro Kit for smaller cell numbers. When starting with

Using RNA Sequencing to Characterize the Tumor Microenvironment 253 fewer than 100,000 cells, we vortex the cells in lysis buffer at full speed for 1 min to homogenize in place of using a QIAshredder in order to minimize nucleic acid loss.
5. The Qiagen RNeasy kits can be used as directed, and variations
are available that include an extra step utilizing a genomic DNA eliminator column (RNeasy Plus kits) or on-column DNA digestion with DNase (Qiagen RNase-Free DNase Set).
6. Molecular biology grade water should be used for eluting RNA
and should be pipetted directly onto the column filter. During this step, care should be taken not to touch the filter or the sides of the column with the pipette tip. The elution volume should be chosen carefully based on the amount of input material. If the eluent is too dilute, the RNA may need to be concentrated in order to perform QC.
7. RNA should be stored at −80 ° C and should always be ali-
quoted to avoid unnecessary freeze-thaw cycles. 3.1.3 QC Three methods of quality control should be used for the most comprehensive measure of RNA quality:
1. Qubit or similar method for high sensitivity fluorometric
quantification.
2. Spectrophotometer (NanoDrop or similar) for purity
assessment.
3. Fragment analyzer (TapeStation, LapChip, etc.) measuring
electrophoretic mobility to determine RNA integrity. Ideally, 2 μL of sample should each be used for Qubit quantification and NanoDrop to improve accuracy of the readings. Also ensure the sample concentration is within the working range of the instrument since many of the corresponding instrument kits have minimum and maximum cutoffs beyond which the reading is unreliable. Follow the temperature requirements of the reagents required to operate the QC instruments, as the readings are often temperature sensitive. Some RNAseq library preparation methods will be more sensitive to contamination than others. NanoDrop measures contaminants and reports the ratio of absorbance of a sample at 260 and 280 nm and the ratio at 260 and 230 nm. A 260/280 ratio of 2.0 ± 0.02 is generally accepted as pure RNA while expected 260/230 values are typically in the range of 2.0–2.2 [46, 52]. Many library prep methods recommend a 260/280 and 260/230 ratio of at least 1.7. A low 260/280 ratio indicates contamination, often with protein or extraction solutions such as phenol, while low 260/230 rations indicate presence of compounds that absorb light at 230 nM such as EDTA, carbohydrates, and/or phenol. RNA integrity number (RIN; electropherogram-based quality

254 C. C. Smith et al.

metric), devised by Agilent [53, 54], and the DV200 metric (the number of nucleic acid fragments greater than 200 nucleotides long), developed and recommended by Illumina [55], are two measures commonly reported by fragment analyzers to assess RNA degradation. Fully intact RNA has a RIN score of 10, while partially degraded RNA and strongly degraded RNA will have a RIN of 5 and 3, respectively. 3.2 Library Two factors largely determine which RNA-seq library preparation Preparation kit one should use: quality and quantity of the starting material. Some recommendations for kits can be seen below in Fig. 1. Though there are many more library preparation kits than those listed below, these are recommendations based on standard operating procedure at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill’s High Throughput Sequencing Facility (see Notes 2–6). 3.3 Sequencing We use an Illumina sequencing platform for the vast majority of our RNA-seq analyses, given the exceptional amount and quality of data provided. Below is a summary of current Illumina platforms (also refer to Table 2) and when we would select each for sequencing.
1. HiSeq 4000: Used for the majority of our whole transcriptome
RNA-seq runs. Good cost/performance ratio, but relatively slow run-times compared to NextSeq and NovaSeq 6000 instruments. However, is known to have an increase in duplicates compared to the earlier HiSeq2500 due to the patterned flow cell.
2. HiSeq 2500: A less optimal option, as it provides fewer reads
without considerable decreases in cost. Typically, the HiSeq 4000 is favored in place of the HiSeq 2500, unless library preparation methods are only compatible with the HiSeq 2500.
3. Nextseq: Occasionally used when sequencing a small sample set
(<8 samples per run). Fast run-times and low instrument costs make this an ideal option for groups with relatively lower throughput sequencing experiments.
4. MiSeq: Not used for whole transcriptome RNA-seq due to lim-
ited sequencing depth but can be used for TCR/BCR amplicon studies.
5. Novaseq 6000: Likely to replace the HiSeq 4000 as our primary
whole transcriptome platform within the coming years. Relatively higher instrument costs but substantially higher reads per run makes this an ideal option for groups with very high run throughputs. For the majority of human and murine RNA-seq analyses, paired-end 2 × 50 bp sequencing chemistry will provide adequate

The exceptions to this are (1) if the focus of one’s sequencing run is to identify novel splice variants or resolve genomic regions with many long repeated elements, or (2) the reference genome/transcriptome for the derivative organism is not well characterized, for which longer reads may be optimal. The length of sequencing can also be influenced by the type of RNA. It is easier to have longer reads on higher quality fresh frozen samples than from FFPE samples which are inherently fragmented to sizes around 130–150 bp. 3.4 Data Processing Before raw sequencing data is converted to downstream formats, and Quality Control several sequencing metrics should be considered. 3.4.1 Read Quality 1. Cluster density: Metric for DNA density on sequencing flow Metrics cell. Lower cluster density maintains quality but sacrifices data output, while overloading can result in poor image resolution and base quality. Recommended cluster densities vary for each Illumina machine and optimal loading concentrations should be consulted prior to sequencing. Improper library quantification can result in inaccurate loading concentrations—we typically rely on NanoDrop and fragment analyzers to determine library quality but Qubit for concentration calculations. We additionally use the KAPA library quantification kit (KK4824) to quantify libraries with suspected low qualities or contaminations, as it can accurately quantify the concentration of libraries specifically, without quantification of non-library DNA content.
2. Quality score: The quality score per sequencing cycle as well as
a histogram of quality distribution are provided for each run. This Q30 (Phred) quality score represents the likelihood of

Using RNA Sequencing to Characterize the Tumor Microenvironment 257 error for each particular base call. Optimally, scores should reach 30 (99.9% accuracy) or greater across all cycles and base pair positions. 3.4.2 BCL to FASTQ Conversion from Illumina sequencing instrument generated base- Conversion, Demultiplexing call files (BCL) to downstream FASTQ format is performed using the bcl2tofastq software, which simultaneously demultiplexes samples based upon sequence index. To properly demulitplex samples, a sample sheet must be provided to the software, containing a row for each sample included within the run and the following columns (description given after colon).
1. FCID: Flow cell ID.
2. Lane: Lane number as an integer 1–8.
3. SampleID: ID of the sample.
4. SampleRef: Reference used for alignment of the sample.
5. Index: Index used for generation of a particular library. If two
indices were used, they should be separated by a hyphen (e.g., ACCAGTAA-GGACATGA) (see Note 7).
6. Description: Description of the sample.
7. Control: “Y” indicates sample is a control; “N” indicates
sample is not a control.
8. Recipe: What library preparation method was used for this
sample.
9. Operator: Name/ID of the operator of this sample.
10. SampleProject: Name of project under which this sample
belongs. For details of how to install and run bcl2fastq, please refer to the Illumina bcl2fastq conversion software support page (https:// support.illumina.com/sequencing/sequencing_software/bcl-2fastq-conversion-software.html) (see Note 8). 3.5 Prealignment QC After conversion into FASTQ format, quality control is performed to identify potential issues arising from the sample preparation and sequencing process. Typically, we perform this using the FastQC software, which provides a simple and fast method to identify per base sequence quality, GC content, per base N content, sequence length distribution, sequence duplication levels, overrepresented sequences, and adapter content. Commonly used filters for excluding samples from downstream analysis in transcriptome profiling experiments include: (1) less than 30 million mapped reads in the sample, and (2) mean PHRED base quality ≤35. Other filters are additionally applied after sample alignment, as described below (see Note 9).

258 C. C. Smith et al. 3.6 Alignment Many computational methods exist to map RNA-seq data to the and Quantification reference genome, allowing for splice aware alignment of both mRNA and other RNA types (rRNA, intronic and intergenic 3.6.1 Alignment Methods RNAs) [56]. In recent years, our group has transitioned from exclusively using Mapsplice to STAR for RNA-seq alignment, which is primarily rooted in their equivalent ability to accurately align reads while dramatically improving alignment times [14, 57, 58]. Apart from STAR, many other aligners have been compared in terms of speed and performance [56], demonstrating that the most reliable general-purpose aligners include STAR, CLC, Novoalign, and GSNAP. While accuracy of these other popular aligners are similar to STAR, runtimes for human-derived data are significantly faster by STAR than the other three aligners. More recently, tools such as Sailfish, Salmon, and Kallisto allow for extremely fast but approximate quantification of genes directly from the FASTQ file, without alignment to a reference genome [18–20]. Sailfish and Salmon make use of a quasi-mapping approach while Kallisto uses pseudo alignment for estimated quantification of genes. Both of these methods use mathematically similar, k-mer based algorithms, with the key difference that quasi-mapping uses suffix arrays while pseudo alignment implements de Bruijn graphs. While these methods can provide very fast and fairly accurate estimates of gene expression, they do not perform as well from FFPE derived data, do not have the accuracy of genome aligners, and do not generate read-level data (BAM/SAM file). As such, we typically still rely on STAR for alignment of FASTQ files. STAR requires a single-ended or pair-end FASTQ file(s) for alignment to the reference genome. Additionally, a reference genome must be supplied and further “built” by STAR for alignment, currently mm10 for murine and hg38 for human data. If a STAR generated genome has not been previously built, reference genome sequences (in the form of FASTA files) and optionally an annotation file (in the form of a GTF file) need to be input into STAR for generating genome indexes. While the annotation file is not necessary to build the reference genome, it should be included to improve mapping accuracy. Limited STAR genomes are available from the creators of STAR (http://labshare.cshl.edu/shares/ gingeraslab/www-data/dobin/STAR/STARgenomes/), but users are encouraged to generate their own genome indexes using the most up to date assemblies and annotations. The NCI’s Genome Data Commons (GDC) also provides references genomes that they use for their harmonization pipelines (https://gdc.cancer.gov/about-data/data-harmonization-and-generation/ gdc-reference-files).

Using RNA Sequencing to Characterize the Tumor Microenvironment 259 3.6.2 Post-Alignment QC After alignment, several quality control metrics are collected to ensure results can be interpreted without significant bias from technical outliers. Given that each sample set can vary dramatically, there are no strict cutoffs for any of these metrics. We try to determine the presence of technical outliers within the set and remove samples or are just aware of the sample quality when interpreting downstream analyses. The following metrics are commonly analyzed.
1. Proportion aligned vs. unaligned: Performed to ensure there
are not an over-abundance of unaligned reads among all data.
2. Percent of alignment by region: Comparison of percentage of
total bases aligned to mRNA versus intergenic, intronic, or ribosomal RNA to ensure the transcriptome coverage is conserved between samples. These metrics are measured using output from Picard Tools [22]. Typically, we want at least 10% of reads to map to mRNA, but the other metrics will vary by library and RNA type (see Note 10).
3. Number of non-zero genes: Performed to determine coverage
among all genes and identify low diversity samples.
4. Relative log expression: Analysis of total aligned reads per sam-
ple to ensure read distributions are similar across samples. This gives an intuitive view of the global variation in relative expression [59].
5. Upper quartile comparison: Calculated as
Median(allUQvaluesacrosscohort), where UQ denotes the UQforagivensample upper quartile (75th percentile) value among all read counts per sample. This metric provides a scaling factor for each sample representing the relative multiplier necessary for UQ readnormalization of that sample relative to all other samples in the set. Alternatively to the above method, DESeq2’s sizeFactor function can also be utilized to calculate a scaling factor. Samples with particularly high scaling values generally have lower mRNA mapping and normalization of these samples will result in amplification of noise.
6. Principle component analysis: Performed to identify potential
technical outliers. 3.6.3 Quantification Gene expression profiling experiments require generation of quan- Methods tified gene expression values for all genes represented in the sequencing data. In recent years, the use of RSEM and Cufflinks as quantifiers has widely been replaced by newer, faster quantifiers such as Sailfish and Salmon [18, 19, 60, 61]. All of these tools are

260 C. C. Smith et al. orders of magnitude faster in run time compared to older quantifiers while maintaining similar or better accuracies [62]. As mentioned earlier, Sailfish and Salmon can directly quantify FASTQ files without genome alignment; however, they can additionally be used downstream of an aligner strictly as a transcript quantifier. We typically pair Salmon quantifier (quant mode) downstream of STAR alignment. Salmon requires an unsorted BAM file as input, and we use the transcriptome-space BAM file as input, with an hg38 or mm10 reference transcriptome FASTA file as reference. 3.7 Select Methods 1. Prior to analysis, gene expression matrices are derived through of Analysis combining the raw count data for each sample into a matrix.
2. From this raw matrix, some threshold can be applied to drop
lowly expressed genes, such as filtering by a minimum read count threshold or dropping all genes with zero expression for all samples (i.e., tissue specific genes). For tumor experiments, we typically have relied on dropping all genes which are not expressed in >70% of all samples, which provides a conservative cutoff to filter out lowly expressed genes but may in some instances introduce bias away from these rare genes.
3. Next, this raw, filtered expression matrix is normalized.
Common methods include upper quartile normalization (UQN), median normalization, normalizing RPKM (reads per kilobase million), FPKM (fragments per kilobase million), TPM (transcripts per kilobase million), or relying on a software package such as DESeq2 (varianceStabilizingTransformation; VST) or edgeR (Trimmed Mean of M; TMM) [23, 27]. These software package normalization methods lead to a more stable normalization than the other methods [63].
4. If not using DESeq2 VST or edgeR TMM for normalization,
the normalized matrix is log2(x + 1) transformed for a final expression matrix (see Note 11). 3.7.1 Differential Gene A wide variety of differential gene expression analysis tools exist, Expression Analysis with popular tools including edgeR, DESeq2, limma and voom, NOISeq, SAMSeq (samr), EBSeq, bayseq, and sleuth, among others. Direct comparison of these popular methods suggests NOISeq, DESeq2, and limma+voom have the best sensitivity/specificity performance metrics, with further suggestions that integration of multiple methods may further improve overall performance [64]. Another common tool for differential gene expression analysis is edgeR, which has been shown to have similar performance compared to DESeq2 [27, 65]. We perform differential gene expression analysis using DESeq2, using a gene expression matrix of raw count as input [23]. This matrix is automatically normalized by DESeq2 prior to differential

Using RNA Sequencing to Characterize the Tumor Microenvironment 261 expression analysis. In the case of Salmon derived expression data, counts need to be converted to an integer DESeq2. 3.7.2 Immune Gene Immune gene signatures are composed of a set of genes, typically Signature Analysis specific to an immune cell or pathway of interest combined with a method to transform expression levels of signature genes into a single score for each sample. We calculate immune gene signatures using a normalized matrix and perform screening such that signatures where >30% of respective genes demonstrate zero expression in a particular sample are not considered for downstream analyses. The IGS score is calculated as the mean of the expression of all genes within a particular signature [66]. Alternatively, genes within each signature can instead be scaled across the cohort, taking the median value as the IGS score. This extra normalization step can help reduce biases incurred by highly or lowly expressed genes, but may also reduce sensitivity if those genes have a high degree of biological significance. The following list of citations contains gene signatures we regularly use in our analyses:
1. Palmer C et al. BMC Genomics 2006; PMID:16704732 [67].
2. Schmidt M et al. Cancer Res 2008; PMID:18593943 [68].
3. Beck et al. Clin Cancer Research 2009; PMID:19188147 [69].
4. Rody A et al. Breast Cancer Res 2009; PMID:19272155 [70].
5. Chan et al. PNAS 2009; PMID:19666525 [71].
6. Prat A et al. Breast Cancer Res 2010; PMID:20813035 [72].
7. Fan C et al. BMC Med Genomics 2011; PMID:21214954 [73].
8. Rody A et al. Breast Cancer Res 2011; PMID:21978456 [74].
9. Bindea G et al. Immunity 2013; PMID:24138885 [75].
10. Iglesia MD et al. Clinical Cancer Research 2014;
PMID:24916698 [76].
11. Kardos J and Chai S et al. JCI insights 2016; PMID:27699256
[77].
12. Charoentong P et al. Cell Reports 2017; PMID 28052254
[78].
13. Vesteinn et al. Immunity 2018; PMID: 29628290 [79].
14. MSigDB gene sets [80].
15. Gene Ontology terms 0050853—GO:0050853; PMID:NA.
16. Gene Ontology terms 0050852—GO:0050852; PMID:NA.
3.7.3 Gene Pathway Gene pathway analyses provide a measure for pathways which have Analysis genes expressed at levels higher than by chance. Among immunogenomic-r elated pathways, we typically use MSigDB gene sets for the bulk of our analysis [80]. Of particular relevance are the

262 C. C. Smith et al. C7 immunologic gene sets, C2 curated gene sets, C5 gene ontology gene sets, and the hallmark gene sets. There are several methods for performing gene pathway analysis, among which include (1) standard GSEA analysis, (2) weighted analysis, and (3) network-based approaches. Below, we will provide a summary and examples for each approach. Commonly use pathway analysis tools for standard GSEA analysis include GSEA, single sample GSEA (ssGSEA), and GSVA for gene pathway analysis [28, 30, 31]. Standard GSEA analysis takes in a discrete and predefined gene set that typically represents a biological state, comparing whether RNA-seq or microarray expression data between two biological groups show phenotypic differences based upon those gene sets. Additionally, ssGSEA and GSVA are able to generate gene signature expression values for each individual sample, which GSEA is not. Thus, GSEA is only able to compare signature expression among predefined groups. While GSEA, ssGSEA, and GSVA are among the most popular gene set analysis tools, other gene pathway analysis software such as PLAGE, GLOBALTEST, and PADOG have demonstrated greater sensitivity under certain conditions [81–84]. As such, the accuracy of each analysis method may be dependent upon the biology of the sample set, and thus the chosen method may require optimization and validation for the optimization of results. Alternatively to standard GSEA, weighted approaches such as GSEAPrerank take into account a predefined list of rank-ordered genes to calculate the enrichment score [29]. The gene’s rank thus defines the weight of its contribution to the enrichment score. This can be particularly useful when the ranking metrics provided by standard GSEA are not appropriate for the data, or if the expression data is derived from a nonstandard approach (targeted methods, ChIP-seq, GWAS studies). Another method for gene pathway calculation is a network-based approach, as exemplified by DawnRank, which ranks potential driver genes based on their impact on differential expression of downstream genes in a molecular interaction network [32]. DawnRank performs these analyses on a per-patient basis, allowing for identification of personalized driver genes without biases from the rest of the cohort. It should be noted that to call driver mutations, DawRank additionally requires variant call files, which typically is derived using DNA data. 3.7.4 Deconvolution The incredibly complex cellular composition of a tumor microenvironment underscores the difficult question of how to deconvolute the proportional signals from each cell type. Among cellular deconvolution tools currently available, CIBERSORT and TIMER are the most popular for characterization of the tumor microenvironment [1, 2]. CIBERSORT is designed to infer the relative proportion of individual immune populations among total leukocytes,

Using RNA Sequencing to Characterize the Tumor Microenvironment 263 while TIMER instead aims to infer immune population abundance amount the total tumor microenvironment. The limitation of both tools is their reference is derived from peripherally collected leukocytes from healthy donors, with the assumption that these transcriptional patterns do not substantially differ from their tumor infiltrating counterparts. At this time, it is not clear which of these two methods provides more accurate estimates of tumor infiltrating immune populations from bulk RNA-seq data. 3.7.5 TCR/BCR Inference We have directly compared the performance of several TCR/BCR Tools inference tools, including MiXCR, MiTCR, TRUST, and V’DJer [33, 34, 85, 86]. Based on these comparisons, our preferred inference method is MiXCR for TCR calling and MiXCR/V’DJer for BCR calling. MiXCR-based TCR inference is performed according to recommended settings from the Mi lab for short-read RNA-seq data (https://mixcr.readthedocs.io/en/master/rnaseq.html; subheading “Typical analysis workflow”), which typically yields 100 to 102 total clones, depending upon sequencing depth and RNA quality. From the MiXCR export file output, we perform diversity and clonotypes sharing calculations through standard diversity calculation formulas (species evenness, and diversity indices such as Gini– Simpson or Shannon entropy). We have found that analyses from samples with very few identified clones (101–102) results in inaccurate diversity calculations, and thus a minimum clone cutoff should be optimized and implemented. We avoid the use of TRUST because of its identification of a large frequency of “noncanonical” CDR3 regions, which can be as short as a single aminoacid residue and are unlikely to be truly derived from TCR sequences. BCR inference is performed using both MiXCR and/or V’DJer. Unlike MiXCR, V’DJer uses an assembly-based inference method for calling full length BCR calls from fresh-frozen derived RNA. As a result, V’DJer is able to provide full-length BCR sequences into the constant region for isoform calling, which allows for single base resolution of the BCR. In a comparison of these two tools, MiXCR was demonstrated to have greater sensitivity and less computational intensity compared to V’DJer [87], and therefore may be more relevant in situations where population levels statistics are of primary interest rather than identification of full length BCR-sequences (see Note 12). 3.7.6 HLA Inference HLA typing has historically been performed through the use of PCR, Sanger sequencing, or flow cytometric approaches, with next generation sequencing recently emerging as a potentially higher throughput and more cost effective approach [88]. The majority of these approaches rely upon the use of HLA region targeted DNA sequencing, preventing the identification of biologically

264 C. C. Smith et al. meaningful data outside of HLA typing. Additionally, targeted sequencing requires the use of capture probes, which may result in loss of capture for polymorphisms within the MHC genes. Whole exome/genome approaches suffer from their requirement of very high read depth, with nearly half a billion sequencing reads necessary for accurate calling [89, 90]. As a result of these limitation, RNA-seq derived MHC calling methods have been recently developed, which allows for accurate calling of alleles without limiting data for uses beyond this purpose. One example of such a tool is PHLAT, which can use both DNA and RNA as input for HLA calling [35]. Another recent tool is HLAProfiling, which takes a k-mer approach to allow for identification of both common and rare alleles from RNA-seq data [36]. 3.7.7 Neoantigen Several published neoantigen prediction pipelines exist, Prediction although they almost all require additional tumor-derived whole-exome sequencing data in order to accurately call mutations. As such, we will discuss several neoantigen prediction tools currently available, without enumerating on the exact DNA inputs necessary for running the software. A more recent approach comes from Neopepsee, which attempts to increase calling accuracy through incorporation of amino acid level immunogenicity information derived via a machine learning algorithm trained on a dataset of reported class I MHC epitopes known to exhibit a positive T-cell effect [39]. Another tool is pVACtools, which also integrates DNA and RNA data to call class I and II neoantigens, importantly with the inclusion of point mutations, indels, gene fusions, and frameshift mutations derived epitopes [40]. Lastly, another tool is INTEGRATEneo, which is a neoantigen prediction pipeline with a focus on gene fusion derived epitopes [41]. Most neoantigen calling pipelines work through a similar process, which we have simplified below:
1. Variant calling: Mutations are identified using a variant calling
program, with DNA-seq and RNA-seq inputs. DNA sequences corresponding to peptides are retrieved and translated in silico into protein sequences.
2. Analysis of variant expression: RNA-seq data is used to quantify
read coverage of all called mutations. The expression levels of each peptide generated are determined by the lowest mutation RNA sequencing read coverage. Peptides which do not meet a minimum read coverage are filtered out.
3. HLA typing: For human samples with unknown HLA type,
HLA typing software is applied as described in the above section.
4. Enumeration of possible variant peptides: Generally, 8–11mers
are considered for class I epitopes, while 15mers are consid-

Using RNA Sequencing to Characterize the Tumor Microenvironment 265 ered for class II epitopes. Several groups rely upon the use of long peptides (closer to 30 amino acid residues in length), with the idea that these longer peptides will allow for better antigen-presenting cell processing and presentation.
5. MHC binding prediction: Binding affinity to MHC molecules
expressed by the tumor for all possible peptides generated from mutations is predicted. Perhaps the most widely used MHC binding affinity prediction software is NetMHCpan (version 4.0) and NetMHCIIpan (version 3.2) for class I and II epitopes, respectively [37, 38]. Peptides are filtered by their binding affinities IC50 which is a measure of the relative binding energy between a test and standard peptide for a specific MHC protein. These values are expressed in nM units with peptides with increased binding to MHC proteins having a lower IC50. The IC50 values are then determined for each HLA allele in the tumor sample. Peptides with an IC50 value of less than 500 nM for at least one allele are typically considered potential neoantigens. 3.7.8 Viral Quantification Expression of viral and human endogenous retroviral (hERV) RNA can drive immunological phenotypes in cancer [6, 42]. We have developed tools for quantification of vertebrate viral and human endogenous retroviral (hERV) transcripts from RNA-seq data. The first of these tools is VirDetect, which specifically detects viruses from RNA sequencing [42]. Reads are aligned to the human genome and reads that do not align to the human genome are then aligned to the masked viral genomes. The novelty of VirDetect is the masking of the viral genome for areas of human homology and areas of low complexity. The masking allows for higher specificity and limits the need for manual curation. The commands can be found here: https://github.com/ dmarron/virdetect/blob/master/VirdetectManual.pdf. The second tool is hervQuant, which allows for quantification of nearly 4000 full-length, intact hERVs from short read RNA-seq data [6]. hervQuant has currently been optimized and validated for 2 × 50 bp fresh-frozen RNA-seq data, making it relevant for the majority of TCGA RNA-seq samples. Information for running hervQuant can be found at: https://unclineberger.org/vincent/ resources. 4 Notes
1. For RNA extraction from FFPE, we prefer the use of blocks
rather than slides, as the greater surface area exposure to the outside environment on slides is associated with more degradation. We have greatest success from using freshly cut blocks, discarding the first scroll and collecting toward the center of

266 C. C. Smith et al. the block. Typically, we take 4–6 slides of 10 μm for RNA extraction.
2. We and others have contributed to the NCI’s Biorepositories
and Biospecimen Research Branch best practices for assessing nucleic acid quality from FFPE tissues [91]. In many degraded RNA samples, the average fragment size of the RNA is around 130–150 bp. However, we have still been able to generate successful total RNA-seq libraries even with low DV200s. For mRNA based library strategies, it is best to start with RINs >7 for best quality, though RINs 5–6 are occasionally successful but not as consistent. RIN cutoffs of 7 have been used in TCGA projects. For more degraded RNAs, it is better to use total RNA or capture based protocols that do not have a strong requirement on intact RNA and can be used with samples of low RIN or DV200. We typically are successful with 80–90% of FFPE libraries, particularly with doubling the max starting amount of RNA (ex 200 ng for RNA exome, or 500– 1000 ng for Total RNA). When a protocol calls for fragmentation, this is based on the suspected quality of the RNA and the desired length of sequencing. In general, we typically do not fragment samples with RINs less than 5.
3. For kits that require the starting RNA to be concentrated into
a small volume, there are a number of concentration methods including column methods, like Qiagen’s RNeasy MinElute Cleanup kit, bead purifications, like KAPA’s Pure Beads or Beckman Coulter’s RNAClean XP, or ethanol precipitation.
4. Some samples, including RNA from blood, might produce
more desirable results following the depletion of unwanted transcripts, such as ribosomal RNA or Globin RNA. Using a depletion kit, like one from NuGEN’s AnyDeplete line, will selectively deplete unwanted transcripts, enriching for sequencing reads of choice. Total RNA input may need to be increased if using a depletion kit.
5. If multiple kits from Fig. 1 would work for a given quality and
quantity of starting RNA, other factors such as price, kit availability, and laboratory familiarity should be considered in selecting the right kit as well as desired RNA analysis—coding vs. noncoding transcriptome, alternative transcripts, or structural alterations.
6. It is not recommended to compare sequencing analysis across
different library preparation kits for the same project, as each kit will have its own biases. Comparing data across multiple library preparation methods may result in preferential upregulation/downregulation of certain genes between different kits. Similarly it is not recommended to compare sequencing analyses longitudinally using different high throughput sequencers.

Using RNA Sequencing to Characterize the Tumor Microenvironment 267
7. The use of dual indexes is preferred, as it reduces the preva-
lence of index hopping/library switching.
8. FASTQ format is a text-based format for storing read data,
and is comprised of four lines per sequenced read: (a) S equence identifier, preceded by a “@” character. Often lists the coordinates on the sequencing chip (e.g., @ UNC20:291:000000000-AKVVA:1:1101:16893:1549 2:N:0:AGGCANACTCTCTA). (b) N ucleotide sequence letters (e.g., AGCGTTGGG). (c) A “+” character, followed optionally by the same sequence identifier in line 1. Often left blank (e.g., +). (d) Q uality scores for each base value from line 2. For current Illumina derived FASTQ files, a PHRED score between 0 and 40 are given, which provides the error probability for each respective base (e.g., >>3>>ADFB).
9. Of QC metrics provided by FastQC, we focus most closely on
the per-base sequencing quality (typically given as a PHRED score), overrepresented sequences, and adapter content. Sequencing quality should ideally remain high across the full length of the read; however, we have noticed that amplicon sequencing methods frequently demonstrate a dramatic drop in quality in the last 25–50% of the read length, without significant issues with downstream processing. Particularly in peripheral blood, ribosomal RNA and globin-related genes can often appear as overrepresented genes. Overrepresented sequences can be input into NCBI nucleotide BLAST to identify the source, correcting for future preparations if necessary. Lastly, high adapter content can result from non-ideal PCR conditions or RNA fragments shorter than the sequencing length. If high adapter content is present, a trimming software to remove adaptor contamination should be considered (we most frequently use bbduk from the BBMap suite [57]).
10. Depending on the library and the quality of the RNA, differ-
ent amounts of reads will map to mRNA [92]. In mRNA or exon capture based methods, typically 60–80% of reads will map to mRNA. However, in total RNA–seq, this number is much lower and varies by RNA quality. Total RNA-seq can range from ~10–30% of reads mapping to mRNA in FFPE and ~30–50% in fresh frozen, with corresponding increases in intron and intergenic regions compared to mRNA-seq. At minimum, to reach an equivalent amount RNA expression data as in microarrays, it is important to aim for at least 15–30 million reads mapping to mRNA and to aim even higher for all the additional benefits one gets from a sequencing vs. array based approach.
