## Chapter 13


274 Sarah Warren et al. based on profiling RNA can be useful because transcriptional regulation is highly dynamic and can be easily multiplexed, thus allowing for the development of biomarkers that report on complex signaling events. This chapter focuses on the development of predictive diagnostics assays based on transcriptional biomarkers measured on the nCounter® platform (NanoString Technologies®, Inc.), However, many of the principles presented here are not specific to the nCounter platform and will be useful more generally to investigators embarking on the development of novel diagnostic assays. For more general information about biomarkers, please see [1–6]. 1.1 Clinical Utility Because biomarkers can be developed on multiple sample types, of Biomarkers used at different times in the natural history of the disease, and measure a range of biological activities, they can be deployed for a variety of different purposes. The most common application is patient selection for a specific treatment based on the ability of the biomarker to predict response to a therapeutic intervention. These predictive biomarkers can be developed as either companion or complementary diagnostics, depending on the biomarker performance and the intended use of the associated therapy. Companion biomarkers are those which were used in clinical trials to identify a particular population enriched with patients who experienced clinical benefit from the therapeutic. As a result, the regulatory approval for that therapeutic requires that the patients first be tested with the companion diagnostic and be identified as biomarker positive prior to receiving treatment. In contrast, complementary diagnostics are used to identify subgroup of patients with higher clinical benefit from a treatment, but the therapeutic was shown to be effective in an all-comers trial design, so administration of the complementary diagnostic is not mandated prior to treatment [2]. Therefore, depending on the clinical trial design, the same predictive biomarker can serve as companion or complementary diagnostic. Biomarkers can serve a variety of other functions in drug development; they can be used to identify whether a patient has an increased susceptibility to a disease (predisposition biomarker), confirm a disease state (diagnostic biomarker), estimate likelihood of disease progression independent of therapeutic intervention (prognostic biomarkers), and monitor treatment efficacy (pharmacodynamics biomarkers). 1.2 Regulation In addition to different applications of biomarkers as diagnostic of Biomarker Assays tests that can lead to different classifications, biomarker assays can be classified based on the level of evidence generated in support of their efficacy, which impacts their downstream applications. The lowest level of evidence is for Research Use Only (RUO) assays, which are produced with limited claims about their level of analytical validation. These assays are usually used as tool for sample

Transcriptional Biomarkers for Immuno-Oncology 275 characterization and hypothesis generation but cannot be used in clinical decision-making. On the other extreme are in vitro diagnostics (IVD), which are cleared by regulatory agencies for the diagnosis of a disease or in the cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention of disease. Between RUO or IVD designations, an assay can exist as a clinical trial assay (CTA), which can be further designated as a lab developed test (LDT) or an Investigational Use Only (IUO) assay. LDT assays may be used for the diagnosis and treatment of patients, but they have been developed and can only be deployed within a single clinical lab (i.e., the lab which analytically validates them). IUO are newly developed IVD assays (or existing IVDs for a different intended use) that are being used to enroll patients in registrational clinical studies that could lead to submissions to regulatory agencies for approval of the drug and the companion diagnostic. 1.3 Rationale As biomarkers are detecting a molecular state or event, it is imporfor Transcriptional tant that the appropriate biomarker be developed for the clinical Biomarkers question at hand (i.e., “fit for purpose”). In parallel, consideration must be made of the practical deployment of a diagnostic assay. For example, when a biomarker is being used to measure a germline mutation that changes the coding sequence of a protein in a way that predisposes an individual to a disease (e.g., BRCA1 mutations, which are correlate with increased risk of breast cancer), the diagnostic assay could detect the mutation in the DNA, the RNA, or in the protein. However, the fact that the DNA sequence is informative and can be easily and accurately measured with existing technology makes it the logical choice for the diagnostic assay. Similarly, levels of prostate serum antigen (PSA) protein levels in the blood have been used as a diagnostic biomarker for prostate cancer as a consequence of androgen receptor signaling. As there are not specific mutations associated with PSA overexpression, DNA is unsuitable as a biomarker, and since circulating cell-free RNA is not stable in blood, it is also unsuitable. Thus, protein-based biomarkers for PSA have been developed for the clinical applications. RNA based biomarkers are particularly useful when measuring a complex, dynamic physiological response, where DNA does not change, and proteins may be temporally dysregulated and/or have particularly challenging assays. RNA can also be easily multiplexed, permitting the creation of complex signatures that integrate multiple RNA targets into a single assay. For example, the Prosigna® assay (NanoString Technologies, Inc.) provides information about the risk of recurrence to postmenopausal breast cancer patients with hormone receptor positive (HR+) locally disseminated disease via multiplexed measurement of 50 genes on the nCounter platform, integrating their expression levels with the PAM50 algorithm to determine intrinsic molecular subtype, then correlating subtype plus nodal involvement into a signature that predicts probability of 10-year recurrence at a distant site [7–9].

276 Sarah Warren et al.

2 RNA Quantitation on the nCounter Platform The NanoString nCounter platform enables digital quantitation of RNA using enzyme-free hybridization of optical reporter barcodes to the RNA transcript of interest in a sequence-specific manner [10]. The assay utilizes RNA isolates from a biological sample, including circulating blood cells, fresh tissue, or formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue. Although the samples can be RNA from any biological source, for immuno-oncology applications this generally means a tissue sample from the tumor preserved by FFPE, as this is the tissue type that is routinely used for diagnostic surgical pathology. The biological signature or pathway being measured by the nCounter system can be easily adapted by simply changing the probe sequences to bind to different RNA targets. Furthermore, the nCounter platform provides a rapid turnaround time (~3 days) with minimal hands-on time (~4 h), and can be deployed in a decentralized fashion, all of which are important clinical considerations for diagnostics development. In comparison to other RNA profiling technologies, the nCounter platform has advantages that may be beneficial in the clinical setting. The nCounter platform can multiplex up to 800 genes, which facilitates the development of nuanced gene signatures. Additionally, the rapid turnaround time and ability to be run as a decentralized assay can provide the rapid time-to-results needed for some clinical assays that may be difficult to achieve on other platforms. The key reagents in the nCounter system are the capture probes and reporter probes that are designed to specifically detect each gene transcript of interest, and these collectively are called the CodeSet (Fig. 1). The reporter probe consists of a 35–50 base sequence that is complementary to the mRNA target and a unique backbone DNA sequence that hybridizes to six RNA segments labeled with one of four fluorescent dyes: red, yellow, blue, or green. The fluorescent segments create a six position/four color fluorescent code that is unique to each target. A separate Capture Probe consists of a 35–50 base probe sequence that is complementary to the mRNA target as well as a biotinylated tag oligo Capture Probe Reporter Probe 3 Target-specific 5 Repeats oligos Single-stranded DNA backbone Repeats B Target 6 Fluorescently labeled RNA mRNA segments Fig. 1 Schematic of the tripartite complex of target mRNA, nCounter capture, and reporter probes

Transcriptional Biomarkers for Immuno-Oncology 277 each observed barcode is one read measured nucleic acid

Fig. 2 Representation of the capture probe–reporter probe–RNA complex and image of the surface of the sample cartridge sequence which is used for purification and immobilization onto a streptavidin- coated slide. During the execution of the assay procedure, a predetermined amount of RNA as set by the assay specifications is hybridized to the capture and reporter probes via overnight incubation in a thermocycler. Tripartite complexes form between the RNA and target-specific capture and reporter probes based on sequence homology. The samples are then loaded into the sample prep instrument, where the complexes are purified and distributed across the surface of the streptavidin-coated visualization chamber where they are immobilized via the biotin tag on the capture probe. An electrical current is then applied to the surface which aligns the barcodes in a common orientation based on the negative charge of the DNA and the free end of the complex is also immobilized to the cartridge surface. The cartridge is then moved to a digital analyzer where the barcodes are scanned and deconvolved to their respective targets to provide a digital count per gene (Fig. 2). 2.1 Assay Controls To control for technical variability within the assay, probes with sequences designed by the External RNA Controls Consortium (ERCC) to mimic, but not interfere with, mammalian RNA are included in the assay [11]. The negative ERCC probes do not have target sequences included in the assay and are used to evaluate the level of background or nonspecific signal in the assay. The assay also includes synthetic ERCC targets at different concentrations and corresponding ERCC probes that are used as positive controls to assess the linearity of the assay. Furthermore, endogenous housekeeping genes expressed at stable levels by the sample of

278 Sarah Warren et al. interest are also measured as part of the assay and used to correct for variations in sample input that could skew results. Finally, for some assays, a reference sample made of pooled synthetic DNA oligos or in vitro-transcribed RNAs is run in parallel to the clinical samples(s) to allow for normalization across assays to control for reagent lot variability. 3 Development of Diagnostic Assays on the nCounter Platform As described above, in addition to the target RNA and capture and reporter probes, the assay will also contain internal control targets, housekeeper genes, and one or more reference samples. Thus, the diagnostic assay will be comprised of the following components, each of which must be developed and produced to the desired performance standards: ●● Instrument (prep station and digital analyzer). ●● Reagents (RNA isolation kit, nCounter reagents, internal positive and negative controls). ●● Consumables (plates, cartridges, and plasticware). ●● Reference samples. ●● Assay procedures. ●● Algorithm and associated cutoff(s). ●● Assay report. NanoString has already developed, validated, and received a 510(k) clearance from the FDA for the Prosigna® breast cancer prognostic assay run on the nCounter instrument (including required reagents and consumables). Thus, new multianalyte RNA diagnostic assays on the nCounter platform would not need to focus on development of new reagent chemistry or instrumentation but can instead focus on the assay specific materials and software. Typically, new diagnostic assay design and development follows a stage-gated approach where particular elements of the assay are considered in a systematic way (Fig. 3). In the concept phase, the intended use of the assay is carefully considered with all parameters required for development and deployment identified and considered. Once this is complete, exploratory studies investigate potential patterns of gene expression that correlate with the clinically relevant outcome under investigation. Here, a variety of candidate signatures can be evaluated and iterated on. Once a lead signature is identified, it will move into the feasibility and development phases where various design parameters of the assay are tested and potentially further optimized to define the limits of performance, and assay and manufacturing procedures are established that will ensure its safe and effective use. The goal of these two phases is to design an assay to the point where all performance

Fig. 3 Stages of diagnostic design and development and assay manufacturing requirements are formally specified, or “locked down.” The assay then moves into a verification and validation phase, where the assay demonstrates that it fulfills all performance and assay manufacturing requirements, followed by the commercialization phase where activities are conducted that will lead to approval by the appropriate regulatory agency and the activities required for commercial launch are developed. As necessary, post market reviews are conducted after the diagnostic has been launched which monitor specific aspects of the “real-world” utilization of the assay. This chapter will focus on the concept, feasibility, and development phases as it is here that prior information on the part of the user will be most impactful in an assay’s success. We refer the readers to a number of excellent publications which exist in order to provide more detailed information about the development and validation of diagnostics [12–20]. Ideally, a diagnostic assay is developed in parallel with the accompanying therapeutic, as this will allow the greatest opportunity for sample acquisition and rational assay and study design. However, it is much more common that the diagnostics development is not initiated until later in the development of the therapeutic. In both cases, prior knowledge about how to efficiently develop a diagnostic will maximize the likelihood of a successful assay being developed and deployed in parallel with the therapeutic. 4 Concept Phase 4.1 Defining Success of a diagnostics development process is heavily dependent the Assay Intended upon defining the intended use of the assay at the outset of the Use project, and this encompasses all aspects of assay utilization in the clinic. Most importantly, the clinical decision to be made based on

280 Sarah Warren et al. the results of the biomarker must be defined. For example, an algorithm to predict progression free survival following treatment and an algorithm to predict objective response may require different biology to be measured to maximize the accuracy of the assay in each setting. Furthermore, the characteristics of the biomarker to support the decision must also be defined. For instance, a predictive biomarker which will be deployed early during disease may require a high positive predictive value to select patients because they are likely to have other treatment options available, while a predictive biomarker deployed late during disease may require a high negative predictive value to identify all patients who may benefit from receiving a specific therapy. To enable this definition of intended use, it is necessary to have a thorough understanding of the disease at a genetic, molecular, cellular, tissue, and organismal level, the course of disease, potentially confounding variables (e.g., comorbidities), standard treatment approaches, and how the therapeutic under investigation could change patient outcomes. This will aid the development efforts by ensuring investigators are able to thoroughly define the clinical context in which the diagnostic will be deployed, identify or create relevant datasets for the signature training exercises, and evaluate early results to minimize false positives or false negative results. Additionally, the practical considerations of the assay development and deployment should be carefully considered. This includes preanalytic variables such as sample type, amount of sample available, age of sample, storage conditions, logistics of sample availability, and potential confounding factors such as other tissue types present in the samples. Notably, the sample available for development of the assay may be fundamentally different from what will be used in the clinical assay. For example, much development work can be done on commercially sourced excisional tumor biopsies, but many samples available for clinical testing are core needle biopsies. If these differences are not considered and tested during the development of the diagnostic, it is highly likely that assay performance will suffer as a result. Considerations for intended use also include all aspects of assay execution, including availability of instrumentation, sites or countries of clinical and commercial laboratories, additional characterization that needs to be performed on the sample (e.g., pathological review), frequency with which assay will be run, complexity and hands-on time of the procedure, and time to results. Operational logistics (e.g., a central laboratory or LDT approach) for the test will define how successfully it will be adopted (both in the clinical study and commercial setting), especially in the case of severe diseases where short turnaround time, high accuracy, and robustness of the test are paramount. Finally, it is useful to consider the role of the assay within the natural history of the disease and related patient management,

Transcriptional Biomarkers for Immuno-Oncology 281 other information the patient and physician will have about their disease, the medical expertise of the clinician, the risk to the patient if a clinician misinterprets the test results, how the results of the assay will be used in the decision-making process, and the consequences of an incorrect test result. By integrating these considerations in the upfront thought process of signature development and testing, the risk of encountering unexpected “surprises” later in development is reduced. Once the clinical problem has been well characterized and the desired performance characteristics of the biomarker defined, development work on the biomarker signature can begin. 5 Feasibility Phase In the feasibility phase, a signature training exercise is performed in which gene sets are evaluated for their association with clinical benefit defined by metrics such as tumor response or time-to-event parameters such as progression free survival or overall survival. In immunotherapy, one common strategy is to build a signature that predicts for clinical response to therapeutic intervention. Here, gene expression signatures of responders and nonresponders are compared and genes that are differentially expressed between the groups are identified. Algorithms for weighting genes and potential cutoffs are also evaluated in parallel to gene set selection, so that at the end of the exercise, a candidate signature with content, algorithm, and cutoffs has been created. Development of a “wellbehaved” transcriptional biomarker signature relies on careful selection of genes, development of a robust algorithm, and appropriate selection of a cutoff with regard to the clinical question. The process is sensitive to bias intrinsic to the training sample sets, so it is recommended to collect and preserve as much molecular, clinical and technical data about the training and validation dataset as practically possible to identify and eliminate these sources of bias. 5.1 Selection Identification of the appropriate content for the signature will of Signature Content depend on a number of factors: prior knowledge, effect size, major signals in the transcriptome, and availability of data for training and testing. As discussed in the concept phase, prior knowledge about the biological system being measured will provide information that will increase the likelihood of a robust signature being developed. One highly effective way to learn about the performance of genes is to study their behavior in similar datasets that are available in the public domain (Table 1). More recently, the Google Dataset Search tool (https://toolbox.google.com/datasetsearch) has been developed which can scan the literature for individual datasets not uploaded into other databases. Most of the datasets available are

Another useful strategy is to define groups of genes with similar biology and expression patterns together as metagenes that can then be tested in unison. The genes for inclusion in the metagenes are selected based on the prior knowledge of the system. For example, a biomarker that is measuring cytolytic T cell infiltration into a tumor could start with a metagene signature that consist of CD8+ T cell markers such as CD8A, CD8B, PRF, GZMB, and GZMM [21]. This approach provides several advantages: it can be used to guide gene selection for inclusion in de novo discovery assays, it serves as an independent assessment of the biomarker performance in the datasets, and it reduces the dimensionality of the data, thereby minimizing the likelihood of false discovery. Effect size describes the magnitude of biological change being measured by the signature. Phenomenon with large effect size will be readily detected across many datasets and with minimal interference from other sample characteristics. In contrast, phenomenon with small effect size must be measured with high sensitivity and precision, and potential interference from other tissue characteristics must be carefully considered and controlled. Therefore, assays which measure phenomenon with large effect size are more likely to be sensitive and robust to changes than assays that measure phenomenon with small effect sizes. Nearly all successful gene expression diagnostics measure biological activities with large

Transcriptional Biomarkers for Immuno-Oncology 283 effect size such as proliferation, tumor subtype, immune infiltrate, and activation of signaling pathways. Moreover, even if these events with large effect size are not predictive in the final assay, they can still be used in algorithm training to produce an algorithm that is robust to variability in these signals. Availability of data refers to the type and quantity of data available for training the signature. Whenever possible, using the same sample type and amount of material that will represent the clinical samples is highly recommended to avoid problems in the assay development caused by differential performance of the genes based on technical variations between the training samples and ultimate clinical samples. As an example, core needle biopsies are frequently used in the clinical setting for cancer diagnosis, and thus likely to be the sample available for additional biomarkers profiling. However, many large-scale research datasets are collected using excisional biopsies because of the greater availability of tissue for profiling. Signatures developed on data from excisional biopsies may not perform well on core needle biopsies because the type of material collected (e.g., tumor and tumor-associated tissue harvested with excisional biopsies) or technical variability (e.g., greater RNA degradation with core needle biopsies because of greater temperature fluctuations during collection). In this case, the signature should be tested on core needle biopsy tissue as part of development as early as is feasible. If significant differences are observed between excisional biopsies and core needle biopsies, the cause should be investigated (e.g., by comparing paired core and excisional biopsies from animal models and/or commercially sourced human tumors) and those results incorporated into the assay development (e.g., by clarifying specifications of the assay that were set in the Concept phase). 5.2 Development There are two broad approaches to developing a signature: one of an Algorithm: based on canonical knowledge of the biology and one based on a Selection of Model data-driven approach with no prior assumptions about the data; combinations of the two approaches are also possible. Often, signatures defined purely based on biology, while simple and possibly less sensitive, will be easily interpreted and are less sensitive to false discovery. In contrast, data-driven signatures are optimized to the task at hand, but may suffer from complexity, lack of interpretability and overfitting. In general, relying on simpler models that are grounded in biological knowledge is preferable to more complex and less interpretable models. However, computational approaches to signature development may be viable when the simple models do not prove effective. In such cases, one should carefully consider the choice of computational approaches available (Table 2). A full treatment of this subject is beyond the scope of this chapter, but we refer the reader to the numerous other publications that address the approaches [22–29]. Careful consideration of the strength and limitations of each approach and the requirements for a specific biomarker will have significant impact in successful development and application of the signature. 5.3 Development Cutoffs are typically set based on the intended use of the assay, that of an Algorithm: is, they will be placed to maximize either the positive predictive Development value or negative predictive value of a biomarker so as to select the of a Cutoff appropriate clinical population. An additional consideration when selecting a cutoff is the benefit of placing it in regions of the dataspace where few samples are found. This will provide some insurance against variations in signature score caused by tissue intrinsic differences, reagent batch effects, and/or sample prep protocols. 5.4 Evaluation Development of a biomarker signature is divided up into three steps: of a Biomarker training, testing, and validation. The training phase is used for the Signature initial development of an algorithm and to gain some confidence in its utility. The testing phase uses a dataset not used for training of the algorithm to verify the accuracy of the signature by confirming that it achieves the necessary performance in a sample setting independent from the one in which it was developed. In practice, training and testing often occur in datasets that are related to each other, such as different phases from the same clinical trial. Consequently, validation in independent data is crucial because algorithms emerging from the training/testing phase are at risk of having been overfit or driven by some unique signal in the training/testing data that does not generalize to other populations. The best practices of biomarker development call for the establishment of a “bright line” between training/testing and validation studies, with validation studies using fully mature and locked algorithms, reagents and protocols [3, 36]. 5.5 Signature If the biomarker discovery exercise begins with collecting data on Training the nCounter, it affords the opportunity to generate an analysisready dataset that will simplify signature development. This method allows for the design of a CodeSet that measure specific gene expression to adequately capture the relevant biology of interest. In addition, the introduction of artifacts due to technical variability into the data is minimized by standardization of the RNA extraction procedure, instrument operating settings, reagent lot changes, CodeSet gene content changes, or probe sequence redesign against the same gene. Development of a gene expression signature for use on the nCounter platform can start with data from the nCounter system, RNA-sequencing (RNAseq), or microarray. There are numerous advantages for transferring an assay to the nCounter platform,

286 Sarah Warren et al. including the simplicity and rapidity of sample processing and the ability to deploy the assay on a distributed platform that can facilitate clinical trials and commercial use. If a signature is developed from data on another platform then transferred to nCounter, care must be taken to “correct” for platform specific differences. Most platform effects are well described by a scale difference between the alternative platform (e.g., RNAseq) and nCounter dataspaces. For example, RNAseq may read one gene with 50% greater efficiency than nCounter, while the reverse is true for another gene. In most cases, this gene-by-gene difference in efficiency can be adjusted for by simply adding a constant to each gene’s log-transformed expression. This rule does not hold at very low counts—nCounter data falls into the range of background noise whereas RNAseq data does not, likely due to the RNAseq sample being amplified enzymatically. Also, RNAseq data may be subject to outlier effects due to variations in PCR efficiency between targets, and these effects may be nonlinear. These assumptions about data linearity between platforms can also fail for microarray data, and thus translating these signatures will require additional consideration, such as expression level of the target, dynamic range of the assays, and background introduced by sample type [37]. As a rule, having access to bigger relevant datasets will result in a more robust signature, and well-annotated datasets will minimize the likelihood of signature performance being compromised by spurious artifacts. 5.6 Signature Repeated sampling of the training dataset allows for the signature Testing to be refined experimentally. Furthermore, it is desirable for the training exercise to not only produce an algorithm, but also generate evidence that the algorithm will succeed in validation. This goal is especially important for complex algorithms derived using machine learning, as they are at the greatest risk from overfitting. There are two primary approaches for developing confidence in a trained algorithm: a train-test split, and cross-validation. In the train-test split approach, the training data is split into training and test sets, and an algorithm is trained on the training set and evaluated in the test set. In instances where data are plentiful, it is better to train on a large dataset and then test on an entirely separate dataset. When that is not possible, it is appropriate to split the available datasets such that most samples are used for training efforts and a fraction of samples are reserved for testing activities. The risk in this approach is that underlying factors in the data which are unique to a particular dataset cannot be incorporated into model and the signature may appear to have better performance than what will be observed in real world applications. If data is too limited to set aside samples for a test set, cross-validation can be used to gain some confidence that a trained algorithm will succeed in the validation phase. In cross-validation

Transcriptional Biomarkers for Immuno-Oncology 287 schemes, the data is split into a small number (usually 5–10) of subsets. The subsets are then combined into cohorts where one subset is omitted, and the algorithm development process is applied to each cohort. Each of the algorithms derived from this process is then tested on the remaining subset of the data. For example, ten algorithms are trained, with each time omitting one of ten subsets of the data from the cohort, then each algorithm is tested on the subset omitted from its training. Once satisfactory performance in the cross-validation test sets is attained, the same algorithm training approach is applied to the full training set. Another strategy to extend small datasets is to use a bootstrapping approach where virtual datasets are created based on an existing dataset with artificial noise introduced computationally to mimic other datasets. This approach can be useful for estimating the performance characteristics of a signature when data available for training are extremely limited. No matter which strategy is employed for testing in the discovery phase, the locked assay must be validated on an independent dataset. 5.7 Signature The problem of small datasets is one of the most frequent and chal- Validation lenging aspects of biomarker development. Although a number of suggestions are provided here as strategies when working with small datasets, at the end of the day, discretion will have to be applied throughout the training and testing of a signature. For that reason, no matter how much data is available for the early work, it is essential that the signature be validated in an independent dataset that was not previously used to develop the algorithm. This is crucial because the signature will almost certainly be overfit to the data used in training. In the training phase, model biomarkers can be built, tested, and retested repeatedly to generate an optimal signature to predict outcome, but a single algorithm should be advanced to the validation phase. 6 Development Phase During the feasibility and development phases, assay components, procedures, robustness, and performance are defined, and sources of variability are identified and tested. The assay conditions should be set to support the smallest amount of tissue expected in routine clinical testing, have the simplest assay workflow, employ quality controls commensurate with clinical use, and yet still give robust results. Throughout feasibility testing, it is beneficial to prespecify and follow an execution and analysis plan because it facilitates completion of the regulatory requirements as the diagnostic assay progresses toward clearance by the regulatory agencies. One important component of this plan is to record any assay failures that occurred and identify the source of those failures (e.g., failure in RNA

288 Sarah Warren et al. isolation, sample swap, low yield, low purity). If any of the samples passed all external checks but failed the assay QC, it is important to investigate the cause of that failure as it can give valuable insights into the performance of the assay and lead to a more robust and stringent performance specifications. 6.1 Clinical Reagents Once a gene expression signature has been trained and tested in the discovery datasets, a clinical grade CodeSet should be designed and built using good manufacturing practices (GMP). If a signature has been developed on another platform or using an nCounter CodeSet that is different from the final clinical CodeSet, it is important to assess any differences caused by the redesign of the assay. For this step, samples which were originally profiled with the discovery assay should be rerun on the clinical assay and the results compared at the level of normalized counts and at the level of the signature score. In addition to any considerations of CodeSet design between the discovery and clinical CodeSet, it is also important to identify and evaluate sources of variability that arise during the manufacture of the clinical assay in its entirety. This should include understanding the effects of different manufacturing builds such as process related probe variance, low signal, high background, and poor linearity on the outputs of the assay in the context of the intended use of the assay. This assessment should be primarily based on results from experiments with control sample tested on different lots of critical reagents (such as CodeSet, prep plates, and cartridges) with as much material variance as possible but can rely on simulations, assuming a deep understanding of the capabilities of the manufacturing process. The outcome of this assessment should be the establishment of appropriate manufacturing process specifications. 6.2 Tissue Input It is important to define samples specifications that will ensure Criteria passing and accurate results for the assay. For tissue-based assays, this includes characterizing the amount of tissue that is needed to obtain the appropriate RNA yield to run the assay. Both a nominal input value and a range should be developed, where the nominal tissue input amount is defined by balancing a desire to maximize assay pass rate (e.g., a 95% pass rate) while maintaining assay performance and ensuring that the amount specified can be routinely supported by current clinical practice. The minimum and maximum input range would be set based on the amount of tissue necessary to ensure reliable assay performance while potentially trading off what is an extreme tissue amount or what may provide a lower pass rate. Furthermore, it is important to test the tissue input specifications on every tumor type the clinical assay will be run on. Different preanalytic variables such as tumor types, collection, fixation or

Transcriptional Biomarkers for Immuno-Oncology 289 storage conditions could all affect RNA yields and routinely used methods should be tested. For example, if the assay will be run in the clinic on excisional, incisional, or core needle tumor biopsies, all three input types should be tested. If one or more of the sample types are not available for development, it should be approximated as closely as possible and potential risks to the assay performance addressed throughout development. For example, if core needle biopsies are not available, they can be approximated by sectioning excisional biopsies into small fractions and comparing the score of each fraction to that of the whole tissue. Although the nCounter platform is relatively robust to different degrees of RNA degradation when compared to other methods for gene expression analysis, it is best to store tissues mounted on slides at ambient temperature in a desiccator to minimize any potential impact on assay performance. Nevertheless, it is best to demonstrate assay robustness to tissue sample storage using time course studies with a minimum suggested time of 1 year, but different studies may be warranted based on the intended use. Another important variable to evaluate on tumor samples is the impact of the amount of adjacent nontumor tissue (or tumor surface area) on the assay result. FFPE samples commonly comprise a mix of both tumor and nontumor tissue especially in case where the tumor margin is included in the FFPE block or in the case of multifocal tumors. Inclusion of nontumor tissue could bias the assay results by changing the biomarker gene expression profile. This can be remedied by adding a requirement for macrodissection where the tumor tissue is enriched in the RNA isolation if the amount of nontumor tissue is above a threshold that is shown to affect assay performance. Macrodissection, where the nontumor material is cut away from the slide, can generate a more uniform sample, but does require additional steps in the assay procedures. Furthermore, contamination from other potentially tumor type specific interferents, such as stroma, fibrotic areas, necrotic tissue, lymphoid tissue, or adipose tissue, should also be assessed for the impact on assay performance. This is usually a regulatory requirement and the results might be incorporated in the assay label as precautions. Tumor cellularity, or the proportion within the histopathologically defined tumor focus or foci that is comprised of tumor cells, may also affect the performance of the assay, and should be evaluated. The methods for determining tumor surface area, defining tumor specific interferents and tumor cellularity should be specified in the assay procedure, so they can be applied consistently to all samples. 6.3 RNA Input The develop process should also consider which variables influence Criteria RNA quality and quantity and can subsequently have a negative impact on assay performance. To minimize variability due to pre-analytical factors, it is best to choose a GMP-grade RNA isolation

290 Sarah Warren et al. kit to be used throughout the development and specified for commercial use of the assay. Once the RNA has been isolated, specifications should be developed around the RNA yield, purity and concentration of sample input. Ideally, RNA input conditions should be tested across the reportable range of algorithmic results and in each tissue type that will be used in the clinical assay. Common sources of assay variability, such as contamination from residual genomic DNA due to improper RNA isolation or failure to adhere to critical parameters in the RNA extraction procedure (e.g., the amount of time required for protein digestion) should be evaluated by simulating common ways the assay protocol may be improperly executed and measuring their effects on the algorithm output. Additionally, RNA storage conditions after isolation should also be evaluated experimentally as a potential source of variability because RNA isolation and assay procedures may occur on different days or even in different labs. For example, the effects of storing the RNA at −20 °C for varying lengths of time should be compared to −80 °C, where RNA is known to be stable. Also, the effects of freeze-thaw on the purified RNA are another potential source of variability that may be introduced in the clinical lab and should be evaluated. 6.4 Assay Procedure There are a number of steps in the hybridization, sample process- Variables ing, and data collection procedure that may also contribute to variability of the assay performance. Variation in the hybridization time should be investigated. Typically, 15–24 h is standard time used in nCounter assays which generally fits within 2 standard working days. Longer hybridization times may result in greater sensitivity, which can improve detection of low abundance targets, but have a risk of increasing background and extend turnaround times of the assay. It is best to define a range of hybridization times rather than a single fixed time to allow for flexibility of the procedure in routine execution. Since both sensitivity and background can be affected by hybridization time, it may be useful to test samples with a range of input amounts and across the reportable range of algorithmic results to robustly test both limits of the system. Finally, there are settings in the nCounter system which could also affect assay sensitivity. For instance, the prep station can be run in standard or high sensitivity mode which affect the efficiency of the capture probe–reporter probe–RNA complex binding to the cartridge surface. Also, the digital analyzer programmed to scan either a low or high number of fields of view from the cartridge surface which impact the time to results and total counted RNA molecules. Both variables should be tested for their effect upon the assay results and specified based on the intended use of the assay. 6.5 Control Samples A critical component of the assay is a reference sample which is used in normalization to control for reagent lot to lot or assay run- to- run variation that could lead to incorrect reporting by

Transcriptional Biomarkers for Immuno-Oncology 291 the algorithm. The reference sample that is most similar to a patient sample (and thus the recommended path), will be in vitro-transcribed RNAs containing the endogenous probe binding sequences flanked by additional endogenous target sequence. These sequences can then be cloned into plasmids for rapid and reproducible synthesis of the reference sample material via PCR followed by IVT synthesis. Each step of the PCR and IVT will also need to be standardized and compared against a sample which has been declared to be the gold standard to ensure future lots of the reference sample are suitable for use in normalization. Alternatively, the reference sample could consist of a standardized biological sample (such as universal reference RNA), but the challenges around producing sufficient quantities of this material, sufficient signal for all biomarker genes, consistency of lots of a biologically derived sample, performing quality checks, and storing it for long periods of time are sufficiently challenging that this is rarely the preferred option for commercial diagnostic assays. Additionally, assays with bimodal signatures typically include two clinical control samples, one that falls into each classification, that laboratories can use to verify the assay is providing the expected results. Assay with more outcome possibilities may need different clinical control sample strategies. Ideally, the reference sample and clinical controls would be developed early and used throughout the development process. 6.6 Housekeeping Housekeepers are genes that should be constitutively express in all Genes samples and not changing in response to the fundamental biology being measured. Housekeepers are included in the assay to normalize variations in sample input that could lead to incorrect assay results, that is, they are used to normalize the counts from the biomarker genes that may be different from one sample to the next due to different amounts of RNA mass used. This prevents biased resulting from overloading or underloading of the sample into the assay. If a signature is made of a balanced mix of genes with positive and negative weights that are associated with the outcome being measured, then the contribution of the housekeeper genes is minimal. For example, if too much sample was used in an assay where the signature was made of genes with a mixture of positive and negatively coefficients, then the counts would be too high for both sets of genes and the effects of overloading on the signature score would be minimal. However, if the signature was made up entirely of genes that were positively associated with the outcome, then the housekeepers would be necessary to correct the overload and accurately measure the signature score. In this example, if a score was being developed to measure proliferation but all the genes in the score were increased with proliferation, then adding a greater amount of the sample could cause all of the counts to be too high and the sample would be misclassified without the use of housekeepers to control for differences in sample loading.

292 Sarah Warren et al. In addition to controlling for sample input amount in the assay, housekeepers are important in the development process for determining the sensitivity of the assay. This is true especially when the input amount of RNA may be low, or the expression level of genes close to the limit of detection. The selection of housekeepers can be conducted in TCGA or other large datasets using similar sample types to identify a core set of expression invariant genes. The GeoNorm algorithm is a standard way to select housekeepers with invariant expression in relation to the biology being tested [38]. 6.7 Assay It is important to characterize both the limit of detection (LOD) Performance and the limit of blank (LOB) in the context of the intended use of the assay. LOD refers to the lowest amount of material that can be reliably detected on the system. LOB refers to the highest counts generated by a blank (water) sample and is a measure of the background of the system. Typically, these assays would be performed with a high number of replicates to allow for an accurate assessment of mean and standard deviation of counts for each target. The relative importance of the calculated LOD or LOB at the gene level should be assessed in the context of the reportable range of algorithmic assay results and likelihood of misclassification at any clinical decision threshold. For example, if genes are routinely below the LOD in a subset of samples, but those samples always fall so far from the cutoff that loss of that gene from the algorithm would never cause misclassification, then this event would be deemed not impactful to the assay. Another metric that should be verified is the specificity of each of the target probes for its intended gene target. Although each probe is designed to be specific for a single transcript, this should be confirmed for clinical assays by running the entire CodeSet but only a single target IVT transcript at a concentration equivalent to its concentration in the reference sample and comparing it against the counts generated with the reference sample containing all the targets. This should be repeated for each of the targets independently, and the resulting data analyzed for both cross reactivity and contamination. Based upon the results from development studies such as RNA 6.8 Algorithm Data input testing, assay procedure tolerance testing, reagent Quality Controls development, various controls in the assay should be considered along with individual specifications to ensure assay performance and to troubleshoot failures associated with the user. These specifications should be sensitive enough to identify issues that would affect assay performance but not so stringent as to falsely fail assays with results that are not impacted. These quality controls and corresponding specifications should be built into the software code or data analysis pipeline of the assay, and failure to pass one or more

Transcriptional Biomarkers for Immuno-Oncology 293 of these specifications should result in assay failure. Examples of these quality controls include: ●● ERCC positive linearity specification—measure acceptable assay linearity using the positive ERCC controls. ●● ERCC negative signal specification—measurement of the maximum allowable signal generated by the negative technical control probes to limit the impact of background. ●● Negative sample signal specification—measurement of the counts from the water lane as a test of background thresholds in the biomarker genes. ●● Housekeeper gene signal specification—measurement to ensure sufficient signal in the reference sample or test sample lane to ensure assay performance. ●● Reference sample score profile specification—measurement to ensure the individual biomarker genes are being measured as expected based on a canonical dataset generated from running the reference sample across many reagent lot/assay condition combinations 6.9 Assay Precision Once an assay has been established and locked down in the devel- Testing opment lab, it is important to test external factors which may contribute sources of variability. These could include variability associated with different runs by the same operator, different operators in the same lab, or different lab sites (different environment and a different instrument). Testing should be performed in a controlled setting with an identical set of biological samples to ensure any intrinsic variability between the samples in minimized. 7 Assay Finalization Based on all of the data from the testing described above, assay procedures and specifications should be set for manufacturing of all assay components, reagents, execution of the assay, data analysis, and interpretation of the results. Labs that will be utilizing the assay in the clinical setting should be trained on the final assay procedure. This development work will support clinical evaluation of the locked assay in the IUO setting and help determine the right testing that will be used to validate the assay performance to support future regulatory filings for full commercialization. 8 Example of Immuno-oncology Signature Development As an example of diagnostics development on the nCounter platform, the Tumor Inflammation Signature (TIS) can be used as a case study. The TIS is an 18 gene signature that enriches for

294 Sarah Warren et al. response to pembrolizumab across a variety of solid tumor indications [30]. The assay was developed from retrospective analysis of pretreatment tumor biopsies of patients enrolled in the clinical trials KN-001, KN-012, and KN-028, which provided access to >350 patient samples across 11 indications. The initial signature was trained based on data collected from a melanoma cohort (n = 62) profiled with a custom CodeSet, and the signature was further tested and refined in cohorts of gastric tumors (n = 33) and head and neck tumors (n = 43), and a multitumor cohort (n = 220) consisting of tumors from gastric, triple negative breast, head and neck, urothelial, anal, biliary, colorectal, esophageal, and ovarian tumors. The signature was validated in an independent cohort from the KN-028 trial. The signature was designed to segregate responders from nonresponders (to limit potential prognostic confounding effects inherent in using time to event as clinical outcome endpoints), and the final model is a penalized linear regression of the 18 genes plus 10 housekeepers. The TIS measures an activated but suppressed adaptive immune response in the tumor microenvironment by integrating genes associated with antigen-presenting cell abundance, T and NK cell abundance, IFN signaling, and T cell exhaustion (Table 3). As the test was intended to be used originally for patient selection in the advance metastatic setting, the cutoff was set at a point which maximized the negative predictive value of the assay. As part of the assay development, the analytical performance of the assay was interrogated by the methods described above. First, the performance of the individual probes was assessed across a pool of in vitro-transcribed targets and found to be linear across a wide range of concentrations (Fig. 4a). Additionally, pooled probes were tested for specificity by spiking in in vitro-transcribed targets individually to the assay (Fig. 4b). All of the probes were found to have minimal cross reactivity that was within the tolerances of the assay. 9  Conclusion This chapter presents an overview of diagnostics development of RNA-based assay using the nCounter platform with a focus on immune-oncology and provides guidance on the overall developmental efforts up to lock of the assay design and prior to analytical and clinical validation. It has illustrated some of the considerations which are common to all biomarker development programs, but it is not possible to introduce all the steps for biomarker development here, so interested readers are encouraged to follow up with the additional resources referenced for much more in depth information. As diagnostics play an increasing role in medical research and patient care, it is important for a wide audience to be familiar with their utility and involved development process, and we hope this chapter provides a simple and practical introduction to the field. ## Chapter 14


302 Vitaly Balan and Jianbin Wang out PD1 gene in mice [3, 4]. These discoveries together with findings by other scientists established the solid foundation for cancer immunotherapies targeting inhibitory checkpoint molecules. Dr. Allison and Dr. Honjo were awarded the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their outstanding contributions in the field. Now, cancer immunotherapy becomes the fourth pillar of cancer treatment in addition to surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy following a series of FDA’s approvals in recent years, such as anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody (mAb) ipilimumab (Yervoy, 2011), anti-PD-1 mAbs pembrolizumab (Keytruda,
2014) and nivolumab (Opdivo, 2014), anti-PD-L1 mAb atezoli-
zumab (Tecentriq, 2016), and anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T cells (CAR-T) Tisagenlecleucel (Kymriah, 2017) and axicabtagene ciloleucel (Yescarta, 2017). Relatively high rate of 5-year survival can be achieved in treating certain hematological cancers using anti-CD19 CAR-T cells and certain types of solid tumors such as melanoma using anti- PD-1 mAbs. In addition, many types of previously untreatable cancers can now be cured with unprecedented rate of success. Nevertheless, there are a significant portion, often more than 50% of many different types of late stages solid tumors, of patients that do not respond to any available treatment including immunotherapy or show serious side effects. The proposed mechanism includes low immunogenicity of the tumor, high expression of negative regulators of immune responses in tumor cells and immune cells, as well as the presence of other immune suppressive cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME), physical barrier in TME, and higher production of inhibitory cytokines or other factors. Cancer immunotherapy is still in its early stage of development and it is very important to have proper set of biomarkers that allows reliable diagnosis, prediction of response to treatment, and monitoring of progression of disease. Recent development of an easy to use gene editing tool as described below provided an opportunity to evaluate existing biomarkers and to discover novel biomarkers to accelerate cancer research, diagnosis, and treatment. 2 A Brief History and Introduction of the CRISPR-Cas9 System Originally discovered as a bacterial and archaeal adaptive immune system to viral infection, the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) system immediately evolved into the most popular genome editing tool once the basic biological mechanism was mostly revealed. Nowadays, hundreds if not thousands of laboratories are utilizing the technology to help answer various biological questions, and numerous institutes and companies are also trying to use

CRISPR and Cancer Biomarker 303 it for therapeutic purpose. The history of CRISPR-Cas9 system has already been reviewed in details by others [5–7]. Briefly, a new type of repeated sequence was initially reported in 1987 [8], but it was uncharacterized until later by Francesco Mojica and other groups [9]. Importantly, the origin of the spacer sequences (analog to sgRNA target-specific sequences) was unknown until later discovered by three groups [10–12]. Remarkable progress was made in the following years revealing part of the mechanisms and providing further evidence that the CRISPR-Cas9 is an adaptive immune system of bacteria and archaea by multiple research groups. In 2012, a landmark paper demonstrated in vitro CRISPR-Cas9 is a RNAprogrammable DNA nuclease which can potentially be used for genome editing [13]. A similar conclusion was also reached in another 2012 paper a month later [14]. Few months later, in 2013, the type II prokaryotic CRISPR-Cas system was used for the first time for RNA-guided site-specific genomic DNA cleavages and modifications including homology-directed repair in eukaryotic cells [15–18]. CRISPR-Cas9 is a RNA-guided programmable endonuclease. Similar to other programmable endonucleases such as ZFN and TALEN, its primary application in cells is to cleave genomic DNA at a predetermined target site to cause double-strand break (DSB) on a target chromosome [19]. Cells recognize DSB as a threat and will try to repair it as soon as possible. There are two main DNA repair pathways: nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) and homology- directed repair (HDR) [20]. NHEJ is usually the more efficient DNA repair pathway in mammalian cells but with less fidelity and will result in mostly small insertions and deletions (indels) at the break site. HDR requires the presence of a homologous template for DNA repair, which can be a sister chromatin or an engineered donor DNA molecule. HDR occurs during active cell cycle and is usually the desired events with high fidelity but lower efficiency. For genome editing application, the CRISPR system can be utilized to knock out a target gene using single guide RNA (sgRNA) targeting the exon regions of a gene. Most indels (NHEJ DNA repair pathway) induced by Cas9/sgRNA treatment cause frame-shift in the open reading frame leading to disruption of the target gene. Supplied with a donor DNA molecule as homologous template in addition to Cas9/sgRNA, the CRISPR system can also be utilized for gene correction or knockin through the HDR DNA repair pathway. Under certain circumstances, the entire donor DNA molecule can also be knocked in at the target site through the NHEJ DNA repair pathway as observed using the ZFN technology [21]. The crystal structure of Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) protein in complex with sgRNA and target DNA revealed that the protein has recognition (REC) and a nuclease (NUC) lobes.

The REC lobe is responsible for DNA target recognition, whereas the NUC lobe is responsible for DNA cleavage and interaction with protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) (Fig. 1) [22]. A nucleasenull dead Cas9 (dCas9) variant can be simply generated by two point mutations [23]. One point mutation inactivates the RuvC and the other inactivates the HNH nuclease domain. A nickase can also be generated if only one of the two sites is mutated. It can be used to preferentially induce high-fidelity genome editing through the HDR pathway [24]. The dCas9-based CRISPR system can be utilized to activate or repress gene expression without changing the DNA coding sequences. The dCas9-based CRISPR system can be utilized for transcriptional gene regulation. A protein fusion of dCas9 and a transcriptional activator such as VP64, P65, VPR (VP64-P65-RTA), or P65-HSF1 can be used to upregulate gene expression [25–27].
