CRISPR and Cancer Biomarker 305 In contrast, a protein fusion of dCas9 and a transcriptional repressor such as KRAB can be used to downregulate gene expression [25]. There are also RNA-editing Cas variants such as Cas13a, which can be utilized to disrupt transcribed mRNA to downregulate target gene expression [28, 29]. The dCas9-based system can be utilized for epigenetic modification. A protein fusion of dCas9 with certain epigenetic modifiers such as methyltransferase DNMT3A and/or its cofactor DNMT3L [30], other methyltransferases (DOT1L, SMYD3, and PRDM9) [31], demethylase TET1 [32], acetyltransferase P300 core [33], histone demethylase LSD1 [34], and histone deacetylases (HDACs) [35] can either activate or repress target gene expression. Gene regulation efficiency of the dCas9-based system can also be significantly enhanced using some signal amplification system. For example, the SunTag system adds epitope tail to dCas9 that is responsible for recruiting transcriptional activators fused with single- chain variable fragment (scFv) [36]. The SAM system added RNA aptamers to 3′ of the sgRNA that create binding sites for activator domains fused with MS2 bacteriophage coat protein (MCP) [27]. The dCas9-based system can actually be transformed back into a genome editing tool again. For example, fusion of cytidine or adenosine deaminases to dCas9 will generate a base editor. These dCas9-deaminase fusion proteins were used for targeted base editing, C-to-T conversion, or A-to-G conversion without DNA double stranded cleavage [37]. Fusion of dCas9 with FokI endonuclease catalytic domain can reconstitute the nuclease activity of the system. It functions as dimers which is somewhat similar as ZFN and TALEN. This system can markedly reduce potential off-target cleavage, since FokI is only active as a dimer and recruitment of two FokI-dCas9 monomers to adjacent “half-sites” by two sgRNAs is essential for the nuclease activity and subsequent DNA cleavage [38, 39]. 3 Application of CRISPR-Cas9 in Tumorigenesis Research and Cancer Biomarker Discovery The application of CRISPR/Cas9 technology in biomedical research notably benefited from the previous research on other genome editing tools such as meganucleases, ZFN and TALEN as well as the RNAi technology. In addition, the advance in next generation sequence (NGS) technology also significantly facilitated the rapid progress of CRISPR research. The CRISPR technology was almost immediately adapted by scientists from various research fields and applied to their projects after the initial demonstration that the programmable endonuclease can work in tubes in 2012

306 Vitaly Balan and Jianbin Wang [13, 14] and in eukaryotic cells in 2013 [15–18]. As expected, numerous studies were focused on cancer research. Genes involved in cancer development including oncogenes, tumor suppressive genes, and other cancer-associated genes are potential important biomarkers for cancer diagnosis and treatment. Tremendous efforts are invested in identification of oncogenes and other cancer-associated genes as potential therapeutic targets. The relative easiness to generate sgRNA library and the long-lasting effects (permanent) of genome editing by the CRISPR system made it a favorite tool for genome-wide screens. CRISPR knock-out screens were shown to outperform shRNA in identifying essential genes [40]. Various genome-scale CRISPR-based screens were performed by different research groups to address some of the fundamental questions relevant to cancer biology and immune biology. For example, which gene(s) is(are) essential for tumor cells to thrive. Many genes in different signal pathways were identified as essential genes in genome-scale CRISPR knockout screens [41–44]. Hart et al. performed CRISPR fitness screens in five human cell lines and identified 1580 human core fitness genes. They also demonstrated that context-dependent fitness genes accurately recapitulated pathway-specific genetic vulnerabilities induced by known oncogenes and revealed cell-type-specific dependencies for specific receptor tyrosine kinases, even in oncogenic KRAS backgrounds [43]. Due to the loss of a specific tumor suppressor or the activation of an oncogene as most tumor cells have, some of the nonessential genes can become essential. This is the basic concept of synthetic lethality. Genome-scale CRISPR screens based on such synthetic lethality can identify additional potential cancer drug targets [45–47]. For example, pancreatic cells with a mutation in the ubiquitin-ligase RNF43 are particularly vulnerable to Wnt-FZD5 knockout [46]. Human T cells are central effectors of immunity and cancer immunotherapy. Shifrut et al. performed CRISPR screens and identified essential T cell receptor signaling components, genes that negatively tune proliferation following stimulation, and perturbations that enhanced cancer cell killing. They also adapted the CRISPR screening platform to identify mediators of immunosuppression, revealing genes controlling responses to adenosine signaling [48]. Somatic gene mutations can alter the vulnerability of cancer cells to T-cell-based immunotherapies. Patel et al. performed a genome-scale CRISPR screen to identify genes whose loss in human cancer cells impaired the effector function of CD8+ T cells. The most enriched genes in the screen have key roles in antigen presentation and interferon-γ signaling including the apelin receptor encoding gene APLNR, which was shown to interact with JAK1 and modulate interferon-γ responses in tumors. Loss of APLNR reduced the efficacy of adoptive cell transfer and checkpoint blockade immunotherapies in mouse models, suggesting APLNR

CRISPR and Cancer Biomarker 307 is a potential biomarker and cancer immunotherapy target [49]. Kearney et al. performed CRISPR screens in vitro and in vivo to identify mechanisms of tumor immune evasion from cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells. They found that deletion of key genes within the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling, interferon-γ (IFN-γ) signaling, and antigen presentation pathways in tumor cells provided protection from CD8+ T cell-mediated killing and blunted antitumor immune responses in vivo, whereas deletion of a number of genes in the TNF pathway emerged as the key mechanism of immune evasion from primary NK cells [50]. Besides the classic gene knockout screens, an alternative way is to use the dCas9-based CRISPR activation/interruption (CRISPRa/i) screening system. Gene expression is knocked down instead of being knocked out in a CRSIPRi system, which allows scientists to study essential genes whose knockout is lethal to cell survival. Upregulation of gene expression is possible with the CRISPRa screening system, which cannot be achieved with the classic gene knockout method using the nuclease-active Cas9 or shRNA/RNAi technology. For example, the majority of disease-associated sequence variants are enriched in enhancers [51]. It was shown that identification of regulatory elements upstream of TSS can be very useful in understanding of mechanisms involved in cancer drug resistance [52]. High-throughput CRISPRi screens identified proximal and distal regulatory elements of MYC1 and GATA1 that regulate gene expression and cellular proliferation. This kind of approach allows researchers to study transcriptional networks and evaluate the contribution of noncoding genetic variations to human diseases [53]. In addition, in contrast to the classic gene knockout using nuclease-active Cas9 where the editing is permanent, the CRISPRa/i system mediated gene regulation has the flexibility to be reversible and inducible [54]. The system can allow temporal transcriptional control of target gene expression and can potential be an invaluable tool in evaluating gene functions in a context specific condition and in the development of precision medicine [55]. A typical way to evaluate whether a gene is really important for tumorigenesis is to knock out the candidate gene in a relevant tumor cell line or primary cells in vitro or in vivo and then check for functional changes, such as cell survival and proliferation, tumor formation, and metastasis in an animal model system. For example, Zuckermann et al. utilized CRISPR technology to delete single (Ptch1) or multiple genes (Trp53, Pten, Nf1) in the mouse brain, resulting in the development of medulloblastoma and glioblastoma, which confirmed the function of these tumor suppressive genes in vivo [56]. Chromatin-modifying genes are frequently mutated in human lung adenocarcinoma, but the functional impact of these mutations on disease initiation and progression is not well understood. Using a CRISPR-based gene knockout approach in

308 Vitaly Balan and Jianbin Wang two Kras(G12D)-driven mouse models of lung adenocarcinoma, Walter et al. demonstrated that loss of either Brg1 or Arid1a were selected against in early-stage tumors, but Brg1 loss continued to limit disease progression over time, whereas loss of Arid1a eventually promoted development of higher grade lesions. They also identified Setd2 as a potent tumor suppressor in lung adenocarcinoma [57]. 4 Application of CRISPR-Cas9 Technologies in Cancer Cell Model and Animal Model Generation As described above, the CRISPR system is extremely useful for generation of knockout or knockin cell lines, which are valuable tools for general cancer research including biomarker studies. One or multiple genes can be knocked out or knocked in in primary cells to generate novel tumor cell lines. For example, genome editing of cultured human intestinal organoid with CRISPR-Cas9 can transform the cells into colorectal cancer cell lines [58, 59]. Ogawa et al. used CRISPR/Cas9 technology to target an HRas(G12V)- IRES-td Tomato construct by homologous recombination into the TP53 locus of human cerebral organoids, resulting in transformed cells that rapidly become invasive and destroy surrounding organoid structures, overwhelming the entire organoid. Tumor cells in the organoids can be orthotopically xenografted into immunodeficient NOD/SCID IL2RG(−/−) animals, exhibiting an invasive phenotype and gene expression profiles consistent with mesenchymal subtype human glioblastoma [60]. Oldrini et al. showed that somatic deletion in neural stem cells of a variety of known tumor suppressor genes (Trp53, Cdkn2a, and Pten) leads to high-grade glioma formation [61]. Chromosome rearrangement such as translocation, inversion, deletion, and duplication are potential causes of tumorigenesis. Tumor cell lines can be established using CRISPR system with sgRNAs targeting two different chromosomes or two distal sites in a single chromosome to generate desired chromosome translocations, inversion, or large deletion. For example, utilizing the CRISPR technology, Torres et al. generated human cell lines and primary cells bearing chromosomal translocations resembling those described in acute myeloid leukemia and Ewing’s sarcoma [62]. A fusion between the genes echinoderm microtubuleassociated protein like 4 (EML4) and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) can be generated by an inversion on the short arm of chromosome 2: inv(2)(p21p23). The EML4-ALK oncogene is detected in a subset of human non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC) and is clinically relevant because it confers sensitivity to ALK inhibitors. Maddalo et al. generated a mouse model of Eml4-Alk-driven lung cancer using viral-mediated delivery of the CRISPR/Cas9 system

CRISPR and Cancer Biomarker 309 to somatic cells of adult animals [63]. The reciprocal t(2;13) (q36.1;q14.1) in human alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (A-RMS) creates a pathognomonic PAX3-FOXO1 fusion gene. Lagutina et al. recreated such a chromosome translocation model using a combination of Cre/LoxP and CRISPR-Cas9 systems in mice [64]. Engelholm et al. delivered CRISPR/Cas9 vectors targeting the DnaJ heat shock protein family member B1 gene (Dnajb1) and the protein kinase cAMP-activated catalytic subunit alpha gene (Prkaca) via hydrodynamic tail vein injection to livers of 8-weekold female FVB/N mice. They found generation of the Dnajb1- Prkaca fusion gene in wild-type mice to be sufficient to initiate formation of tumors that have many features of human fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma (FL-HCC) [65]. Animal model systems are one of the most valuable tool to study tumorigenesis and evaluate potential therapeutic agents. With the advance in CRISPR technologies, it is now much more efficient and faster to generate cancer-specific animal models. Furthermore, some more complex animal model involving multiple genes can also be generated in a much shortened time frame. For example, Heckl et al. generated mouse models of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) by delivering combinations of sgRNAs and Cas9 with a lentiviral vector to modify up to five genes in a single mouse hematopoietic stem cell (HSC), leading to clonal outgrowth and myeloid malignancy. Utilizing a Cre-dependent Cas9 knockin mouse, in vivo knockout Tp53 and Lkb1 as well HDR-mediated introduction of Kras(G12D) mutations lead to macroscopic tumors of adenocarcinoma pathology [66]. Hydrodynamic injection to deliver a CRISPR plasmid DNA expressing Cas9 and sgRNAs to the liver that directly target the tumor suppressor genes Pten and Tp53 induced liver tumors in mice [67]. Pancreatic cancers were induced in Ptf1aCre/+;KrasLSL- G12D/+ mice by codelivering of Cas9 and 15 sgRNAs targeting two neutral genetic loci as well as a set of 13 tumor-suppressor genes, which were previously reported to be involved in pancreatic tumorigenesis [68]. Schokrpur et al. showed that a CRISPR/Cas9mediated knockout of von Hippel Lindau (VHL) in the RENCA model lead to morphologic and molecular changes indicative of epithelial- mesenchymal transition (EMT), which in turn drives increased metastasis to the lungs. A better understanding of the mechanisms involved in this phenomenon can guide the search for more effective treatments to combat metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) [69]. 5 Application of CRISPR/Cas9 Technologies in Cancer Diagnosis The CRISPR system can also potentially be directly utilized as biomarker detection tools for cancer diagnosis or following up disease progression during and after therapeutic interventions.

310 Vitaly Balan and Jianbin Wang 5.1 Live Cell The dCas9-based CRISPR system has been utilized for live cell Chromosome Labeling labeling and imaging studies of chromosome organization and and Imaging location. For example, using an EGFP-tagged dCas9 and a structurally optimized sgRNA, Chen et al. showed robust imaging of repetitive elements in telomeres and coding genes in living cells. Furthermore, an array of sgRNAs tiling along the target locus enabled the visualization of nonrepetitive genomic sequences [70]. Subsequently, a two color imaging method was developed using nuclease-deficient orthologous spCas9 and saCas9 fused with different fluorescent proteins [71]. Additional systems such as CRISPRainbow and CRISPR-Sirius for labeling DNA in living cells were also developed using engineered chimeric sgRNA scaffolds that can bind sets of fluorescent proteins [72, 73]. The dCas9-based live cell chromosome labeling and imaging technique can potentially be developed into assays for cancer biomarker detection. 5.2 DNA/RNA The CRISPR system can be utilized for target-specific DNA detec- Detection tion. For example, Pardee et al. developed an assay to detect Zika virus utilizing a novel CRISPR/Cas9-based module, which is able to discriminate against closely related Dengue virus sequences with single-base resolution [74]. Guk et al. later developed a dCas9/ sgRNA-SYBR Green I (SGI)-based DNA-FISH method to detect methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), which is crucial for guiding effective patient treatment and preventing the spread of MRSA infections. The approach can potentially be applied to any target such as various pathogens other than MRSA by simply changing the sgRNA sequence [75]. Deng et al. used in vitro constituted dCas9-sgRNA complexes as probes to label sequence-specific genomic loci fluorescently without global DNA denaturation (Cas9mediated fluorescence in situ hybridization, CASFISH). They demonstrated rapid and robust labeling of repetitive DNA elements in pericentromere, centromere, G-rich telomere, and coding gene loci. Assembling dCas9 with an array of sgRNAs tiling arbitrary target loci, they were able to visualize nonrepetitive genomic sequences. This technology can potentially be developed into a cancer genetic biomarker assay for cancer diagnosis [76]. Besides DNA detection, the CRISPR system can also be utilized for RNA detection. For example, the RNA-guided, RNAtargeting CRISPR effector Cas13a (previously known as C2c2) exhibits a “collateral effect” of promiscuous ribonuclease activity upon target recognition. Gootenberg et al. combined the collateral effect of Cas13a with isothermal amplification to establish a detection platform, termed Specific High-Sensitivity Enzymatic Reporter UnLOCKing (SHERLOCK), to detect specific strains of Zika and Dengue virus, distinguish pathogenic bacteria, genotype human DNA, and identify mutations in cell-free tumor DNA [77]. Later, a field-deployable as well as an updated SHERLOCK version 2 was developed [78, 79].

CRISPR and Cancer Biomarker 311 5.3 DNA Barcoding The CRISPR system is not only an adaptive immune system but and Lineage Tracing also a genetic recorder in bacteria and archaeal. The spacer information is indeed a record of past bacteriophage infections [80]. To enables the elucidation of lineage relationships via the patterns of mutations shared between cells (lineage tracing), McKenna et al. used CRISPR-based genome editing to progressively introduce and accumulate diverse mutations in a DNA barcode (synthetic target arrays for lineage tracing, GESTALT) over multiple rounds of cell division in cell culture and zebrafish [81]. Kalhor et al. developed an approach for engineering evolving DNA barcodes in living cells, using a homing guide RNA (hgRNA) scaffold that directs the Cas9-hgRNA complex to target the DNA locus of the hgRNA itself. This integrated approach can potentially have wide ranging applications, such as in deep lineage tracing, cellular barcoding, molecular recording, dissecting cancer biology, and connectome mapping [82]. Michlits et al. generated complex sgRNA libraries with unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) that allowed for screening of clonally expanded, individually tagged cells, which is named as CRISPR-UMI, a single-cell lineage-tracing methodology for pooled screening to account for cell heterogeneity [83]. The CRISPR-based barcoding and lineage tracing continued to evolve, and whole mouse clone tracing is now possible as demonstrated by Alemany et al. [84] and Kalhor et al. [85]. Intratumor genetic heterogeneity underlies the ability of tumors to evolve and adapt to different environmental conditions. Using CRISPR-based DNA barcoding and lineage tracing technology, Guernet et al. recapitulated and traced the emergence of subpopulations of cancer cells containing mutations of interest [86]. 6 Application of CRISPR/Cas9 Technologies in Cancer Therapy 6.1 Drug As discussed before, the CRISPR system is an important tool in Development (Evaluate discovery and identification of genes important for tumorigenesis, Candidate Drugs or which are essentially potential drug target genes. Besides identifi- Predict cation of potential drug targets, the CRISPR system can also be Drug-Resistance) used to evaluate candidate drugs or predict drug resistance, which is important for guiding the design and development of next- generation drugs [87]. For example, a CRISPR screen of 192 chromatin regulatory domains in murine acute myeloid leukemia cells identifies six known drug targets and 19 additional dependencies [88]. Programmable dCas9-deaminases used with pooled sgRNA libraries targeting PSMB5 enabled directed evolution of a bortezomib-resistant mutation [89]. Similar approach was used to target BCR-ABL and identified known and new mutations conferring imatinib resistance in chronic myeloid leukemia cells [90]. Jost et al. developed a two-tiered CRISPR-mediated chemical-genetic strategy for target identification: combined genome-wide

312 Vitaly Balan and Jianbin Wang knockdown and overexpression screening as well as focused, comparative chemical-genetic profiling. Application of these strategies to rigosertib, a drug in phase three clinical trials for high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome whose molecular target had remained controversial, pointed singularly to microtubules as rigosertib’s target. They have also showed that expression of tubulin with a structure-guided mutation in the rigosertib-binding pocket conferred resistance to rigosertib, establishing that rigosertib kills cancer cells by destabilizing microtubules [91]. Zimmermann et al. used CRISPR screens to identify genes and pathways that mediate cellular resistance to olaparib, a clinically approved PARP inhibitor. In addition to an expected enrichment for genes related to homologous recombination, they discovered that mutations in all three genes encoding ribonuclease H2 sensitized cells to PARP inhibition due to impaired ribonucleotide excision repair. These finding can potentially be exploited for therapeutic purposes due to the frequent deletion of RNASEH2B in metastatic prostate cancer and chronic lymphocytic leukemia [92]. 6.2 Gene and Cell One simple concept to utilize the CRISPR system for cancer ther- Therapy apy is to knock out or knock down the causative gene(s) or essential survival gene(s). Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) presents 6.2.1 Genome Editing the poorest prognosis among the breast cancer subtypes and no current standard therapy. Castro et al. used CRISPR system to knock out Cripto-1, an embryonic stem cell marker, which was present in spindle-like areas and its promoter showed activity in primary TNBC-like mouse tumors. Cripto-1 knockout inhibited tumor growth and pulmonary metastasis, suggesting Cripto-1 as a potential TNBC target [93]. Pan et al. used a genome-scale CRISPR screen to identify mechanisms of tumor cell resistance to killing by cytotoxic T cells, the central effectors of antitumor immunity. They found that inactivation of >100 genes-including Pbrm1, Arid2, and Brd7, which encode components of the PBAF form of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex sensitized mouse B16F10 melanoma cells to killing by T cells [94]. Manguso et al. performed in vivo CRISPR screen and identified tyrosine phosphatase PTPN2 as a potential immunotherapy target. They found deletion of PTPN2 in tumor cells increased the efficacy of immunotherapy by enhancing interferon-γ-mediated effects on antigen presentation and growth suppression [95]. Chemotherapy resistance presents a difficult challenge in treating epithelial ovarian cancer patients, particularly when tumors exhibit resistance to multiple chemotherapeutic agents. A few studies have shown that elevated serum levels of the ovarian cancer biomarker HE4 correlate with tumor chemoresistance, response to treatment, and survival. Ribeiro et al. used CRISPR/Cas technology to knock down HE4 in HE4-overexpressing SKOV3 cells, which partially reversed the chemoresistance [96].

CRISPR and Cancer Biomarker 313 6.2.2 Oncogenic Virus One of the causative agents for tumorigenesis is certain chronic Infection virus infection. For example, Epstein–Barr (EB) virus is a cause of Hodgkin’s disease and Burkitt’s lymphoma [97]. Wang et al. used the CRISPR/Cas9 system to target the genomes of latent EB viral infections in patient-derived cells from a Burkitt’s lymphoma and showed dramatic proliferation arrest and a concomitant decrease in viral load after the treatment [98]. High-risk human papillomaviruses (HPVs), including HPV-16 and HPV-18, are the causative agents of cervical carcinomas and are linked to several other tumors of the anogenital and oropharyngeal regions. Kennedy et al. used the CRISPR system to target two viral oncogenes E6 or E7 region in viral genome in HPV-16- and HPV-18-transformed cells and lead to cell cycle arrest and eventual cell death [99]. Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection causes liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in humans. The CRISPR system was used to target HBV genome in infected cells and significantly reduced viral replication in cell culture and a mouse model [100–102]. 6.2.3 CAR-T Cells One of the exciting recent advancements in cancer immunotherapy and T-iPSCs is the production of CAR-T cells for treating various hematologic cancers. The successful rates for certain hematologic cancers are relatively high in historic point of view. One challenge is the necessity to produce autologous CAR-T cells for each individual patient. To broaden the application of the technology to more patient population in a more convenient way, scientists are trying to generate universal CAR-T cells utilizing programmable endonucleases including ZFN, TALEN, and the CRISPR system. Eyquem et al. utilized CRISPR-mediated knockin to direct a CD19-specific CAR to the T-cell receptor alpha constant (TRAC) locus, which not only results in uniform CAR expression in human peripheral blood T cells, but also enhances T-cell potency, with edited cells vastly outperforming conventionally generated CAR-T cells in a mouse model of acute lymphoblastic leukemia [103]. Ren et al. combined lentiviral delivery of CAR and electrotransfer of Cas9 mRNA and gRNAs targeting endogenous TCR, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and PD1 simultaneously, to generate gene-disrupted allogeneic CAR-T cells deficient of TCR, HLA class I molecule and PD-1. The simultaneous triple genome editing led to enhanced in vivo antitumor activity of the gene-disrupted CAR-T cells [104]. Ren et al. also generated TCR, HLA class I, and Fas triple knockout CAR-T cells and attempted TCR, HLA-I, PD-1, CTLA-4 quadruple knockout CAR-T cells [105]. Another challenge is the application of CAR-T cells to treat solid tumors other than hematologic cancers. The efficacy is generally low for most solid tumors. Possible reasons including the physical barrier for CAR-T cells to migrate into tumors, the presence of immune inhibitory microenvironment at the tumor sites such as inhibitory checkpoint proteins, immune inhibitory cytokines, and

314 Vitaly Balan and Jianbin Wang the presence of myeloid-derived suppressive cells, and antigen escape due to tumor heterogeneity. To overcome part of the problem, scientists are testing combinations of CAR-T with various other treatments, such as anti-PD1, anti-PD-L1, and anti-CTLA-4. An alternative way is to knock out PD1 or other inhibitory check-point genes in CAR-T cells using the CRISPR system. Rupp et al. demonstrated that CRISPR-mediated PD-1 disruption augmented CD19 CAR T cell mediated killing of tumor cells in vitro and + enhanced clearance of PD-L1 tumor xenografts in vivo [106]. Guo et al. generated PD-1 knockout glypican-3 (GPC3)-targeted CAR and demonstrated that the disruption of PD-1 enhanced the in vivo antitumor activity of CAR T cells against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cell PLC/PRF/5 and improved the persistence and infiltration of CAR-T cells in the NSG mice bearing the tumor [107]. Zhang et al. generated LAG-3, another inhibitory check-point molecule, knockout CAR-T cells using CRISPR-mediated gene editing and found that the LAG-3 knockout CAR-T cells displayed robust antigen-specific antitumor activity in cell culture and in murine xenograft model, which is comparable to standard CAR-T cells [108]. In a recent study, Jung et al. used CRISPR/ Cas9 to potentiate CAR-T-cell function by increasing CD3 signaling via knockout of diacylglycerol kinase (DGK), an enzyme that metabolizes diacylglycerol to phosphatidic acid [109]. At Refuge Biotechnologies, we are actively pursuing the next-generation CAR-T cells with higher efficacy and better safety profile by utilizing a dCas9-based CRISPR system to conditionally upregulate or knock down target gene expression, such as PD1 [110]. Such CAR T cells will have normal levels of PD-1 expression in health tissues, but will have reduced PD-1 expression once the cells encountered with tumor cells. Another challenge of chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy is the associated toxicities including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurotoxicity. Sterner et al. generated GM-CSF deficient CART19 cells through CRISPR/Cas9 disruption of GM-CSF during CAR-T cell manufacturing. These GM-CSF knock-out CAR-T cells maintained normal functions and had improved antitumor activity and overall survival compared to conventional CART19. This approach may potentially enhance CAR-T cell function and reduce unwanted treatment associated toxicity, since GM-CSF and its target cells such as monocytes and macrophages are contributors to the development of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurotoxicity [111]. Related to toxicity, the absence of cancer-restricted surface markers is a major impediment to antigen-specific immunotherapy using CAR-T cells. Kim et al. used CRISPR for knocking out CD33 from normal hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), thereby generating a hematopoietic system resistant to CD33-targeted therapy and enabling specific targeting of AML with CAR T cells [112].

CRISPR and Cancer Biomarker 315 Limited T cell availability and proliferative exhaustion present major barriers to successful T cell-based immunotherapies and may potentially be overcome through the use of “rejuvenated” induced pluripotent stem cells derived from antigen-specific T cells (T-iPSCs). Minagawa et al. used CRISPR to knock out a recombinase gene in the T-iPSCs to prevent additional TCR rearrangement and generated CD8αβ T from monocytederived iPSCs that were transduced with an antigen-specific TCR. The regenerated CD8αβ T cells effectively inhibited tumor growth in xenograft cancer models, suggesting these approaches could contribute to safe and effective regenerative T cell immunotherapies [113]. 7 Limitation of the CRISPR-Cas9 Technologies There is no doubt that the CRISPR system is a very powerful tool for cancer research and potential cancer diagnosis and therapy. Notable features of the system include its simplicity in constructing sgRNAs and its capacity to target many genomic loci simultaneously, which enables the simultaneous study of numerous genetic modifications in one step. However, there are also a few main challenges the technology is facing. (1) Reasonable genome editing efficiency can be obtained for a lot of different primary cell types ex vivo, but it is still very challenge to deliver the CRISPR system to some specific target cells/tissues/organs in vivo. In addition, the relative large size of Cas9 protein is apparently not helpful for efficient delivery. (2) Off-target effect is still a concern. However, tremendous progress has been made in generating new Cas9 variants with significantly improved specificity [114, 115]. (3) Due to the complexity of and the involvement of multiple genes/pathways in tumorigenesis, multiple genes often need to be knocked out simultaneously to observe desired phenotype. Multiple double strand breaks in a cell are known to facilitate chromosome translocation [62, 116], which will be a concern for experimental data interpretation as well as future clinical applications. 8 Concluding Remarks The CRISPR technology has become a basic molecular biology tool for biomedical research in general. It has already been applied to the discovery of potential novel cancer biomarkers. We expect to see the CRISPR technology being more broadly adopted by researchers in the biomarker field. More progress in both cancer diagnosis and therapy is expected in the foreseeable future.

# Part V

Phenotyping of Tumor and Immune Cells

## Chapter 15 HLA


326 Barbara Seliger and Soldano Ferrone EMT Epithelial–mesenchymal transition ERAP ER-resident aminopeptidases ER Endoplasmic reticulum HC Heavy chain HDAC Histone deacetylase HDACi Histone deacetylase inhibitors HLA Human leukocyte antigen HNSCC Head and neck squamous cancer iCP Immune checkpoint iCPI Immune checkpoint inhibitor IHC Immunohistochemistry IFN Interferon JAK Janus kinase LOH Loss of heterozygosity LMP Low molecular weight proteins mAb Monoclonal antibody miRNAs MicroRNAs NLRC5 NOD-like receptor caspase recruitment domain containing protein 5 NSCLC Non-small cell lung carcinoma OS Overall survival PLC Peptide loading complex RBP RNA-binding proteins RCC Renal cell carcinoma SNP Single nucleotide polymorphisms TA Tumor antigen TAP Transporter associated with antigen processing TIL Tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte TNBC Triple negative breast cancer tpn Tapasin UCP2 Uncoupling protein 2 β2 -m β2 -microglobulin 1 Introduction It has been known for many years that malignant transformation of human cells is frequently associated with changes in the expression and/or function of the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I antigen processing machinery (APM). These changes, which are in most, but not in all cases due to a partial or complete loss of expression and/or function of the HLA class I APM, are not unique for human cells, since they have been described in many other species [1]. The conservation of these alterations through phylogenetic evolution suggests that they play an important role in the malignant transformation of cells, in the growth of tumors and in the metastatic spread of cancer cells. Despite their importance, only a limited number of investigations have so far characterized the underlying molecular mechanisms of these abnormalities. In in vitro studies,

HLA Class I Abnormalities and Immunotherapy 327 experiments in animal model systems, and some clinical evidence indicate that defects in HLA class I APM may affect the interactions between target cells and cognate T cells. These effects may provide tumor cells with escape mechanisms from recognition and destruction by immune cells in vitro and by host’s immune system in vivo [2]. These escape mechanisms have been suggested to underlie the correlation found in many malignancies between HLA class I APM component defects and clinical course of the disease. In spite of the major role played by HLA class I APM in the interactions of tumor cells with host’s immune system, interest in the analysis and characterization of HLA class I APM expression in malignant cells waned at the end of the last century and at the beginning of the present one. This attitude of the tumor immunology scientific community most likely reflects the limited, if any success of T cell-based immunotherapies for the treatment of malignant diseases. The disappointing clinical results obtained in many large clinical trials shook tumor immunologists’ confidence in the ability of host’s immune system to control tumor cell growth and more importantly increased clinical oncologists’ skepticism about the efficacy of immunotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of cancer. This scenario has drastically changed in the last few years, since therapies with immune checkpoint (iCP)-specific monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) have induced impressive clinical responses in a variable, but significant number of patients with various types of cancer [3, 4]. These clinical results have restored tumor immunologists’ confidence in the role of immune surveillance in the pathogenesis and clinical course of malignant disease and in the ability of patients’ immune system to recognize tumor cells, mount a response against tumor antigens (TA) and eradicate tumor cells. More importantly, the significant clinical responses have convinced clinical oncologists including the most skeptical ones that immunotherapeutic strategies are a viable and clinically effective approach for the treatment of various types of cancer. As a result, immune checkpoint inhibitor (iCPI)-based therapies either as an individual treatment or in combination with other strategies, which enhance host’s immune responses and/or tumor cell susceptibility to immune recognition and/or destruction, have become a major component of the armamentarium routinely used by clinical oncologists for the treatment of cancer [5]. Furthermore, the use of therapies like chemotherapy and radiotherapy, which have been considered for many years to be nonimmunological in nature, has changed, since they are being applied in order to take advantage of their immunomodulatory properties in addition to their cytotoxic effects [6]. The emphasis on the role of TA-specific T cells in the design of immunotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of malignant diseases has rekindled interest in the expression, regulation, and

328 Barbara Seliger and Soldano Ferrone function of HLA class I APM in malignant cells, since this machinery plays a crucial role in the interactions of tumor cells with cognate cytotoxic T cells [1, 7]. This machinery generates 8–11 amino acid long peptides from mostly, although not exclusively, endogenous proteins, loads them on β2 -microglobulin (β2 -m)-associated HLA class I heavy chains (HC), and transports them to the cell membrane for presentation to CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL). Convincing evidence has shown that the efficient sequence of the latter steps requires a fully functional HLA class I APM, since abnormalities in the expression and/or function of its components results in a defective synthesis and/or expression of β2 -m/HLA class I HC/TA derived peptide complexes. Alterations in HLA class I APM components will lead to a downregulation of HLA class I surface expression and can also alter the repertoire of antigenic peptides presented and thus affect the recognition of tumor cells by cognate CTLs. Therefore, in this chapter we first describe the organization and functional properties of HLA class I APM with a discussion of the available methods to assess the expression of its components in tissues. Then we summarize the information related to the frequency of defects in HLA class I APM component expression in cancer and about the underlying molecular mechanisms. Lastly, we discuss the impact of HLA class I APM defects on the response to T cell-based immunotherapies and the rational design of strategies to counteract these defects in order to enhance tumor visibility and efficacy of immunotherapies to eliminate cancer. 2 Organization and Functional Properties of HLA Class I APM β2 -m HLA class I HC tumor antigen (TA)-derived peptide trimolecular complexes synthesized by HLA class I APM mediate the recognition and eradication of tumor cells by CTL. Mostly, not exclusively endogenous proteins are degraded by the multicatalytic proteasome and their active subunits into peptides. The three catalytic subunits β1, β2, and β5 are responsible for the proteolytic activity of the 20S subunit core of the proteasome and initial peptide proteolysis yielding peptides with a correct C-terminal residues. Interferon (IFN)-γ can promote an upregulation of specific catalytic subunits termed the low molecular weight proteins (LMP)2, LMP7 and LMP10, which are incorporated into the 20S proteasome thereby replacing the constitutive β1, β2, and β5 proteasome subunits [8, 9]. The exchange of subunits results in the generation of the immunoproteasome, which has an impact on the quantity and quality of peptides presented by MHC class I molecules. The proteasomal degradation products are shuttled by the heterodimeric transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP) complex consisting of the TAP1 and TAP2 subunits from

HLA Class I Abnormalities and Immunotherapy 329 the cytosol into the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Peptides are then loaded on β2 -m-associated HLA class I HC dimers as part of the multi-subunit peptide loading complex (PLC) [10], which is responsible for loading, editing and final proof reading, before the stable HLA class I peptide complexes are released. The recent characterization of its structure demonstrates a symbiosis of TAP, the ER resident chaperone network in the HLA class I assembly [11]. To generate optimal peptide antigens for binding to HLA class I alleles, peptides are “fine-tuned” through processing at the N-terminal residue by other cytosolic (e.g., leucine aminopeptidase) and/or the ER-resident aminopeptidases ERAP1/2 prior to its association with MHC class I antigens. This step is assisted by various chaperone molecules, such as ERp57, calnexin (CNX) [12], calreticulin (CRT), and tapasin (tpn). The ER-resident CNX and CRT are involved in the stabilization, folding and association of immature HLA class I HC and β2 -m prior to the generation of the PLC. Tpn serves as a bridge between MHC class I, β2 -m, TAP, and CRT and is essential to form a stable PLC [13]. Furthermore, tpn plays a key role in the quality control of peptides and thus influences the presented peptide repertoire presented to cognate CTL [14, 15]. Upon peptide binding the PLC dissociates and the resulting HC/β2 -m/TA trimer then travels via the trans- Golgi to the plasma membrane of target cells and is there presented to CD8+ CTLs. 3 Methodology to Analyze HLA Class I APM Component Expression in Tissues Both molecular and immunohistochemical techniques have been developed and used to analyze HLA class I APM component expression in tissues. RNAseq or Nanostring analyses provide information about the expression of the components analyzed at the RNA level. They require a limited amount of tissues. Frozen tissues are preferable to formalin – fixed tissues, although techniques have been developed to extract RNA from fixed tissues. Structural alterations or epigenetic changes of HLA class I APM components are determined using DNA extracted from either formalin- fixed or fresh frozen tissues. DNA and RNA are generally extracted from a mixture of malignant or dysplastic cells with normal stromal cells and infiltrating immune cells. This contamination may lead to false positive results. Furthermore, these techniques do not provide information about the degree of heterogeneity in the expression of a tested molecule in the cell population analyzed. However, this limitation can be overcome by recently developed techniques, which allow the analysis of the expression of a molecule at the single cell level, but their routine use is generally limited by their high costs. Lastly, the results from RNAseq and Nanostring analyses are an indirect

330 Barbara Seliger and Soldano Ferrone indication of HLA class I APM component expression, since mRNA levels do not necessarily correlate with protein expression. This possibility has been further strengthened by the identification of microRNAs (miRNAs) and RNA-binding proteins (RBP) affecting the expression of HLA class I APM components [16–18]. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) measures HLA class I component expression at the protein level utilizing antibodies as probes. The evaluation of the results generally relies on the microscopic reading of the stained tissues although reading with machines is being developed. IHC techniques provide information about the expression level of a molecule in a cell population and its degree of heterogeneity. The results are reliable and reproducible when the molecule being tested is not expressed or is homogeneously expressed in a tumor cell population. On the other hand, the results are limited by the subjective evaluation, when a molecule is weakly expressed and/ or has a heterogeneous expression. An additional limitation is represented by the fact that IHC techniques provide only limited information about the functional properties of the molecule analyzed. A number of HLA class I APM component specific antibodies have been developed [19–23], from which the majority can be successfully implemented for the analyses of paraffin-embedded tissues. In contrast, the W6/32 antibody recognizing HLA class I HC (HLA-A, -B, -C, -E and -F) in association with β2 -m could only be used on fresh frozen tissues [24]. The development of novel immunohistochemical based methods, like the multispectral imaging (MSI), allows deeper insights into the tumor microenvironment in association with the expression of, for example, APM components in specific cell populations as well as their spatial distribution [25]. 4 Frequency of Defects in HLA Class I APM Component Expression in Various Cancer Types and Underlying Mechanisms Cancers can hijack mechanisms to protect themselves from immune cell attack. Many studies have been reported loss or downregulation of HLA class I surface expression in a large number of cancer types of distinct origin. These defects have often been associated with disease progression, reduced survival of patients and level of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL). The literature about this topic has been recently reviewed and discussed by one of us (SF). The interested reader is referred to the pertinent publications [2]. It is noteworthy that aberrant HLA class I APM component expression has not been systematically analyzed across various cancers (Table 1). The studies vary regarding the number of tumor lesions and HLA class I APM components analyzed. The major amount of information exists regarding the frequency of defective HLA class I HC and β2 -m expression across different tumor types

In contrast, the expression of the proteasomal subunits LMP2 and LMP7 and the chaperones calnexin, calreticulin, and ERp57 have been investigated to a limited extent in tumors. The events leading to impaired HLA class I expression could be at the genetic (mutations, gene deletions, loss of heterozygosity (LOH)) or at the regulatory level. These effects can be (1) directly on HLA class I genes, or (2) as a result of altered peptide generation by targeting immunoproteasomal components LMP2, LMP7 and LMP10 and other peptidases, such as ERAP1/2, (3) peptide transport and loading of HLA class I involving the TAP1/2 subunits as well as the chaperones CNX, CRT, ERp57, and tpn,

332 Barbara Seliger and Soldano Ferrone and (4) defective export via the trans Golgi. Here we will summarize the most important conclusions. Recently, NLRC5 (NOD-like receptor (NLR) caspase recruitment (CARD) domain containing protein 5) has been identified as an MHC class I transactivator, which induces not only MHC class I genes, but also APM components including LMP2, TAP1 and β2 -m [26, 27]. In addition, NLRC5 expression is highly correlated with MHC class I and APM component expression in many tissues [28]. Lastly, NLRC5 expression positively correlated with CD8, granzyme B and perforin mRNA levels in CD8+ T cells [28]. Regarding abnormalities of HLA class I antigens, HLA class I loss has been reported in 92% of cervical cancers as an early occurring event in cervical carcinogenesis [29], in 71% of breast cancer, which was inversely correlated with HER-2/neu expression [30] and in 64% of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [31]. Furthermore, allele-specific loss of HLA class I antigens was found in 40% of early NSCLC, which was associated with a subclonal neoantigen burden and an altered immune reactivity due to a high selective pressure [32]. In melanoma, HLA-A2 loss was associated with a complex rearrangement of chromosome 6p [33] or simultaneous mutations in TAP1 [34]. Recently, a strong correlation of HPV-associated cervical cancer with risk and protective HLA haplotypes has been reported in a genome-wide association study [35, 36]. Furthermore in this disease, the expression of HLA-A and -B is also often transcriptionally downregulated, which has a significant impact on the HPV16-related pathogenesis of cervical cancer [36]. Epigenetic changes in HLA class I APM components including increased methylation and altered histone acetylation cause reduced expression of this pathway [37]. In addition, a diminished expression of the constitutive and IFN-γ inducible proteasome subunits significantly impacts the quantity of suitable peptides available for loading on HLA class I dimers. This results in a downregulation of MHC class I surface expression and has been found in a large number of different c ancer types. Next to the (immune)proteasome subunits, loss or down-regulation of ERAP1 results in qualitative and quantitative changes of HLA class I surface expression in tumors [38–40]. This could occur at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional level [39]. However, it is noteworthy that ERAP1 expression is highly variable in tumors and can be found either upregulated or downregulated in tumors [40]. In cervical cancer and head and neck squamous cell cancer (HNSCC), the reduced expression and function of ERAP1 is associated with low HLA class I surface antigen expression. Loss or downregulation of TAP1 and/or TAP2 is found in many tumor cell lines, primary tumors and metastases when compared to corresponding normal or tumor adjacent cells. This is associated with a reduced function and diminished HLA class I

HLA Class I Abnormalities and Immunotherapy 333 surface expression as shown in particular for cervical cancer, renal cell carcinoma (RCC), melanoma and colorectal cancer (CRC) [34, 41–45]. A synchronous loss or downregulation of both TAP1 and TAP2 expression or a single subunit defect has been detected in tumor cells. In addition, a coordinate downregulation of TAP, β2 -m and HLA class I HC was found, for example, in CRC [46]. All these distinct phenotypes lead to impaired HLA class I surface expression due to changes in the availability of antigenic peptides for loading of the HLA class I dimer in the ER suggesting that TAP is essential for the formation of stable HLA class I trimeric complexes [47]. This was further underlined by reconstitution of HLA class I expression following TAP gene transfer [48]. The expression of other components of the PLC, like CRT and CNX, is altered not only in different solid tumor types including melanoma, bladder, prostate, hepatocellular, esophageal, colon, cervical, and breast cancers but also in hematopoietic malignancies. However, these changes might be associated with other cellular functions, such as cell cycle regulation, cell migration and adhesion, and ER stress. In addition, impaired tpn expression severely affects most HLA I alleles resulting in fewer stable HLA class I surface antigens [49]. Heterogeneous but an overall downregulation of expression of tpn levels is detected in HNSCC, NSCLC, CRC, RCC, and pancreatic carcinoma when compared to control tissues [50], which directly correlate with HLA class I surface expression and reduced CD8+ T cell responses [51]. Since HLA class I abnormalities are mainly driven by regulatory mechanisms, alterations in NLRC5 expression, which globally affect the MHC class I pathway have been suggested. Indeed, NLRC5 mRNA expression levels are often downregulated in solid tumors compared to healthy controls. This could be due to promoter methylation, copy number loss, somatic mutations, or transcriptional downregulation. These defects are strongly associated with the a diminished expression of the majority of HLA class I APM components [28] suggesting that NLRC 5 expression in tumors is important for HLA class I expression as well as for the recruitment of CD8+ T cells [52]. 5 Clinical Relevance of HLA Class I APM Component Defects in Malignant Tissues with Special Emphasis on Its Impact on Clinical Response to T Cell-Based Immunotherapy HLA class I APM component downregulation/loss has been shown to be associated with a shorter disease free interval and/or overall survival (OS) in many types of cancer. However, exceptions to this rule have been reported. For instance, HLA class I down-regulation has been shown to be associated with a prolonged OS in CRC and NSCLC [53].

334 Barbara Seliger and Soldano Ferrone Reduced expression of the immunoproteasome in early disease stage correlates with an increased metastasis formation and disease recurrence [54]. Furthermore, SNPs in LMP2 and LMP7 are associated with a worse OS in cervical carcinoma. This association appears to be a consequence of altered protein functions [55, 56]. Loss of ERAP1 expression associated with a poorer prognosis and OS in human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive cervical carcinoma may restrict the ability to generate TA derived peptides, thereby reducing HLA class I surface expression [57]. This was due to an SNP in ERAP1, which has been associated with poorer prognosis and disease progression in this disease. Furthermore, a combination of SNPs in ERAP1, LMP7, and TAP2 is associated with an increased risk of developing HPV+ cervical cancer. In addition, the presence of a homozygous ERAP1 haplotype (ERAP1-56 major and ERAP-127 minor) correlates with a significantly worse OS, highlighting ERAP1 as an independent predictor of survival. The functional consequences of these SNPs are currently unknown but may alter the generated TA derived peptide repertoire and reduce TA-specific CTL responses suggesting a significant role of ERAP1 in the control of tumors. In triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), ERAP1 low levels were also associated with a significant shorter recurrence free and overall survival [58]. Defective TAP1 and TAP2 expression is also associated with a poor patients’ prognosis in many types of cancer [59]. For example in melanoma, HNSCC, esophageal cancer, NSCLC and CRC, TAP1 and/or TAP2 downregulation was significantly correlated with the development of metastases and a poor patients’ survival, suggesting that TAP might serve as an independent prognostic marker in these diseases [45, 60–65]. A systematic meta-analysis of TAP1 polymorphisms demonstrated that the allele of TAP2-rs4148876, but not TAP1-rs1135216, TAP1-rs4148873, TAP2-rs2228396, TAP2-rs241447, and TAP2-rs4148873, might be a potential biomarker for assessing cancer risk [66]. A role of CNX in ER stress has been implicated in cancer. An increased CNX expression is linked with poor prognosis in CRC and serves as a diagnostic marker in lung cancer. The reduced expression of the thiol oxidoreductase, ERp57 involved in the PLC formation is an independent predictor of OS in cervical carcinoma and is associated with disease progression in gastric cancer [67, 68]. Low levels of tpn expression are also frequently found in human tumor cell lines, which may be associated with other HLA class I APM component downregulations [69]. More recently, a reduced tpn expression, which has been found in 48% cases of CRC, has been shown to be correlated with prognosis and CTL responses in CRC; high tpn expression levels correlate with a degree of CD8+ T cell infiltration independent of HLA class I expression levels [70]. An association of functional tpn loss with

HLA Class I Abnormalities and Immunotherapy 335 disease progression is observed in melanoma with a significant downregulation in advanced disease stages [71]. However, tpn expression is not always associated with a positive outcome: Increased tpn expression in the murine pancreatic tumor cell line Panc02 reduced the presentation of an immunodominant TA resulting in lack of immune recognition. Therefore, the activity of tpn in tumors can modulate both the quality and quantity of TA derived peptides presented by MHC class I surface antigens to cognate CD8+ T cells [72]. Concerning NLRC5, TCGA data analysis also indicated that its expression was associated with an increased patients’ OS in melanoma, HNSCC, bladder, rectal, and cervical cancer [28], but with a worse patients’ survival in brain cancer and NSCLC [28, 73]. 6 Immune Resistance Mechanisms to T Cell-Based Immunotherapy It has been suggested that during clonal evolution and selection cancer cells can acquire defects in antigen processing and IFN signaling pathways [74]. There exists a functional landscape of mechanisms as described above that endow tumor cells with the ability to evade immunosurveillance leading to intrinsic (Table 2) and acquired immune resistances (Table 3) [75, 76]. Recently, a number of novel immunotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of cancer have been established, which are based on inhibiting Table 2 Intrinsic immune resistance mechanisms Tumor cell-based Absent/low TA expression Low mutational burden Loss of viral antigen and TA expression Methylation of TA Absent/low HLA class I Mutation/downregulation of TAP antigen presentation Deletion/mutation/downregulation of β2 -m Deletion/mutation/downregulation/LOH of HLA class I molecules Methylation of HLA class I molecules Mutation/downregulation of IFN signaling components Altered oncogenic signaling (e.g., MAPK, WNT), altered expression of major APM components Cell extrinsic mechanisms (TME-based) Lack of T cells with TA specific TCR Altered expression of iCPs Immune suppressive cells Immune suppressive cytokines and metabolites Acidic pH Hypoxia Altered composition of the immune cell repertoire

336 Barbara Seliger and Soldano Ferrone Table 3 Acquired immune resistance mechanisms Molecule Mechanisms Immunotherapy Tumor entity References HLA class I HC loss/ Mutation iCPI, ACT Melanoma [75] downregulation TA loss Methylation peptide vaccination, ACT Melanoma [70–72, 78] β2 -m Mutation iCPI Melanoma [70, 71] JAK1/JAK2 Mutation iCPI Melanoma [74] HLA downregulation Transcriptional iCPI, ACT Melanoma [77, 78] APM downregulation Transcriptional iCPI, ACT Melanoma [77, 78] APLNR Downregulation, iCPI Melanoma [76] mutation processes, through which cancer adapts and evades from an immune response. Thus, intrinsic and adaptive resistance mechanisms are key clinical barriers to improve the outcome of cancer patients and their in depth identification might lead to the development of personalized immunotherapies tailored to overcome therapy resistance and block the evasion process of a particular cancer protecting itself from the immune system [77, 78]. Despite the recent success of immunotherapies with increased response rates, 30–40% of patients who initially objectively responded to this treatment relapse over time even under continued treatment [79]. This might be due to intrinsic resistance to immunotherapies, which can be, for example, predetermined by irreversible changes in HLA class I APM and IFN signal pathway components [80]. This might lead to loss of T cell function and lack or impaired T cell recognition. Already in the 1990s it was reported that some patients who initially responded to immunotherapy with IL-2, TIL, or peptide vaccination could develop resistances through the loss of HLA class I molecules, β2 -m or TA [81–83]. Inhibition of adaptive immune resistance is the mechanistic basis of responses to PD-1 or PD-L1 blocking antibodies and may be of relevance for the development of other cancer immunotherapy strategies. Based on experimental models as well as on human tumors, mutations such as loss of either the maternal or paternal HLA haplotype have been shown to limit the susceptibility to immunotherapy. For example, LOH at HLA loci have been found in resistant lesions from tumors treated with tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL) targeting the KRAS gene [84]. Since the presence of the HLA-C∗08:02 allele was required for the presentation of the KRAS- G12D neoantigen and tumor recognition by T cells, its loss was

HLA Class I Abnormalities and Immunotherapy 337 proposed to be directly associated with immune evasion. Thus, there is a link between haplotype, antitumor immunity, and neoantigen prediction. This was further strengthened by McGranahan and coauthors’ report demonstrating that LOH plays a key role in the initiation as well as in the evolution of NSCLC [32]. However, the high mutational load and low levels of HLA class I expression in tumors without HLA LOH suggest alternative mechanisms of immune evasion and/or disruption of neoantigen presentation including mutations in β2 -m, janus kinases (JAKs), and NLRC5 or downregulation of HLA class I APM components. Recently, the development of resistances during immunotherapies has become into focus of research. So far, it has not been clear how important these abnormalities of HLA class I APM molecules are in tumor evolution of different cancer types. In a melanoma model, loss of HLA class I in metastasis, but not in primary tumors prevents T cell recognition of neoantigens [85]. Zaretsky and coauthors described a new and homozygous truncating mutation in β2 -m and loss-of-function mutations in JAK1 and JAK2 leading to lack of HLA class I surface expression upon iCPI therapy [86]. In contrast, in a cohort of lung cancer patients resistant to iCPI, recurrent mutations or copy number changes of HLA class I APM components were not detected. An acquired homozygous loss of β2 -m leading to loss of HLA class I cell surface expression was found in one tumor and a matched patient-derived xenograft (PDX), while β2 -m downregulation was also detected in two additional PDXs established from iCPI-resistant tumors [87]. A CRISP/Cas screening approach recently identified loss of function mutations in the apelin receptor (APLNR), which can interact with the JAK1 that modulates responses to T cells. Downregulation of APLNR expression results in resistance to immunotherapy [88]. Next to rare structural alterations of HLA class I and IFN pathway components, dynamic transcriptional suppression of HLA class I genes presenting the targeted viral epitope in the resistant tumors as a consequence of high CTL-mediated immunologic pressure has been recently shown, which is reversible. Transcriptional suppression of HLA class I loci and APM components may underlie resistance to other immunotherapies, including checkpoint inhibitors and adoptive T cell therapy (ACT). This will have also an impact on the design of improved immunotherapy treatments [89, 90]. Based on transcriptional profiling of iCPI treated patients and experimental models, a role of MHC class II expression on tumor cells in the prediction of response to anti-PD1 treatment has also recently been discussed [91]. This is mediated by the recruitment of CD4+ T cells and development of dependency on PD-1 and LAG-3 expression, which was upregulated in anti-PD1 resistant MHC class II expression tumors. This was due to an enhanced expression of the HLA class II receptor FCRL6 expressed on NK

338 Barbara Seliger and Soldano Ferrone and T cells, suggesting an MHC class II-mediated context-dependent mechanism of adaptive resistance to PD-1-targeting immunotherapies [91]. In addition, the cellular heterogeneity and plasticity involved in shaping the TME and in controlling antitumor immunity has to be taken into account. Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of tumor cells might also contribute to immune escape by shaping the TME and decrease the susceptibility to immune effector cells. Thus, EMT might serve as a candidate predictive marker for monitoring of the immunotherapies or as a target to overcome therapy resistance to optimize treatment efficacy [92]. Indeed, there exists evidence of EMT as a known mechanism of immune escape in melanoma tumors not responding to iCPI. This might be due to elevated histone H3 lysine (27) trimethylation (H3K27me3), decreased E-cadherin and other protein expression indicating a more mesenchymal phenotype in nonresponding tumors [93]. 7 Modulating Resistance Mechanisms Underlying T Cell-Based Immunotherapy There exists evidence that monotherapies using iCPI, ACT or other immunotherapeutic strategies are not that effective and result in the development of acquired resistances [94]. Combinations of immunotherapies and/or with other therapies might overcome resistance associated with treatment with single-agent efforts [95–97]. There exists a large array of possibilities to revert the resistance of immune escape, which depend on the underlying mechanisms. On the one hand, loss or downregulation of HLA class I APM components due to their structural alterations could be reverted by gene transfer. For example, restoring tpn expression in murine lung carcinoma (CMT.64) restored MHC class I antigen expression and increased the CD8+, CD4+ and CD11C+ infiltrate to the tumor site. In addition, when both tpn and TAP functions were restored, a significantly greater protective response was generated [98] suggesting that proper function of multiple components of the MHC class I pathway are required to generate a maximal response. Similar results were obtained by restoring TAP expression levels in human tumor cells resulting in enhanced MHC class I expression associated with increases of TA-specific immune responses and survival [34, 48, 65]. However, this approach is only applicable in experimental models and human tumor cells as proof of principle, but not in the clinical implementation. Recently, NLRC5 has been shown to be a major transcriptional regulator of HLA class I APM components [28]. Since NLRC5 alterations were found in many tumors, high NLRC5 expression levels might restore HLA class I APM component expression. Indeed, stable overexpression of NLRC5 in B16 mela-

HLA Class I Abnormalities and Immunotherapy 339 noma cells expressing very low levels of APM components [99] resulted in their reconstitution, which was also associated with a reduced tumor growth in vivo [100]. Furthermore, reconstitution of the transcription factor E2F1, which is involved in modulating tpn expression, leads to an increased MHC class I surface expression [101]. Not only the enhancement of the expression of HLA class I APM components, but also rather their inhibition might result in an increased immunogenicity. Inhibition of ERAP1 activity by respective inhibitors might provide a tool to induce CD8+ T cell responses [102], since in some experimental models upregulation of ER was associated with a reduced T cell response. Emerging evidence suggests key roles of tumor extracellular matrix (ECM) components and their proteolytic remodeling products in regulating the cancer-immunity cycle [103]. Indeed, the small leucine rich proteoglycan family member biglycan (BGN) has recently been associated with an altered MHC class I expression [104]. BGN expression could be downregulated by oncogenic transformation [105]. Reconstitution of BGN in oncogenic transformants or treatment with exogenous recombinant BGN resulted not only in a reduced tumor formation, but also in increased expression of MHC class I APM components, which is also accompanied by enhanced T cell infiltration of tumors [104]. Next to reconstitution of structurally altered APM components, expression of transcriptional regulators and ECM molecules, deficient expression mediated by deregulation could be restored by treatment with cytokines, in particular IFN-α, IFN-γ, and TNF-α [106, 107]. Most of the HLA class I APM components are regulated by IFN-γ due to IFN-γ responsive elements in their promoters [108–110]. Thus, IFN-γ stimulation is often able to restore expression of antigen-processing machinery (APM) in tumor cell lines, furthermore, IFN-γ secreted by TIL might be responsible for HLA class I APM expression in tumor lesions. Therefore, targeting HLA class I APM components and enhancing their expression might increase the sensitivity of tumor cells to T cell-based immunotherapies. Hypermethylation and alterations in histone acetylation, of HLA class I APM components have been reported in various cancers. For example, epigenetic changes in the HLA class I APM pathway play an important role for impaired expression of these components as recently shown in Merkel cell carcinoma [111]. The silencing of HLA class I APM components is due to histone deacetylation and could be restored by HDAC inhibition suggesting the use of HDACi in combinatorial strategies to enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy [112]. This holds also for the treatment with demethylating agents, such as azacytidine or guadecitabine, which either directly or indirectly upregulates HLA class I APM component expression [113–115].

340 Barbara Seliger and Soldano Ferrone This further promotes the recruitment of CD8+T cells in the TME and potentiates T cell responses. Therefore, the combination of demethylating agents with immunotherapies might potentiate TA-specific T cell immunity. Recently, modulating the metabolism pathway might enhance immunogenicity of tumors. The mitochondrial uncoupling protein 2 (UCP2) expression levels have been shown to be associated with an increased survival of tumor patients, correlated with the IFNregulated gene expression as well as an enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration. Overexpression of UCP2 in tumors promotes an inflammatory microenvironment, which counteracts acquired resistance to T cell-based immunotherapies [116]. Due to an increase in understanding of the tumor immune escape mechanisms and their modulation leading to intrinsic and acquired immune resistances [86, 117, 118] (Tables 2 and 3), strategies to combat therapeutic resistance to immunotherapy are currently investigated including the reprogramming of immunologically “cold” tumors (low immune cell infiltration, low TCR diversity) into “hot” tumors (high immune cell infiltration, high TCR diversity) [119–121]. This involves an enhancement of endogenous T cell function [77, 122–124] or efficacy of adoptive transfer of TA-specific T lymphocytes by ex vivo expansion of TIL [125] or by the use of TA-engineered T cells mediated by transduction with chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) or TCRs [126, 127]. For example, the combination of anti-CTLA-4 and anti- PD1 results in significantly higher response rates to therapy associated with an improved patients’ survival [128, 129] due to inhibition of several iCP inducing the activity of tumor-specific T cells [130–132], which have both overlapping and unique effects on TA-specific T cells [122]. Furthermore, combining immune modulation of the TME with iCPI and/or vaccinations or even targeted therapies are currently tested in diverse clinical trials [133]. The rationale for combining these treatments is based on their substantial synergistic effects on antitumor immunity due to increased HLA class I antigens and reprogramming of the immune suppressive TME by increasing T cell infiltration and reducing immune suppressive cytokines and metabolites [134] and enhancing T cell function [135]. Emerging strategies to enhance responses to immunotherapy are being developed based on novel insights into T cell and overall immune function. Examples of this include insights into metabolic reprogramming of T cells to enhance therapeutic responses [136, 137] and via modulation of the gut microbiome to augment responses to cancer immunotherapy [138–140]. One challenge is to validate the different combination strategies due to the distinct kinetics of immune responses as well as the limited human and technical resources available. Therefore, there exists an urgent need to test these combinations in appropriate preclinical models

HLA Class I Abnormalities and Immunotherapy 341 and expedite clinical translation through novel approaches to clinical trial design. Ex vivo profiling of iCPI blockade or combinations using organoids might help to develop novel combinations [141]. Recently, patients’ specific responsiveness can be predicted through readily assayable proteins and histone epigenetic marks, and pathways activated in nonresponders, which can be used as targets to enhance responsiveness [93]. For example, the histone methyltransferase Ezh2 has been shown to control several tumor cell-intrinsic and extrinsic resistance mechanisms. Notably, T cell infiltration selectively correlated with high EZH2-PRC2 complex activity in human melanoma. During anti-CTLA-4 or IL-2 immunotherapy in mice, intratumoral tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) production and T cell accumulation resulted in increased Ezh2 expression in melanoma cells, which in turn silenced their own immunogenicity and antigen presentation. Ezh2 inactivation reversed this resistance and synergized with anti-CTLA-4 and IL-2 immunotherapy to suppress melanoma growth by PD-L1 down-regulation suggesting that Ezh2 serves as a molecular switch controlling melanoma escape during T cell-targeting immunotherapies [142]. Furthermore, HDAC inhibitors could upregulate PD-L1 ligands and augment immunotherapy with PD-1 blockade. Mice receiving this combination therapy had a slower tumor progression and increased survival compared with control and single-agent treatments. Comparable results were obtained in a lung carcinoma model and a triple negative breast cancer [143, 144]. These results highlight the ability of epigenetic modifiers to augment immunotherapies, providing a rationale for combining HDAC inhibitors with PD-1 blockade as a promising strategy for the treatment of different tumor entities [145]. 8 Conclusions Malignant transformation of cells is often associated with diminished expression of HLA class I APM components, but variable frequencies. These have functional relevance leading to reduced antitumoral T cell responses and are of clinical significance by their correlation with disease progression and poor prognosis of patients. Recently, these abnormalities have been reported to play a role in the resistance to iCPI-based immunotherapies. Indeed, despite the impressive advances of durable clinical responses, a large number of patients develop resistances during therapy. The underlying resistance mechanisms have a high proportion of overlap with the general immune escape strategies of tumors. Increased knowledge into these processes might provide insights into the acquired resistance mechanisms, which could then help to develop strategies to overcome these resistances by their reprogramming.

High-Parameter Immune Profiling with CyTOF 355 The advantages of adopting mass cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF) methods as opposed to high dimensional flow cytometry include [2]:
1. Negligible signal overlap between parameters, creating a lower
background and little or no need for signal compensation.
2. A higher number of parameters, allowing single-tube analysis
of 40+ markers. 1.1 Markers Our goal for developing this reference panel was to perform comto Identify prehensive immune monitoring, covering all major immune cell and Characterize populations, while providing flexibility for project-specific markers Immune Cell Subsets to be added. Our reference panel (Table 1, Fig. 1a–c) was designed to comprehensively and reproducibly identify:
1. Major lineages of T and B cells, natural killer (NK) cells,
myeloid and granulocyte populations found in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and other tissues.
2. Minor T cell subsets such as regulatory T cells, and exhaustion
markers such as PD-1 and TIM3.
3. Cytokine-producing cells (optionally).
4. Blood cell tumors in the context of other immune cell types.
5. Functional markers of antigen presenting cells such as mono-
cytes and dendritic cells.
6. Other study-specific markers using the ten empty channels.
After identification of live single cells, all immune cell subpopulations expressing CD45 are identified, through cell surface and intracellular markers, including the lymphoid lineage in which T cells could be further subdivided into CD4+ T-helper (Th) cells, CD8+ T cells, natural killer T (NKT) cells and γδ T cells. Additionally, using differential expression patterns of CD27, CD45RA, CD45RO and CCR7, several maturation states of T cells such as naïve, effector, effector memory and central memory can be discriminated [3]. In addition, regulatory T cells (Tregs) are identified through high expression of CD25 (interleukin-2 receptor alpha chain), low to negative levels of the IL-7 receptor CD127, and expression of the lineage defining transcription factor FoxP3. Figure 1a shows a general T cell subsetting strategy using this panel. Furthermore, other immune cell lineages and various functional subsets of each population are identified. B cell maturation is characterized via CD27 and CD38 expression. Monocyte subsets are distinguished based on their expression of CD14 and CD16, and NK cell subsets based on their combinatorial expression of CD16 and CD56 (Hartmann et al., manuscript submitted).

356 Bita Sahaf et al. Other functionally relevant proteins may be investigated using this panel. CD25, HLA-DR, and CD38 can help determine the activation state of T cells, while Ki-67 expression identifies actively proliferating cells across multiple cell types. This panel allows for quantification of the immune checkpointrelated molecules and exhaustion markers such as PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4, and TIM-3 in various cell types (Hartmann et al., Cell Reports, in press [7]). The robustness and reproducibly of this panel has been confirmed in staining of different tissue types such as PBMC, whole blood, bone marrow, and tissue biopsies, all relevant for investigating immune modulation after immunotherapy. Several modifications to the panel have also been tested. As shown in Fig. 1b, intracellular cytokines are detected in T cells after in vitro stimulation with PMA + ionomycin while 1a shows gating strategy for T cells. Figure 1c shows the gating strategy for a modified reference panel for phenotypic characterization of CAR-T cells. 1.2 Minimizing In addition to considerations taken to develop a comprehensive Experimental panel, minimizing experimental variability is necessary for compa- Variability rability of high dimensional data and down-stream automation of data processing. Our efforts to minimize experimental variability include the following experimental strategies:
1. Processing batched samples as a single composite of multi-
plexed barcoded samples to reduce intersample variability.
2. Inclusion of a labeled spike-in sample as an internal reference
control to monitor variability between separately stained samples.
3. Lyophilization of the antibody cocktail, reducing the variabil-
ity introduced by errors in pipetting or degradation of liquid reagents. 2 Materials
