2. Run Eu Beads (151Eu and 153 Eu) for 120 s; the bead count
needs to be <10,000 and singlet mean dual count should be 1000 and 1500 respectively.

360 Bita Sahaf et al.
3. If these parameters are not met, the machine needs to be
cleaned and retuned.
4. Immediately prior to acquisition, resuspend each sample in
1 mL CSM; spin for 5 min at 600 × g 4 °C, aspirate.
5. Resuspend each sample in 1 mL ddH O; spin for 5 min at
2 600 × g 4 °C, aspirate.
6. Resuspend each sample in 1 mL ddH O; spin for 5 min at
2 600 × g 4 °C, aspirate.
7. Keep samples on ice until CYTOF acquisition.
8. Make 1× EQ beads solution: add 1 mL 10× EQ beads to
9 mL ddH O. 2
9. For each sample acquisition: resuspend each sample at a con-
centration of 750,000 cells/mL with 1× EQ beads solution.
10. Filter sample through a cell strainer cap into a 5 mL tube and
load onto the CyTOF instrument.
11. Acquire 250,000 events/sample.
12. Postacquisition: normalize FCS files using Fluidigm normal-
izer (software version 6.5.358). 3.9 Data Analysis 1. CyTOF FCS files can be analyzed using a variety of approaches. In general, analyses focus on identifying defined immune subsets on the basis of canonical marker expression patterns, and evaluating changes in the expression of dynamic markers within these cell subsets. This can be accomplished through manual gating (Fig. 1) or automated clustering approaches (Fig. 5; Note 9). 4 Notes
1. Cell thawing media: It is critical to add the benzonase right
before thawing the cells into the thawing media. Benzonase may be deactivated if heated to denaturation and kept too long in warmed media.
2. Rhodium-103 is a nucleic acid intercalator that will preferen-
tially permeate and accumulates in cells with compromised membrane integrity, hence allowing dead cell discrimination based on higher staining intensity in these cells. When staining thawed cells, we recommend at least a 1 h cell rest at 37 °C for better results. Typically, we acquire stained samples within 24 h; however, rhodium intercalation is reversible, and Rh103 signal may be diluted out if samples are stored too long prior to CyTOF acquisition. An alternative approach for dead cell labeling is the use of cisplatin, which binds covalently to proteins and may offer more flexibility in postponing sample acquisition.

High-Parameter Immune Profiling with CyTOF 361
3. Generally, pooling samples will improve sample processing
efficiency and reduce technical variability, facilitating more accurate comparisons of samples within the pool. Barcoding refers to tagging individual samples with unique combinations of metals, after which the cells are pooled, processed, stained and acquired as a multiplexed single sample. Advantages of barcoding include: (a) S ince all the samples are stained in a single tube, all cells will be exposed to the same concentration of antibodies. Uniform antibody exposure eliminates tube-to-tube variability in staining. (b) A cquiring the specimen as one multiplexed sample abrogates any detector sensitivity drift during the time it takes to acquire the whole sample. This protocol uses live-cell barcoding, where a combination of antibodies against cell surface markers sodium– potassium pump (CD298) and β2-microglubulin (b2m) is used to barcode the cells [4]. Indium conjugation of the anti-CD298 (clone 2M2, BioLegend) and anti-b2m (clone, LNH-94; BioLegend) is performed using the MaxPar X8 antibody labeling kit obtained from Fluidigm and following the manufacturer’s instructions. Monoisotopic platinum conjugation of anti-CD298 and anti-b2m of four different platinum isotypes (194Pt, 195Pt, 196Pt, and 198Pt) is done via direct covalent binding of platinum isotype to the antibodies as described [5]. Briefly, 1 mM stock solution of isotopically enriched cisplatin in DMSO (custom order Fluidigm) is preconditioned for 48 h in 37 °C and stored at −20 °C. Buffer exchange is performed on anti-CD298 and anti-b2m in a 50 KD MW cut off filter, and reduced with 4 mM TCEP (ThermoFisher) for 30 min at 37 °C and washed 2 times with C buffer (Fluidigm). 20 μL of the 1 mM monoisotopic cisplatin solution (equivalent to 20 nmol) is diluted in 1 mL of C buffer and added to the antibody for 1 h at 37 °C for conjugation. Cisplatinconjugated antibodies are then washed four times with 400 μL W buffer (Fluidigm) and the antibody is collected by two centrifugations (2 min, 1000 × g, RT) with 50 μL of W buffer with an inverted column into a new collection tube. Protein content is assessed by NanoDrop (Thermo Fisher) measurement, antibody stabilization buffer (Candor Bioscience) is added to a final volume of at least 50 v/v %, and antibodies are stored at 4 °C. Both indium and cisplatinum-conjugated antibodies are titrated to define the optimal working concentration. A 6-choose-3 scheme [6] can be used to identify and tag up to 20 samples in combination of 3 channels for barcoding.

362 Bita Sahaf et al. The debarcoding algorithm such as Permessa and Fluidigm debarcoder may be used for sample deconvolution and exclusion of doublets.
4. While barcoding samples is a useful strategy to reduce sample
variability within a batch, the number of samples that can be barcoded and pooled is ultimately limited. Spike-in reference controls are therefore a useful experimental strategy to control for variability between batches. There are several potential options for spike-in reference controls such as multiple aliquots of PBMCs derived from leukapheresis, which can potentially be banked and cryopreserved. This protocol uses a commercial source of lyophilized healthy donor PBMCs that have been prelabeled with Tantalum, a channel that is generally not used for mass cytometry analysis (Fig. 2). These lyophilized cells offer the advantage of ease of preparation and long term reproducibility, and are a versatile resource for monitoring staining variability across samples, particularly in the setting of multicenter studies. However, one of the limitations of this approach is that healthy PBMCs may not express some of the dynamic checkpoint markers that are of interest in monitoring immunotherapy. To address this, PBMCs can be stimulated with CD3/CD28 Dynabeads (ThermoFisher Scientifics; catalogue number 11131D) for 4 days to induce upregulation of T cell activation/checkpoint markers. Further stimulation with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) and Ionomycin can be used to induce production of intracellular cytokines. A reference sample consists of 1:1 resting and stimulated PBMCs may therefore allow for monitoring of a broader range of immunotherapy- relevant markers than healthy control PBMCs alone.
5. An antibody panel for comprehensive immune monitoring
will ideally allow identification of all major immune cell populations, characterization of dynamic markers that are relevant in the setting of immunotherapy (e.g., PD-L1). Our proposed reference panel is designed to identify major and minor immune lineages, while providing flexibility for project-specific markers to be added.
6. The large number of antibodies in a typical CyTOF panel
increases the potential risk of pipetting errors when prepare antibody cocktail and represents a major source of potential intersample technical variability in large scale monitoring studies. One strategy to reduce these issues is lyophilization of antibody panels, which streamlines sample processing and reduces the potential for tube-to-tube pipetting variations. We have successfully validated the robustness and durability of this antibody panel in a lyophilized state (Fig. 3). The lyophilized panel can be stored desiccated at −20 °C for over 1 year

Lotze One of the earliest origins of the understanding of antibody complexity had to do with studies of the breadth of responses associated with diphtheria toxoid immunization, spanning protective and nonprotective immunity, specified by avidity and affinity by Jerne and others [2]. Subsequent work led to some highly speculative studies [3–7] that defined the Network Theory of Immunity, suggesting that a cascade of antibodies (Ab1) and anti-antibodies (Ab2) and anti-antiantibodies (Ab3), etc. were generated by templates off the antigen and its “internal reflection.” This led to the Nobel Prize for Jerne [8]. Real progress was not made until a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms of generating diversity in the B cell receptors (BCR) were understood in pioneering studies from Tonegawa et al. performed in the mid-1970s [9–11]. Similar studies were generated for the alpha beta [12–19] and gamma delta T cell receptors [20–22] This diversity could be described as the “miracle of immunology,” originally thought to be due to stochastic processes, but now recognized to be due to combinatorial diversity of encoded germline elements with “trimming” and N-region diversification (additional nucleotides). The BCR is expressed on the surface of B cells with diversity generating possibly as great as 1026 different antibody molecules [23]. Adult B cell numbers in any individual are actually <1012 cells, with similar numbers predicted of T-cells, bearing as many as 1015–1025 different receptors [24–27]. 2 The Complexity of the Adaptome By rearranging germline genes (Fig. 1, B cell receptor), each one of the matured T and B cells will have a unique surface receptor. The receptor for an individual cell is usually coded by two genes. There are conventional Tαβ cells where the receptors are coded by alpha and beta chain genes to form a heterodimer; there are also dual alpha expressing T cells where two rearranged alpha chains form a dimeric receptor [28]. There are also Tγδ cells that express gamma and delta genes. Dual delta-expressing T cells have also been observed [29]. For B cells, heterodimers are usually encoded by a heavy chain gene and a light chain or a kappa chain gene. There are a total of seven chain genes forming what we have now termed the “adaptome” associated with the adaptive immune response, distinguishable from the “myelome” associated with innate and acute inflammation. Interestingly, plants have no migratory inflammatory cells [30, 31]. Each receptor gene locus is composed of mini gene segments (Fig. 1), with many variable (V), diversity (D), juncture (J), and constant (C) genes. Each cell will randomly use one of the V, D, and J genes to form one of its receptor chains. The CDR3 region (complementarity-determining region 3) is at the juncture of VDJ

Fig. 1 Germline VDJ genes at the B cell heavy chain locus are rearranged and generate multiple unique CDR3s. Use of germline segments derived from variable diversity, joining, and constant regions by recombinases allows extraordinary diversity to be generated genes which provide the basis for repertoire diversity. Additional diversity was introduced by recombination activating genes (RAG)1 and RAG2 at the CDR3 region by first deleting a few bases and then adding random sequences at the 3′ end of the V, both ends of the D, and the 5′ end of the J genes. As a result of VDJ rearrangements, deletion and additions, in addition to chain combinations, human beings are capable of producing a diverse repertoire at an astronomical scale. it is estimated that the overall human adaptome may have more than 1015–1025 clonotypes! In a person, there are maybe a total of 5 × 1011 T cells, the majority of which would be in different tissues, maybe with as many as 1010 different T cells that could be found in the peripheral blood. A sample of 1 mL of peripheral blood may have as many as one million T cells, which may define 50,000 to 350,000 clonotypes, depending on the diversity of the individual’s repertoire. To study the repertoire distribution in one person, we (JH) performed an exhaustive sequencing study on T cell receptor beta chain genes (Fig. 2). We took two blood draws of the same individual, one in the morning and one in the afternoon. We divided each sample into 20 aliquots, each including about one million T cells. After multiplex PCR and NGS sequencing to analyze five million reads (molecules), we found on average 350,000 unique CDR3 sequences from each aliquot, the clonotype overlap between two samples is about 50%. This result suggests a long-tailed distribution of clonotypes in a person, that is, a small number (~10,000 clonotypes out of 350,000 observed repertoire) of active and memory T cells that will be expanded and therefore represented more in the sequencing library. The majority of the naive T cells may be randomly discovered in each sequencing experiment, and thus found only in the tail. In other words, the signal-to-noise ratio is about 1:35. 3 Methods to Study the Adaptome With the signal to noise ratio so low, it is critical to develop inclusive and quantitative methods. The goal is to analyze as many cells as possible and not to introduce analytical bias. Given that the proximal more abundant clonotypes are present at higher numbers and with greater amount of message, even small sample sizes including fingerstick samples blotted on filter paper may be adequate to provide a snapshot of active clones [32]. Some evidence of the TCR in neutrophils has accumulated over the last few years whose biologic significance is uncertain [33–35]. Recent work suggests that this might also be true in a subpopulation of monocytes [36]. Table 1 lists a few commonly used methods to prepare libraries for NGS. The RNASeq method, although providing more comprehensive gene expression information, does not provide the sequence of the entire transcriptome which is necessary in order to identify low abundance CDR3 sequences in more cells. Therefore, it is not fully sensitive, nor quantitative enough for serious repertoire analysis. With the 5′ RACE method [37, 38], since the first strand of cDNA synthesis is conducted with reverse transcriptase and one primer (usually targeting the C gene, or using OligoT), rates of synthesis are believed to be uniform and unbiased. However, careful examination of all of the V gene segments on a locus, allows recognition that some may have short 5′ un-transcribed regions (as short as 30 bp), and some may have very long 5′UTR (up to 9 kb). Therefore, the libraries made by this method may be biased toward shorter sequences. These “moonlighting” functions are performed with less efficiency and accuracy. 4 Repertoire Analysis For repertoire analysis, the regular multiplex PCR method faces four major challenges: (1) each primer that is designed needs to perform, amplify, and be validated; (2) each pair of primers that amplifies one target needs to be compatible with other pairs that target other unique loci in the same reaction system; (3) the method must utilize primers that do not bind and amplify background sequences that are not resident in the TCR; and (4) it must use primers that do not amplify among themselves. By targeting genomic DNA, clonotype distributions can be studied from almost all kinds of samples, including FFPE. However, when using genomic DNA as templates, the entire genome goes into the PCR reaction, while the real targets are those of the rearranged CDR3 regions, those V genes that do not participate in the rearrangement may also bind the available primers

The Adaptome as Biomarker for Assessing Cancer Immunity and Immunotherapy 375 and initiate background synthesis. It is also difficult to make primers performing with the same efficiency and not introduce amplification bias, requiring calibration based on previous experiments that may not align with the new amplification, requiring algorithms to calculate disparities from the individual PCR. 5 Multiplex PCR Methods We (JH) have developed sequentially two improved and novel multiplex PCR methods called amplicon rescued multiplex PCR (arm-PCR) and dimer avoided multiplex PCR (dam-PCR). In arm-PCR (Fig. 3), we designed nested primers for each intended target, with a common tagged sequence on the inside primers of all targeted loci. The purpose of the nested primers was to increase compatibility among each of the individual target loci. One pair of primers can only offer one optimal amplification condition, two pairs of nested primers, however, will provide four opportunities and conditions to allow the target to be amplified. After rescuing the amplicons, the targets are further amplified with the common primers and therefore, the exponential phase of amplification of all targets will have the same efficiency. We use the C gene specific primer for reverse transcriptase arm-PCR, this give inclusive and semiquantitative amplification of T and B cell receptor sequences. Typically, when 0.5–1 μg of total RNA from a PBMC sample is used, after obtaining about five million reads per sample, 100,000– 350,000 unique CDR3 (uCDR3) sequences could be identified. The five million reads obtained are not all useful sequences, it includes almost 50% analytical noise introduced during the experiment. To identify analytical noise, we conducted an experiment where four synthetic TCRB clones were mixed at different ratios, amplified and sequenced separately (Table 2). The first experiment yielded 36,439 unique CDR3 sequences from the mixture of 4 clones after 5,729,613 reads were obtained. Other than the 4 original clones we included in the multiplex PCR reaction, all other clone types were errors. The second experiment yielded 50,354 unique clones from 9,131,681 reads. Based on this observation, we developed five software filters called SMART (Sequencing Error Filter; Mosaic Sequence Filter, Amplification Filter, Reference Filter, and Frequency Threshold Filter) filters to remove noise. 6 Applying Suitable Filters to Data Taking the first experiment as an example, the Sequencing Error Filter (or Pair-end filter) will remove sequences where the overlap regions from the paired end sequencing (Illumina) were not identical. The removed sequences were errors introduced during PCR or

The Adaptome as Biomarker for Assessing Cancer Immunity and Immunotherapy 377 N-addition filter looks into the N addition region (not overlapped in pair-end sequencing, and no reference sequences) and finds the major peaks of sequence distribution and some minor satellite peaks. If the satellite peak is less than 5% of the main clone, the associated sequences get removed. After this filter, 2,926,309 reads and 83 unique CDR3s remain. The Mosaic sequence filter or Chimera filter removes artificial sequences formed during PCR by joining two unrelated clones. After this filter 66 unique CDR3s remains. The last filter is the Frequency Threshold Filter. If the CDR3’s frequency is too low (only 1 or 2 reads), we will not trust it. There are 13 CDR3 unique sequences that pass this filter. If we increase the stringency of the frequency filter, allowing only those CDR3s with more than 10 reads to pass, there will only be the 4 synthetic clones left (the input sequences). In practice, we set the frequency filter to 2 to allow some noise to be included, otherwise, we may remove too many sequences and miss real signals as well. 7 Dimer Avoided Multiplex PCR Dimers are easily formed during a multiplex PCR reaction when hundreds of primers interact with each other at high concentration. Once formed, dimers are preferentially amplified due to their small size and readily available substrates. After each additional cycle, they will occupy more and more polymerase molecules that would otherwise be used to amplify the intended targets. At the plateau phase of a PCR reaction, there are usually substantially more dimers produced than the intended products. Sometimes, more than 80% of the PCR products are composed of primer dimers. In fact, dimers are the primary reason why a PCR reaction reaches a plateau. This is especially problematic for single-cell analysis, which only bears low copy numbers of the intended targets. To address this problem, we sequenced the dimers with NGS, with the hope of identifying patterns or rules of dimer formation in order to improve primer design. Surprisingly, we did not find any obvious rules but discovered that many dimers were formed with as little as one base pair overlap at the 3′ ends of the two individual primers. This means that the primer-dimer problem is so common that it could not be resolved by finding better ways to design the primers. Therefore, we introduced radical steps to prevent the formation of dimers at the very beginning of a PCR reaction. To carry out dimer avoided multiplex PCR (dam-PCR), we would add only the 3′ end primer mix first, allowing them to fully extend upstream with the available polymerase (for DNA templates) or reverse transcriptase (for RNA templates). We then, taking advantage of the huge difference in molecular weight and charge between the amplicons and primers, remove and wash away all of the unincorporated primers by physical and chemical means. Then, we add the 5′ end primer mix, allow

378 Jian Han and Michael T. Lotze them to extend to the ends, and then remove and wash away all of the unused primers again. A nucleotide tag on the primers introduced during the first two steps serve as common priming sites for further amplification. Since the primers or dimers formed at the very first cycle were removed immediately, dimers were avoided during subsequent amplification cycles. Because virtually no dimers formed during dam-PCR, the amplification sensitivity for intended targets actually increased, and a more quantitative analysis also become possible by adding a unique molecular identifier (UMI), a short random sequence in the primer, to the primers. Use of UMI also make it easy to identify and remove errors generated during library prep and sequencing. Figure 4 shows the difference between arm-PCR and dam- PCR for single cell analysis. With the dam-PCR method, we can achieve high levels of success (~95%) in single T or B cell analysis, pairing the receptor genes (alpha/beta, gamma/delta, or heavy and light chain genes) and at the same time, profiling 30–150 genes that defines the phenotypes of the cells, including cytokines, surface markers, and transcription factors. 8 Measuring the Diversity of a Repertoire Because each individual can only allocate a finite number of cells to the adaptive immune system, our adaptome also must have an upper limit (Fig. 5). Each of the 7 chains that contributes to the overall adaptome have their own limited repertoire of clonotypes. If a particular clone expands, it will displace other clonotypes and reduce repertoire diversity. Figure 6 is an iR-Map (immune Repertoire map) which shows the relative frequencies of all the clonotypes within a repertoire. In Fig. 7, we show two repertoires with extreme diversity scores. There are several well-established statistics used to describe diversity. A diversity index is a statistic to assess the diversity of a population in which each object belongs to a unique category [39]. D50, Simpson’s and Shannon’s diversity index range from 0 to 50, from 0 to 1, and from 0 to lnN respectively where N is the size of the underlying population. In all three diversity indices, values near 0 correspond to the highly biased population (less diversity), while values near its maximum correspond to the highly heterogeneous population (more diversity). It is clear that the values for Simpson’s diversity indices is packed in the high-end, which is likely due to the large population size. On the other hand, Shannon’s and D50 are of relatively even distribution. To make diversity index even more easily understood and more visual, we introduced yet another diversity index, iR-Di, labeled as Di in Fig. 7. The iR-Di is 100(%) minus the area under the red curve, where the X axis is the percentage (%) of unique CDR3s, and Y is the percentage (%) of total reads. 9 Diversity as a Biomarker How diverse our T-cell receptors are varies in individuals and in the setting of various diseases including cancer [41–44], autoimmunity [45–47], and following transplantation [48–53]. Patients with the same active disease may be exposed to the same endogenous or exogenous antigens. Thus, convergent evolution, under substantial selection pressure, may produce a range of similar disease-specific clonotypes. When compared to nondisease control samples, those patients with the same active disease may have increased percentage of their repertoire sharing individual disease-specific CDR3s. Some of these TILs can also be found in peripheral blood monocytes and NKT, CD8, CD4, or Tr subsets nose and guide therapy in individuals with chronic inflammation. We have developed an analytical method, called the disease-specific linklets analysis (DSLA), to identify disease-specific signals. Linklets are two unique CDR3 sequences coappearing in a single sample. They are not a biological unit, but rather exist in silico. Instead of using a single unique CDR3 as the basic analytical unit, we used the link between two CDR3s as the basic analytical unit. The purpose of using linklets is that it enhances the biological signal (because TCR CDR3’s targeting an individual disease, will allow convergent evolution and coappearance among samples). This also removes analytical noise, especially noise introduced by barcode bleeding. Figure 16 outlines the DSLA process. Figure 17 demonstrates in one illustrative example, how a deep analysis of a lung cancer patient’s TIL reveals complete absence of γδ T-cells and skewed repertoire with emergence of defined clonotypes.

Fig. 16 Positive and negative linklets. Linklets are formed between any two CDR3s that coappeared in a sample. Number 1 ranked CDR3 and number 2 ranked can form a linklet (SARDLTPGVTFSNQPQH/ASSELETDTQY). This kind of top-to-lower ranking linklets are called positive linklets; those from bottom ranked to higher ranked CDR3s are negative linklets Fig. 17 Disease-specific linklet (DSLA) analysis. Surprisingly frequent convergent evolution of unique CDR3’s is observed in many diseases. Here, we “link” two individual shared TCR CDR3’s among individuals with an individual disease and “count” the number of pairs of shared linklets to determine the range of receptor sharing. 400 Limor Cohen et al. lacking [2]. Such early on-treatment biomarkers of anti-tumor immune response could have broad utility in immuno-oncology from guiding individual treatment regimens and managing immune-related adverse effects to focusing drug development. One of the major reasons that an on-treatment biomarker strategy can have immediate clinical utility, in addition to providing mechanistic insights into PD-1i responses, is related to the kinetics of treatment responses in immuno-oncology. The indirect anti-tumor action of stimulating the innate and adaptive immune systems means standard radiologic measures are less reliable indicators of early on-treatment response [3]. CT scans can falsely overestimate disease burden in the presence of a brisk inflammatory response and a subset of responding patients will show long-term stabilization of disease, even after a mild initial increase in tumor burden [3]. The PD-1i mechanistic action of invigorating the antitumor immune response can be observed as tumor microenvironment (TME) gene expression and cellular changes, with potential for blood-based detection. Compared to pretreatment tissue analysis, early on-treatment tumor biopsy immune profiling of lymphocyte density and composition as well as gene expression analysis shows greater accuracy for predicting response [4, 5]. A large proportion of genes that are differentially expressed between responders and nonresponders in on-treatment biopsies are soluble immunologic signaling molecules: cytokines and chemokines [4, 5]. Even though the mechanistic site of action for PD-1i is the TME, there appears to be systemic evidence of PD-1i action. Flow and mass cytometry studies of peripheral blood lymphocytes show differences in T cell subpopulations according to PD-1i response [6, 7]. Whether these cellular changes are a direct or indirect effect of PD-1i and emanate from the TME remains to be seen. Taken together, these findings suggest a possible role for early noninvasive response profiling by assessing soluble immune factors in peripheral blood. Liquid biopsy is traditionally the approach of sampling blood or bodily fluids to detect and characterize trace amounts of nucleic acids emanating from a solid tumor. Liquid biopsy is in clinical use as a method for the detection of epidermal growth factor receptor mutations in lung adenocarcinoma needed for rationale assignment to therapy and may have expanded indications across diagnosis and monitoring of solid tumors, obviating the need for a fraction of invasive tumor tissue sampling [8]. The refinement of sensitive DNA detection technologies including single molecule-encoded next generation sequencing and droplet digital PCR have enabled the adoption of liquid biopsy for tumors with recurrent genomic driver mutations [8]. Analogously, with advances in ultrasensitive protein detection technology, changes in soluble immunologic signaling molecules emanating from the tumor microenvironment can potentially be detected in systemic circulation and unlock a

Single-Molecule Arrays for Ultrasensitive Detection of Blood-Based Biomarkers… 401 proteomic liquid biopsy approach for monitoring responses to immuno-oncology agents. Such a liquid biopsy adapted to soluble immune signaling molecules can potentially be generalizable across malignancies treated with immuno-oncology agents, regardless of genomic makeup. Detection limits are a major technical barrier to accurate measurement of cytokines in cell-free blood (serum or plasma) and, as with the case of DNA-based liquid biopsy, can be mostly overcome by the digitization of assay signal. Many cytokines and chemokines are below the limits of detection of conventional assays, especially in the absence of a systemic inflammatory response, as in PD-1 blockade [9]. Compared to conventional plate-based ELISAs, multiplexed immunoassays such as the Luminex and Meso Scale Discovery platforms reduce specimen volume requirements per analyte and enable screening approaches but only moderately improve sensitivity and may have decreased reproducibility [9]. Ultrasensitive methods such as Single Molecule Array (Simoa, Quanterix), also Erenna (Singulex), V-plex (MSD), and others greatly increase the yield of accurate cytokine measurements from plasma [10]. A recent study by our group found that Simoa assays for IL-6, IL-10, IL-2, and IFNγ could reliably quantitate these cytokines in 100% (74/74), 100% (79/79), 68% (46/68), and 82% (53/64), respectively, of randomly selected patient samples [11]. Simoa assays are bead-based immunoassays with the major advance of signal detection by single molecule counting, a digitized output that results in ultra-high sensitivity. Antibody-coated capture beads are added in excess to a sample containing low concentrations of target analyte molecules such that one or zero target protein molecules will bind to each bead. Next, an enzyme labeled immunocomplex is formed by using a biotinylated detection antibody followed by streptavidin-β-galactosidase. Then the beads are deposited into an array of 50 fL-sized microwells that can each only accommodate one bead. Active wells are counted digitally because of the local accumulation of fluorescent product within immunocomplex-containing wells. The inactive beads are also counted and the ratio of fluorescent bead-containing wells to nonfluorescent bead-containing wells correlates to the protein biomarker concentration. The assay dynamic range can be extended by measuring the fluorescence intensity of the entire array, thereby switching to an analog mode at higher concentrations of target analyte. The signal output is measured on the Simoa instrument using the standard unit of average enzymes per bead (AEB) [12, 13]. Simoa assays can be customized and commercial ELISAcompatible antibody pairs can be used, however, not all assays are compatible and empiric testing is necessary in the matrix of interest [14]. Our laboratory’s standard approach to first-step analytic validation of new Simoa assays includes dilution linearity, spike and

402 Limor Cohen et al. recovery, and adjusting calibrator concentrations to ensure healthy patient samples are reading in the assay linear range. A major consideration in the investigation of circulating cytokines as disease biomarkers is discerning disease-associated variation from the substantial physiologic variation in concentrations of these proteins, both within and across individuals. Diet, exercise, sleep, and diurnal variation have all been described to influence the concentrations of various circulating cytokines [15–17]. The difference in baseline concentrations of circulating cytokines between healthy individuals can be as much as three orders of magnitude, as has been described for interleukin-8 [18], and many of these differences relate to genetic polymorphisms [19]. Given these potential sources of variation and prior limitations on accurate quantitation from serum, our group undertook a longitudinal study of healthy volunteers, collecting serum weekly for 14 weeks and assessing levels of 15 cytokines by Simoa [18]. For the 13 cytokines that could be reliably quantitated in the majority of samples, this study demonstrated minimal interindividual weekly variation. A narrow baseline cytokine concentration range was apparent for each individual and for the two individuals who showed spiking cytokine concentration changes in association with cold symptoms, their cytokine levels returned to a baseline within 20 days [18]. This study illustrates two important concepts moving forward in cytokine biomarker development: (1) for high interindividual variation cytokines, a comparison to an individual’s baseline will enable a personalized approach to capturing significant changes (2) to build sensitivity and specificity when measuring these pleiotropic proteins influenced by viral illness, exercise, and other factors, a multicytokine profile will likely be necessary. With evidence that measuring changes from an individual’s baseline will be important, we next sought to characterize the effects of clinical specimen handling and processing on plasma cytokine levels. This study, using random patient whole blood specimens, was designed to mimic the preanalytical factors envisioned in a planned clinical study of patients treated with PD-1i. Sample stability over a range of 2–10 h after venipuncture, pneumatic tube transport, vigorous handling, and freeze–thaw were assessed [11]. We found that within an 8-h window, levels of four cytokines were decreasing an average of 5–18%, that this change could be mitigated by cold storage or by rapid separation to plasma, and that whole blood specimens required no special handling [11]. Other components of clinical fit-for-purpose validation included interference (in this case by mixing study with hemolyzed, icteric, and lipemic specimens) and an accuracy comparison [20]. With a validated specimen collection and processing protocol, we sought to minimize cytokine changes owing to in vitro factors to better assess significant biological changes occurring in patient samples.

Single-Molecule Arrays for Ultrasensitive Detection of Blood-Based Biomarkers… 403 Ultrasensitive immunoassays are enabling precise quantification of circulating cytokines with great promise for immuno-oncology applications. Through analytical and preclinical validation studies of Simoa cytokine assays, we identify the importance of baseline measurements and confirm the broad compatibility of standard clinical blood collection methods. Here we describe the Simoa assay and a blood processing protocol that we have adapted for ultrasensitive cytokine measurement in plasma. 2 Materials

Monoclonal Protocol antibodies can be used to target a specific epitope, while polyclonal antibodies can be used to target numerous different epitopes on a 3.1.1 Select a Matched protein. High-affinity antibodies, which are designed to target Antibody Pair native proteins, will have higher chances of success than antibodies that target denatured proteins. Therefore, antibodies optimized for sandwich ELISA or immunoprecipitation are generally preferred over antibodies optimized for western blots. Additionally, the dissociation constant of the antibody is particularly important. An antibody pair that works well in a traditional sandwich ELISA is highly likely to provide improved sensitivity when used in a Simoa assay. 3.2 Prepare This step describes the conjugation of the capture antibody to car- Antibody-Coated boxylated paramagnetic beads (2.7 μm in diameter). Capture Beads 3.2.1 Buffer Exchange This step is designed to remove any amine containing molecules, the Antibody such as azides, which will interfere with the conjugation. Antibodies containing BSA will need to be purified using other methods first. Start with 30% excess antibody to account for losses during antibody purification. Suggested antibody concentrations for coupling are 0.3 mg/mL, 0.5 mg/mL, or 0.7 mg/mL in a 200 μL volume, corresponding to 78 μg, 130 μg, 182 μg of capture antibody, respectively. The amount of antibody used will determine the coating density on the bead. Add the required volume of antibody to an Amicon filter. Add up to 450 μL of Conjugation Buffer to the filter. Centrifuge the columns at 14,000 × g for 5 min. Discard the supernatant. Repeat for a total of three times. The antibody is now concentrated on the filter. Proceed immediately to the next step. Remove the filter from the tube, invert it, and place it into a clean Amicon tube. Place the filter device in the centrifuge, aligning the open cap toward the center of the rotor. Centrifuge inverted at 1000 × g for 2 min to transfer the concentrated sample from the filter to the tube. Remove the filter, invert, and wash both sides of the membrane with 50 μL of Conjugation Buffer by pipetting. Invert the filter and place it into the tube of antibody concentrate. Centrifuge the tube inverted at 1000 × g for 2 min. Remove the filter from the tube and discard the filter. The tube contains the buffer-exchanged antibody to be conjugated to the beads. Measure the antibody concentration using a spectrophotometer. Dilute the antibody to the desired concentration (for example 0.3 mg/mL, 0.5 mg/mL, or 0.7 mg/mL). Place the tube of antibody on ice until ready for use.

Single-Molecule Arrays for Ultrasensitive Detection of Blood-Based Biomarkers… 405 3.2.2 Prepare the Beads Add 2.8 × 108 well-mixed carboxylated paramagnetic beads into a tube. Briefly centrifuge the tube of beads. Place the tube in the magnetic separator for at least 1 min to collect the beads to the side of the tube and aspirate the supernatant. Remove the tube from the magnet and add 200 μL Bead Wash Buffer. Cap the tube and vortex well to disperse the beads. Repeat this washing procedure two times. Then, wash the beads two times with Conjugation Buffer. Resuspend the beads in 190 μL of Conjugation Buffer. Remove the tube from the magnet and vortex well. Briefly centrifuge the tube to remove all liquid from the cap. Place the beads on ice until ready for use. 3.2.3 Conjugate Use ice-cold buffers for all steps. Add 1 mL of Conjugation Buffer the Antibody to the Beads to 10 mg of EDC for a final concentration of 10 mg/mL. It is important to use fresh EDC that has been equilibrated to room temperature. Vortex until the EDC is completely dissolved. Use immediately after reconstitution. Add 10 μL of EDC to the iced tube of beads. Cap and vortex vigorously. Place in the rotator for 30 min. Place the tube in the magnetic separator for at least 1 min to collect the beads to the side of the tube and aspirate the supernatant. Remove the tube from the magnet and add 200 μL of ice-cold Conjugation Buffer to the tube. Vortex for 5 s to disperse the beads and centrifuge. Place the tube in the magnetic separator with the bead pellet adjacent to the magnet for approximately 15 s, to collect the beads to the side of the tube and aspirate the supernatant. Timing is critical for this step. Proceed to next step immediately. Remove the tube of activated beads from the magnet. Add 200 μL of ice-cold buffer-exchanged capture antibody to the beads. Cap the tube and vortex for 10 s. Place the tube in the rotator and mix for 120 min at room temperature. NOTE: this protocol uses a final concentration of 0.5 mg/mL of EDC during the activation step. However, the EDC concentration can be reduced for optimal conjugation. The conjugation step can also be done in a cold room at 4 °C for improved coupling efficiency. 3.3 Block the Beads Briefly centrifuge the tube of beads. Place the tube in a magnetic separator for at least 1 min to collect the beads to the side of the tube. Aspirate the supernatant to a new tube. Add 200 μL of Bead Blocking Buffer. Vortex for 5 s and centrifuge the tube. Place the tube on a rotator and incubate for 30 min. Briefly centrifuge the tube. Place the tube in a

Single-Molecule Arrays for Ultrasensitive Detection of Blood-Based Biomarkers… 409 Prepare Protein standards should be reconstituted based on the manufacthe Calibration Curve turer’s instructions, aliquoted, and stored at −80. Avoid freeze– thaw cycles of protein standards. Prepare a serial dilution of the protein standards for a calibration curve. Often, different proteins require different buffers to expose the epitopes and allow the antibody to bind. Some buffers can be PBS based and others can be Tris based. In most cases, empirical testing is required to obtain maximal results. Calibration curves can be fit to a linear fit, 4PL, or 5PL with different weighting factors. The detection limit is calculated as three standard deviations above the background. Calibration curve range can span about four orders of magnitude but should be optimized to ensure samples are reading in the linear range. Prepare the Samples It is desirable to dilute the samples to reduce interference arising from matrix effects. Commonly, samples are diluted four-fold. However, if protein levels are low, samples can be diluted less. Additionally, larger volumes can be used to ensure the analyte is detectable. In a typical Simoa assay, 100 μL of sample is used. However, larger sample volumes will have more molecules and can improve detection. Other parameters that can be optimized include buffer composition and addition of heterophilic blockers. Additional discussion can be found in reference [22]. Assay Validation Here, we outline suggested assay validation parameters. Additional information can be obtained in reference [23]. Assay validation includes the following: (1) Optimization of assay parameters to achieve sufficient analytical sensitivity. (2) Determination of assay dynamic range. (3) Limit of detection (LOD), three standard deviations above the background, is calculated as the upper 95% confidence interval (CI) obtained from ten runs on ten different days. (4) Limit of quantitation (LOQ) is calculated as lowest concentration at which the analyte can be reliably measured with <20% coefficient of variation (CV) in concentration obtained from 20 samples. (5) Dilution linearity of three unique endogenous serum samples is performed over four dilution factors. Acceptable linearity has an R2 value greater than 0.9. (6) Spike-and-recovery. Three different concentrations of low, medium, and high amounts of recombinant protein are spiked into three unique samples. Acceptable recovery is between 70% and 130%. (7) Interassay variation. Three unique serum samples are measured on five different days. Acceptable CVs are below 20%. Intra-assay variation. Three unique serum samples are measured five times on the same day. Acceptable CVs are below 20%. Additionally, all measurements should be obtained in duplicate or triplicate and calibrator and sample CVs should be below 20%.

We chose to validate the following protocol with plasma for its simplicity. Draw peripheral blood into a 2.0 mL lavender EDTA collection tube (BD Vacutainer) and invert gently to mix. Alternatively, clinical specimens remaining after standard hematology testing are also compatible. Centrifuge whole blood at 2000 × g for 15 min at room temperature and immediately aliquot plasma (see Note 1) and freeze at −80 °C such that the time from blood collection to freeze does not exceed 4 h (see Note 2). The EDTA whole blood specimens do not require special handling and plasma cytokine levels are unaffected by mild hemolysis and up to three freeze–thaw cycles. We validated this approach by measuring IL-2, IL-6, IL-10, and IFNγ [11] however, our findings may not be broadly applicable to all cytokines and other proteins. 3.7 Data Processing Longitudinal changes in cytokines levels are compared as a percentage change from baseline. In the case of PD-1i treatment, a pretreatment baseline is collected just prior to drug infusion and prior to every subsequent dose. This approach has the benefit of incorporating the high interindividual variation in cytokines levels; however, individuals with lower baseline levels will have greater relative changes. Other possible data processing approaches include comparing absolute differences from baseline and analysis of covariance with a baseline level covariate [24]. Our current approach has been

Single-Molecule Arrays for Ultrasensitive Detection of Blood-Based Biomarkers… 411 to screen for individual cytokine changes associated with response/ nonresponse in retrospectively collected patient samples with defined clinical outcomes. The cytokine changes with statistical association to response are being assessed in a prospectively collected patient cohort. Further work will seek to understand how to combine these markers into predictive panels with clinical utility. 4 Notes
1. When aliquoting plasma avoid disturbing the buffy coat layer.
Freeze–thaw of leukocytes can release cytokines into the cell-free fraction. Plasma can also be isolated by gentle centrifugation as in peripheral blood mononuclear cell collection without affecting circulating cytokine levels.
2. We find that a 4-h maximum interval between specimen collec-
tion and freeze is a feasible clinical workflow. Cold storage of whole blood for up to 10 h is comparable [11]. Some cytokines will undergo partial degradation in this timeframe; therefore, to understand the range of in vitro degradation, stability studies should be performed by splitting samples and either freezing immediately or leaving as whole blood for the desired time interval. By capturing the maximal degradation, an empirically defined threshold is applied and only changes cytokine level changes greater than this cutoff are considered significant. ## Chapter 19


414 Dong Liu et al. who are enrolled in the clinical trials but do not respond to these immunotherapies [3–5]. In addition, as “living drugs,” CAR-T cell products can be activated and release a variety of cytokines upon engaging with specific antigens after adoptive transfer into patients, which correlates with antitumor therapeutic efficacy but also may cause life-threatening immunotoxicity such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurologic toxicity [6–8]. Therefore, there is an urgent need for a precise quality check for CAR products before the infusion to the patients. Thus, an optimal biomarker to predict the response to the therapies and the quality of CAR products is critical for benefiting more patients and reducing potential side effects. It has been demonstrated that cytokine secretion of T cells by antigen stimulation is one of the primary parameters to evaluate T cell activation and function [9, 10]. In particular, polyfunctional T cells, defined as single cells coproducing at least two cytokines, are recognized as key effector cells contributing to the development of potent and durable cellular immunity against various infectious diseases as well as cancers [10–12]. Currently, the leading technologies for measuring functional T cell responses are ELISpot and flow cytometry-based assays [13]. The major limitation with these methods is their inability to simultaneously measure all relevant cytokines secreted at live single cell resolution and to identify highly polyfunctional cell subsets [13, 14]. While the most advanced multicolor flow cytometry-based assays have advantages in the ability to measure many surface markers per cell, limitations in the measurement of intracellular cytokines per cell exist due to the inherent background and nonspecific signal of intracellular staining [15, 16]. Importantly, since flow cytometry-based assays do not measure true secretion, these may not reflect the true secretory patterns in vivo. IsoPlexis’ IsoLight system employs its IsoCode® chip, a singlecell, highly multiplexed chip consisting of an antibody barcode array patterned in the parallel line fashion on a polylysinefunctionalized glass slide and a microchamber chip fabricated in polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). By combining sandwich ELISA and fluorescence signal detection (Fig. 1), the IsoCode technology uniquely addresses the above cytokine detection limitations with its ability to measure a large panel of 40+ key secreted proteins from live single cells [17] and to deeply decipher the functional heterogeneity and key functional subsets of responding immune cells among individual patients (Figs. 2a). In addition to quantitative assaying of a large array of secreted proteins per cell, the IsoCode chip is designed to fit various types of immune cells and requires samples totaling ~10,000 cells. The IsoCode chip measures Polyfunctional Strength Index (PSI™), a unique single-cell metric defined as the percentage of polyfunctional cells

Single-Cell PSITM can Predict Patient Response to Cell… 415

Fig. 1 Schematic representation of the method used in IsoCode chip technology. (left) The IsoPlexis platform isolates thousands of single cells into individual microchambers, each of which is prepatterned with a complete copy of a 32-plex antibody array. (right) Following incubation, fluorescent ELISA detection is used to determine which combinations of proteins are being secreted by each individual cell (2+ proteins per cell) in a sample, multiplied by the average signal intensity of the proteins secreted by these polyfunctional single cells (Fig. 2b). Recently, PSI™ has been employed in the anti- CD19 CAR-T cell preinfusion products manufactured from apheresis of patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) and demonstrated a statistically positive association predictive of objective response (OR) as well as CRS in these patients after anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy, outperforming other preinfusion flow cytometry-based and bulk-level metrics in p-value of ability to differentiate responders and nonresponders (Fig. 2a, c, [18]). Using PSI™, IsoPlexis revealed previously unobserved deep functional heterogeneity and successfully predicted the clinical response and toxicities of engineered CAR products as well as tumor relapse in patients with melanoma after T cell receptor (TCR)-modified T cell therapy [18–20]. In a recent study, we are also able to use IPSIs of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells to distinguish the patients who responded to PD-1/CTLA-4 checkpoint inhibitor therapy from nonresponders (manuscript in preparation). In addition to the importance of in cancer therapy, the single-cell deep profiling reveals the crucial role of polyfunctional monocytes or NK cells in multiple sclerosis or Crohn disease, which helps better understanding the pathogenesis of these inflammatory autoimmune disorders [21, 22]. Herein, we detail the materials and methods involved in preparing and running samples on the IsoCode chip integrated with the IsoLight automation platform. Since the benchtop IsoLight instrument is a sample-in, result-out automation system which automates the imaging, incubation, and ELISA fluidics steps of the IsoCode assay (Fig. 3), we mainly focus on the sample preparation steps prior to loading the IsoCode chips.

(b) The PSI™ (polyfunctional strength index determined by IsoCode chip) of each sample is computed using a prespecified formula defined as the percentage of polyfunctional cells, multiplied by mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of the proteins secreted by the polyfunctional cells. right) by sliding them into the respective slot of the tray until they come to a full stop. (a) C arefully remove the protective clear film from bottom of chip without touching the optical surface before loading into the IsoLight. (b) V erify that each chip is pushed all the way to its stop. (c) E ach chip is held in position by a magnet.
13. Press “Close Chip Tray” and the instrument will start scanning
the chip barcodes.
14. Press “Start Assay” after all tray positions were scanned and the
chips displayed.
15. The instrument now executes all the required steps from cell
loading to post-run cleaning and informs the user of the run status using color coded progress bars.
16. The “Next” button becomes activated after the run completed
(see estimated time of completion).
17. Remove the IsoCode chips and liquid consumable conical
tubes (except “dummy tube” R2) from the reagent bay and dispose of any waste in the external waste bottle.
18. Follow the instructions to transfer the data to the IsoSpeak
Computer to be analyzed using the IsoSpeak software using the provided USB drive or over Ethernet.

426 Dong Liu et al. 3.4 Data Analysis/ Raw data from the IsoCode is automatically processed using Report Generation IsoPlexis’ IsoSpeak software. The software interface allows users to easily create a project file to consolidate the results from each sample. Once data is transferred from the IsoLight computer to a file location accessible by the computer running IsoSpeak, users can simply select this raw data to import it into the project. One experiment is created per sample and displayed in a table with the associated raw data images and antibody panel information. Each of these experiments can be optionally annotated with additional metadata, such as patient ID, clinical outcome information, and stimulation information. At this point, the software automatically processes the raw data of these experiments, without any user involvement. Automated image processing steps include detecting the location single-cell chambers on the chip, aligning them with corresponding signal readouts from those chambers, and quantitating these signal readouts. Data is appropriately quality controlled at each step to ensure only high quality single-cell data is output in the final data analysis. The processed data is output in the form of a matrix, with each row corresponding to a single cell, and each column corresponding to a cytokine’s signal intensity coming from that cell. Signal intensities are background subtracted to distinguish true secretions from noise. The background thresholds are computed per cytokine and are three standard deviations above the background level in empty chambers on the chip. At this point, a suite of analytics tools available through IsoSpeak gives the users the ability to parse through and visualize the single-cell results. The user interface facilitates sorting and selecting subsets of the full dataset, with filters generated based on the experiment annotations input by the user. A collection of tables and graph types is provided to display the data at various levels of detail and complexity. In particular, many of the visualizations revolve around the polyfunctionality of the sample. Polyfunctional cells are defined as cells cosecreting at least two proteins from the prespecified panel. Knowing the functional profile of each cell enables the calculation of other metrics, including a breakdown of each sample according to cell polyfunctionality (i.e., what percentage of cells are secreting multiple cytokines versus nonsecreting or monofunctional cells), and a breakdown of the sample by functional groups (i.e., which monofunctional and polyfunctional groups are being secreted by cells in the sample, and their frequency). A single cell functional profile is determined for each analyzed sample. For human immune-oncology samples, profiles are categorized into effector (Granzyme B, IFN-γ, MIP-1α, Perforin, TNF- α, TNF-β), stimulatory (GM-CSF, IL-2, IL-5, IL-7, IL-8, IL-9, IL-12, IL-15, IL-21), regulatory (IL-4, IL-10, IL-13, IL-22, TGF-β1, sCD137, sCD40L), chemoattractive (CCL-11, IP-10,

Single-Cell PSITM can Predict Patient Response to Cell… 427 MIP-1β, RANTES), and inflammatory (IL-1b, IL-6, IL-17A, IL-17F, MCP-1, MCP-4) groups. The PSI (polyfunctional strength index) of each sample is computed using a prespecified formula defined as the percentage of polyfunctional cells, multiplied by mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of the proteins secreted by those cells: PSIsample=(%polyfunctional cells in samples)× n ∑ (MFIof secretedd proteinIof the polyfunctional cells)/n, i=1 where n is the number of evaluated cytokines. IsoSpeak users can visualize the polyfunctionality and PSI of each sample as bar graphs, as well as a breakdown of PSI per cytokine, to see each cytokine’s contribution to the overall PSI. Other graphs are also provided, such as bar graphs with the percentage of single cells secreting each analyzed cytokine, or vertical scatterplots with the single-cell signal intensities of each cytokine. More complex visualizations are provided specifically to help analyze highdimensional, single-cell, protein secretion data. These include polyfunctional heatmaps and PAT (polyfunctional activation topology) PCA plots and provide more granular information about the polyfunctional subsets driving the overall response, highlighting key similarities and differences across the samples (see Fig. 4 for an example of these visualizations). All visualizations and corresponding data tables can be exported from IsoSpeak for further analysis and for report generation. 4 Notes
1. In this chapter, we described the whole process of sample
preparation, stimulation, staining, loading, acquisition, and data analysis for human single cell analysis using IsoCode chip on IsoLight automation system (see Fig. 3). Theoretically, this protocol can be used for any type of cells including primary cells and cell lines with some modifications. This procedure can also apply to mouse immune cells. The single-cell data of mouse T cells suggests the stimulation with immobilized anti-mouse CD3 and soluble anti-mouse CD28 at 37 °C, 5% CO 2 for 48 h generate a polyfunctional response that correlates to each experimental condition.
2. The investigator should follow the standard protocols
described in this chapter as starting point for their given cell type, however, it is highly recommended for each individual lab to optimize the protocol based their specific scientific questions. For example, we have extensively tested different time courses of in vitro stimulation from 4 h to 48 h.

3. If work with fresh cells, skip Subheading 3.1.1 (the thawing
and overnight recovery steps).
4. Each cell product contains chip chips: CD4+ or CD8+ T cell
subsets with either antigen specific or nonspecific stimulation. For example, for anti-CD19 CAR-T products using K562cell- based assay system, CD4+ or CD8+ T cells are stimulated with either CD19-K562 or NGFR-K562 cell, for TCR-T products using T2 cell-based assay system, CD4+ or CD8+ T cell subsets are stimulated with either peptide-pulsed or unpulsed T2 cells.
5. Antibodies for magnetic bead conjugation need to only recog-
nize molecules that are exclusively expressed on target cells but not on T cells. Antibody-conjugated Dynabeads should be washed and resuspended in 0.1% BSA to avoid nonspecific binding. Keep tube upright and beads fully submerged to avoid beads drying.
6. Cells can be stained with either Fluorochrome-conjugated
antibody that specifically binds to a surface marker on cells or membrane dye including CFSE, CellTracker™ Violet Dye or CellTracker™ Red CMTPX Dye for cell detection on chip.
7. The use of a viability dye to check cell viability for every step is
strongly recommended since cell viability is critically important for the success of the assay. We found that lower viability is correlated with lower levels of secreted proteins. If there are still too many dead cells after Ficoll (>20%), a DNA-binding dye is recommended for on-chip staining to gate out dead cells for later IsoSpeak data analysis.
8. For TILs isolation, the pieces of tumor tissues should be as
small as possible, <1 mm3, to increase the surface area that is exposed to the dissociative enzymes. If the pieces of tissue are too large, it will result in incompletely digestion and reduce the yield of TILs.
9. Alternatively, if the pieces TIL samples are too difficult to
remove with forceps, you can attempt to pour them from the tube into the petri dish or carefully use the serological plastic pipette to transfer smaller pieces to the dish. Use forceps to hold the tissue in place while you mince the tumor into small pieces using a sterile scalpel and/or sterile scissors.
10. Using scissors, carefully cut across one side of the pouch
without damaging the chip. Do not touch the optical surface of the bottom of the IsoCode chip and verify that the optical surface of the IsoCode chip is clean. If necessary, the optical surface can be gently cleaned with acetone and or 70% Ethanol using a lint-free, nonscratching tissue (Kimwipes, lens cleaning tissues).

11. When open the IsoCode chips, inspect the inlet port to verify

12. The IsoCode chip needs to be used within 4 h after breaking
the vacuum seal or be discarded.
13. The supernatants from all the experimental conditions can be

434 Takahiro Yamazaki et al. completely inherent to dying cells. First, dying cells must be sufficiently antigenic, that is, they must express epitopes that are not covered by central tolerance and are properly presented on MHC Class I molecules [8–10]. Although for the purpose of this discussion the proteomic profile of a cell population can be simplistically considered a purely cell-intrinsic feature, central tolerance is determined by the negative selection of thymocytes in the course of T cell development [11, 12], implying that antigenicity is largely influenced by the host. Thus, normal cells succumbing to stress are essentially unable to drive adaptive immune responses in syngeneic hosts (although they can initiate innate inflammatory responses) [13–15]. Conversely, cancer cells are often characterized by genetic instability and hence express antigenic epitopes that are not covered by central tolerance [16–20]. Second, cell death must be accompanied by the emission of immunostimulatory signals that orchestrate the recruitment and activation of the cellular components required for the initiation of adaptive immune responses, notably, antigen-presenting cells (APCs, most often dendritic cells, DCs) and naïve CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) [21–23]. This reflects the ability of dying cells to expose or secrete damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) [24–26] that de facto operate as immunological adjuvants upon binding to their cognate receptors on the surface of immune cells [21–23]. Importantly, whereas DAMP emission in response to stress is completely inherent to dying cells, the ability of DAMPs to drive immunostimulation depends on the expression of their cognate receptors by the host [27–30]. Third, cell death must occur in a microenvironment that is compatible with the recruitment and activation of APCs, CTL priming, as well as CTL effector functions, including the establishment of immunological memory [31–33]. This is particularly relevant as cancer cells succumbing to a variety of chemotherapeutics in vitro are often able to initiate adaptive immunity associated with the establishment of immunological memory when inoculated in syngeneic tumor-naïve hosts as a prophylactic intervention [34–36]. Conversely, the same anticancer agents generally fail to drive productive ICD when employed in therapeutic settings, reflecting the robust immunosuppressive circuitries established by developing tumors [37–40]. In specific cases, however, ICD inducers are potent enough to subvert cancer-driven immunosuppression and enable the establishment of tumor-targeting adaptive immunity in vivo [41–43]. In this context, one particularly relevant example is provided by radiation therapy (RT), which—in a limited percentage of cancer patients—can generate the immunological eradication of nonirradiated lesions (the so-called “abscopal responses”) [44–48]. Collectively, these observations suggest that (1) although DAMPs emitted by cancer cells dying in vitro can be harnessed to screen for potential ICD inducers, the ability of cell death to drive

Immunogenicity of Cancer Cell Death 435 adaptive immunity against dead cell-associated antigens largely depends on host-related factors, and hence can only be assessed in vivo, and (2) the presence of established neoplastic lesions considerably lowers (but may not completely abolish) the ability of dying cancer cells to drive productive ICD associated with CTL effector functions including immunological memory. Here, we detail two distinct models that can be used to assess ICD in vivo in prophylactic (vaccination) and therapeutic (abscopal responses) settings, based on murine mammary carcinoma TSA cells and immunocompetent syngeneic BALB/c mice. The vaccination model is advantageous in that it provides improved experimental control on cell death induction (which occurs in vitro), and increased sensitivity (hosts are tumor-naïve and hence devoid of cancer-driven immunosuppression), but its clinical relevance is limited. Conversely, the abscopal model is highly relevant from a clinical perspective but is limited in that local delivery is required for at least one of the agents (i.e., it cannot be employed for systemic therapies). 2 Materials Unless otherwise specified, chemicals are obtained from Sigma- Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA), cell culture media and supplements from Gibco®-ThermoFisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA), and fluorophores from Invitrogen™ Molecular Probes™-ThermoFisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA). 2.1 Common 1. 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes. aspirate culture medium, wash adherent cells with 10 mL prewarmed PBS (see Note 20), and add 3–5 mL 0.25% (w/v) trypsin–EDTA solution (see Note 21).

2. Twenty-four hour after seeding (see Note 28), treat cells by
substituting the culture medium with 12 mL complete growth medium supplemented with the potential ICD inducers of choice (see Note 29).
3. A convenient negative control (non-ICD inducer) is 150 μM
CDDP; convenient positive controls (established ICD inducers) are 1 μM MTX or RT in a single dose >20 Gy (see Notes 30–32).
4. At the end of the incubation period, transfer culture superna-
tants to 50 mL conical centrifuge tubes (see Notes 33 and 34) and detach adherent cells with 3–5 mL trypsin–EDTA upon washing with 10 mL prewarmed PBS (see Notes 20 and 21).
5. Upon detachment, add 5 mL complete growth medium (see
Notes 22–24) and collect cells from each flask into the 50 mL conical centrifuge tube containing the corresponding supernatant.
6. Centrifuge cell suspensions at 800 × g, room temperature, for
5 min (see Note 35).
7. Discard the supernatant, resuspend each cell pellet in 10 mL
prewarmed PBS and repeat step 6 (see Note 36).
8. Discard the supernatant, carefully resuspend the cell pellet in
2 mL prewarmed PBS, and mix 10 μL of each cell suspension with 200 μL complete growth medium supplemented with 0.5 μg/mL PI into individual FACS tubes (see Notes 37–39).
9. Incubate FACS tubes for 5 min at 37 °C and analyze each
sample by flow cytometry for forward scatter (FSC), side scatter (SSC), and PI fluorescence (see Notes 40–42).
10. Alongside, use 10 μL of the cell suspension mixed with
10 μL TB to load a disposable counting chamber (see Notes 43 and 44).
11. Establish the concentration of cells by averaging the number of
TB− and TB+ events from no less than three counting fields (see Notes 45 and 46).
12. Use prewarmed PBS to resuspend dying TSA cells at a final
concentration of 10 × 106 cells/mL, and inoculate 5–10 BALB/c mice with 100 μL of this cell suspension s.c. as a vaccination injection to the left flank (see Notes 47 and 48). Include as an additional negative control condition a group of 5 BALB/c mice receiving 100 μL PBS only.
13. Two weeks later, pre-expand TSA cells in 75 cm2 flasks to
obtain approximately 5 × 106 cells at <75% confluence (see Note 49).
