Once the primary tumor reached a surface area of 25 mm2 (D1), mice were randomized to the following treatments: systemic vehicle (i.p., on D1, D4, and D7), focal radiation therapy (RT) to the primary tumor (8 Gy X 3, on D1, D2, and D3), systemic CTLA4 blockade (9H10 antibody i.p., on D1, D4, and D7), and focal RT to the primary tumor plus systemic CTLA4 blockade, as detailed in Subheading 3.3. Primary and abscopal tumor growth was monitored over time. Data are reported as means ± SEM (n = 3–15 mice per group); ∗p < 0.05, as compared to vehicletreated mice (linear mixed-effect modeling)

440 Takahiro Yamazaki et al.
9. Once primary tumors reach a surface area of 20–40 mm2 (D1),
mice are allocated to receive either of the following treatments (see Notes 60 and 61): (a) P BS only (100 μL, i.p., on D3, D6 and D9) (see Notes 62 and 63); (b) P otential ICD inducer to the primary tumor (see Notes 64 and 65); (c) 9 H10 antibody (200 μg/mouse, i.p., on D3, D6 and D9) (see Notes 66 and 67); (d) P otential ICD inducer to the primary tumor plus 9H10 antibody.
10. A convenient positive control is fractionated focal RT to the
primary tumor (3 fractions of 8 Gy, on D1, D2, and D3) plus 9H10 antibody (200 μg/mouse, i.p., on D3, D6, and D9) (see Note 68);
11. Tumor growth at both the primary and abscopal site is moni-
tored routinely with a standard caliper (see Notes 52 and 69) (Fig. 2).
12. Mice that reject both the primary and abscopal tumors can be
rechallenged 30 days after tumor clearance with 0.1 × 106 TSA cells in 100 μL PBS, inoculated s.c. at either flank, and/or 1 × 106 mouse colorectal carcinoma CT26 cells in 100 μL PBS, inoculated s.c. at the contralateral flank (see Subheading 3.2, steps 11–19 and Notes 45–54). 4 Notes
1. Small animal irradiation platforms with comparable technical
features from alternative providers can also be employed. One such instrument is the X-RAD SmART from Precision X-Ray, Inc. (North Branford, CT, USA) [49, 50].
2. Flow cytometers with comparable technical features from
alternative providers can also be employed. Examples include the Attune NxT Flow Cytometer from ThermoFisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA) and FACSCelesta™ from BD Biosciences (Frankin Lakes, NJ, USA).
3. As an alternative to mouse mammary carcinoma TSA cells,
vaccination experiments have successfully been performed with mouse colorectal carcinoma CT26 and CMT-93 cells [51, 52], which are syngeneic to BALB/c mice, as well as with mouse fibrosarcoma MCA205 cells [53], which are syngeneic to C57BL/6 mice. Similarly, abscopal responses in the double lesion model have been successfully observed with mouse mammary carcinoma 4T1 cells [54, 55], which are syngeneic

Immunogenicity of Cancer Cell Death 441 to BALB/c mice, as well as with mouse colorectal carcinoma MC38 cells [41, 55–57] and mouse melanoma B16-OVA cells [55], both of which are syngeneic to C57BL/6 mice. Growth medium requirements for these cell lines may not necessarily match those of mouse mammary carcinoma TSA cells.
4. Stored at −20 °C and under protection from light, trypsin–
EDTA is stable for no less than 18 months. Repeated freeze-thawing is not recommended by the manufacturer. Upon thawing, trypsin–EDTA is stable at 4 °C for approximately 2 weeks.
5. The National Toxicology Program (NTP), the International
Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), or the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) do not currently list EDTA as a carcinogen.
6. MTX, a cytostatic anthracenedione that causes double-strand
DNA breaks by stabilizing the cleavable complex of topoisomerase II and DNA [58–60], is currently employed as a chemotherapeutic agent against leukemia and various solid tumors [61, 62].
7. MTX may cause heritable genetic damage, harm to the unborn
child and may be harmful if inhaled, swallowed, or absorbed through skin. Therefore, MTX should always be handled with care by using protective gloves, clothing and eyewear.
8. CDDP, a platinum-based alkylating compound, is commonly
employed in the clinic against a wide spectrum of solid neoplasms [63–67]. The main mechanism of action of CDDP involves the generation of intrastrand/interstrand DNA cross-links and DNA-protein cross-links [68–70].
9. CDDP is currently listed as a carcinogen by the IARC, the
NTP, and the OSHA. CDDP is mutagenic, potentially fatal if swallowed, harmful if inhaled or absorbed through skin and may cause serious eye damage. Thus, CDDP should always be manipulated with appropriate protective equipment (gloves, clothing, and eyewear).
10. Undissolved CDDP (a yellow-to-orange powder) is stable for
no less than 2 years if stored at 4 °C and under protection from light. Under appropriate storage conditions (room temperature, vials hermetically sealed and protected from light), CDDP stock solutions in DMF are stable for several months.
11. DMF is not listed as a carcinogen by the IARC, the NTP, or
the OSHA, but is readily absorbed by inhalation as well as through the skin, and can behave as an irritant for the eyes, skin, gastrointestinal tract, and respiratory system. Thus, DMF should always be handled with appropriate protective

442 Takahiro Yamazaki et al. equipment (gloves, clothing, and eyewear) under a chemical fume hood. DMF is also inflammable, and hence should be stored within hermetically sealed containers in cabinets designed for inflammable reagents.
12. PI is not currently listed as a carcinogen by the IARC, the
NTP, or the OSHA. However, PI may have mutagenic effects, is harmful if swallowed, and behaves as an irritant to the eyes, respiratory system, and skin. It is therefore recommended to manipulate PI with care while wearing protective equipment (gloves, clothing, and eyewear).
13. Undissolved PI (a dark red powder) is stable for no less than
12 months under appropriate storage conditions (room temperature, protected from light). PI stock solutions are stable for no less than 6 months (if stored at 4 °C, under protection from light).
14. TB is not currently listed as a carcinogen by the NTP, the
IARC, or the OSHA. Information on the effects of TB on human health is limited. Upon direct contact, TB may behave as an irritant to the eyes, skin, gastrointestinal tract, and respiratory system.
15. Undissolved TB (a dark purple-brown powder) is highly stable
under appropriate storage conditions (room temperature, protected from light). TB stock solutions are also very stable but tend to form precipitates with time. Such precipitates dissolve quickly upon agitation unless solvent has evaporated to a significant extent (and hence TB concentration has trespassed maximal solubility). In this case, stock solutions should be prepared de novo.
16. The 9H10 antibody, which is specific for mouse cytotoxic T
lymphocyte associated protein 4 (CTLA4) [71], is not currently listed as a hazardous substance by the NTP, the IARC, or the OSHA.
17. As per manufacturer recommendations, the 9H10 antibody
stock solution should be stored undiluted at 4 °C, protected from prolonged exposure to light, and never frozen.
18. A 75 cm2 flask of mouse mammary carcinoma TSA cells con-
fluent to 80% contains approximately 6–8 × 106 cells. Routine cell maintenance can also be performed in 25 cm2 or 175 cm2 flasks. These can be instrumental if space in the incubator is limited or a high number of cells is required for experimental determinations, respectively.
19. It is important to avoid both underconfluence and overconflu-
ence at passaging because the former may introduce a bottleneck effect that favors genetic drifts in the cell population [72, 73], while the latter may be associated with at least some degree of

Immunogenicity of Cancer Cell Death 443 nutrient deprivation and contact inhibition, potentially resulting in cell death. Of note, the sensitivity of different cell lines to overconfluence varies considerably.
20. Washing with PBS minimizes serum leftovers that may inhibit
enzymatic detachment by trypsin–EDTA.
21. Detachment can also be achieved with alternative enzymatic
reagents, such as Detachin (from Genlantis, San Diego, CA, USA), as well as mechanically, with dedicated cell scrapers.
22. The time required for complete detachment varies significantly
with cell line. It is recommended to visually inspect flasks for detachment before adding complete medium. This will ensure maximal yields.
23. Prolonged, unnecessary exposure to trypsin–EDTA should be
avoided as this is generally associated with reduced attachment on seeding and (in at least some cell lines) some degree of toxicity. For cell lines that are very sensitive to trypsin–EDTA, scraping should be preferred (see also Note 22).
24. This step is important as the FBS contained in complete cul-
ture medium inactivates trypsin–EDTA (see also Note 23).
25. It is recommended to avoid both overdilution (seeding less
than 5% of the original culture) and underdilution (seeding more than 30%) in the context of cell maintenance. Overdilution may introduce a bottleneck effect that favors genetic drifts in the cell population (see also Note 19). Conversely, underdilution may call for passaging every 1–2 days, which over time may negatively affect viability and/ or cellular functions. As a rule of thumb, biweekly passaging is adequate for most cancer cell lines.
26. As cells are reseeded in complete medium, removing trypsin–
EDTA leftovers is generally not required. For particularly sensitive cell lines, this can be achieved by centrifuging suspensions at 400 × g, room temperature, for 5 min, discarding the supernatant and resuspending the cell pellet in 1–2 mL prewarmed PBS or complete growth medium before seeding.
27. Depending on the final amount of cells needed for vaccina-
tion, alternative cell culture containers can be used, including 6-well plates and 10-cm petri dishes.
28. Twenty-four hours is generally adequate for seeded cells to
reattach to the substrate and recover normal cellular functions including proliferation. However, this may vary with specific cell lines, and cells that have not yet fully adapted to culture are generally hypersensitive to a variety of stressors, which may confound the interpretation of results.
29. Growth medium should be replaced in all experimental condi-
tions (including control conditions) in order to remove cells

444 Takahiro Yamazaki et al. that are dead or dying because of passaging. The percentage of cells unable to adapt to passaging is generally marginal (<5%), but this may nonetheless constitute a confounding factor at data analysis.
30. CDDP at overtly cytotoxic doses is unable to induce ICD
because CDDP-driven cell death is not associated with prominent endoplasmic reticulum stress and consequent exposure of calreticulin (CALR) on the plasma membrane [74–77].
31. MTX at overtly cytotoxic doses is a bona fide inducer of ICD
associated with CARL exposure on the plasma membrane, ATP secretion, as well as release of high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), annexin A1 (ANXA1) and type I interferon (IFN) into the microenvironment [78–83].
32. Cells exposed in vitro to overtly cytotoxic radiation doses are
highly immunogenic as they emit all the signals associated with bona fide ICD (see also Note 31) [34, 84, 85].
33. Dose and incubation time are major determinants of the
immunogenicity of cell death driven by a variety of agents [36, 86, 87]. Indicatively, cells succumbing to established ICD inducers such as MTX and RT have maximal immunogenicity 24–48 h after treatment, while immunogenicity fades with longer incubation times. This does not necessarily apply to other hitherto uncharacterized ICD inducers.
34. Supernatants must not be discarded at this step, as most dead
and dying cells are detached and would therefore be lost.
35. Slightly higher centrifugation speeds (as compared to speeds
normally employed for cell passaging) ensure that apoptotic cell corpses (which are lighter and hence sediment at reduced speed) are not lost at this passage [88].
36. This passage is required to carefully wash cells from potential
drug leftovers that may interfere with subsequent experimental steps.
37. PI is a DNA-binding exclusion dye, meaning that it only enters
cells with an irreversibly permeabilized plasma membrane. Irreversible plasma membrane permeabilization is the most widely accepted operational definition of cell death [14].
38. PI exhibits excitation/emission peaks at 482/504 nm, respec-
tively, in aqueous solution, and 535/617 nm, respectively, when bound to DNA.
39. 4′,6-Diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) is a convenient alter-
native to PI for the assessment of cell death on flow cytometry based on plasma membrane permeabilization. DNA-bound DAPI exhibits excitation/emission peaks at 350/460 nm, respectively.

Immunogenicity of Cancer Cell Death 445
40. FSC and SSC are indicative of cell size and granularity,
respectively.
41. General gating strategy is as follows: (1) gate on cell-like
events based on FSC-H and SSC-H, (2) discard doublets based on FSC-H versus FSC-A; and (3) estimate the proportion of dead (PI+) singlets of the cell suspension.
42. Our experience suggests that <50% and >80% cell death are
not compatible with vaccination assays for the detection of ICD. When cell death is insufficient, indeed, tumors form at the vaccination site (and the subsequent challenge injection is not rejected). Similarly, excessive degrees of cell death (such as those obtained with freeze-thawing) are not compatible with the establishment of protective antitumor immunity [89]. Dose and incubation time should therefore be adjusted to achieve 50–80% cell death (see also Note 33). The amount of cell death required for optimal vaccination efficiency may vary with cell line and treatment.
43. TB is a colored exclusion dye that is appropriate to provide a
rough estimate of cell death in control conditions.
44. A variety of nondisposable counting chambers also exist,
including classical devices such as the Bürker and Neubauer hemocytometers.
45. Cell death should be quantified in no less than three counting
fields and among no less than 200 cells per field to ensure statistical significance.
46. Tabletop automated counters compatible with disposable
chambers and capable of quantifying TB+ cells are also commercially available. Examples include the Cell Counter model R1 (from Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) as well as the TC20™ Automated Cell Counter (from Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA).
47. The left flank is chosen arbitrarily, but we strongly recommend
making sure the choice is consistent and respected (to avoid issues at data analysis).
48. It is important for the vaccination injection to be performed
s.c. as (at least in part) immunogenicity seems to be reduced with i.d. injections. Potentially, this reflects the differential composition of the epidermal versus dermal immune infiltrate [90, 91].
49. We recommend to avoid confluence levels >75% in this setting
as (at least in some cell lines) they are associated with reduced proliferation rates upon in vivo inoculation.
50. The challenge injection must be performed on the oppo-
site flank as compared to the vaccination injection (see also Note 47).

446 Takahiro Yamazaki et al.
51. It is paramount to inject living cancer cells s.c., as i.d. injec-
tions will result in tumors that cannot be easily detected at early stages (they grow deep into the dermal layers and are not simple to locate when they are small), which may confound data analysis.
52. Tumor incidence and growth can also be monitored with more
sophisticated devices, including microCT scanners [92, 93].
53. Bona fide ICD driven by MTX and RT is generally associated
with high rates (>85%) of tumor rejection at the challenge site. CDDP-driven cell death offers protection to a limited (<20%) fraction of mice. Intermediate extents of protection can also be observed.
54. Besides incidence, vaccination with dying cells may also alter
growth rates at the challenge sites. Reduced tumor growth at the challenge site can be interpreted as a sign indicative of a mild immunological reaction against the tumor.
55. Re-challenging mice with a syngeneic TSA-unrelated cell line
informs on whether rejection of the primary challenge with TSA cells reflected the activation of a tumor-specific adaptive immune response associated with long-term immunological memory (as compared to some form of non-tumor-specific protection potentially linked to the innate immune system).
56. Gathering cultures from different flasks is important to
homogenize as much as possible cell suspensions employed to establish tumors in vivo (and hence to contain experimental variance).
57. Abscopal lesions must be established in the opposite flank as
compared to primary lesions (see also Note 47).
58. As an alternative, primary and abscopal lesions can be estab-
lished on the same day. In this setting, 100 μL of a TSA cell suspension at 0.5–0.7 × 105 cells/mL should be employed for abscopal lesions.
59. The delay between the establishment of primary and abscopal
tumors can be altered as per specific experimental requirements. However, please note that spontaneous rejection of the abscopal lesions may occur when such delay is excessive, most likely reflecting activation of a tumor-specific immune response that can control freshly injected cells (but is not able to counteract the growth of established tumors).
60. Indicatively, in this experimental setting, primary TSA tumors
reach a surface area of 20–30 mm2 8–10 days after inoculation.
61. In our experience, when surface area at treatment is >50 mm2,
therapeutic efficacy at both primary and abscopal lesions is dramatically reduced.

Immunogenicity of Cancer Cell Death 447
62. Timing in this specific case reflects the administration schedule
of the 9H10 antibody.
63. When intratumoral chemical agents are tested (see also Note 64),
negative control conditions should include i.t. injections of the drug vehicle plus PBS i.p.
64. Bona fide abscopal responses can only be measured when at
least one of the treatments is administered locally or i.t. This reflects the potential of agents administered systemically to have a direct effect on both the primary and abscopal lesions (see also Note 63).
65. Treatment dose and schedule may have a profound effect on
the ability of agents that induce ICD in primary lesions to drive abscopal responses [41, 94, 95].
66. The 9H10 antibody interrupts immunosuppressive CTLA4-
dependent signaling on the surface of T cells, hence rendering them more susceptible to cross-priming by DCs [96, 97].
67. As an alternative, the 29F.1A12 antibody (from Bio X Cell),
which is specific for mouse programmed cell death 1 (PDCD1; best known as PD-1), can be also employed [98, 99]. The 29F.1A12 antibody is delivered i.p., on D3, D6, and D9 at 200 μg/mouse.
68. Focal RT delivered to the primary tumor in 3 fractions of 8 Gy
on D1, D2, and D3 together with the 9H10 antibody (200 μg/ mouse, i.p., on D3, D6, and D9) mediates a highly immunogenic form of cell death associated with robust type I IFN secretion [41, 95]. Higher RT doses delivered in a single fraction are not as efficient at enabling the initiation of tumor- specific immunity owing to the upregulation of the exonuclease three prime repair exonuclease 1 (TREX1), which limits type I IFN production by degrading cytosolic DNA [41, 95, 100].
69. Bona fide abscopal responses can vary in degree from a relative
reduction in the growth of abscopal lesions to complete tumor eradication at both primary and abscopal sites. # Part VI

Tissue Imaging Methods

## Chapter 21


456 Sanjay S. Patel and Scott J. Rodig density, and to evaluate their distribution. The most recent, and perhaps most significant, example of the clinical significance of this approach for immuno-oncology has been the evaluation for PD-L1 expression in a variety of tumor types [1–6]. However, single-marker IHC has its obvious limitations, and the need for multiple antibody labeling (i.e., multiplexing), recognized since the advent of IHC itself [7, 8], has become especially acute for the evaluation of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) in which dozens of types of immune cells may reside and impact disease progression and response to therapy. In most instances, each of the antibodies used in multiplexing are directly or indirectly labeled with a unique fluorophore. Spectrally resolved imaging, whereby two or more distinct colors can be “unmixed” on the basis of their individual spectral characteristics, is necessary to visualize tissues stained with multiple antibodies [9]. The benefits of multiplexing include, but are not limited to: (1) more precise identification of specific cell types through the application of multiple phenotypic markers; (2) identification of and the spatial relationship between multiple cell types; (3) colocalization of phenotypic and activation markers on individual cell types for to define functional states (e.g., proliferating Ki67+ cells within a tissue section) [1]; and (4) tissue preservation (i.e., simultaneous evaluation of multiple markers using a single tissue section). In spite of these clear benefits, there is no single “gold standard” approach to multiplexing, and each technique now in practice is not without its caveats. In this section, we will introduce several methodologies that have been largely perfected and are widely utilized, and also a few newer, “cutting-edge” techniques that may enter routine use in the future. A portion of these will be discussed in greater detail in subsequent sections. 2 Multiplex Colorimetric IHC (mCIHC) Multiplex chromogenic immunohistochemistry (mCIHC) involves the application of two or more antibodies that are conjugated to enzymatic reporter systems (e.g., horseradish peroxidase [HRP], alkaline phosphatase [ALP]) using molecules such as 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (DAB) or 3-amino-9-ethylcarbzaole (AEC) as substrates/chromogens for visual detection and methyl green or hematoxylin as counterstains. The protocols for this approach are similar to those used in monolabeling. mCIHC is limited by the fact that typically only two markers can be reliably evaluated by the human eye, and particularly only when they mark distinct cell types. Spectral deconvolution, or unmixing, can be helpful; however, the widely accepted maximum even with this added step is 3–4 markers. The reasons for this limitation include (1) the relatively low signal-to-noise ratio, or narrow dynamic range, of

Overview of Tissue Imaging Methods 457 substrates such as DAB and (2) spectral overlap between DAB and other commonly used chromogenic dyes. Sequential tissue staining, stripping of the colorimetric dyes, followed by additional staining is one method that has been utilized to overcome these limitations. One such protocol termed multiplexed immunohistochemical consecutive staining on single slide (MICSSS) has been recently developed [10]. MICSSS can be performed on any FFPE tissue and involves iterative cycles of staining, image scanning, and destaining of chromogenic substrate, and enables multiparametric characterization of antigens on a single tissue section while preserving tissue antigenicity and maintaining architecture. A more detailed discussion of this methodology will be provided in a subsequent section. 3 Multiplex Immunofluorescence IHC (mIF) Classical multiplex immunofluorescence immunohistochemistry (mIF) has been used as a research tool in cell biology for decades, but only recently adapted to staining FFPE tissue samples. Formalin-fixed samples are characterized by autofluorescence which has traditionally limited the visualization of specific tissue staining with fluorescently conjugated antibodies. However, the combination of spectral deconvolution and computer-assisted subtraction of autofluorescence has largely overcome this limitation. MIF relies on either direct (i.e., primary antibody conjugated to fluorophore) or indirect (i.e., secondary antibody conjugated to fluorophore) antigen labeling with subsequent target visualization using a fluorescent microscope with paired excitation/emission filter sets designed to emit and capture only specific wavelengths of light. Individual fluorophores are excited by one specific wavelength and emit at a longer specific wavelength (a phenomenon known as Stokes shift) [11]. Whereas direct antibody conjugation ensures specificity of tissue staining, the intensity of fluorescence is such that only a subset of protein targets, generally those with the highest cellular concentration, are reliably detected with subsequent imaging. Indirect staining allows for signal amplification and thereby the detection of a wider range of protein antigens. Common fluorophores used in mIF include Alexa or Cy dyes, and fluorescent quantum dot nanocrystals. As a result of the wider dynamic ranges of fluorophore-conjugated antibodies, and the reduced spectral overlap, the multiplexing capability of mIF is superior to that of mCIHC; at present, up to seven targets (i.e., six proteins plus 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole [DAPI] for visualization of nuclei) can be reliably interrogated on a single tissue section. Traditionally, the labeled, secondary antibody used in indirect mIF is directed against the primary antibody species. For instance,

458 Sanjay S. Patel and Scott J. Rodig a fluorescently labeled goat anti-mouse secondary antibody may be used to detect a primary mouse antibody used to stain the tissue. An obvious limitation with this approach is that only a combination of primary antibodies from distinct animal species (e.g., rabbit, mouse, or goat) can be used together with multiplexing. Tyramide signal amplification (TSA) is one method that has been used to work around the aforementioned issue. This approach first involves application of a primary antibody and an HRPconjugated secondary antibody, followed by HRP-mediated conversion of a subsequently introduced tyramide-based reagent (tyramide-biotin, tyramide-DNP, tyramide-fluorophore, etc.) into highly reactive free radicals that form covalent bonds with tyrosine residues immediately proximal to the enzyme. As a result, multiple tyramide- conjugated molecules are laid down at the site of the primary antibody. Multiplexing is enabled by the fact that multiple primary/secondary antibody complexes can be sequentially applied and removed, while the covalently bonded tyramide molecules remain. Direct imaging of fluorophores or downstream application of individual fluorophores linked either to anti-biotin or anti-DNP molecules, for example, allows for subsequent visualization of the amplified signal [11]. Benefits of this method include: (1) ability to profile a greater number of markers than by mCIHC on one tissue section; (2) favorable signal- to-noise ratio; (3) amplification of weaker antigen signals; and (4) detection of multiple primary antibodies of the same species (i.e., mouse) simultaneously. The utility of TSA-based mIF was recently utilized to characterize the immunosuppressive environment and to profile the PD-L1 expression pattern of classic Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) [12]. In this study, Carey et al. FFPE material from 20 diagnostic whole lymph node excision specimens and applied a panel of Opal (TSA) fluorochrome-conjugated primary antibodies (PerkinElmer, Hopkinton, MA) sequentially, including: anti-PD-L1/Opal-520, anti-CD30/Opal-540, anti-CD68/Opal-650, and anti-CD163/ Opal-690. The nuclear counterstain 4′,6-diamidino-2- phenylindole (DAPI) was subsequently applied to all slides. Matched tissue sections from each case were stained for CD30 by chromogenic immunohistochemistry and used to identify two target regions for mIF analysis. Two regions from each case were imaged using a multispectral imaging platform (Vectra 3, PerkinElmer, Hopkinton, MA) at 4× resolution. Additionally, for each region of interest, four tiled fields of view were acquired at 20× resolution as multispectral images. Following image capture, the fields of view were spectrally unmixed and analyzed using a pathologist-directed supervised machine learning algorithm (InForm 2.1, PerkinElmer). Pathologist-directed machine learning is based on an iterative training/test process during which a small number of cells (training phase, typically 15–20 cells) are manually selected as being

Overview of Tissue Imaging Methods 459 most representative of each phenotype of interest, allowing the algorithm to subsequently predict the phenotypes for all remaining cells (testing phase). In brief, individual cells are identified with nuclear DAPI staining, and cellular identity assigned according to a combination of features including (1) positive staining for specific cell lineage markers, (2) lack of staining for additional cell lineage markers, and (3) histomorphological features of the cellular staining. The latter criterion is an integral and important characteristic of the supervised machine learning algorithm. Decisions made by the software can be manually overruled to refine and optimize the algorithm. In this study, unique cell phenotyping was performed for each tumor and then applied to both tiled and study images to account for intersample variability of signal intensities. The commercial software automatically derives maps of cell membranes and Cartesian coordinates for each cell phenotype within a given image that can be further subject to quantitative spatial analysis. The combination of mIF, pathologist-directed automated cell phenotyping, and quantitative spatial analysis was recently employed by Carey et al. to identify a novel micro-anatomic structure within tumor biopsy samples of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL); a tumor highly sensitive to PD-1 inhibitors. Visually, the bulk tumor mass of cHL is composed of a multitude of nonneoplastic inflammatory and stromal cells, with only occasional neoplastic Hodgkin Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells that are intermixed in an apparently random fashion. MIF, image, and spatial analysis of the tumor mass revealed that the HRS cells specifically reside within an enriched population of PD-L1+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) that are in contact with a similarly enriched population of “exhausted” PD-1+ T-cells. This result implies an “immune-protective niche” wherein PD-L1+ TAMs augment the pool of available PD-L1 to engage PD-1 on T-cells within the immediate vicinity of HRS cells and prevent immune-mediated elimination of the neoplastic cells. The effectiveness of PD-1 blockade in cHL may be due, in part, to disruption of this novel micro-anatomic structure. Additional details regarding mIF methodologies will be provided in a subsequent section. 4 Cyclic Immunofluorescence (CycIF) As the name implies, cyclic immunofluorescence (CycIF) combines iterative cycles of tissue staining and three-channel mIF. More specifically panels of fluorophore-conjugated primary antibodies are sequentially applied (typically 4–5 cycles) and imaged, with intervening steps of fluorophore inactivation by oxidation using hydrogen peroxide [13–15]. Unlike in the TSA approach to mIF,

460 Sanjay S. Patel and Scott J. Rodig primary antibodies remain bound to their targets in the course of a CycIF assay. A more detailed discussion of this methodology will be provided in a subsequent section. 5 Multiplexed Ion Beam Imaging (MIBI) Multiplexed Ion Beam Imaging (MIBI) is a revolutionary and distinct technology from those described above with the capability to detect and visualize and exceptionally large number of proteins in situ. It uses secondary ion mass spectrometry to image antibodies tagged with isotopically pure elemental reporters, rather than HRP or fluorophore conjugates, and is based on the mass cytometry technique that preceded it [16]. In brief, primary antibodies are conjugated to a water-soluble polymer bearing multiple metal-chelating ligands [17]. The polymer is comprised of a terminal maleimide group for coupling to cysteine-SH groups on the Fc portion of a given antibody; this approach is considered much more efficacious for preserving antibody reactivity than covalent attachment to amino groups of lysine residues. The chelating ligand component of the polymer is designed to form high-affinity complexes with lanthanide (Ln3+) ions. This family of elements is particularly useful for the purpose of labeling primary antibodies given their low natural abundance in tissue and the broad choice of elements and isotopes. Furthermore, the metal-chelating ligand enables attachment of multiple numbers of a given elemental ion, thereby increasing the sensitivity of detection. After staining FFPE tissue with the labeled antibodies, these elemental tags are subsequently detected and quantified using inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (ICP- TOF- MS) [16]. This methodology is theoretically capable of analyzing up to 100 differentially tagged antibodies simultaneously in a single tissue section. An additional benefit of MIBI is the capability of achieving as low as parts-per-billion sensitivity over a five-log dynamic range at a very high resolution [18, 19]. In comparison, mCIHC and mIF have dynamic ranges of approximately 1–2 and 2–3 logs, respectively. A slight variation on this technique using a modified ArF excimer GeoLas C laser system (i.e., laser ablation) rather than an ion beam has also been reported with similar results [20]. In contrast to standard mCIHC and mIF protocols, sample preparation involves one-step, rather than sequential, application of a cocktail of elementally tagged primary antibodies. Samples are subsequently mounted in a sample holder and subjected to a rasterized oxygen duoplasmatron primary ion beam. As this beam strikes a sample, lanthanide adducts of the bound antibodies are liberated as secondary ions and recorded by a TOF-MS. For each physical pixel in the analyzed tissue, a mass spectrum is recorded,

Overview of Tissue Imaging Methods 461 and reflects the abundance of queried antigens in that location. Spectral data is converted into Tagged Image File Format (TIFF) files, with each image depicting expression of one protein in the field of view. Cell segmentation is performed using a convolutional neural net. Similar to image analysis in mIF, this process is initiated with manual annotation, and thereafter the trained network is applied to the segmentation of new images. Following segmentation, additional cellular features including size protein expression can be extracted allowing subsequent clustering and assignment of distinct cell populations (e.g., tumor cells vs. immune cell subsets). Cell populations are annotated within the context of analyzed tissue by way of pseudocoloring. For each sample, quantitative information regarding cell types and their locations within the tissue can be extracted [18]. In the initial report by Angelo and colleagues, a NanoSIMS 50 L mass spectrometer (Cameca) was used in conjunction with a primary ion beam source. This instrument utilized seven detector trolleys tuned to the elemental peaks corresponding to each metal isotope-conjugated antibody, limiting contamination by organic elements present in the analyzed tissue, and images were captured in cycles. In the first cycle, for example, detectors were tuned to the following masses: detector 1, 27Al; detector 2, 139La; detector 3, 143Nd; detector 4, 137Sm; detector 5, 158Gd; detector 6, 166Er; and detector 7, 176Yb. Regions of interest in each sample were identified on serial sections using brightfield microscopy and were then located using a charge-coupled device camera in the NanoSIMS analysis chamber. Ion images were acquired for fields of view from 50 to 100 microns, with up to 10 repeat scans over a single area. The total scan time for a single field of view ranged from between 5 and 25 min. Larger areas could be assembled by stitching together multiple contiguous fields of view. Using breast tumor samples, images were acquired for hematoxylin (used as a nuclear counterstain given its aluminum content), and labeled monoclonal antibodies recognizing ERa, PR, Ki-67, E-cadherin, HER2, and dsDNA in one scan, followed by antibodies recognizing keratin, vimentin, and actin in another. Pseudo-brightfield images analogous to DAB staining were generated by coding hematoxylin on a white-to-blue scale and the desired marker on a white-to-brown scale. Similarly, pseudo-fluorescence images were generated using a dsDNA channel (red), a hematoxylin channel (blue) and a marker channel (green). Composite pseudo-brightfield and pseudo-fluorescence images were then created, for each antibody used in the study, within a single field of view. Angelo’s group recently utilized MIBI to more comprehensively generate a 36-marker proteomic profile of the immune microenvironment of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) [21]. An analysis of FFPE samples from 41 patients with TNBC revealed

462 Sanjay S. Patel and Scott J. Rodig variability in the composition of tumor-immune populations across individuals. Subsequent, spatial analyses identified tumors that were either “mixed” or “compartmentalized” with respect to immune infiltrations and expression patterns of PD-1, PD-L1, and IDO. Perhaps most importantly, these data revealed a correlation between a quantifiably defined “compartmentalized” architecture and improved overall survival. 6 Codetection by indexing (CODEX) Codetection by indexing (CODEX) is another novel technology for highly multiparametric in situ analysis of protein expression using tissue sections. One of the benefits of this technique is its use of a standard fluorescence microscope rather than an ion beam coupled to a mass spectrometer. Unlike the other platforms described above, published reports involving CODEX have only utilized frozen tissue cut onto glass slides, rather than FFPE tissue. Like the other multiplexing methods, multiple antibodies are applied to a single tissue section for visualization simultaneously; however, the antibodies are tagged with unique DNA oligonucleotides, rather than fluorophores or rare metal elements, and then crosslinked to their cellular targets. The process typically involves a single step of immunostaining with up to 40-antibodies each labeled with distinct oligonucleotide tags. Visualization of a tissuebound antibody requires specific PCR-based extension of each antibody- bound oligonucleotide followed by annealing to a complementary strand of DNA coupled to a specific fluorophore. Analysis typically involves imaging 2–5 DNA-tagged antibodies with 2–5 fluorescently labeled complementary oligonucleotides at a time with a standard fluorescent microscope, followed by enzymatic cleavage of the fluorescently labeled oligonucleotides, specific PCR-based extension of an additional set of 2–5 unique antibody tags, and rehybridization with the fluorescently labeled complementary oligonucleotides. Complete analysis of the single tissue section requires approximately 30 h to image a 1 cm2 area at 400 nm resolution. At the conclusion of the multicycle rendering protocol, each group of antibodies is visualized at a known, predefined cycle of the indexing protocol and the multiparameter image is reconstructed [22]. Using this methodology, Nolan and colleagues recently examined normal and lupus (MRL/lpr) murine spleens [22]. With a 30-antibody panel designed to identify splenic-resident cell types (e.g., lymphocytes, macrophages, microvessels, conduit system, and splenic stroma) the four classic anatomic compartments could be resolved: red pulp, B cell follicle, periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS), and the marginal zone (MZ). Using a clustering algorithm, the expression profiles of hundreds of thousands of

Overview of Tissue Imaging Methods 463 segmented cells were categorized according to 27 broadly defined phenotypic groups. Through application of pairwise and combinatorial (i-niches) statistics of cell-to-cell contacts in splenic samples, the study revealed a significant non-random distribution of cells in the murine spleens whereby specific cell types were either selectively associating with, or avoiding, each other. Importantly, a subset of these cellular mapped cellular interactions varied between normal (BALBc) or diseased (MRL/lpr) splenic tissue revealing previously unrecognized reorganization of the cellular architecture in the diseased state. Additional details can be found in the published report [22]. 7 Digital Spatial Profiling The abovementioned techniques all use antibody-based methods to detect antibody–protein complexes in a tissue section. Digital Spatial Profiling (DSP) is a recently developed technique based on the nCounter® barcoding technology developed by NanoString that enables spatially resolved digital characterization of proteins or mRNA in a highly multiplexed (up to 1000-plex) assay. In brief, antibodies or mRNA probes are coupled with UV photocleavable oligonucleotide tags. Upon hybridization of probes to slide-mounted FFPE tissue, UV exposure is used to liberate the oligonucleotide tags within small, predefined regions of interest (ROIs). The collected probes are quantified on a standard nCounter system, and counts are mapped back to tissue location, which produces a spatially resolved digital profile of analyte (protein or mRNA) abundance within each ROI. A more detailed discussion of this methodology will be provided in a subsequent section. 8 Conclusions Over the past several decades, tissue imaging methods have progressed from single marker-based immunohistochemical techniques to more recently developed highly multiplexed and multiparametric approaches to simultaneously profile upward of 35–40 protein targets in a single tissue section. While the former remains generally sufficient for diagnostic purposes, the latter has been largely driven by an ever-increasing need to more fully capture the biological heterogeneity of the tumor microenvironment in a quantifiable manner and thus to support rational selection of targeted therapeutics and precision medicine. While such sophisticated approaches to tissue biomarker evaluation are exciting, and hold tremendous promise, they are nonetheless in their infancy and therefore come with one or more caveats at this time including, but not limited to, (1) high cost; (2) lack of standardized

464 Sanjay S. Patel and Scott J. Rodig approaches across laboratories; (3) time- and labor-intensive protocols; and (4) lack of widespread accessibility. The subsequent chapters in this part of the book discuss in greater detail the methodologies introduced here and include expanded commentaries on the benefits and drawbacks of each of these approaches. hensive multiplexed technologies that allow for simultaneous visualization of an even larger number of biomarkers from a single tissue section, as well as to streamline, automate, and reduce the time spent on tissue staining and processing [6]. Multiplexed technologies are being used to identify the presence of multiple biological markers on a single tissue sample or an ensemble of different tissue samples [7]. They provide unique in situ biological information that in many cases cannot be attained by other methods or by single chromogenic immunohistochemistry (IHC) techniques. In routine pathology workflow, singlet chromogenic IHC is the bright-field microscopy method (absorption spectrometry, Fig. 1a) for the visualization of specific proteins expressed in discrete cell types of different tissues. The visualization of these proteins is frequently made by an indirect detection through a conjugated secondary antibody and polymers that will amplify the signal of the epitope (antigen) of interest [8]. The evaluation and analysis of IHC slides in the predigital era is dependent on standard optic microscope with a semiquantitative scale that captures the Fig. 1 A simplified diagram that illustrates the energy transmission in spectroscopy and the graphic representation of a multispectral image. This methodology can be problematic due to observer subjectivity, inter- and intraobserver variation, and limited range data (usually quantified by 0–4 grades scale) [9]. Recent advances in digital pathology have made possible a quantitative IHC through the absolute quantification of the revealed chromogen by digital image analysis and automated average scoring reaching a similarity to the standardized pathologist-based visual assessment [9, 10]. The role of the pathologist is evolving from the traditional task of correlation between morphological changes with clinical manifestations and morphological-based diagnosis to the current necessity of a quantitative morphology in order to provide prognostic and predictive information from small biopsies or whole tumor tissue sections. Translational research is transforming the practice of pathology and has necessitated the validation of new forms of digital image analysis, incorporation of molecular-based methods to in vivo microscopy, as well as, guiding the drug development from preclinical to clinical stages by the in situ quantification of biomarkers in different pre- and post-treatment time-points [11, 12]. The pathologist’s participation in the daily work with clinicians is growing at the same level of preanalytical workflow with accelerated fixation devices, automated IHC stainers, the development of tissue microarrays, whole slide digital scanners, and, finally, the automated digital image analysis of spectral imaging [13]. 1.1 Multiplexed Multiplex is an adjective involving or consisting of many elements Labeling and the in a complex relationship. The multiparametric analysis of individ- Immunome ual cells has been available since the detection and quantification tools provided by flow cytometry. The ability to increase the number of parameters able to recognize a single cell subpopulation started in 1960 with the development of the fluorescence activated cell sorter (FACS) [14]. It consisted on flow microfluorometers that simultaneously measured light-based physical parameters of individual cells traveling in a narrow fluid jet, most of these parameters as a consequence of fluorescence intensities (emission spectroscopy, Fig. 1b) caused by fluorochromes attached directly to the cell components (direct fluorescence), or indirectly through secondary fluorescent antibodies (indirect immunofluorescence) [14–16]. This technology initiated the concept of multiplexing (more than two labeling antibodies, N > 2) applied to a single cell level in a fluorescence- based methodology in order to define properties and functions of subsets of different cells coexisting in blood and organs [14]. The need to study more than two markers on one specific cell began with the idea that thymocytes could be divided into series of more or less distinct subsets or subpopulations. In other words, advancements in immunology and cell biology pushed the development of multiplexed platforms at the same time that the immunomic concept started to be defined [16].

470 Alejandro Francisco-Cruz et al. Tumors are complex mixtures of cells, and consist of stromal cells, endothelial cells, and tumor infiltrating immune cells interacting with malignant cells known as intratumoral immune landscape. Understanding the complex interactions of tumors with their microenvironment is of major importance to understand not only the protective immune response against tumors but also how to leverage and amplify that response to combat the tumor [17]. An unsupervised correlation matrix of the intratumor immunome revealed that, the spatial–temporal analysis of 28 cell types, cytotoxic T cells, T follicular helper cells, and B cells had the strongest correlations with disease-free survival in colorectal carcinoma [18]. In addition, the participation of other protective immune cells such as T helper type 1 cells, and other soluble factors such as chemokines, cytotoxic and adhesion molecules, can portend prognostic and predictive information for several types of tumors (e.g., breast, ovarian, melanoma, lung, and hepatocellular tumors) [17]. After characterizing the majority of the immune subsets infiltrating tumors by multiplexed methods, a new perspective of host defense would reveal the central role of protective and non-protective immune phenotypes within the tumor [18]. 1.2 Fundamentals The central component for multiplex immunofluorescence workof Multispectral flow is multispectral imaging. Spectral imaging combines spectros- Imaging and Unmixing copy and imaging (Fig. 1b) [19]. Imaging is the science and Techniques technology of acquiring two-dimensional spatial (X and Y) and temporal data information from objects depending on parameters 1.2.1 Multispectral such as the spatial resolution, field of view, dynamic range, and Imaging (MSI) lowest detectable signal [19]. Optical spectroscopy studies the spectral characteristics of matter, mainly in the spectrum of the visible light range or the collection of light intensities at different wavelengths (λ) [19]. The number of captured wavelengths distinguishes multispectral (10–30 bands of data) from hyperspectral (hundreds to thousands of bands of data) imaging systems [20]. Essentially, in multispectral imaging the imaging system provides the intensity wavelength spectrum at every pixel of the image, in addition of the typical two dimensional position of every pixel [19]. To obtain the third dimensional information for every pixel, conventional cameras store data corresponding to red, green, and blue signals (RGB), approximating the range of color perception of the human eye [21]. However, the analysis of wavelengths of light beyond the components RGB is only obtained with specialized digital camera known as charged-coupled device (CCD) that incorporates a liquid crystal tunable filter for specifying desired wavelengths of light [20, 21]. The commercially available liquid crystal tunable filter-based system Nuance™, CRi, system is suitable for both bright-field and fluorescence imaging, usually attached to a microscope with a standard digital camera port. Under automatic control, a series of images can be taken within a

Multiplex Immunofluorescence 471 spectral range that can extend from the blue out into the nearinfrared [13]. Finally, after the execution of processing algorithms at each pixel of digitized signals, the multispectral image is created similar to a cube that contains spatial information associated with a spectrum at every pixel within the three-dimensional space [19, 21, 22]. 1.2.2 Spectral Library For multiplex immunofluorescence, it is necessary to excite all the and Linear Unmixing fluorophores contained in a single slide after the staining, but the emission spectral range cannot overlap with the excitation range [19]. To overcome this complexity, multiband filters are used to detect more than one fluorochrome by band in the filter [19]. Every pixel contained in the multispectral image should be classified within a linear combination of the spectra using a spectral library as a reference (similar to a standard curve for normalization in quantitative PCR, Fig. 2a). In this way, the percentage of each basis spectrum contributing to each pixel can be determined. Using these percentages, a total intensity at a pixel can be determined since the amount of each specific pixel from the stained tissue can be quantitatively measured with reference to the spectral library (Fig. 2b) [21]. Generating an appropriate spectral library can be simple, and it requires imaging single samples stained with a primary antibody directed against a well-known and highly prevalent antigen (e.g., CD20, CD3, etc) using only one fluorescent dye at a time (Fig. 2a). Additionally, the spectra from each dye can be extracted using automated spectral software (e.g., InForm™, PerkinElmer; Fig. 2b) [13]. Once the spectral library is correctly built-in, to process the multispectral image (with all the fluorophores from a panel already stained) the key task is to partition the overall visual signal at each pixel into its different components. This partitioning is achieved by a methodology known as linear unmixing, also termed spectral unmixing, which is an algorithm that can unmix the data quickly and accurately within seconds, generating individual abundance images for each of the unmixed components, as well as a component image containing and combining all the unmixed species in one single image file or display (Fig. 3) [13]. The linear unmixing method is based on the assumption that the measured signal from each color is linearly proportional to the concentration of that color in the object [19, 23]. This method or algorithm is based on fluorochromes stained either separately (spectral library) in addition to the mixture in the images of the study. Therefore, the linear decomposition algorithm is able to determine the specific amount of each fluorochrome at each pixel through measuring and saving the emission spectra of every distinct fluorochrome prior to the actual analysis of the multiplexed slide [19, 23, 24]. After the linear unmixing, the individual components (i.e. the signal from each individual fluorophore) can then be turned on or off, and can be

In this regard, it is likely that multiplex fluorescence-based techniques will become increasingly part of the standard pathology workflow in the near future. 1.3.1 Amplification For the visualization of proteins or nucleic acids, fluorescence is of the Epitope Detection, associated with a lower background, lower detection threshold, Tyramide Signal and easier quantification than absorption [26]. For immunofluo- Amplification, rescence (antibodies conjugated with fluorophores as reporters), and Interpretation there are two basic approaches to antigen detection: direct or indirect labeling. In direct immunofluorescence, a fluorophore is directly conjugated to a primary antibody. In indirect immunofluorescence, the fluorophore is conjugated to a secondary antibody, which is species-specific directed against the constant region(s) of the primary antibody. In addition, if an enzyme reaction is applied as part of the signal detection, the best term for the methodology is fluorescent IHC. There is a direct relationship between the concentration of an epitope and the amount of fluorescence intensity in the direct fluorescence and chromogenic IHC. At low concentrations, this relationship is linear; therefore, reliable quantitation is possible (Fig. 4a) [19, 26]. Indirect immunofluorescence, without t yramide signal amplification, has a marked amplification of the signal, leading to a 20% higher intensity of the signal than that for direct fluorescence or chromogenic IHC. As such, the linear range for the indirect immunofluorescence is 9–10 times greater than that for the direct fluorescence requiring fewer target molecules for signal detection (Fig. 4a) [26]. Modified from [26] immunofluorescence, a maximal signal is present at the highest concentration of antigen. In addition, the ability of an immunoassay coupled to an enzymatic reaction, such as IHC, to detect an antigen depends not only on the antigen concentration but also on the affinity of the antibody used and the catalytic activity of the reporter enzyme used [27]. The fluorescent signal amplification can be achieved if a secondary antibody is conjugated with an enzyme instead of fluorophores. Robust amplification approaches, such as the avidin–biotin complex and/or the tyramine system amplification, result in signal amplification and improved detection [26–28]. Tyramide signal amplification was described in the 1990s [27, 28]. It is a catalyzed reporter deposition and it involves utilizing the antigen-dependent reporter enzyme (e.g. horseradish peroxidase) to catalyze the covalently binding of an additional reporter (fluorescence-labeled tyramide) on the surface of a solid-phase immunoassay system [27, 28]. The fluorochrome-tyramide complex is insoluble in water and once the deposit is attached to the antigen, the product is highly stable. The reaction with the solid-phase (e.g., tissue section) only occurs in the location where it is generated (where the primary antibody is located) with a detection limit of 8–16-fold for fluorescent systems and one single cycle of amplification [27]. The introduction of tyramide signal amplification increased the

476 Alejandro Francisco-Cruz et al. sensitivity of chromogenic IHC (Fig. 4), and it is ideal for fluorescent multiplexing with similar species of primary antibodies because the primary and secondary antibody complexes (attached to the tissue by non-covalent bonds) can be removed by heat energy such as by microwave treatment [29]. Repeated microwave treatment (in conjunction with the antigen retrieval) has the additional advantage that it completely eliminates endogenous peroxidase activity and removes immunoglobulins, avoiding the cross-reactivity between two or more detection sequences (Fig. 5). This system coupled with tyramide signal amplification at every cycle, enables the detection of very low expressed antigens without affection of the fluorescent intensity [30]. At the end of each cycle, only the tyramide–fluorochrome complex, covalently attached to the antigen, will remain surrounding the epitope site (Fig. 5) [30]. It is important to note that tyramide signal amplification is driven by enzymatic reaction, the same way diaminobenzidine deposition is driven by the horseradish peroxidase, but only tyramide signal amplification is uniquely suited for serial staining [6, 31]. Staining intensity can be dependent on the amplification system used and not necessarly on the quantity of the antigen. The relationship between the amplification system and signal intensity is graphically illustrated in Fig. 4. With tyramide amplification, the difference in epitope concentration between a negative and a strong positive staining intensity can be scored to either negative or positive (Fig. 4b) compared with other staining methods without signal amplification where the intensity of the signal will increase as the quantity of the antigen does. Proper titration of primary antibody is essential, and enhancement components are broadly used in most of the labs. A strong amplification system, such as tyramide signal amplification, may in some cases reveal a positive test result, while an approach using a less strong signal enhancement (e.g., chromogenic IHC or direct immunofluorescence) may be negative. In fact, by tyramide signal amplification, the detection of the proteins is increased more than 10 times compared to standard biotin-based staining methods [32]. 1.3.2 Fluorescent There are multiple fluorophores available for multiplex immuno- Multiplex IHC or Multiplex fluorescence (Table 1). The principle to select the correct fluoro- Immunofluorescence phore involves the evaluation of the property of each individual fluorophores wavelength to be excited and emit at a longer wavelength (a phenomena known as a Stokes shift) [6]. Tyramides can be conjugated to biotin or fluorescent labels and revealed by streptavidin–HRP system [6, 31]. The HRP catalyzes the formation of tyramide into highly reactive tyramide radicals that covalently bind to electron-rich tyrosine moieties close to the epitope of interest on FFPE tissue. Tissue surfaces with anchored biotinylated tyramide must be further treated with fluorescent or enzyme tagged proteins that have a high affinity for biotin as streptavidin before to microscopic visualization [6, 31]. Fluorescent multiplex IHC, known as well as multiplex immunofluorescence or quantitative immunofluorescence, allows researchers to use antibodies raised in the same species, and creating different panels for different targets [4, 31]. The manual-staining protocol involves detection with fluorescent TSA reagents, followed by microwave treatment that removes the primary and secondary antibodies between cycles and any nonspecific staining that reduces tissue autofluorescence for each antibody cycle. In the automated protocol using Leica Bond RX or other autostainers the time is reduced drastically when compared with manual staining. Selection of Antibodies The first step to build a staining panel for multiplex immunofluofor Multiplex rescence IHC starts with the research question defining the group Immunofluorescence Panel of immune cells that are needed to target. Central to the success of this approach is the selection of the most specific targets (epitopes) with the lowest redundancy to best define the subpopulation of cells.

Multiplex Immunofluorescence 479 In this regard, the support of experts on immunology is essential to define the expected pattern of colocalization of the selected markers (Fig. 6a). The selection of the primary antibodies is the second step for the development of the panel, and it implies a careful selection and testing of antibody clones that will give the best staining pattern evaluated by experienced pathologist (Fig. 6b). The initial goal in this step is to establish the optimal antibody conditions, including titration, detection system, blocking regimen and antigen retrieval protocol. For initial testing, it is necessary to determine the expected expression of the antibody and must include the tissue-type, cell type, cell compartment whether the antigen is normally expressed, overexpressed or lost in the target tissue by chromogenic IHC (Fig. 6a, b). For the first tests, it is crucial to determine which tissues are required for validation. Tissues for validation are a mix of positive and negative tissues, depending on the biomarker, and cell lines (including overexpressing and knock-out lines) should also be utilized. For a well-characterized antibody with a limited spectrum of antigenic targets and robust historical performance in FFPE tissues (e.g., CD3 or CD8), the validation process can be pragmatic. For an antibody that is not well characterized and/or has a wide range of reported reactivity, a more extensive validation may be required. Regarding immune-cell markers, it is very important to consider that signaling pathways, cytokine and cytokines receptors, and some of cell-membrane markers (cluster of differentiation) may exhibit pleiotropy (multiple biological actions) and redundancy (shared biological actions). To overcome this, a well-defined immunologic background and specialized support team is necessary to select the biomarkers that will answer a specific question. Optimization of Primary Chromogenic IHC analysis should be performed preferably by an Antibodies by IHC automated staining system, with well provider validated antibodies. The expression of all cell biomarkers can be detected with polymers (e.g., Novocastra Bond Polymer Refine Detection Kit, Leica Microsystems) and with a diaminobenzidine reaction and hematoxylin counterstaining. The correct titrations of antibodies for IHC analysis can be chosen on the basis of the minimum to maximum range of staining in negative and positive control specimens, respectively, combined with the uniformity of staining within the specific cell expression with the different antibodies to obtain a correct staining pattern. Positive and negative controls should be used for IHC validation considering native expression of markers on normal tissues, special specimens with overexpression of the marker of interest (malignant tumors, placenta, etc.), and/or transfected cell lines as positive controls, and tumors lacking expression or knockout cell lines as negative controls. For the immune cell markers, the IHC expression usually can be evaluated in lymphoid organs such as spleen, tonsil, lymph node, and/or

Automated Multiplex Once each target of interest was optimized in uniplex slides (by Immunofluorescence chromogenic IHC and single IF), the Opal 7 multiplexed assay can Staining Protocol be used to generate multiple staining slides. Briefly, primary antibodies to tonsil specimens as controls should be stained to optimize concentrations previously determined on the uniplex control tissues (Fig. 6b). Staining should be performed consecutively by using the same steps as those used in uniplex immunofluorescence (Fig. 5), and the detection for each marker should be completed before application of the next antibody. The best sequence of antibodies for multiplex staining is determined for each panel combination depending on the intensity of the fluorophore and the prevalence of the antigen following the general criteria of the brightest fluorophore for low expressed antigens (rare antigens, e.g., B7-H4) and less bright fluorophores for highly expressed antigens (e.g., cytokeratin). To control for variations of the staining over time, slide tissues from sequential FFPE tissues sections stained at 1-week intervals is recommended. Controls should include: positive controls, in the case of immune cell markers positive controls can include tonsil or lymph node, however, depending on the prevalence of the biomarker other controls should be included, such as placenta or transfected cell lines; and negative controls including the unstained autofluorescence tissue section which should be the same type of tissue than the group of cases to analyze. Slides should be stained maintaining the same conditions and using the same kit of staining (e.g., Opal 7 kit) than in the uniplex protocol. RX instrument enables small volumes of reagent (as little as 150 μL per slide) to be uniformly applied over the tissue sections on a slide and has continuous batch processing, allowing for independent start and finish times for each batch of 10 slides. Advantages The advantages of the multispectral imaging for the analysis of and Disadvantages multiplex immunofluorescence incudes the possibility to separate of Multiplex the image into distinct spectral signals, improvement of the quality Immunofluorescence of the final images compared with other fluorescence-based imaging systems, and the possibility to eliminate background staining and counterstaining. Multiplex immunofluorescence offers the possibility to study the cell biology through capturing multidimensional data related to tissue architecture, spatial distribution of multiple cell phenotypes, and co-expression of signaling and cell cycle markers at the same time [21, 34]. Importantly, this method is similar in cost to standard chromogenic detection methods, it allows the use of multiple similar species primary antibodies, it supports the assessment across an entire tissue section [6], and it reduces the amount of sample required for analysis that is often limited [21]. The most important disadvantage when multispectral imaging is applied to the analysis of pathological tissue sections is that a spectral image contains significantly more information and data than a single two-dimensional image, and therefore requires a significantly longer time to acquire, process and analyze [19]. On the other hand, the number of wavelength band passes that can be fit into the visible wavelength range limits the number of fluorophores without crosstalk between them or DAPI [6]. More than seven probes resulted in difficulties for the panel optimization and validation due to the spectral overlap [21]. The balance between information and time can be resolved when well-developed software are available; however, most of the available free software use a metadata interference which can be cumbersome. Improvements on novel dye chemistries, stability of fluorophores, filter technology and imaging spectroscopy software, will support a wider parameter able to analyze by multiplex immunofluorescence. Currently, new methodologies are available for multiplexing with a light-based principle and others with mass-based principle (Fig. 7). Changing the light (fluorescence) as a reporter by the mass (atomic mass from isotopes) helps to overcome the overlapping issues of the visible spectrum and to increase the number of biomarkers able to study. Clinical Applications Multiplex immunofluorescence methodologies are expanding our of Multiplex knowledge of tumor immune contexture. Mapping the tumor Immunofluorescence microenvironment and studying the predictive value of immune checkpoints expression in malignant cells and tumor infiltrating immune cells has proven to be informative in patients with melanoma, lung cancer, breast cancer, gastric cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma and other tumors treated with immune modulatory

Multiplex Immunofluorescence 485 therapies [35–39]. Although PD-L1 expression determined by chromogenic IHC has shown to be predictive in non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) to anti-PD-L1/PD-1 blockage, a negative test does not exclude response to immunotherapy [40, 41]. Using a multiplex immunofluorescence panel to detect malignant cells and lymphocytes expressing Granzyme B (GZB) and Ki-67, a dormant lymphocyte signature characterized by high CD3 infiltration but low expression of GZB and Ki-67 was associated with sensitivity to PD-L1/PD-1 blockade in NSCLC [42]. This phenotype was independent from the tumor mutational burden and PD-L1 expression on malignant cells [42]. By multiplex immunofluorescence, it is possible to study the relationship between phenotypes of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and the independent roles affecting the clinical outcomes in NSCLC. At the same time, multiplex immunofluorescence enables the study of targetable biomarkers, such as PD-L1, to study the effect of neoadjuvant treatment in immune-cell subpopulations and its impact on clinical outcomes [43–46]. The immunophenotypic findings of the tumor associated immune infiltrate determined by multiplex immunofluorescence can further be correlated with genomic or transcriptomic data from the same patients. For instance, the protein and mRNA expression of PD-L1 in NSCLC and immune cells by multiplex immunofluorescence and in situ mRNA hybridization has prognostic relevance since tumors with PD-L1 positivity and increased TILs (hot tumors) infiltration are associated with better survival [47]. Similarly, it was demonstrated that NSCLC with high PD-L1 expression and inactivated T-cell response (cold tumors) are associated with an activated EGFR signaling pathway [45, 47]. The spatial relationship between immune cells infiltrating tumors by multiplex immunofluorescence has been correlated with clinical outcomes or the pathological grade in NSCLC and pancreatic intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), respectively [43, 48]. It has been demonstrated that the spatial proximity between tumor and T regulatory cell spatial proximity predicts worse NSCLC patients’ survival, while spatial proximity between CD8 and T regulatory cells predicts survival in these patients [48]. On the other hand, spatial proximities between epithelial cells and cytotoxic T cells are predictive of the dysplasia grade for IPMN [43]. 1.4 Other Multiplexed staining bleaching techniques were developed with Multiplexed Staining different platform to study tumor tissue specimens [49]. The basic Methods Without concept of these techniques is to eliminate the staining marker Signal Amplification once complete to allocate the next biomarker in consecutive cycles after finishing the desired biomarkers to identify multiple antigens in a single sample. 1.4.1 Multi-Epitope- The multi-epitope-ligand cartography (MEL) [50, 51], is one such Ligand Cartography bleaching or erasing techniques, that is capable of colocalizing different proteins in one single tissue sample using consecutive rounds

486 Alejandro Francisco-Cruz et al. of conjugate biomarkers with fluorescent labels [52]. Sample of cells or sectioned tissue is incubated with one or more antibodies (conjugated to different dyes); followed by image acquisition of the sample using a high-sensitivity digital camera. After this, the sample is bleached with phosphate buffer saline to eliminate the excitation wavelengths, after which a new cycle of staining is started. One limitation of MELC technique is that the photobleaching step can only be applied to the microscope’s field of view, meaning that the multiprobe image is limited to a single microscopic medium-to-high power field [52]. MELC can be applied on FFPE and frozen tissue sections, and it has been coupled to RNA extraction to combine RNA and protein expression analysis [53]. MELC has been used as a very efficient methodology to study immune cell markers and intracellular signaling pathways in infectious contexts [54, 55] and to perform systematic high-c ontent proteomic analysis of colorectal cancer as well as the T cell-related protein expression patterns and their modification in the tissue of Barrett’s esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma patients [56, 57]. 1.4.2 Sequential Sequential immunoperoxidase labeling and erasing (SIMPLE) is a Immunoperoxidase multiplex IHC approach with sequential labeling bleaching tech- Labeling and Erasing nique that enables simultaneous marker visualization [58]. SIMPLE combines 5–12 markers using alcohol-soluble peroxidase substrate 3-amino-9-ethylcarbazole, with a fast nondestructive method for antibody–antigen separation. In in each labeling, a given precipitate is assigned a pseudo-color, and all colors are overlapped at the end of the process to visualize all the target antigens used. This method showed the ability to erase the results of a single stain while preserving tissue antigenicity for repeated rounds of labeling [58]. Using SIMPLE platform in a head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) cohort, differential immune profile complexity was able to evaluate. Three different immune profiles of HNSCC tumors were characterized by two panels with 12 markers in each, where lymphoid-inflamed, myeloid-inflamed, and hypoinflamed subgroups correlated with distinct clinical outcomes. In addition, geometrical mapping analysis revealed that the immune complexity status was associated with therapeutic response to vaccination therapy in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, where myeloid-inflamed and T cell exhaustion status correlated with shorter overall survival [59]. 1.4.3 MultiOmyx™ Created by General Electric Global Research has developed an Staining or Hyperplexed erase methodology platform called MultiOmyx™. MultiOmyx™ is Immunofluorescence a multiplex direct immunofluorescence approach where up to 60 Assay targets can be interrogated from a single FFPE section and uses primary conjugated antibodies with fluorochromes to stain different biomarkers of interest in batches of two or four at one time. After deactivating the tissue autofluorescence and completing the

Multiplex Immunofluorescence 487 first cycle of stain, the tissue is imaged followed by deactivation of the fluorochromes via alkaline oxidation to initiate a new cycle of staining. The MultiOmyx™ platform can stain multiplex rounds of biomarkers repeating the same procedure until the desired targets have been imaged in a multiplexed iterative manner [60, 61]. The MultiOmyx™ platform was applied to medullary colorectal cancer tissue and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition pathways were demonstrated, including coexpression of cytokeratin, Cadherin 3, Vimentin, and cytosolic Placenta-specific 8 protein. This provided evidence that excess PLAC8 expression was an important driver of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. An additional application of this technology is in the hematopathology lab where the routine diagnosis of hematological neoplasms includes several IHC markers, for example CD30, CD15, PAX-5, CD20, CD79a, CD45, B cell-specific Octamer Binding protein-1, OCT-2, and CD3 antibodies in the diagnosis of classical Hodgkin lymphoma. MultiOmyx™ shows equivalent performance for routine morphologic and IHC evaluation of cases in which classical Hodgkin lymphoma was included within the differential diagnosis [12]. 1.4.4 Codetection CODetection by indEXing (CODEX) is a fluorescence-based by Indexing or Fluorescent imaging approach that uses oligo-DNA-conjugated antibodies. Immunohisto-hybridization The oligonucleotide duplexes encode uniquely designed sequences with 5′ overhangs [62]. Fresh frozen tissue and isolated cells were used for validation of this methodology, but application on FFPE tissue is under development. Cells or fresh frozen tissue are stained with a cocktail containing all conjugated antibodies (up to 50 antibodies) at the same time. This methodology is based on secondary detection index cycles where tags are iteratively revealed in situ by using indexing nucleotides (adenine and guanine) and rendering fluorophore-conjugated nucleotides (uracil and cytidine) with the combination of a polymerization cycle and a fluorescent channel, at which a given DNA tag incorporates one of two fluorescently labeled dNTP species. Specifically, the antibody-matched overhangs (indexes) include a region to be filled by blank letters and a dedicated position for a dye labeled nucleotide at the end. The antibodies to be revealed first generally have shorter overhangs than the antibodies to be visualized later. Each extension and bleaching (with TCEP) cycle takes 10 min. Imaging in each cycle takes minutes to hours depending on sample dimensions, resolution, and microscope (a standard fluorescent microscope). The platform can be performed on any three-color fluorescence microscope enabling conversion of regular fluorescence microscope into a tool for multidimensional tissue rendering and cell cytometry [62], giving a good advantage to user this platform. CODEX is an innovative platform that has achieved and reported a deep immune profiling of mouse splenic architecture comparing normal murine

488 Alejandro Francisco-Cruz et al. spleen to spleens from animals with systemic autoimmune disease [14]. There is no cancer-related published studies using this method, but it is a promising and highly efficient methodology to study the tumor-associated immune contexture. 1.5 Conclusions Multiplex immunofluorescence and other multiplexed methods can provide important and efficient means to apply in disease diagnosis, prevention, and translational research. These systems are increasingly showing different capabilities from bench to the clinic, improving our understanding of the tumor microenvironment. Multiplex immunofluorescence and digital pathology image analysis supports a comprehensive study of the immunome, and the spatial-pattern distribution in the tumor microenvironment and their corresponding impact on clinical outcomes. The development of these new methods requires a multidisciplinary team, well-trained lab staff, pathologists with experience in digital image analysis, and the interaction with oncologists and immunologists to determine the clinically relevant biomarkers that delineate patients who will respond versus those who will not, and this will facilitate a more rapid transition into the clinical setting to directly benefit patients. In addition, these methodologists demand automation to provide efficient and fast information with a strong statistician and IT support to process, interact and save large amounts of data. Characterizing and validating these multiplex immunofluorescence staining using immune system-based biomarkers has several critical implications for clinical translation and has emerged as one of the most potent tools for immunoprofiling, offering simultaneous detection of up to seven markers in the same tissue section in FFPE tumor tissues. 2 Materials 2.1 Optimized 1.
