3.2 Manual 1. Unload slides from the instrument and place into 1× TBS Completion Steps Buffer.
2. Wash and clear sections through 3 changes of TBS Buffer.
3. Mount sections with cover glass using ProLong® Diamond
Antifade Mountant (Opal Mount medium). 3.3 Digital Image 1. Multiplex immunofluorescence slides can be imaged using the Analysis and Immuno Vectra 3.0 spectral imaging system (PerkinElmer). After low phenotyping (See magnification scanning (at 10×), the slides and tissue sections can Note 2) be sampled to select regions of interest. For the analysis of tumor tissues we recommend the selection of at least five individual fields (0.669 × 0.500 μm, 0.3345 mm2 each) in the intratumoral compartment avoiding necrotic and hemorrhagic areas.
2. Necrotic areas are not suitable for digital image analysis due to
the loss of the morphology that difficult the generation of tissue segmentation and the cell segmentation maps, in addition, necrotic areas are the main sources of several common pitfalls that can lead to wrong or misinterpreted results.
3. Hemorrhagic areas usually contain high autofluorescence due
to the concentration of hemoglobin. For selection of regions of interest, it is critical to engage an experienced pathologist who is able to distinguish the tumor components and artifacts comparing with a hematoxylin and eosin slide from the same tissue section.
4. After the selection of regions of interest and the scanning at
high magnification (20× or 40×), the image can be analyzed. InForm software couples the linear unmixing and the digital image analysis in one single project primarily specified by the user to personalize the analysis.

Multiplex Immunofluorescence 491
5. Every project is divided in different consecutive steps: prepara-
tion of the image (linear unmixing), tissue segmentation, nuclei and cell segmentation, phenotyping, and scoring. Once obtained the unmixed images (component images) it is possible to use other available software for digital pathology image analysis such as HALO (IndicaLab), VIS (Visiopharm), or other open source software such as ImageJ, Fiji, Icy, CellProfiler, and QuPath.
6. Before the deep analysis of the unmixed image, it is recom-
mended to evaluate separately the expression of every marker and signal obtained from every fluorophore by a pathologist in order to confirm that every marker is expressed in the expected group of cells and they are showing the correct pattern of expression (Fig. 6c).
7. By InForm software, it is possible to segment the tissue section
into different compartments depending on the expression of a specific marker such as the cytokeratin expression in carcinomas to define the malignant cell compartment (Fig. 6d).
8. The nuclear and cellular segmentation can be achieved relatively
easily by InForm that considers the expression of DAPI in all the nucleated cells to individualize every cell. The nuclear and cellular segmentation is the most critical step for the image analysis because those parameters determine the subsequent quantification of the density of cellular phenotypes and the percentage of expression of biomarkers in specific subpopulation.
9. Finally, an automated cell density per phenotype (colocaliza-
tion) can be obtained after repeated training steps to allow the software to recognize with a high confidence every colocalization observed by a well-trained pathologist (Fig. 6d). We have observed an excellent correlation between HALO, VIS and InForm software regarding the cell segmentation and the cell densities per phenotype obtained from the same images stained with a multiplex panel with 7 markers. 4 Notes
1. Several factors can adversely impact the quality of the staining
of the multiplex immunofluorescence and quality and reliability of the digital image analyses. Specifically, multiple factors that significantly affect the staining are the same that affect the chromogenic IHC staining. (a) L ong periods of fixation and long periods between the cut section and the staining. (b) S pecificity of antibodies and not well-optimized antibodies. (c) O rder of the antibody labeling.

492 Alejandro Francisco-Cruz et al. (d) S election of fluorophores and order of staining. (e) D ilution of the amplification system used. (f) A ntigen retrieval time and pH and appropriate blocking
2. For the accurate digital image analysis, is the following are
recommended: (a) T he selection of regions of interest, the cell segmentation, and phenotyping should be done under pathologist supervision. (b) F or confirming the specificity and reproducibility of the analysis, each area examined can be overlapped with the sequential chromogenic IHC slides to quantify each marker at the same location of the tumor specimens. (c) T he autofluorescence can be resolved with the multispectral camera; however, it demands the use of tissue specific autofluorescence controls per batch of staining or per study such as bone marrow or mixoid component in cases of sarcomas. (d) T he histologic assessment of each analysis area should be performed to ensure that the tumor tissue (at least 85% malignant cells) is included in the selected intratumoral region. References

498 Guray Akturk et al. 1 Introduction Characterization and spatial organization of molecular targets and cellular subsets in and around tissue lesions is of great significance, as shown by examples in tumor immunology such as the immunoscore [1], that is, the quantification of CD8 memory T cells in and around colorectal tumors as a prognostic marker [2], or as PD-L1 as a predictive marker of various solid tumors responding to immune checkpoint blockade of the PD-1 pathway [3, 4]. This characterization requires high-dimensional analysis of immune cells and cells from the tissue microenvironment, including diseased cells (tumor), immune cells, stroma, and vasculature, to elucidate their lineage by detecting specific markers of these cells in situ. Single-cell methods such as time-of-flight mass cytometry (CyTOF) can analyze cells of a given tissue with high precision and accuracy but require fresh tissue and do not provide information about tissue architecture [5]. Geographic location of cells and their relationship with other cells is also of interest. Many methods allowing for high-dimensional tissue analyses often rely on expensive equipment and proprietary reagents [6–10]. There is a need for an assay capable of showing multiple marker expressions on a single cell level including spatial features but concurrently affordable and simple, that can be performed in most labs with minimal requirements. Chromogen-based immunohistochemistry from formalin-fixed, paraffin embedded tissues is a perfect fit for this definition and it is used routinely in every pathology laboratory worldwide in daily diagnostic routines. However, it is most commonly used as a singleplex staining in which single antibody is performed on a single section and this approach is limited by tissue availability and insufficient for complex exploration such as immune cell subpopulations or colocalization of multiple markers in the tissue microenvironment. We have developed a multiplex immunostaining system named “multiplexed immunohistochemical consecutive staining on the same slide (MICSSS)” as simple and cost-effective as singleplex immunohistochemistry but robust and powerful at the same time for characterizing up to ten markers on the same tissue section [11]. MICSSS can be done on any formalinfixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) section and it relies on iterative cycles of immunostaining with various antibodies that can be selected in a mix-and-match fashion, scanning, and removal of chromogenic substrate (Fig. 1). High-dimensional coexpression analysis can be done on processed whole slide images since all antibodies are applied on the same section. Moreover, this method does not negatively affect marker intensity and can be performed for up to ten markers even on delicate tissue structures. Whole slide images belonging to the same section can be analyzed by AI-powered image analysis software such as QuPath to reveal

Multiplexed Immunohistochemical Consecutive Staining on Single Slide (MICSSS)… 499

markers within the microenvironment of a tissue lesion with spatial features visually and to further analyze in the form of data files rather than images [12]. MICSSS provides a tremendous opportunity and potential for tissue-based research worldwide as it makes multiplexed analysis of tissue markers affordable and simple. 1.1 Immunostaining MICSSS is a sample-sparing multiplex immunohistochemical method developed for formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) 1.1.1 Iterative Cycles tissue sections based on iterative cycles of immunostaining with of Immunostaining primary and secondary antibodies using standard chromogen amplification, scanning, and destaining of tissue slides (Fig. 1). Each staining cycle starts with optimized pH and heat-induced antigen retrieval conditions to reveal epitopes tailored to the primary antibody, followed by imaging of slides. Organic solvent soluble chromogens are used for MICSSS protocol since chromogenic substrate must be easily removable by destaining between cycles. Amino ethyl carbazole (AEC) is a red-colored chromogen ideal for this purpose; however, any soluble chromogen can be used for MICSSS immunostaining. Harris hematoxylin is used for counterstaining in each cycle and it includes ethanol in its preparation formula; one should be careful for the duration of hematoxylin counterstaining since it can decrease the intensity of chromogenic Fig. 1 MICSSS pipeline

500 Guray Akturk et al. color due to the effect of ethanol. While this bleaching step removes the chromogenic substrate, it does not guarantee removal of all antibody bonds to antigen on a given cellular compartment along with the chromogenic substrate. Heat-induced antigen retrieval likely contributes to additional partial removal of primary and secondary antibody pairs. Nevertheless, proper blocking must be included in the protocol after the first cycle and thereafter to block all residual antibodies belonging to the previous cycle. Peroxidase block and serum-free protein block are used in all cycles including the first one to eliminate possible nonspecific background staining. MICSSS system is capable of performing up to ten antibodies by this method without the interference of residual antibodies from previous cycles of staining, and before tissue damage from repeated cycles may start precluding analyses. Each cycle lasts for an average of 6–7 h, and approximately 30 slides can be processed simultaneously. Automated immunostaining platforms allow for batch process, and multiple slides can be stained with different antibodies simultaneously, in contrast to manual immunostaining in which just one antibody can be performed on multiple slides simultaneously. 1.1.2 Does Not Affect Antigen quality loss can be a major concern since destaining and Antigenicity/No Steric heat exposure are used after every cycle of MICSSS immunostain- Hindrance ing. MICSSS method has been validated with multiple markers constitutively expressed on immune cells by testing them in permutation of order of staining on consecutive slides from the same tissue block. Number of cells per mm2 for each marker tested was comparable for each marker regardless whether immunostaining was performed first, second, or even after 10 cycles, thereby establishing that MICSSS can be used as a reliable test for markers used to detect immune cells. MICSSS also provides similar signal intensity level for a selected marker after several cycles of immunostaining and it is validated by testing signal intensity for various antibodies in permutation of order by performing color deconvolution and comparing signal intensity histograms for different orders. This validation has revealed MICSSS provides robust evidence for antibody signal preservation even after tenth cycle and there was no significant difference between different orders of a selected immunostain. However, quantitative markers relying not only on density but on signal intensity, like PD-L1 and HER-2, should be prioritized, preferentially first in the iterative cycles before performing destaining, since even minimal signal intensity loss could affect interpretation based on guidelines for these markers. Another concern of iterative cycles can be damage on tissue sections after prolonged handling, in particular due to repeated need for removal of coverslips, which contributes to the recommended limit of a maximum of ten markers per slide.

Multiplexed Immunohistochemical Consecutive Staining on Single Slide (MICSSS)… 501 MICSSS panels can include immune markers that stain different compartments of a cell like nuclear, cytoplasmic, and nuclear.

While other multiplexing methods with depot effect amplification could experience steric hindrance, MICSSS does not appear to suffer from this problem due to effective destaining and blocking between cycles. MICSSS allows for routine testing of membranous expression of CD2, CD3, CD8, PD-1 quadruple positive T cells or cytoplasmic expression of HLA-DR, CD206, CD68, CD163 quadruple positive histiocytes without obvious steric hindrance. 1.1.3 Can Be Performed Pathology archives host a tremendous amount of IHC slides Along with a Fixed Marker worldwide which are acquired during diagnostic workflows. They are mostly singleplex immunostained slides in which browncolored DAB is used as a chromogen, as it is the most commonly used chromogen in the world. However, DAB is a permanent chromogen and is not removable by organic solvents the way AEC can be. MICSSS may be performed along with DAB staining using sets of antibodies from non-cross-reactive species in the first cycle, and double-colored (brown-red) multiplexed images can be acquired. This may be useful for example when performing cytokeratin immunostaining for tumor cells with DAB brown staining which remains preserved throughout MICSSS (insensitive to solvent- based destaining), while in parallel querying iteratively several markers for the immune microenvironment using standard MICSSS with AEC red staining. 1.2 Image Image acquisition is done after every cycle of immunostaining Acquisition since bleaching takes place between cycles and removes the immunostain (Fig. 2). It is performed by a whole slide scanner in which Fig. 2 Comparison of several markers on the same ROI of a triple negative breast cancer case

502 Guray Akturk et al. slides are scanned at 20× or 40× magnification and saved as full images in formats depending on the scanner type/brand. Certain points should be taken into consideration during the whole slide scanning process. Proper naming of image files is important to prevent any confusion, and it should ideally include at least antibody name, cycle number, and date, and including important immunostaining conditions like antibody incubation duration and dilution levels can be useful. Every project should have a specific folder/ subfolder system, and they should be kept in a cloud with backup system. Slide labels should also be included in the scanning since they can provide an image info backup. The size of image files can become an issue in time by accumulating data from several projects. Instead of scanning the entire slide area, selecting actual tissue area first and limiting the scan to this region can save some disk space without affecting the analysis. Tissue selection can be made by manual annotation or automatically. Most scanning systems provide automatic tissue detection feature. If automatic tissue recognition is used for detecting the scanned area and tissue is thin or faintly stained, thresholding should be used. Thresholding can also be used for the opposite scenario of having dark-colored dirt or pen lines on the slides. Artifacts on the slide like dust, excessive residual stain, and/or curled tissue areas should be discarded as much as possible since they can create false-positive detection during image analysis on the next step. Focusing is important since blurry areas negatively affect the image analysis quality. It can be done automatically or manually. Putting multiple focus points on the tissue area can minimize blurring in newer scanners. When there is more than one tissue on the slide, each tissue piece can be selected and focused separately to increase quality, otherwise the scanner recognizes all tissue pieces as a single tissue and sets one common focal plane. There are many whole slide image formats depending on the selection of digital slide scanner. Scanner specific formats usually have file size limitation advantages when compared with uncompressed raw images. Selected objective magnification level is the main factor for resolution of images and digital slide scanners most commonly have 20× and 40× options. 20× is the most commonly used magnification level of scanning since it usually provides enough detail for image analysis in addition to providing images with optimal file sizes. 1.3 Image Analysis MICSSS produces individual images of full tissue immunostaining per marker, up to ten markers per slide (Fig. 2). A challenge is then to be able to analyze these images, either individually to establish density (per mm2) or percentage (out of all nucleated cells) of stained cells expressing the marker, or for coexpression of markers on the same cell. Manual counting is feasible for individual markers but can quickly become overwhelming, pointing to the growing use of digital pathology solutions when multiple

Multiplexed Immunohistochemical Consecutive Staining on Single Slide (MICSSS)… 503

markers are involved. MICSSS-generated image analysis can be performed with a variety of software tools and suites, most of which include steps of image segmentation based on nucleus detection (hematoxylin or optical density), detection of chromogen, and, in some cases, image coregistration. Because one of the goals of MICSSS is to democratize access to multiplex immunohistochemistry, the following pipeline is based on open-source software developed by Dr. Bankhead named QuPath [12]. 1.3.1 Color Vectors QuPath performs color deconvolution for channel separation for RGB images. Default stain vectors for MICSSS brightfield images are hematoxylin, AEC chromogen, and residual channel (Fig. 3). Default values for these stain vectors should always be checked since accuracy of cell segmentation and positive cell detection depends on these vector values. QuPath has a useful feature named “estimate stain vectors” in which color vector values can be automatically estimated depending on a sampling ROI on the whole slide image. However, this sampling ROI must be small and include a balanced level of positive and negative cells as well as a blank white area. 1.3.2 Annotation Scanned tissue area can include many different tissue compartments such as tumor, normal organ parenchyma, normal epithelium, and tumor/normal stroma. Annotation of compartments of interest correctly holds significance since annotated areas are used in cell segmentation and further image analysis. QuPath has many tissue annotation features including rectangle, circular selection tools in addition to special annotation tools like wand tool which can detect the sharp tissue compartment borders like tumor or normal parenchymal border automatically and makes the annotation around these tissue compartment types easier (Fig. 4). Annotation is also performed or double checked by a pathologist to prevent errors. Any error made in this step can lead to cascade of errors image analysis since everything is dependent on annotated areas. If annotation of specific area of interest is not considered and just whole tissue annotation is needed, QuPath has a Fig. 3 The ROI selected above is used for estimating stain vectors (hematoxylin, AEC, residual). Hematoxylin and AEC channels are produced by using these stain vectors with color deconvolution

504 Guray Akturk et al. Fig. 4 Various annotation tools provided by QuPath are demonstrated here including line, circle, rectangle, wand, polygon, and brush tools “simple tissue detection” feature that can automatically annotate the whole tissue and this feature can be used in batch mode to make whole tissue annotation for all project images in one run. However, double check must be done to prevent errors that might happen during batch run. Peritumoral lymphocytic accumulation can be significant in some tumors and special annotation methods can be used to analyze peritumoral region. QuPath allows to expand the tumor border outward and/or inward for a selected diameter, and this feature allows for quantifying the tumor border TILs and comparing them with intratumoral ones in detail. This feature can provide important data in terms of geographic configuration of TILs. 1.3.3 Cell Segmentation Cell segmentation refers to identification of cells in an image, and it is one of the most important steps of image analysis. It is performed as nuclear segmentation, and cytoplasmic and membranous portions are included in the segmentation by expanding nuclear segmentation border for a selected diameter. Hematoxylin and chromogen color intensity values for nuclear, cytoplasmic, and total cellular compartment in addition to several shape features are recorded in each cellular detection of segmentation. QuPath provides two types of segmentation based on optical density and hematoxylin color intensity (Fig. 5). Cell segmentation quality depends on multiple factors including accuracy of stain vector values, image scanning quality, and number of artifacts. Some dense tissue types like lymph node require diligent setting testing to reach optimal segmentation. If cell segmentation is done on each

Multiplexed Immunohistochemical Consecutive Staining on Single Slide (MICSSS)… 505

Fig. 5 Colorectal carcinoma stained with Ki-67. Cell segmentation is performed based on optical density, and positive cell detection is made by finding a cutoff value with using the mean nuclear chromogen color intensity feature IHC image belonging to the same slide separately, this can cause slight change in number of total cells per image. Moreover, chromogen color can obscure the nuclear details for some antibodies like CD68 and cause false positive segmented cells. Pure hematoxylin staining without immunostaining can be included in MICSSS panel as a separate cycle and this channel can be used as a common segmentation layer. Once cell segmentation is done on a hematoxylin-stained image, segmentation layer can be moved onto other images of the project. Uniform total cell number can be calculated by using this methodology; however, it requires processing on all images to fix minimal elastic changes occur during cycles of MICSSS. Fiji software’s Trakem2 plug-in can be used for fixing the elastic changes and aligning all images and ultimately all cells on the same coordinates [13, 14]. 1.3.4 Phenotyping Phenotyping refers to detection of certain type of cell(s) depending on their features including color intensity and shape features; however, it is most commonly used for detection of positive cells in an image (Fig. 5). Correct cell segmentation and recorded shape and intensity values in segmented cells are extremely important for the accuracy of phenotyping. Thresholding is the most commonly used phenotyping method; however, machine learning-based classifier methods can be performed for phenotyping as well. Thresholding is simpler and faster method than the latter;

506 Guray Akturk et al.

however, it bears some caveats as well. Thresholding basically uses feature values recorded in each cell during cell segmentation including shape features like nuclear size and nuclear/cellular size rate and intensity features like nuclear chromogen intensity or total cellular intensity. Operator finds a cutoff value for a desired feature to differentiate them from other cells by using QuPath’s measurement maps function. Once the cutoff value is achieved, that value can be used for phenotyping. For example, CD3 positive cells can easily be differentiated from other cells by using thresholding on cellular chromogen color mean value. Requiring minimal tweaks for different slides stained with the same antibody in a project is the major drawback of this method and it leads to bias. Machine learning classifier method can be performed to prevent bias for a project including a lot of case (Fig. 6). This method depends on training a classifier by selecting features like intensity and/or shape values and using them in training by processing with a selected machine learning or deep learning algorithm. For example, detection of positive immunostained cells can be made by using chromogen color intensity features. A classifier can be created after training it with a proper number of positive and negative cells, and this classifier can be used throughout the project in an unbiased way. Thresholding method allows only dual classification like positive and negative, whereas a trained classifier is capable of Fig. 6 ROI from a normal tonsil tissue including a germinal center which is diffusely positive stained with Ki67 as expected. Yellow circle shaped dots are used to train the machine learning based classifier for positive and negative cells. After marking 11 cells as positive and negative, this algorithm classified the rest of the cells correctly

Multiplexed Immunohistochemical Consecutive Staining on Single Slide (MICSSS)… 507 classifying infinite number of categories depending on the training. This can help us phenotyping not just positive and negative but also subcategories like positive immune cells or morphological categories like tumor, normal epithelium, and normal parenchyma. It can even allow us to train for artifacts on tissue section and categorize them. Moreover, shape and intensity features like nuclear-to-cellular ratio and intensity values can be combined, and this helps in yielding more precise results for immunostains like cytokeratin to detect tumor cells. 1.3.5 Multiplexing Multiplexing methods bear the purpose of demonstrating coex- MICSSS Images Belonging pression data of cells in a tissue, and MICSSS is capable of providto the Same Slide ing it with spatial information in a unique way. However, a visual demonstration of multiplexed immunostaining requires image processing steps since MICSSS is based on cycles of immunostaining and removal of antibodies between these cycles. This causes elastic changes on tissue at the microscopic level. The placement of the slide in the scanner after every immunostaining cycle can also be slightly different which can cause the tissue section to be located in a slightly different area in the image. All these conditions should be fixed to align IHC images belonging to the same tissue section for visualizing multiple immune markers on the same image. The purpose of alignment is to fix coordinates of the same cells on different IHC images belonging to the same section for visualizing coexpressions. Fiji Trakem2 plug-in is a good option for alignment of images automatically and/or manual by using landmarks [14]. After alignment, images must be registered on top of each other; however, since every image uses the same red-colored AEC chromogen, registration of these raw images do not give the desired multiplexed image which has a different color code for each antibody. Color deconvolution is performed for this purpose to extract hematoxylin and AEC chromogen channels as 8-bit images. Hematoxylin channel can be yielded best from pure hematoxylin stained image and chromogen channels are extracted from immunostained sections. After assigning different color codes for each IHC image, color inversion takes place to achieve pseudofluorescent channels ready for merging. Merging these channels after these steps will result in a perfect image visualizing all antibody expression in one focal plane. Cell segmentation is made on hematoxylin channel to achieve the most accurate results. Cell segmentation performed on hematoxylin channel will record all intensity values for other IHC channels, and this allows to obtain detailed coexpression data for each cell. This method’s drawback is being able to perform only in a selected ROI. However, whole slide image coexpression data without visual image can be still provided by using same cell segmentation layer for all images. This whole slide image data can be analyzed more in detail by mass cytometry approaches like viSNE analysis.

4. Wash the slide in TBS20 for 5 min. Repeat wash step two
times. 3.1.7 Antibody Staining Repeat steps of “Primary Staining,” “Secondary Antibody and Antigen Detection Staining,” and “Antigen Detection.” (Subsequent Cycles) For every subsequent staining, the procedure should be repeated beginning with “Dehydration/Destaining/Rehydration” step.

Multiplexed Immunohistochemical Consecutive Staining on Single Slide (MICSSS)… 513 3.2 Scanning After every cycle of immunostaining, scanning of immunostained slide is carried out in a whole slide scanner (Hamamatsu NanoZoomer S60). NDPScan is used as the scanning software in our workflow.
1. The glass slide is inserted in the tray and loaded into the
scanner.
2. Destination location for output image, and slide name which
includes antibody name, order of cycle, and protocol details like primary antibody incubation duration and concentration optionally are set.
3. Magnification level of scanning is selected as 20× or 40×. 20×
is preferred since it results in optimal file sizes.
4. Scan area is set by automatic tissue recognition or manual
selection.
5. Focusing is done by focus points. It can be done automatically
by selecting the number of focus points or manually. These focus points can be reviewed to increase the quality and prevent any sort of blurriness.
6. NDPI extension is used by Hamamatsu scanner in default
mode; however, it can be changed to raw image extensions like TIFF images. NDPI is the preferred extension type since it provides small file sizes and acceptable image quality together.
7. Output images are reviewed for quality control.
3.3 Image Analysis Image analysis is performed by using QuPath (0.1.2) which is an open-source software. 3.3.1 Project Regardless of organized image folders for each project, QuPath has Management a feature of project management feature to group images belonging to a project together and save every single image analysis data in that project to work on them anytime needed. It creates “qpdata” file for every image in a project to save image analysis data like annotations, cell segmentation, and phenotyping data. QuPath stores project folder in a different location than the image files.
1. Project is created with a specific name.
2. Related images are imported into the project. QuPath pro-
vides several methods to import images like selecting files one by one or importing a selected folder of images altogether.
3. Metadata like antibody name, date, and order of cycle are
encoded in each image to sort them in different desired orders. 3.3.2 Stain Vectors Chromogenic immunohistochemistry images are basically RGB images per their background pixel values, and three important stain vectors (hematoxylin, chromogen, and residual) are used for immunostaining separation. Since QuPath uses color deconvolution for

514 Guray Akturk et al. stain separation, stain vector values are extremely important for further steps of image analysis. QuPath has a very useful feature for estimating these values named “Estimate Stain Vectors” for the purpose of improving stain separation.
1. Default stain vector type should be selected as Brightfield
H-DAB.
2. Representative tissue ROI is selected on tissue. This ROI must
include a balanced amount of positive and negative cells as well as a blank (white) area. Moreover, it should not be a large region since it results in downsampling of pixel values and it should be avoided for best results.
3. “Estimate Stain Vectors” feature is used for automatic estima-
tion of stain vectors. Results are shown in 2D scatterplots belonging to three vectors.
4. Scatterplot shows stain vector values by dots and two stain
vectors per scatterplot. Most of the dots should fall ideally between two stain vectors in each scatterplot.
5. Quality control is made by visualizing each vector in
Brightness/Contrast tool. NOTE: If there are many images in a project that are acquired with a similar staining, one representative ROI can be used to estimate stain vectors in batch mode by using a script. 3.3.3 Annotation Annotation can be made in different ways according to the purpose of a project. It is needed for further steps of image analysis since analysis is performed on created annotations in the image.
1. Simple tissue detection: This tool can automatically recognize
and annotate whole tissue on the slide (Fig. 7).
2. Annotation tools: QuPath provides many basic annotation
tools like rectangle, circle, and line tool as well as more advanced ones like wand tool which detects sharp changes in tissue and annotate it by moving the pointer around the interested area (Fig. 4).
3. TMA annotation: TMA cores can automatically be annotated
by the TMA support of QuPath (Fig. 8).
4. Annotation of specific tissue structures like tumor should be
done by using the annotation tools mentioned above by a pathologist to prevent possible errors. NOTE: Tumor annotation can be expanded inward and outward for a desired diameter to analyze the tumor border and peritumoral regions (Fig. 9). 3.3.4 Segmentation Cell segmentation refers to detection of cells in an image. QuPath basically makes nuclear segmentation and expands the nuclear border of detection by a selected diameter to create a cytoplasmic zone.

1. Detection image type is set to either “Hematoxylin OD” or

2. Nuclear parameters are tweaked according to the tissue type.
(a) B ackground radius value estimates the background color and improves the cell segmentation. It makes this estimation pixel by pixel and propagates the information through-

4. Cell expansion value sets the area of cytoplasmic region of

Thresholding 1. Measurement maps are used to set a cutoff value for a desired feature (Fig. 10).
2. Once a cutoff value is set, it is applied to the image to differ-
entiate the cells for a selected feature like shape or intensity.

Smoothing reduces the noise of measurement of shape features like nucleus–cell ratio. It takes weighted average of detection measurements of adjacent cells.
1. Smoothed features can be added according to the aim of the
project.
2. Detection classifier is created by selecting a classifier type.
Random forest method is the default classifier algorithm.
3. Desired features are selected from advanced options according
to the aim of the project.
4. Cell/tissue type classes are created in annotations tab.
5. Different cell classes are annotated using annotation tools.
Using dots for different classes is useful for detection of positive immune cells.
6. The classifier system will autoupdate classification in annota-
tions which include segmented cells during the annotation of different classes. Once the desired classification is achieved, classifier and training objects are saved separately.
7. Saved classifier can be applied to other images in the project
file. Batch run of a saved classifier can be performed to save time; however, review is always needed for quality control.

continue training the classifier, if there is any inaccurate classification in other images in the project. 3.3.6 Data Analysis Final data can be extracted as annotation or detection measurements and exported as a data file. 4 Notes
1. It is important to ensure that the tissue on the slide at no point
becomes dry. The slide or the tissue should remain covered in the solution/reagent from the previous step until it is ready to proceed with the next step. Avoid processing too many slides at once in between steps without applying the next appropriate reagent/solution in order to prevent tissue desiccation.
2. If a certain antibody produces a faint signal at baseline, stain-
ing with this antibody should be performed as one of the initial rounds of staining with this consecutive staining method.
3. AEC is toxic and carcinogenic. Make sure to use appropriate
personal protective equipment when handling the solution or slides that have been treated with this solution.

## Chapter 24


522 Jennifer Eng et al. 1 Introduction 1.1 Introduction Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues in histopathology is most widely used 1.1.1 Standard Practice for clinical diagnosis and biomedical research, and is often supplein Histopathology mented by chromogen development-based immunohistochemistry (IHC). Tissue architecture and cellular morphology in H&E-stained and protein expression in IHC-stained tissues are observable by bright-field microscopy, can be preserved for many years, and can be digitally archived through optical camera or CCD imaging systems. IHC-staining is typically a single channel colorimetric stain limited to cellular resolution, and is not suitable for colocalization analysis of multiple protein expressions. 1.1.2 Development Immunofluorescence (IF) is a specialized type of IHC that uses a of Immunofluorescence fluorescent dye to visualize antibody binding. The localization of a protein in tissue and cells, as well as any variations thereof, provides insights into the function of this protein. In early 1950, Albert H. Coons and his colleague paved the way for the future of immunofluorescent staining by developing a fluorescein-labeled antibody and fluorescence microscopy technique(s) to identify antigens in tissue sections, followed by the development of indirect IF, which uses secondary antibodies conjugated to fluorescent dyes. This technique, which is no longer limited to protein detection, is now the most widely used immunofluorescent method. Indirect IF permits multiplexed tissue staining, as well as screening and titrations of patient sera with fluorescently labeled antibodies, just as in any other serologic method, and has contributed to a variety of biomedical research and clinical studies. 1.1.3 Tumor Infiltrating TILs in cancer tissues can be examined with H&E staining [1]; Lymphocytes (TILs) however, better delineation of lymphocyte subsets and their functional status can be achieved by staining for various cell surface markers using a series of single channel IHCs onto serial tissue sections [2]. A larger set of biomarkers can be more efficiently interrogated by the highly multiplexed immunofluorescent procedure that enables linear quantification of multiple protein expression at subcellular resolution using a single tissue section [3–6]. To examine the states of immune and tumor cells in cancer specimens, tissues are often dissociated into single cells for flow cytometry analysis, which can also be applied to the bulk analysis of genomic and epigenetic state. However, the context of the tissue architecture will be lost, and as a result, the spatial distribution of the microenvironmental landscape, including TILs and stromal compositions representing the tumor microenvironment state, cannot be analyzed.

Cyclic Multiplexed-Immunofluorescence (cmIF), a Highly Multiplexed Method… 523 1.1.4 Cyclic Multiplexed- Recent advances in digital pathology and whole-tissue scanning Immunofluorescence technology have allowed the development of the cyclic multiplexed- (cmIF) immunofluorescence (cmIF) workflow, which can be used to assess the histopathological architecture at a subcellular level and the interactions between tumor cells and their microenvironments in the tissue context. Highly multiplexed imaging will be used to achieve quantitative single-cell analysis of the spatial pattern of all cellular compositions, which will be classified into the categories of heterogeneous tumor cells, immune cells, fibroblast, endothelial cells, and other mesenchymal cells in the tumor microenvironment. The cmIF is a powerful, robust, quantifiable, and reproducible staining tool for highly multiplexed immunofluorescence imaging of tissues and cells. This method has been optimized to quantify the expression of 60 protein biomarkers and apply single cell-based multivariate analysis [3, 4], all within the same section from an archive of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues (Fig. 1). Further analysis of the spatial patterns of immune effector cells and aggressively proliferating tumor cells beyond cellular composition, colocalization, and proximity assessment is the current subject of machine learning algorithm development, and will help identify spatially defined subpopulations and their associations with clinical outcomes. 1.2 Background The modulation of the immune system for checkpoint inhibition through therapeutic monoclonal antibodies has rapidly revolution-1.2.1 Cancer ized treatment strategies in various malignancies over the last Immunotherapy decade. Several immunotherapeutic antibodies, namely, “immune checkpoint inhibitors” or “immune modulators,” have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and have led to outcomes with significantly better efficacy and patient tolerance than chemotherapy among advanced cancer patients, such as those with melanoma, lymphoma, or cancers in the lung, bladder, kidney, colon, and rectum. However, increased experience in the use of immunotherapy agents in clinical settings has revealed several limitations, such as treatment resistance and undesirable immunogenic reactions [7]. 1.2.2 Immunotherapy Particularly in breast cancer (BC), a retrospective analysis of TILs for Breast Cancer by H&E in prospectively collected ~4000 tissues from clinical trials revealed the influence of host immunosurveillance on breast cancer biology while undergoing treatment [8]. Analyses of past trial results have been generally consistent; TNBC and HER2 positive BC are most strongly associated with better outcomes, while the association in HR+ BC is potentially limited by the substantial nature of luminal BC subtype. The expression of certain genes in luminal BC subtype—such as p53 mutation, and the amplification of FGFR and CCND1—drive tumor cell proliferation and genomic instability, resulting in aggressive cancer phenotype and resistance

526 Jennifer Eng et al. Fig. 1 (continued)

to treatment. Interestingly, high-grade luminal BC that achieved a pathological complete response (pCR) showed better long-term survival compared to grade 1 or 2 luminal tumors [9]. In general, there are far fewer TILs in luminal BC that are of the HER2+ BC or TNBC subtypes, and the prognostic benefit of TILs has been shown to be quantitative in nature [10]. A number of clinical trials involving immune checkpoint inhibitors for locally advanced and metastatic BC patients are currently ongoing to determine whether immunotherapy provides a clinical benefit in BC treatment, and preliminary analyses of the trials have shown contradictory results between subtypes. The use of immune checkpoint inhibitors, both with and without cytotoxic agents, has shown promising results in TNBC, while the rate of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors is lower in HR+ BC, even when combined with molecular targeting agents [11–16]. These results may reflect a fundamental difference in the landscape of tumor heterogeneity, TILs, angiogenesis, and stromal microenvironment between BC subtypes. The defined tumor area is divided into a stromal region and an enriched tumor cell region, typically referred to as “Stromal TILs” and “Intratumoral TILs” in most studies. Since stromal TILs are generally more abundant, they are readily assessed in H&E stained tissues, in contrast, intratumoral TILs are generally lower in number, more heterogeneous across samples, and less visible. A significant association with clinical outcomes has been established with stromal TILs [2]. A study of cytotoxic neoadjuvant setting for BC reported that both TIL types were independent predictors for pCR in TNBC, but only intratumoral TILs was an independent predictor in luminal BC. Interestingly, neither TIL type predicted pCR in Her2+ subtype [17].

Cyclic Multiplexed-Immunofluorescence (cmIF), a Highly Multiplexed Method… 527 Fig. 1 (continued)

528 Jennifer Eng et al. Intrinsic gene expression analyses suggest that there are 4–6 molecular subtypes in TNBC, such as BL1, BL2, IM, M, MSL, and LAR. The BL1 subtype is characterized by elevated cell cycle and DNA damage response gene expression, while the BL2 subtype is enriched in growth factor signaling and myoepithelial markers. The IM subtype is composed of genes encoding immune antigens, cytokine, and core immune signal transduction pathways, and likely represents gene expression from both the tumor cells and infiltrating lymphocytes. Both M and MSL subtypes share elevated expression of genes that are involved in the epithelialmesenchymal- transition and growth factor pathways, but only the MSL subtype shows decreased expression of the genes involved in proliferation and is associated with better outcome. The LAR subtype is characterized by luminal gene expression and is driven by the androgen receptor (AR). LAR, or the steroid receptor subtype conferred poor prognosis in TNBC. The studies identified TNBC cell lines representative of each subtype and demonstrated that they have differential sensitivity to the alkylating agent cisplatin, with BL1 cell lines displaying the greatest sensitivity [18–20]. Another study identified four TNBC subtypes based on mRNA expression and DNA profiling: (1) LAR, (2) mesenchymal, (3) basal-like immune suppressive, and (4) basal-like immune active, in which immune-suppressive and active basal-like TNBC are associated with the worst and the best prognosis, respectively [21], suggesting that the basal-like immune suppressive subtype might be a target for immune checkpoint inhibition. The development of a relevant TIL evaluation method is critical for stratification of the patient population into those who may respond to immune checkpoint blockade. Most studies measure both stromal and intratumoral TILs; however, stromal TILs are considered to be more representative and reproducible. Certainly, stromal TILs are generally more abundant, whereas intratumoral TILs are typically lower in number, more heterogeneous across samples, and less visible. Consequently, significant associations with clinicopathological parameters and disease outcomes have been better established for stromal TILs than for intratumoral TILs. The evaluation of TILs becomes increasingly relevant with the emerging role of immunotherapy in breast cancer. Early phase trials of checkpoint blockade show promising results; however, some patients may not derive any benefits from immunotherapies. This underlines the importance of the development of predictive biomarkers, which may enable further stratification of these BC subtypes into subclasses. 1.2.3 Immunotherapy Prostate cancer (PC) is one of the leading causes of cancer death in for Prostate Cancer men, second only to lung cancer (https://seer.cancer.gov/statistics/), for which current standard care is based on surgical resection, radiation, and hormone therapy, including castration.

Cyclic Multiplexed-Immunofluorescence (cmIF), a Highly Multiplexed Method… 529 Immunotherapy for advanced PC patients appears promising, as patients with melanoma and other cancers have been shown to respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors [22], resulting in increased quality of life for those patients. The successful management of advanced PC, such as metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), requires an understanding of the complexity of tumor cells and their interactions with the microenvironment, particularly with TILs. Cancer vaccine therapy was first approved for PC, and more have become available in subsequent years, but most fail to meet treatment expectations. However, combining a check-point inhibitor with prostate cancer vaccines appears more beneficial for CRPC patients [23, 24]. Preliminary studies on new drugs that block the immune checkpoints in CRPC indicate that such immune checkpoint inhibition might be a solution for these patients. Synergistic combinations of immunotherapy with conventional cancer treatments may have tremendous potential [25]. 1.2.4 Immunotherapy Contrary to the promising results of immune checkpoint inhibifor Pancreatic Cancer tion among TNBC and CRPC patients, the majority of patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) have never benefited from immunotherapy in clinical trials [20, 26, 27]. These unexpected outcomes are the result of the nature of PDAC: low immunogenicity and abundant stroma induce an immunosuppressive environment through activated cancer-associated fibroblasts and their TGF-β secretion. A new treatment strategy is required for patients with PDAC, such as the combination of checkpoint inhibitors and FOLFIRINOX, which may present some advantages in addition to anti-TGF-β targeting therapy [28, 29]. Therefore, it is necessary to develop new approaches to further stratify various cancer subtypes into those that will or will not respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Improvements in the clinical efficacy of immunomodulation for a majority of advanced cancer patients are critically needed. 1.3 Biomarkers Cyclic IF, including our cmIF, is the most promising approach for highly multiplexed- and single-cell-based proteomic analyses 1.3.1 Overview because it allows for the interrogation of the spatial distribution and interaction of tumor and microenvironment at the cellular and molecular levels using conventional fluorescence microscopy and inexpensive reagents. The quantitative and spatial analyses of intratumor heterogeneity and tumor microenvironment, which is composed of immune cells, fibroblasts, vasculature, and noncellular components in the stroma, is important for the characterization and classification of further subgroups of malignancy or responsiveness to therapeutic agents. Immunotherapy has emerged as a highly promising approach for the treatment of cancer patients. However, the clinical efficacy of immunotherapy is limited to a minority of cancer patients. Thus, new approaches to improve the

530 Jennifer Eng et al. efficacy of immunotherapies for most patients are critically needed. Strategies to improve the efficacy of immunotherapy rely on both an enhanced understanding of the tumor/immune interface at the cellular and molecular levels, and the ability to stratify and select appropriate patients for a specific immunotherapy agent or combination therapy. Optimized biomarker strategies could help elucidate both of these areas and allow cancer immunotherapy to be tailored to each individual patient’s disease. 1.3.2 Tumor Tumor heterogeneity is one of the hallmarks of malignancy [30, Heterogeneity 31]. Cancer tissues differ greatly between patients (intertumor heterogeneity), as well as within each individual tumor (intratumor heterogeneity) [32], and such heterogeneity is caused by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors. For instance, intrinsic heterogeneity may develop from genomic instability at the malignant transition [33, 34] or due to epigenetic plasticity, and extrinsic signals from the tumor microenvironment can introduce additional heterogeneity to these tumor cells as a result of drug treatment-induced stressors [35]. Different cell states can possess distinct drug sensitivities [36–38], making cell-state heterogeneity a challenge for therapeutic management of breast tumors. An additional challenge to therapeutic treatment is the inherent plasticity of tumor cell states [39, 40]. Cytotoxic and molecular targeted therapies have been shown to drive cells into drug tolerant persistor cell states, which can survive drug pressure in a low-proliferative state, leading to incomplete response or recurrence [38, 41, 42]. Early studies— particularly those investigating BC—defined tumor heterogeneity based on several characteristics of intratumor cell populations, including tumorigenicity, treatment resistance, and metastatic potential [43–45]. Recent investigations support the notion that the TILs, stroma cells, parenchyma, and vasculature making up the tumor microenvironment all play important roles in tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis [46]. It is important to understand the state of individual cells among the many tumor cells that may be undergoing differentiation (Keratin subtypes and CD44), hyper proliferation (PCNA and Ki67), evasion of growth repression (pS6RP and pRB), resisting cell death (53BP1 and Rad51), and other cell states, as represented by the many biomarkers listed in Table 1. 1.3.3 TILs TILs are thought to be an important player in prognosis and therapy. TILs have been reported to be positively associated with improved survival in TNBC and other cancers [47–54], while the rates of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors are lower in HR+ BC, even when combined with molecular targeting agents [12, 13]. A successful antitumor immune response requires several key steps, which are (1) the brief capture of tumor antigens by APCs, (2) presentation of tumor antigens to lymphocytes, (3) acti-

532 Jennifer Eng et al. vation and expansion of CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes, (4) direct cell-to-cell contact between activated lymphocytes and tumor cells, and (5) production of inflammatory cytokines (CD4+), cells that kill tumor cells (CD8+), B cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and macrophages [55–57]. However, suppression of tumor growth by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and NKp46+ NK cells involves a complex series of direct and indirect interactions between immune cells. Negative regulation through immune check-point proteins— such as PD1, PD-L1, and FoxP3—occurs in 30–50% of breast cancers and limits CD4+ T cell functions to promote CD8+ T cell activation within tumor microenvironments [58]. Additionally, the tumor cells and their microenvironment often manipulate the successful antitumor immune response through immune check-point proteins. The following biomarkers: CD4, CD8, PD1, FoxP3, CD20, and CD68, can be used to characterize the composition of immune cells in TILs as a minimum set of immune cell markers. The analysis of proximity from those immune cells to tumor boundary, or directly to PCNA/Ki67 positive proliferating tumor cells enables mapping of the spatial organization of tumor cells, immune cells, and cells in the tumor microenvironment. 1.3.4 Angiogenesis Angiogenesis is another hallmark of malignancy, and clinical benefits of antiangiogenetic agents have been reported in colorectal cancer, non-small cell lung carcinoma [59, 60], and renal cell carcinoma [61]. Preclinical studies have confirmed that angiogenesis also plays a central role in breast cancer carcinogenesis and metastatic potential [62–65]. However, the benefit of antiangiogenetic therapy with bevacizumab or protein kinase inhibitors, such as sunitinib, has been controversial because most trials of antiangiogenetic agents in breast cancer have reported improved response rate and progression-free survival, but no increase in overall survival compared to the patients who received chemotherapy alone [66]. Quantitative measures to assess mature and immature angiogenesis by examining endothelial markers (CD31 and CD34) and their pericyte marker (αSMA), the spatial distribution of hypoxic tumor cells expressing HIF1a or GLUT1, and those cells’ proximity to mature blood vessels, to proliferating tumor cells, and to each other are required for the stratification of responses to antiangiogenic therapy. The antiangiogenetic control via bevacizumab or sunitinib enhances the efficacy of cytotoxic agents (nab-paclitaxel, anthracycline, and cyclophosphamide) against tumor cells, and also normalizes cancer-associated vasculature (i.e., vascular normalization), which reduces vascular hotspots, tumor microvessel density (MVD), and immature vessel distribution [67–69]. The density, maturity, and formation of immature lymphatic vessels may also be involved in the mechanisms of tumor resistance to treatment in trials with bevacizumab, of which these vessels’ synergistic or adverse effects are as of yet unclear. Therefore, characterization of lymphatic vessel distribution using lymphatic

Cyclic Multiplexed-Immunofluorescence (cmIF), a Highly Multiplexed Method… 533 endothelial markers (PDPN and LYVE1) and αSMA is required. Increases in lymphatic vessel promotion in the S0800 trial may also induce regional lymph-node or distant organ metastasis through the lymphatic system [70]. 1.3.5 Cancer-Associated Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are the most frequent compo- Fibroblasts (CAFs) nent of tumor stroma, especially in breast and pancreatic cancer [71, 72]. According to the seed-and-soil hypothesis, a permissive microenvironment (soil) facilitates growth of cancer cells (seed) in extended primary and metastatic sites, which interact with not only cancer cells, but also with TILs and endothelial cells in the tumor stroma [73]. CAFs may induce therapeutic resistances against endocrine therapy [74], chemotherapy [75], and molecular target therapy [76]. The tumor microenvironment has been demonstrated to promote breast cancer initiation, growth, migration, metastasis, and therapeutic resistances. CAFs, TAMs, EC, CAAs, leukocytes, etc. are critical components of tumor stroma, comprising the majority of tumor microenvironment and taking part in induction of breast cancer malignancy through various mechanisms [77]. The characteristics of CAFs are not yet fully understood; they may potentially be transformed resident fibroblasts, epithelial-mesenchymal-transformed tumor cells, bone marrowderived mesenchymal stem cells, or other cells in stroma, and should be characterized in order to identify the composition of the tumor microenvironment, and their individual roles therein. At present, no evidence suggests a single dominant origin of CAFs in the tumor microenvironment. Biomarkers considered acceptable for reliably identifying CAFs include αSMA, FSP-1, FAP, PDGFRa, PDGFRb, and vimentin [72, 78]. Some new related therapeutic targets, such as FAP, have been developed and are currently under preclinical evaluation [71, 72]. These targets may potentially augment the existing therapeutic options for cancer treatment and prevention. Several studies confirmed the correlation between MVD and prognosis [79, 80], inflammatory response [81], and immune suppression. Angiogenic factors such as VEGF released by tumor cells and CAFs inhibit dendritic cell (DC) maturation and proinflammatory cytokine production, and promote Treg infiltration. Tumor blood vessels are often functionally compromised and often do not express receptors required for T-cell extravasation into tissues, such as ICAM-1 and VCAM-1, which precludes effective infiltration of cytotoxic T-cells into tumors [82]. 1.3.6 Disease Specific Disease specific biomarkers for tumors and normal tissues in breast, Biomarkers pancreas, and prostate cancers are listed in the table. The markers can be synergistically used with others for characterization, subtyping, and further classification of each cancer tissue [83, 84]. These biomarkers are frequently used for histopathological diagnosis in routine practices of breast, pancreas, and prostate pathology.

534 Jennifer Eng et al. In breast cancer pathology, it is important to characterize stromal invasion, columnar cell lesions, intraductal proliferations, papillary lesions, sclerosing lesions, spindle cell lesions, and prognostic and predictive factors, in addition to molecular phenotypes such as luminal A, B, TNBC (basal and claudin-low), and Her2. In pancreatic cancer pathology, the most widely used biomarkers for the diagnosis of ductal adenocarcinoma are pVHL, maspin, S100P, and IMP-3, and for the diagnosis of pancreatic endocrine neoplasm are synaptophysin, chromogranin, NSE, and beta-catenin. Poor prognostic markers in advanced pancreatic adenocarcinoma are overexpressions of DNMT1, HDAC1, CD166, and nuclear S100A6, and those in endocrine neoplasm are CK19, Ki67, CD99, topoisomerase IIa, and nuclear survivin. In prostate cancer, the recommended biomarkers to distinguish seminal vesicles from prostatic ductal adenocarcinoma and high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia are CK7, PAX2, and MUC6. CK7 and CK20 (epithelial markers) are negative in both normal and neoplastic prostatic epithelia, MUC6 is positive in seminal vesicles but negative in normal prostate and adenocarcinoma, and nuclear PAX2 is positive in seminal vesicles, negative in adenocarcinoma, and high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia. Cancers originating from these three organs are histopathologically and genetically more complex than others, which may be one of the reasons that results of immune checkpoint inhibition in clinical trials are mixed. 2 Materials 2.1 Tissue 1. with 8 core Xeon CPU, 16 GB Graphic board, and 256 GB RDIMM). 3 Methods 3.1 Overview In recent years, methods of simultaneously visualizing multiple biomarkers that have become popular in biomedical research, including brightfield multiplexing technology with sequential

Cyclic Multiplexed-Immunofluorescence (cmIF), a Highly Multiplexed Method… 539 staining [85–87] (see Note 1), fluorescent multiplexing with fluorophores and nanocrystals, and combination of unmixing technology using multispectral acquisition system to image enzymatic amplification of fluorescent signals [88]. However, unlike previous methods, the newly developed method of cyclic multiplexed-immunofluorescence (cmIF) allows iterative rounds of multiplex immunofluorescence staining using directly labeled antibodies without the need for incubation with secondary antibodies or enzymatic amplification. Instead, cmIF only requires fluorophore quenching to achieve highly multiplexed staining of up to 60 protein biomarkers in a single tissue section [3, 4]. The protocol has been optimized for formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples, and a workflow has been developed to process digital images for quantitative single-cell based spatial analysis. The cmIF assay may enter routine use in clinical settings as this technique becomes more widely available in the future. Some potential issues with the cmIF assay are that there is a limit to the number of biomarkers that can be interrogated, and that the procedure is both labor-intensive and time consuming. To overcome these disadvantages, a more robust method of cyclic IF using oligonucleotide- conjugated antibodies is under development (see Note 2). 3.2 Staining Tumor tissues are fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin or 4% formaldehyde in PBS (pH 7). To preserve phosphorylated proteins 3.2.1 Tissue Preparation and prevent tissue autolysis and degradation, the immediate fixation of the tissues with a refrigerated fixative is critical; however, it is also important to maintain cell morphology and tissue architecture over the course of cmIF protocol. The optimal fixation time varies between 6 and 48 hour(s), depending on the tissue size, staining methods, and antibodies being used to target proteins. However, a fixation step that lasts longer than 48 h is not recommended, as overfixation may present difficulties in antigen retrieval following staining. After fixation, the tissues are gently dehydrated in increasing grades of ethanol to minimize cell damage, processed through xylene to clear the tissues of ethanol, embedded in heated paraffin at 60 °C, and then hardened overnight to form tissue blocks. Finally, the tissues are sectioned at a thickness of 4–5 μm using a microtome, placed on slides that are silanized or otherwise coated with a suitable adhesive, and dried at room temperature. The slides may optionally be baked at 55–65 °C for 30–120 min in order to minimize tissue loss during the staining procedure. The sectioned tissues should be stored at 4 °C to prevent tissue oxidation, which may cause the loss of antigenicity in tissues. For long-term storage of sections without loss of antigenicity, the slides can be dipped in paraffin to cover the surface of the tissue sections (see Note 3).

540 Jennifer Eng et al. 3.2.2 Antigen Retrieval The slides should be baked prior to the start of tissue processing in preparation for staining, if they have not been baked already. The paraffin must be completely removed from the tissue, which should then be rehydrated to allow the efficient bonding of antigens and antibodies during the staining steps. Antigen retrieval is necessary for successful immunohistochemical staining of the FFPE tissues, as fixation causes protein-protein cross-linking and masking the epitopes that are specific antibody binding targets. Heat-mediated antigen retrieval (by microwave, pressure cooker, or autoclave) in either citrate buffer (pH 6) or Tris EDTA buffer (pH 9) is the widely accepted standard procedure in most research and pathology laboratories. However, certain antibodies may require processing at lower temperatures, the use of buffers with higher or lower pH, or enzyme-mediated antigen retrieval with the use of proteinase K, trypsin, or pepsin. Antigen retrieval methods that involve enzymatic pretreatment are more difficult to control compared to methods of heat-mediated antigen retrieval. As a large number of antibodies (typically 20–40) will be used in cyclic immunofluorescence staining, heat-mediated antigen retrieval in citrate buffer or Tris EDTA buffer, or both buffers sequentially, is most recommended. A commercial buffer for antigen retrieval will also produce satisfactory staining results. The antigen retrieval process should only be applied once for cyclic immunofluorescence before beginning the staining procedure. 3.2.3 Antibody Selection There are a number of commercially available primary antibodies that are directly conjugated to N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) ester fluorophores. These fluorophores are often Cyanine dyes or similar alternatives, which randomly label lysine resides on antibodies. The desired primary antibodies can be labeled in-house by using NHSactivated dyes or a commercial labeling kit. Several vendors provide a variety of protein- and antibody-labeling reagents, including Cy2, Cy3, Cy5, and, Alexa Fluor (AF). Hydrogen peroxide inactivation of fluorescence, as required for cyclic immunofluorescence, is difficult in certain fluorophores, such as FITC or AF546. The processes of validating antibodies for biomarker expression specificity and selecting fluorophores for labeling are the two most important steps in cmIF. The use of directly labeled antibodies provides greater flexibility in multiplex immunofluorescence, especially in cmIF, because there is greater freedom in selecting the most optimal combination of antibodies to examine. Additionally, directly labeled antibodies are suitable for quantitative analysis of target protein expression because there is no signal amplification in the procedure. The intensity of fluorescence has a linear relationship to the target protein’s expression in stained tissues, so differences in protein expression can therefore be estimated by the difference between fluorescence intensities under constant staining and imaging conditions. However, the use of directly labeled antibodies may compromise the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), so careful antibody selection for

Cyclic Multiplexed-Immunofluorescence (cmIF), a Highly Multiplexed Method… 541

each target protein is one of the most important key factors to obtaining successful results from cmIF. Many labeling kits with Alexa Fluor and their analogs, including all components for antibody labeling, such as a purification column and buffer, are commercially available (see Subheading 2.3 in Materials and Note 4). In-house antibody labeling with the desired fluorophore can also be done if it is not available on the market. 3.2.4 Antibody Validation The validation of antibodies for specificity, reproducibility, and durability is an essential step for the cmIF (Fig. 2). However, this is sometimes difficult, time-consuming, and costly. Cyclic Multiplexed-Immunofluorescence (cmIF), a Highly Multiplexed Method… 543 antibodies often compromise staining results compared to immunofluorescence staining with secondary antibodies, due to the smaller number of fluorophore molecules representing target proteins and the loss of antibody affinity to epitopes in proteins. These problems may be exacerbated when the selected antibodies are confirmation-specific or the target proteins contain fragile epitopes. Positive and negative control tissues and cell lines are also important for antibody validation, and knockout, knockdown, or knockin cell lines may need to be established for this process. A variety of reference images for immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence staining can be found in The Human Protein Atlas (https:// www.proteinatlas.org/humanproteome/tissue/breast). 3.2.5 Staining After antigen retrieval, the tissues are incubated in blocking soluand Acquisition tion with either bovine serum albumin alone or combined with other sera. The tissues are incubated in the directly conjugated primary antibodies for 4–16 h, washed in PBS, stained with DAPI for nucleus imaging, and mounted in antifade mounting media. Immunofluorescent microscopy relies on the detection of light emitted at specific wavelengths from each fluorophore directly bound to a primary antibody when excited by light of another specific wavelength. The emitted light is always of a longer wavelength than the excitation light. This difference between the band maxima of excitation and emission wavelengths, which is known as Stokes shift, is a unique property intrinsic to each individual fluorophore. Selection of an appropriate combination of fluorophores, target antigens, and primary antibodies, and maximizing spectra from target antigen channels with minimal bleeding spectra from others by setting multiband path microscopy filters are factors that are critical to effective cmIF. The optimal components for obtaining high quality digital images with high SNR and dynamic range for the regions of interest (or full tissue sections) from fluorescence microscopy systems, which are systems for which research and pathology laboratories most commonly use widefield epifluorescence microscopes, are an LED light source, a 20× objective with high numerical aperture, an X-Y motorized stage, a 16-bit grayscale CCD or CMOS camera, and multichannel tile-imaging capabilities with autofocus functionality. One of the most promising technologies that has emerged in the last several years for illumination in optical microscopy is the light-emitting diode (LED). Recent advances in illumination technology to expand the LED spectrum to include infrared red enable imaging of signals emitted by Cy7/ AF750 and similar dyes. This ability to use Cy7/AF750 makes 5-channel imaging possible. Most major microscope manufacturers generally make such high-end digital imaging systems available for purchase.

544 Jennifer Eng et al. 3.2.6 Fluorescence After image acquisition, the coverslip is gently removed in PBS and Inactivation the fluorophores are chemically inactivated by horizontal incubation of slides under incandescence light. Following fluorophore

inactivation, slides are washed in PBS. Tissue bleaching is then visually confirmed under a microscope, the next round of primary antibodies is applied, and the cycle of staining, imaging, and bleaching is repeated (Fig. 3). The antibodies from previous rounds of staining are never stripped off from the tissues at any step. 3.3 Image The acquired images should be stored in single- or multichannel Processing grayscale Tagged Image File Format (TIFF), which is a flexible and adaptable file format for handling images and data within a single 3.3.1 Overview file, and can include header tags (size, definition, etc.). Image files in TIFF format can be reviewed, edited, and analyzed in ImageJ, Fig. 3 (a) Pearson’s correlation (CD45 between different rounds). The Pearson’s correlation coefficients for tonsil and jejunum tissues are 0.947 (209,369 cells) and 0.915 (75,879 cells), respectively. The proportions of CD4/CD45 and CD8/CD45 are 58% and 40% in Jejunum-1 tissue, and 60% and 38% in Jejunum-2 tissue, respectively, which demonstrate reproducibility of cellular composition across different rounds of cmIF with differing staining orders

Cyclic Multiplexed-Immunofluorescence (cmIF), a Highly Multiplexed Method… 545 which is an open-source software program. The majority of manufacturer- provided imaging software included with microscopes or image acquisition cameras are capable of saving or exporting the acquired images in TIFF format. It is recommended that the TIFF images be organized by staining cycle, or “round” number (R), and the channel number (C) within each cycle (e.g., R1C1 is the nuclear DAPI image from the first cycle). For single cell-based analysis using image data generated from cmIF, the image registration is the first step of the analysis process. 3.3.2 Registration Registration transforms different sets of image data into a single coordinate system. Typically, all images are registered to the same coordinates in the first DAPI image (i.e., the first DAPI is the registration reference). The other channel images in the same cycle must be aligned with the corresponding DAPI image, regardless of whether they are saved as individual TIFFs or in a stacked TIFF file. The image registration functionality is available through multiple plugins (StackReg or MultiStackReg) for ImageJ [http://bradbusse.net/downloads.html], or from the Computer Vision System Toolbox in Matlab (MathWorks) such as “matchFeatures” and “estimateGeometricTransform.” These functions can be used to automatically identify nuclear features in each DAPI image, such as size, shape, and texture [89, 90] as well as to identify matching features between two DAPI images and find an affine transformation matrix to align those matched features. Once DAPI is registered, the transformation matrix is applied to the biomarker channel images in each respective round. Other algorithms for image registration, such as “wavelet based automatic registration” and “Deep learning-based registration” have been reported and may be of potential use. Once the images have been registered, overlays of biomarkers from any round can be visualized (Fig. 4a, b). 3.3.3 Segmentation Segmentation is the next important step for feature extraction among individual cells. Each individual nucleus is detected and segmented using alternating sequential filters, OTSU thresholding, and seeded Watershed algorithms in CellProfiler [91] or ImageJ [92], which can also be found in Matlab or Python [93]. In the segmentation process, single and multiple nuclear DAPI images are denoised and locally flattened using an alternating sequential filter, which is a mathematical morphology operator, in which alternating transformations of opening and closing are sequentially applied with structuring elements of increasing size. The resulting images are used in OTSU thresholding, creating a binarized image of nuclear masks. The masks are eroded with a mathematical morphology operator to separate touching nuclei, and are then individually labeled to serve as seeds in a watershed algorithm applied to the gradient of a single or multiple DAPI images [35, 94, 95]. The centripetal expansion equation is applied to the nuclear segmentation results to obtain intensity values in the cytoplasmic

More accurate subcellular segmentation may require channel images targeting specific biomarkers, such as: pan-cadherin, sodium–potassium ATPase, and CD45 as biomarkers for the plasma membrane; pan-cytokeratin and S6 ribosomal protein as biomarkers of the cytoplasm; and Cox IV and TOMM20 marking the mitochondria. Biomarkers for subcellular segmentation may be selected according to one’s experimental needs or research interests, and the same algorithms used for nuclear segmentation can be used in subcellular segmentation as well [96]. Following single cell segmentation, moments of each biomarker are extracted from the subcellular component of the segmentation mask as appropriate for the known subcellular localization of the target proteins. 3.4 Analysis Serial digitized cmIF images will be processed using the computational image analysis workflow described above to align and visualize 3.4.1 Overview several markers simultaneously. The biomarker information from each single cell in an FFPE section that has been iteratively stained with a series of antibodies is transformed into a large spreadsheet, which contains mean intensity, pixel number, and x-y coordinates, among a number of other extracted features. Since the antigens in protein biomarkers are detected based on fluorophore- conjugated antibodies, the measured fluorescence intensity in the image is considered representative of the antigen quantity.

548 Jennifer Eng et al. 3.4.2 Clustering The clustering of all cells based on the expression level of each

biomarker (i.e., mean intensity of each single cell) is a widely accepted measure for classifying cells with similar biological phenotypes, such as HR+ and Ki67+ tumor cells. Figure 5a shows the result of K-means clustering with 40 biomarkers to classify all cells from four TMA cores into ten groups, such as CD45 positive immune cells and CAFs in stroma. Each group is coded by a unique color, and the population of clustered cells is plotted on the bar graph in the middle. 3.4.3 Spatial Mapping Cells classified in the same group are mapped to their original locations in the TMA cores on the right (Fig. 5a). Immune cells and CAFs, represented respectively as pink and red, are distributed to four cores. Figure 5b and c show the plot of each cell after reducing high dimensionality by T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (tSNE) algorithm, which indicates that each core tends to carry a unique set of sample-based tumor cells, as well as a small population of shared tumor and other cells, common across the four TMA cores (Fig. 5b). The majority of HER2+, ER+, and CD45+ immune cells are all mutually exclusive. Ki67+ is expressed within, or in close proximity to, HER2+ and ER+ cells (Fig. 5c).
