FoxP3, and CD31 are obtained from segmented single cell, which is then processed to analyze the immune cell composition and spatial information at a single-cell level. Tumor segmentation masks to distinguish intratumoral from peritumoral regions will be generated from the images of cell nuclei and Type I keratins (acidic, low MW) of the same tissue region as the tumor marker. Segmentation of tumor regions and other cell types will be validated by visual assessment to exclude objects falsely annotated due to unspecific staining, background, or errors in annotation overlooked by the automated procedure described above. 3.4.5 Proximity Analysis The distance from the tumor border and evaluated cellular components of the tumor microenvironment will be calculated by spatial proximity analysis. Extraction of spatial proximity and distance measurements will be processed using an automated workflow [97]. For instance, CD8+ T cell positional data can be used to measure distance from each individual T cell to the annotated tumor border. Using the Quickhull Algorithm for Convex Hulls, “dsearchn” function in MATLAB R2016, the shortest distance between T cell centroids and the boundary of the tumor mask can be measured to determine T cell distance to tumor boundaries. Similarly, the shortest distance between other cell types and the

4 Notes
1. Chromogen-based multiplex immunohistochemistry. The
Coussens laboratory at OHSU developed a related multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) platform that enables deep auditing of immune contexture in situ in FFPE sections. Specifically, FFPE tissue sections are iteratively stained with panels of leukocyte lineage-specific and/or function-associated antibodies reflecting ~40 validated targets. An automated computational pipeline for image analysis enables classification of immune cell types using either image cytometry gating or sparse coding strategies [87, 94, 98]. Each stain is detected in a separate channel, and is imaged by digital scanning and bright-field microscopy, followed by chemical-discoloring and antibody stripping. This method allows for evaluation of mm of tissue and millions of cells in situ. As antigen detection is based on precipitated chromogen, measurements of the markers’ expression are less quantitative compared to that of IF-based staining, but is potentially more adaptable for clinical applications. This platform has been applied to multiple clinical and preclinical studies to evaluate immune response to disease and/or therapy [87, 99–101].

Cyclic Multiplexed-Immunofluorescence (cmIF), a Highly Multiplexed Method… 557
2. Next-generation Cyclic IF. A novel labeling and staining
technology has been developed in Drs. Gibbs, Chin and Gray laboratories at OHSU in collaboration with Quantitative Imaging Systems, and uses validated primary antibody-conjugated oligonucleotides (Ab-oligos). In situ hybridization of complementary oligonucleotides labeled with fluorophores (imaging-oligos) facilitates biomarker detection for imaging by conventional fluorescent microscopy. A variety of complementary oligo configurations were validated to remove fluorescent signals from the stained tissue before subsequent staining cycles (2019 SPIE Conference Proceedings). Each Ab-oligo can only be applied once to any given tissue section at the beginning, followed by the cycles of hybridization and signal removal. The novel strategy may solve many of the potential issues currently present in cmIF, such as the time and labor costs required for repeated antibody incubation during each staining cycle. The technology is similar to the codetection by indexing (CODEX) strategy, which was developed in Dr. Nolan laboratory, and employed the combination of DNA barcodes, fluorescent dNTP analogs, and an in situ polymerization-based indexing procedure [102].
3. It is difficult to manage batch-to-batch and day-to-day varia-
tions in staining through mathematical methods, such as normalization for the results from multiple samples. A fundamental underlying issue is the inability to control tissue quality between samples within the same batch in the cmIF procedure. Variations in tissue sample quality likely depend on variations in tissue age, fixation time, leading time until tissue fixation, and laboratory technician skills. To overcome experimental or technical variabilities, a deep learning model has been developed, which enables direct translation of H&E images into realistic predictions of two commonly used prognostic markers (pan- CK and αSMA) and a nuclear counterstain DAPI [90]. Since prediction happens in silico, the method is consistent and does not show the technical artifacts often appear in IF staining caused by improper fixation, improper reagents, or poor preservation. We envision that this technique could alleviate technical challenge and difficulties of cmIF imaging and may facilitate compatibility with clinical histopathology workflow.
4. The cmIF procedure uses primary or prelabeled antibodies
from a large pool of commercial suppliers. The labeling protocol for primary antibodies is well established, and the labeling is inexpensive. The fluorophores used to label antibodies are relatively small molecules, so the potential adverse influence of fluorophores on the antibody’s original affinity is minimal. The cost of all necessary chemicals and reagents for cmIF is very low except for that of the primary antibodies. The required imaging equipment and image processing for analysis are the same as those of other platforms.

558 Jennifer Eng et al. 5 Conclusions The journey to establish a workflow for cmIF that enables the interrogation of the expression of 60 protein biomarkers in individual cells from a single FFPE section since the first time an advanced breast cancer tissue was successfully stained with nine antibodies over three cycles. The assay workflow of cmIF also includes analysis of the spatial distribution of classified cells and their proximity. The antibodies, especially in-house labeled antibodies, have been validated, as have the reproducibility and repeatability of cmIF using a number of adjacent tissues (most of the data for which is not included in this chapter). The cmIF now applies to the SMMART Clinical Trials at the OHSU Knight Cancer Institute for patients suffering from advanced breast, pancreas, or prostate cancer. The ultimate goal of this development is to improve cancer therapy strategies by understanding the mechanisms of cancer progression and drug resistance. We hope this chapter will disseminate our expertise of the cyclic IF procedure and analytics to the broader cancer research community in order to improve cancer patients’ quality of life. ## Chapter 25


564 Joseph M. Beechem predict response to immunotherapies [2–5]. Imaging-based methods, however, have typically resolved a small number of potential biomarkers (≤~10 markers). In contrast, molecular profiling technologies (e.g., next-generation sequencing, NanoString, microarrays), often resolve hundreds to thousands of potential markers simultaneously, yet lack the spatial resolution to directly measure the unique tumor-microenvironment changes that are intrinsic to every current immunotherapeutic method. The development of digital spatial profiling allows the utilization of the high numbers of exploratory biomarkers, similar to NGS and NanoString, yet provides the spatial context so important for immuno-oncology based drugs. The GeoMX DSP system has been developed with hardware, software, and chemistry to allow for up to 800-plex profiling of mRNA or protein using an optical-barcode readout (20, 21) and potential for unlimited multiplexing using the NGS readout. Full results from 10 to 20 slides (depending on number of ROIs and AOIs) can be accomplished within 1.5–2.5 days (assuming approximately 24 AOIs per tissue section). The GeoMx system is highly sensitive, simple to run, and produces direct, digital data for quantitative downstream analysis. Importantly, the technology is nondestructive, allowing multiple cycles of high-plex profiling on the same tissue section or subsequent DNA sequencing on the same section. 2 Materials 2.1 Sample 1. Each primary antibody was coupled to a 70 bp indexing oligo Preparation (NanoString, custom conjugation service). Probe Design From 5′ to 3′, they each comprised a 35–40 bp target complementary sequence, an iSpPC UV photocleavable linker (Integrated DNA Technologies), and a 60 bp indexing oligo sequence. The 60 bp indexing oligo sequence contains a unique sequence that describes the RNA target for which it was designed. For instance, the sequence “GATCCGA” in the photocleaved oligo from a spatially resolved RNA experiment may represent a PD-L1 hybridization probe, whereas “TAACGCT” may represent CTLA4 hybridization probe (see Note 1). 2.3 Sample 1. Each ROI was uniquely indexed using Illumina’s i5 × i7 dualfor Photocleaved Oligo indexing system. 4 μL of the aspirate containing the photo- Counting cleaved oligos was used in a PCR reaction with 1 μM of i5 primer, 1 μM i7 primer, and 1× NSTG PCR Master Mix. Thermocycler conditions were 37 °C for 30 min, 50 °C for 10 min, 95 °C for 3 min, 18 cycles of 95 °C for 15 s, 65 °C for 60 s, 68 °C for 30 s, and final extension of 68 °C for 5 min.
2. PCR reactions were purified with two rounds of AMPure XP
beads (Beckman Coulter) at 1.2× bead-to-sample ratio. Libraries were paired-end sequenced (2 × 75) on an MiSeq with 25.9 M total aligned reads and a median of 0.2 M aligned reads per ROI (range 1128–1.1 M). Each library (or ROI) was demultiplex on-instrument to produce one FASTQ file per ROI.

4. Photocleaved oligos that have been released into aqueous liquid
above the slide are collected via a microcapillary tube and deposited in a 96-well plate for subsequent quantitation (see Note 2).
5. By capturing a vast excess volume (~2500 nL) of buffer, nearly
every photocleaved oligo that is photocleaved can be accurately transferred to an on-instrument microplate well. Since these PC-oligos are being counted using either direct single-molecule methods (NanoString nCounter) or via next-generation sequencing, this dilution factor does not cause any problem with the net sensitivity of the instrument because each will be captured again during the detection-counting process.
6. Localized UV exposure and PC-oligo collection (steps 3–5)
are repeated for each ROI, with extensive washing between each cycle. The average time it takes to collect data for each AOI within an ROI is approximately 30–45 s.
7. After all of the ROIs are collected, the spatially resolved pools
of photocleaved oligos are taken out of the DSP instrument for digital counting. The digital counting is either accomplished by a direct hybridization reaction with NanoString’s fluorescent barcodes (up to 800-plex), or counted using NGS approaches (unlimited multiplexing) [described in Subheading 2 above]. The digital counts obtained from NanoString or NGS-based readout(s) are then mapped back to each ROI and AOI (see Note 3). 3.2 Overview 1. An for Immuno-oncology emphasis here will be to highlight those aspects of ROI-and-AOI Mechanism of Action selection most useful for immuno-oncology applications. and Biomarker Key to understanding the modes-of-GeoMx operation, is a Discovery description of the four fluorescent detection channels of GeoMx. The markers observed in these four-channels are called “Visible Morphology Markers.” The spatial patterns generated from the Morphology Markers are called “masks,” and the masks are imagefiles that can be downloaded directly into the DMDs to control the placement of the photocleavage light on the tissue surface with single-cell resolution. The four fluorescence channels of GeoMx image the morphology markers and are configured as: FITC-channel: The 480 nm (centered excitation), 516 nm (centered emission) channel of GeoMx is usually devoted to the nucleic-acid stain (SYTO13, Molecular Probes) and is used to count cell nuclei. Counting of the total number of cells in the AOI can be a very useful and important way to normalize signals. Cy3-channel: The 538 nm (centered excitation), 564 nm (centered emission) channel of GeoMx is often devoted to visualization of all of the immune-cells in a ROI using a fluorescently labeled CD45. Texas Red-channel: The 588 nm (centered excitation), 623 nm (centered emission) channel of GeoMx is often devoted to visual-

Cy5-channel: The 646 nm (centered excitation), 683 nm (centered emission) channel of GeoMx is devoted to visualization of custom-labeled antibodies of interest. To generate a custom mask to control GeoMx DMDs, one can generate a series of multicolor images (as many as desired) using any outside microscope system as long as the tumor section measured originates from the same FFPE tumor block. This tumor-section needs to be close enough to the serial section placed in the GeoMx, such that the software of GeoMx can align the ImageJ-processed outside image to the four- color fluorescence image of the serial section measured on the DSP. We have found that serial sections as far as 10–20 five-micron sections-away can still be aligned in GeoMx. If the exactly same section (as used in the outside microscope) is utilized in the GeoMx

experiment, this allows very high-dimensional selection of individual rare-cell types that (almost surely) do not exist in serial-sections to be utilized for high-plex AOI profiling. 3.5 Primary Modes Each mode is designed to facilitate different types of spatially of Operating the DSP resolved studies. The system has been developed such that many of (Fig. 2) these operational modes can be combined, generating a very high flexibility in potential experimental designs. 3.5.1 Geometric Profiling Geometric profiling are a suite of general purpose tools that allow (Fig. 3) a pathologist (or knowledgeable scientist) to simply “free-hand” draw geometric shapes (circles, squares, polygons, etc.) over particularly interesting areas of a tissue section. Early versions of this type of geometric profiling can be found in references [6, 7]. More advanced examples relevant for immuno-oncology would be to automatically find immune-deserts, immune-boundary regions, high-infiltrate regions, and low-infiltrate regions. GeoMx is developing automated tools that will assist in this type of profiling. For instance, tools that will allow GeoMx to automatically point out immune-regions of low-infiltrate, medium-infiltrate, and high-infiltrate from a full four-color tissue scan, with adjustable settings for how to define low, medium, and high for each infiltrate type. 3.5.2 Segment Profiling The goal of segment profiling is to decompose a ROI into distinct (Fig. 4) “compartments of biology.” Compartments of biology especially relevant for immuno-oncology applications are the “tumor” and “tumor microenvironment” compartments. Beechem For example, take the case of wanting to perform automated DSP high-plex profiling of proteins or RNA in the tumor-only and tumor microenvironment (TME) compartments of a single FFPE tissue section. This is an application highly relevant for discovering immuno-oncology biomarkers for mechanism-of-action studies or for discovering predictive biomarkers of immunotherapy response. If one of the fluorescent channels measures a dye-labeled pancytokeratin in, say, the Cy3-channel of the DSP, the Cy3-image will uniquely locate all of the tumor-specific cells in many cancer types. Unique to the DSP, the GeoMx system can automatically threshold the Cy-3 image for above-background cells and simultaneously adjust all one million micromirrors of the two DMDs to only shine the photocleavage light on each individual tumor-positive cell in the Cy3 image (Subheading 3.5.3 described below). This allows high-plex profiling of the tumor cells for protein or RNA as if all tumors consist of 100% pure tumor cellularity (i.e., the measured signals will not be contaminated with signals arising from the tumor microenvironment). This operation is called configuring an “area of photocleavage illumination” (AOI). Having obtained the “pure-tumor” molecular profile, the GeoMx system will automatically establish the DMD configuration for the “pure-TME” photocleavage step. This can be accomplished in multiple ways. The simplest method, simply takes the tumor-specific Cy3-channel image utilized to profile the tumor-specific cells and “inverts” the image prior to configuring the DMDs. By inverting the image, one automatically configures all of the micromirrors in the DMDs to change position and shine the photocleavage light only on the nontumor (i.e., TME) region of the tissue section. This approach will hence profile every cell that is in the TME, both immune and nonimmune cells. If one wants to molecular profile only the immune cells in the TME, one can devote one of the other fluorescent detection channels (e.g., the Texas-Red channel) for a dye-labeled anti-CD45 antibody. In this case, GeoMx will then automatically take the Texas-Red image, threshold over background, and simultaneously configure the DMDs to shine photocleavage light on only the immune cells (CD45+) in the TME. The GeoMx software is configured to understand key immuno-oncology terms (tumor, TME, macrophages, Tregs, etc.) and will automatically perform all of the operations above for completely unattended tumor and TME molecular profiling. 3.5.3 Rare Cell-Type • Segment profiling can be combined with cell-type profiling to Profiling (Fig. 5) generate distinct AOIs within a single ROI. For instance, one can combine an antibody labeled for the Texas-Red channel (use CD68 as an example) with a custom-labeled antibody to PD-L1 in the Cy5-channel to generate a cell-type profile mask that will control the DMDs to illuminate only all macrophages (CD68+) with PD-L1 expression (also) on the surface. This type of profiling is very well suited for NGS readout, where a very large number of ROIs can be combined and analyzed in a single run of a NextSeq, HighSeq, or NovaSeq NGS system (Illumina, San Diego, CA). 3.6 Simultaneous To facilitate the simultaneous analysis of spatially resolved RNA Analysis of Protein and protein, we designed the GeoMx DSP software to allow one to and RNA overlay the ROIs-AOIs from one tissue section (performed using for Biomarker high-plex protein panel) directly onto the spatially aligned adjacent Discovery (Fig. 8) tissue section utilized for high-plex RNA profiling (see Fig. 8). The proteinase-K step utilized for in situ RNA hybridization destroys some of the key epitopes for antibody binding rendering simultaneous protein and RNA on a single section viable only for relatively high-abundance protein targets (e.g., pan-cytokeratin). By aligning the adjacent sections images together via software, and then projecting the ROI-AOI geometries (from protein to RNA or vice versa), rigorous simultaneous analysis (differential expression volcano plots, principal component analysis, etc.) can be performed on both digital layers of information. 579 H&E and Sample Annotation Immunostaining Imaging Features Molecular Profiling Digital Pathology Kaplan-Meier Estimator Bulk Expression Survival (days) Clinical Annotation 3.7 Data Analysis A very important component of DSP is the analysis and interpreta- Environment tion of spatially resolved high-plex RNA and protein data. Many Developed for GeoMx software approaches attempt to base all analysis on pure spatial infor- (Fig. 9) mation. The GeoMx approach to data analysis is very different. A

completely interactive data analysis approach has been developed that combines all of the data and sample annotation into a single internally consistent molecular profiling analysis that interacts in real time with the raw spatially resolved images. For instance, the GeoMx software “understands” Kaplan–Meier analysis, principal component analysis, volcano plots, etc., all “staples” of modern molecular profiling analysis. Prospective biomarkers displayed in a volcano plot (for example) representing all of the differential expression of proteins and RNA in the TME of “responders” versus “nonresponders” to immunotherapy can be immediately “transferred-back” to the original spatially resolved images that generated measured the differential response. In this manner, the (rather) abstract molecular profiling analysis can be immediately referenced-back to the raw spatially resolved images generating the molecular profile. lacitsitatS ecnacifingiS lavivruS-% High-Plex Spatially Resolved RNA and Protein Detection Using Digital Spatial Profiling… Fig. 9 GeoMx data analysis environment. Kaplan–Meir plots, volcano plots (lower and upper right), principal component analysis, swimmer plots, etc. are all part of the data analysis structure of GeoMx. 580 Joseph M. Beechem 4 Notes
1. The indexing sequences are arbitrary, and are utilized by the
NanoString software as being associated with specific targets. All RNA detection probes and indexing oligo sequence complements were ion-exchange HPLC purified (Integrated DNA Technologies). Up to ten oligo RNA detection probes were designed per target mRNA.
2. Microcapillary is NOT a spatially resolving DSP element; it is
designed to center over the illumination area and capture approximately 2.5 μL of buffer above the tissue after photocleavage. The approximate volume in which the photocleaved oligos are released is a few nanoliters.
3. Prior to each AOI, a full four-color 20× magnification image of
the tissue slice, enabling the high-plex digital counts to be accurately mapped-back onto the correct tissue section location. 5 Summary The key unique features of the GeoMx DSP are as follows:
1. Unlimited multiplex. The nCounter-based readout of GeoMx
permits multiplexed proteins and RNA to be carried out up to 800-plex. Using the NGS readout mode, unlimited multiplexing is possible. Typical multiplexed protein panels range from 20-plex to approximately 100-plex. Typical RNA panels range from 96-plex to 20,000-plex. With the NGS readout of RNA, multiple RNA-probes spanning the multiple exons permit spatially resolved mRNA isoform splicing.
2. Multianalyte (both RNA and Protein). Both high-plex protein
and RNA analysis can be performed on FFPE slices (minimum
2) obtained from the same tumor block. Data analysis can be
performed on both sets of analytes simultaneously. Both RNA probes and antibodies can be custom labeled. RNA custom is much easier and can be expanded to very high plex.
3. Quantitative. Both RNA and protein barcodes are digitally
counted. The dynamic range is linear over ~106 counts. The DSP chemistry is the only current completely digital chemistry developed for pathology, matching well the initiative to develop digital pathology as a new field of study.
4. Single-cell capable. The one million mirrors of the DMD per-
mit a spatial resolution with a hardware limit of approximately one square micron. T cells are approximately 10 μm in diameter, so it is possible to illuminate single T cells, representing the smallest detection target usually encountered in immuno-oncology studies.

High-Plex Spatially Resolved RNA and Protein Detection Using Digital Spatial Profiling… 581
5. Nondestructive. Since the tissue slice is never “touched” by
anything other than a brief burst of 385 nm light, after performance of a DSP experiment the tissue slice can be stored wet and preserved for further studies. Downstream full NGS sequencing can be performed on exactly the same slide that was examined in the DSP. Similarly, the original antibody cocktail can be “stripped off” and the slide can be stored wet for future studies with differing antibody cocktails and/or different ROIs and AOIs.
6. High throughput. GeoMx has been designed as a high-
throughput device, able to complete approximately 10–20 tissue slices from excisional biopsies in a single 10 h workday (assuming approximately 12–24 AOIs per slide).
7. Ease of Use and Maintenance. GeoMx has been designed to be
operated by laboratory technicians familiar with only standard immunohistochemistry practices. No special laboratory facilities are required, and only standard benchtop instrumentation space is needed. Some limitations of the DSP platform should be noted. Profiling every cell in a tissue slice at single-cell resolution with this system is impractical and cost-prohibitive. One advantage of imaging- based methods over DSP, is the ability to get multiplexed information on each cell in the tissue slice, whereas DSP provides high-plex information of regions of interest and tissue compartments- niches. Hence, we view DSP and imaging-based approaches to be complementary, and in fact, cycling-based imaging approaches can be utilized up-front of a DSP workflow for those cases where high-plex guided region-of-interest selection for DSP is desired. The era of “spatially resolved technologies” are just beginning. Similar to the revolution in understanding of biology provided by single-cell sequencing techniques, we believe spatially resolved high-plex profiling with generate a similar revolution in the understanding of mechanism of action in immuno-oncology and will greatly accelerate the development of high information-content biomarkers capable of predicting response to the vast number of combination immunotherapies currently under development (Tables 1, 2, and 3). To better understand the immune response in cancer cases, multiplexed techniques have been developed to analyze multiple markers on the same sample, enabling deep profiling of the TME [1–7]. Flow cytometry provides a convenient tool to study large numbers of markers (up to 18) and phenotypes in suspended cells, but does not offer insight into their original spatial distribution [8, 9]. In contrast, multiplex IHC (mIHC) can provide in situ multiparametric analysis of the tumor environment. The leading mIHC techniques are based on immunofluorescence, as it offers a higher sensitivity, wider dynamic range for quantification, and better multiplexing capabilities through the spectral separation of fluorescent dyes and their specific wavelengths compared to commonly used brightfield detection methods [10]. A promising approach relies on the enzymatic, covalent deposition of the reporter dyes on the sample, and a sequence of staining and stripping steps to overcome the limitation of using primary antibodies from the same host species [2, 11, 12]. However, the associated workflow is slow and nuance-rich due to the numerous antibody staining steps and the repeated epitope retrieval steps to deactivate the antibodies which can lead to tissue damage [13, 14]. In addition, the development of the multiplex assays requires lengthy optimization [15]. Other fluorescence mIHC techniques have demonstrated high multiplexing imaging in FFPE tissue, using labeled primary antibodies and a cyclical imaging/staining approach where dyes are bleached or cleaved between imaging steps [6, 16, 17]. The main shortcoming of these techniques arises from the lack of signal amplification, which limits the detection of low abundance markers, increases overall imaging time, as well as having an increased risk for tissue damage due to the multiple bleaching/stripping steps [6]. More recently, alternative mIHC methods based on time-of-flight mass spectrometry have demonstrated great potential for highly multiparametric and deep phenotyping of tissue sections [18–20]. However, these methods are limited by very long acquisition times and require dedicated, expensive imaging equipment, preventing routine application to whole-slide imaging and analysis. The InSituPlex technology is based on antibodies conjugated to short oligonucleotides herein referred to as barcodes. Antibodies for each target are associated with a unique, addressable barcode sequence for subsequent labeling and detection. For each barcode, a complementary oligonucleotide probe tagged with a fluorescent dye is used in order to label the antibody conjugates. Different fluorophores are associated with each barcode–probe pair in order to spectrally separate the targets during imaging. Figure 1 is a schematic of the staining workflow. First, the FFPE sections are dewaxed and subjected to heat-induced epitope retrieval using routine laboratory techniques.

The InSituPlex® Staining Method for Multiplexed Immunofluorescence Cell… 587

Fig. 1 InSituPlex assay workflow After a quick blocking step, the sections are then incubated with a mixture of primary antibodies conjugated to barcodes (Fig. 1a, b). Next, the ratio of barcodes per antibody is increased on the tissue through a process that amplifies all targets simultaneously (Fig. 1c). Finally, the fluorescently tagged probes are added to the sample to hybridize and label the targets (Fig. 1d), and the sections are ready for fluorescence imaging. The assay protocol fits into standard IHC workflows and automation instrumentation, while offering a low number of steps compared to other multiplex fluorescent IHC methods. Here, we demonstrate the application of the InSituPlex technology by employing a commercially available multiplex IHC kit (UltiMapper I/O PD-L1) targeting a set of protein markers relevant to the field of immuno-oncology research. The multiplexed panel is designed to detect five protein targets on a single tissue slide with whole slide imaging. The panel comprises DNA-barcoded antibodies against CD8, CD68, PD-L1, pan-cytokeratin, and SOX10 (see Note 1). A typical result using the panel on human non-small cell lung cancer tissue is presented. 2 Materials The UltiMapper I/O kits, utilizing InSituPlex technology, are designed to be platform agnostic. The materials listed below are suggestions and generally can be substituted with those used routinely in histology laboratories. Staining can be performed manually or on an automated platform. Imaging can be performed on any scanner that can read in the DAPI, FITC, TRITC, Cy5, and Cy7 channels. Image analysis can be performed using any software that is capable of accepting the file format from the corresponding scanner (see Note 2). 2.1 Formalin-Fixed, 1. # Part VII

Microbiome

## Chapter 27


596 Manoj Kumar et al. nose, vagina, vaginal secretion, seminal fluid, mammary glands, and the largest number residing in the gut due to the bioavailability of nutrients [3]. It is estimated that collectively the human gut microbiota are at least as numerous as the total cells in the human body by ten to one [4, 5], consisting of about 100 trillion microbes that represent around 5000 distinct species and make up to 2 kg of the human body weight [3]. The human microbiome is often referred to, as “our second genome” due to its size and sheer vastness [5]. In particular, the gut microbiota is now considered an “organ” of its own and is nicknamed “our second brain” due to its role in various immunological, neuronal, and endocrine responses [6]. Studies of the diversity in the human microbiome initially started in 1680, when Antoine van Leeuwenhoek compared his own oral and fecal samples using self-made microscopes [7]. He observed that the two habitats had distinct microbes and this observation led him to compare samples from healthy and diseased individuals where he also noted striking differences in their microbial communities [7, 8]. However, owing to the limitation of the in vitro microbial cultivation, the complex and dynamic nature of our microbiota was not fully recognized up until recently. This was facilitated by the advent of high-throughput sequencing technologies and the undertaking of large-scale metagenomics endeavors such as the Human Microbiome Project (HMP) that was initiated by the National Institutes of Health in the USA [9] and the Metagenomes Human Intestinal Tract (MetaHIT) project developed by the European Commission [10]. These projects have expanded our understanding of the Human microbiome. The MetaHIT study reported gut metagenomes from stool samples of predominantly healthy cohort of 124 European adults [11]. Whereas, in an effort to define the healthy human microbiome, the HMP researchers recruited 242 volunteers (129 males, 113 females) and sampled tissues from 15 body sites in men and 18 body sites in women. By incorporating several complementary techniques and analyses including 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene sequencing, whole-genome shotgun sequencing (WGS) and aligning the assembled sequences to the reference microbial genomes [12, 13] they were able to define the microbiome composition of each body site they sampled from [9]. They showed that, various body sites show a tenfold difference in the estimated microbial richness, with the gut being the richest ecosystem [9]. They also confirmed that a high interindividual variation of the microbiome exists and concluded that a healthy microbiome can be achieved by maintaining a balance between all the factors that contribute to the microbiome makeup (will be discussed later). The most extensive research has been conducted with the gut ecosystem, in order to assess the impact of the gut microbes on

Microbiome as an Immunological Modifier 597 human health and predisposition to various diseases [11, 14]. The gut microbiomes described as part of the MetaHIT cohorts indicated that a large proportion of the microbial genes are shared between individuals of this cohort and that more than 99% of these genes are bacterial, representing 1000–1150 bacterial species [11]. A healthy gut microbiota is mainly composed of strict anaerobes dominated by two main phyla: Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes [13]. In a healthy individual, many other body sites are occupied by microbial communities although not as well studied as the gut [13]. One of the largest human-associated microbial habitats is the skin surface, and is colonized primarily by Corynebacterium, Propionibacterium, and Staphylococcus [15]. The composition of the microbial communities shows more similarity “within habitats” as compared to “between habitats.” For example, samples collected from the oral communities show similar composition between different individuals, whereas compared with other communities within the same person, the oral ecosystem looks vastly different [13]. The oral and salivary microbiomes mirror the gut microbiota in terms of complexity and diversity [13]. An ecologically stable vaginal microbiome is dominated by species of Lactobacillus (L. crispatus, L. iners, L. jensenii, or L. gasseri) or by other microbes including Gardnerella vaginalis and Atopobium spp., among others and is classified in community state types [16]. This microbial diversity is affected by race, ethnicity, pregnancy, hormonal changes, sexual activities, and hygiene practices, among others [16–18]. The vaginal microbiome plays an important role in the prevention of genital and urinary tract infections and in prevention sexually transmitted diseases, and multiple studies have shown that an abnormal vaginal microbial composition is associated with an increased risk of HIV infection [19]. There are body sites particularly difficult to characterize, due to the low microbial load in healthy individuals, for example, the lung microbiota has a low microbial density, especially in the absence of an infection or pulmonary disease, as under normal conditions, the human lungs harbor approximately 2.2 × 103 bacterial genomes per cm2 [20]. It is also worth-noting that the identification of these microbial genomes remains tedious due to the technical challenges associated with the sampling from such sites. Similarly, habitats such as mammary glands, breast milk [21], placenta [22], and amniotic fluid [23] are of great interest due to their potential role in establishment of the early infant microbiome, but most studies have relied on traditional culture dependent approaches and/or single-cell techniques, such as FISH or microfluidics to study their microbiomes. Development of better sampling techniques facilitating the use of larger-scale high-throughput metagenomics studies are thus required to establish the exact composition and functionality of these challenging microbial habitats [23].

598 Manoj Kumar et al. 2 Universal Properties of the Human Microbiome Based on the HMP and other research studies the “universal” properties of a healthy human microbiome have been identified. Dr. Lita Proctor, the coordinator of the HMP, pointed out few of these properties [13]. First, unlike the human genome, the human microbiome is not inherited but acquired upon birth. Newborns are described as “microbe magnets,” where the microbiota of the babies born vaginally resembles closely the mother’s vaginal microbiota, whereas those born via cesarean section (C-section) derive their microbiota from the mother’s skin [13] or the surrounding environment [24]. A second universal property is that, the adult microbial community composition is dictated by specific body sites, each body habitat such as gut, skin, oral cavity and urogenital tract, has a distinct microbial composition, regardless of the host gender, age, weight, or any other factor. HMP 16S rRNA data revealed clustering of specific microbial taxa within each of the body sites, and this clustering was driven by various factors including temperature, humidity, and pH, among others [25]. The final universally applicable property is that the gut microbiome changes over the lifetime, advances in metagenomics techniques have facilitated our understanding of the microbiome composition and its variation from infancy to old age. The ELDERMET project reported that the microbiomes in elderly people (aged 65 and over) are quite distinct from the microbiomes of middle-aged adults [26]. 3 Inception of the Microbial Colonization One of the most essential processes in the human life is the initial colonization of the infant’s gut by microbes, as this sets the stage for the establishment of a stable microbiome later in life [27]. Microbial contact during prenatal life and the inoculum transferred during birth and breastfeeding imprint the infant’s microbiota and the immune system [24, 28]. The gut microbiota of neonates is low in diversity and is dominated by two major phyla such as Proteobacteria and Actinobacteria, while in the weeks following birth, the microbiota becomes more diverse and dominated by Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes [11, 28–30]. Between one to two years of life, the microbial succession begins to vary, coinciding with the transition to a more diverse type of diet [29]. By the end of the second year of age, the taxonomic composition of the gut microbiome stabilizes and converges toward a characteristic adult microbiome [28]. Therefore, the first 2 years of life represents a vital period for any diet-based alteration to potentially impact the human health and immunity in later life.

Microbiome as an Immunological Modifier 599 4 Major Factors Influencing the Development of the Microbiome Several pre and postnatal factors can significantly alter the composition of the gut microbiota including genetics; the mode of delivery at birth; the method of infant feeding; the use of medications, especially antibiotics; and diet, among others. 4.1 Birth Mode Numerous studies have shown that the mode of delivery (vaginally or by C-section) has a strong influence on early gut colonization [24, 28]. Vaginally delivered infants are exposed to their mother’s vaginal and fecal microbiota and have an abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species [24]. Whereas, the very first microbial inoculum received by the infant born via a C-section is distinct; and these newborns become quickly colonized by the bacteria acquired from the skin and the surrounding hospital environment [24]. It is also suggested that the microbial composition in those infants may be disturbed for the first few months in life [31, 32]. Analysis of the meconium in the first few days after revealed that the microbial communities of the infant’s gut mirror either those of the mother’s vagina (Lactobacillus, Prevotella, or Sneathia) in the case of vaginal delivery, or the mother’s skin microbiota (Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, and Propionibacterium) in the case of a C-section [24]. Vaginally delivered infants also share the higher proportion of their gut microbial 16S gene sequences with their own mothers as compared to other mothers [32]. 4.2 Feeding Mode The mode of feeding is another factor that influences the development of the microbiota in the infant’s gut. Not only is mother’s milk the major source of bacteria colonizing the infant’s gut, but it is also considered a major determinant and contributor to the child health status [33]. Analysis of breast milk samples revealed the presence of Streptococcus and Staphylococcus genus, and those are considered among the early colonizers of the infant’s gut [34]. Additional phyla such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus were detected in the breast milk samples and also in the gut of breastfed infants in higher counts as compared to the formula-fed infants [35–37] indicating a major role of breast milk in seeding the gut microbiota early in life. The gut microbial diversity increases with the infant’s age and during the gradual shift from milk to solid food where a higher abundance of Bacteroides and Clostridium species in the toddler’s gut starts to be observed. 4.3 Antibiotics The use of broad-spectrum antibiotics in infants and young children has negative effects on the composition of the gut microbiota, which results in significant drops in taxonomic richness, diversity and evenness of the gut microbial communities [38, 39]. Prenatal/ or maternal antibiotic exposure is shown to increase the abundance of many pathogenic communities (pathobionts) such as

600 Manoj Kumar et al. Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Serratia, and Parabacteroides [40]. Early antibiotic exposure in neonates (such as Ampicillin and Gentamicin administered within the first 48 h of birth) results in significantly lower levels of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus when compared to untreated controls [41]. 4.4 Preterm Birth Compared to full term born infants, the preterm born infant’s microbiota has a reduced microbial diversity and a decreased abundance of bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Bacteroides species [42]. In addition, potentially pathogenic bacteria such as Enterococcus species together with Proteobacteria species increase proportionally as a result of the reduction of the beneficial microbes [41]. Preterm birth is also associated with inflammatory intestinal disorders such as Neonatal Necrotizing Enterocolitis which has been linked to microbial dysbiosis and an increase in Proteobacteria is considered a predictive marker for the disease [43]. 4.5 Host Genetics The contribution of the host genetic makeup in shaping the early microbiota remains a subject of many speculations, as defining the host genotype–microbiota interaction in humans remains complicated. However specific bacteria found in the gut microbiota may be influenced in part, by the genetic makeup of the host, impacting as a result our metabolism and ultimately the health status. Family studies with varying degrees of relatedness along with the twin cohorts’ studies provided a great input on the role of genetics in the microbiome composition. The microbial diversity is similar within family members as compared to unrelated individuals and monozygotic twins share certain the expression of certain heritable taxa compared to the dizygotic twins [44]. However, the overall variance in the microbiome composition is also affected for a few percent by host genetics and mostly determined by environmental factors [45]. A recent study in southern China, showed that the major influence on microbiome composition was due to the geographical localization in different districts and that these differences could simply be accounted by environmental or life style differences among districts [46]. Detailed genome-wide association studies are required to provide a greater insight into the role of the genetic makeup in the microbiome composition and in the mechanism underlying the microbiota–host genetic interactions. 4.6 Environmental Differences in lifestyle due to the geographical location, religion Factors and culture are among the factors impacting the development of an early gut microbiota [47]. Infants from the Northern part of Europe have higher abundance of Bifidobacterium, Clostridium and Atopobium species in their gut microbiome, while infants living in southern Europe have higher percentages of Eubacteria, Lactobacillus and Bacteroides [36]. Similar differences in the gut microbial composition have been reported between German and Finnish infants [36], and between Swedish and Estonian infants [48].

Microbiome as an Immunological Modifier 601 Family dynamics may also act as a relevant environmental factor, where having siblings usually results in a higher percentage of Bifidobacterium as compared to single infants [49]. Exposure to household pets was shown to play a role in shaping the gut microbiome of infants [50]. An emerging spectrum of environmental factors including maternal or infant’s exposures to toxins/pollutants and xenobiotic substances are important to be considered and warrant more studies in order to determine their role in the development of the early gut microbiota. 5 Tools Used to Study the Microbiome Recent advancements in the development of sequencing technologies and bioinformatics tools, fostered the growth of new omics technologies used to study the microbiome composition and its interaction with the host. Omics technology helps to explore the microbiome at various levels including gene expression, gene abundance, protein expression and microbial metabolites [51]. This knowledge is an essential tool used to study the role of the microbiome in many diseases and pathological conditions using various models (described later). 5.1 16S rRNA Gene This is a gene-specific technique, where the bacterial taxonomic Sequencing profile of a sample is characterized by sequencing specific hypervariable regions of the 16S rRNA gene [52]. Amplicons are generated using universal primers used to anneal with the conserved regions of the 16S rRNA gene sequences [43]. Those hypervariable region sequences are highly polymorphic, therefore allowing the classification of the bacterial taxa from phyla to species levels [52]. Illumina MiSeq and ThermoFisher Ion Torrent Personal genomic instruments are the widely used sequencers with a capacity to generate 300–400 bp reads [53]. Sequence reads can be analyzed using the traditional way of operation taxonomic unitsbased clustering approach using QIIME pipeline or calling amplicon sequence variants using DADA2 pipeline [54, 55]. The other available tools used to detect the taxonomic profiles using 16S data are LEA-seq, 16S based oligo typing, Long-read 16S, UNOISE2, and Deblur [56–59]. GreenGenes and SILVA are the most commonly used databases to profile the taxonomic differences among various samples [60, 61]. Eukaryotic organisms (such as fungi and protists) also play an important role in the microbiome. They can be analyzed in a similar manner to 16S studies by either looking at the hypervariable regions of the 18S rRNA or the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) regions between rRNA genes [62–74]. 5.2 Metagenomics: This technology is based on the shotgun sequencing of the whole Which Microbes Are genomic DNA and is used to study all the genetic materials in the There? microbiota [51]. Metagenomic study provides information about

602 Manoj Kumar et al. the taxonomic profile, functional composition and gene abundance of the microbiota [75]. It can also provide information up to species/strain level compared to 16S rRNA gene sequencing [75]. One challenge of metagenomic shotgun sequencing is that of retrieving enough data pertaining to the microbiota from low biomass samples. These low biomass samples are host tissues which present a low concentration of microbes relative to host somatic cells. Because shotgun sequencing is nontargeted, and the size of a mammalian genome is three orders of magnitude larger than that of a bacterial genome, the sequencing effort for a low biomass sample may end up being dominated by the host DNA. Although metagenomics can explore the functional abundance (relative abundance of the microbial genes), it lacks information about the microbial activity (gene expression in live microbes) [75]. Therefore, recent studies are using metatranscriptomics (RNA-based) along with metagenomics (DNA-based) to explore the functionality of the active/viable microbes and their role in the host physiology [51]. Metagenomic sequencing reads can be taxonomically classified using, basically, two approaches, namely, the alignment of reads to reference bacterial genomes, or a comparison of snippets, or “words,” of genome of a fixed small size (known as k-mers) to the ones found in reference bacterial genomes. The HUMAnN pipeline [76] infers presence and relative abundance (quantity) of species by alignment to precomputed clade-specific genes, which are genes exclusive to a species or other higher-level taxonomic levels. Metabolic reconstruction using hits to reference are performed using ASGARD [77]. Classification of reads coming from species which are not in a reference database can be done by k-mer spectrum analysis using Kraken [78] and by assembling the reads into contiguous sequences, called contigs, followed by naive gene prediction and classification using a functional database like InterPro [79]. 5.3 Meta The advent development in the field of RNA-sequencing has protranscriptomics: What vided more exciting opportunities in the field of transcriptomics, Are Those Microbes especially microbial transcriptomics. Metatranscriptomics reflect the Doing? functional activity of microbial communities by assessing the community-wide gene expression [80]. Sample processing for metatranscriptomics is laborious compared to the metagenomics library preparation. After total RNA extraction, bacterial rRNA is removed using specific magnetic probes of rRNAs. The prokaryotic RNA content is only 1–5% of the total RNA content and is enriched with mRNA that is converted into cDNA before proceeding with the RNA sequencing protocol [81]. Sequence reads are mapped to reference genomes, and the expressed genes are identified based on the sequence reads covering these regions. Raw Sequence data is filtered using Trimmomatic and mapped using BOWTIE and GEM [82]. The differentially expressed genes are identified using CuffDiff [83]. HUMAnN and MG-RAST are the most extensively used pipelines for metatranscriptomics analysis [82, 84–86].

Microbiome as an Immunological Modifier 603 This approach can give a panorama for assessing the microbial activity of the human microbiome, the antisense RNAs and small noncoding RNAs, and facilitates a deeper understanding of the host–microbiome interactions in abnormal and diseased states [81]. 5.4 Metabolomics Defined as the analysis of the metabolomic profiles using untargeted and targeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS) methods or nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR); metabolomics is used to explain the mechanism of microbial bioactivity [53]. Of all the previously described omics approaches, the metabolomics approach acts as a bridging gap between the microbiome and host physiology. Metabolomic profiles can be analyzed with biofluids such as plasma, serum, urine, tissue extracts, and fecal supernatant [87, 88]. The output of the metabolomics data allows correlations between microbiota, their metabolites and metabolic routes using multivariate analysis. It can also be used as a diagnostic and prognostic marker for the diagnosis and treatment of various diseases. 6 Microbiota Derived-Metabolites and Small Molecules After completion of the HMP [9], Cimermancic et al. used an advanced computational approach with a moving aim from “who’s there?” to “what are they doing?” and identified more than 14,000 biosynthetic gene clusters in the human microbiome [89]. Of which, 3118 genes were present in one or more of the 752 sequenced samples [9]. While microbes are well known to produce diverse natural molecules mainly enzymes and antimicrobial agents, the recent genome mining have discovered numerous novel unexpected biosynthetic gene clusters and distinct natural molecules, which contribute to the microbial social and competitive interaction with other organisms [89–92]. The microbiota produces a range of molecules from various chemical classes including low molecular weight metabolites, to high molecular weight ribosomally synthesized posttranslationally modified peptides and proteins (RiPP), short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and diverse lipopolysaccharide (LPS) [92]. SCFAs contain acetate (C2), propionate (C3), and butyrate (C4) and are mainly produced by Butyrivibrio, Clostridium, Faecalibacterium, and Bifidobacterium species [93]. Vitamins like vitamin B and vitamin K are produced by various gut microbes including Propionibacterium freudenreichii, Salmonella enterica, Listeria innocua, and Enterobacter species, among others [94–96]. Those metabolites possess a wide range of activities; for example, microcin a narrow-spectrum antibacterial RiPP produced by Escherichia coli inhibits the growth of other closely related microbes; while the LPS and glycolipids released by the gut microbiota target various host immune cells; and the SCFAs produced by Bacteroidetes

604 Manoj Kumar et al. and Firmicutes stimulate a range of host processes such as epithelial cell proliferation, energy metabolism, host immune system (discussed later). We have summarized some of the natural molecules or metabolites produced by different microbiota species that mediate microbe-microbe interaction and host–microbe interactions in Table 1.
