## Chapter 29


650 Alida Palmisano et al. The impact and importance of combining genomic, proteomics, and functional molecular analysis in the field of cancer immunotherapy is demonstrated in efforts like the Cancer Immune Monitoring and Analysis Centers (CIMACs) and the Cancer Immunologic Data Commons (CIDC) Network, an initiative of the National Cancer Institute (NCI) Cancer Moonshot that provides cutting-edge technology and expertise in genomic, proteomic, and functional molecular analysis to enhance knowledge gained from clinical trials in cancer immune therapies [2]. Early stages of cancer biomarker research generally focus on cell lines and animal models. Understanding the influence of molecular alterations in tumor cells on pharmacological responses in cancer cell lines and animal models from the omic perspective is a necessary first step toward making oncology treatment for patients more effective and personalized. Increasingly it is recognized that the host immune response may also play an important role in permitting a tumor to develop and grow. For example, in a recent study on the immunome of colon cancer [3], the authors used multiple databases and bioinformatics resources to characterize colon cancer autoantibody signature between healthy controls and patients with the disease. The authors’ goal was to identify aberrant cellular mechanisms and enriched networks associated with colon cancer in order to gain further understanding of the biological mechanisms that may suggest therapeutic targets or clinical biomarkers. With the goal to inform and support biomedical researchers who engage in comprehensive analyses with a variety of different computational resources, we review several publicly available bioinformatics tools and data resources that are extensively used for integrative multidimensional data analysis and visualization in the field of cancer immunotherapy. In Subheadings 2 and 3, we review online repositories of data generated from cancer cell lines and cancer tissue specimens, respectively. We highlight how each repository provides the capability to explore the resources directly from the online portal, or to download the information for independent analysis. In Subheading 4, we review analysis tools that may be useful for researchers seeking biological insights from genomics data, through pathway analysis. In Subheading 5, we highlight public resources that curate information related to genomic alterations and their impact on therapeutics. In Subheading 6, we discuss some powerful tools to visualize complex genomic information and allow researchers to find patterns of biological importance in large datasets of mutation data. Finally, in Subheading 7 we review several data analysis tools developed for genomics, epigenetics, and neoantigen prediction.

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 651 2 Online Data Analysis Tools for Cancer Cell Lines Understanding changes in gene expression that occur in response to anticancer agents in tumor cell lines may facilitate prediction of patient response and resistance. Data from treated cell lines can also help guide the development of effective drug combinations for further exploration in clinical settings. Therefore, online resources that collect experimental data on drug response of cancer cell lines are an essential tool for the biomedical research community. The NCI Transcriptional Pharmacodynamics Workbench (NCI TPW) [4] is an example of such an online resource. The NCI TPW complements existing platforms by offering a centralized compilation of data on drug sensitivity as well as directly measured longitudinal transcriptional response for a large, common set of cancer cell lines. In particular, the NCI TPW allows researchers to query gene expression data for more than 12,000 genes in the NCI-60 panel of human tumor cell lines at multiple time points following exposure to 15 different anticancer agents. Examining genes that show concerted directional responses to multiple agents may shed light on common mechanisms of drug response or resistance. The NCI TPW (https://tpwb.nci.nih.gov) includes an intuitive web-interface that provides researchers the opportunity to generate heatmaps of genes affected by anti-cancer agents, organized by signaling pathway, or by interactions with a specific transcription factor or receptor type. Querying drug sensitivity data can provide mechanistic insights from gene expression data to identify agent combinations appropriate for further preclinical or clinical studies. Another online resource developed by NCI that contains extensive molecular and pharmacological data on cancer cell lines is the well-established CellMiner project (http://discover.nci.nih. gov/cellminer) and its updated version, CellMinerCDB (https:// discover.nci.nih.gov/cellminercdb/) [5, 6]. CellMiner provides extensive data on the NCI-60 cancer cell lines and the activity information for more than 20,000 compounds, including drugs approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and those used in clinical trials. CellMiner also contains transcript expressions for more than 25,000 genes, genetic variants for more than 15,000 genes, microRNAs transcript expressions, protein levels, DNA copy number variations, and DNA methylation levels. CellMinerCDB, currently contains fewer types of molecular data and analysis tools, but it provides an interactive web-application to explore other large cell line databases, such as Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE, from the Broad Institute and Novartis Institutes for Biomedical Research), Cancer Therapeutics Response

652 Alida Palmisano et al. Portal (CTRP, from the Broad Institute), and Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC, from the Wellcome Trust Sanger and Massachusetts General Hospital). Each of these databases contains about 1000 cell lines, thus broadening the spectrum of cancer types and number of cell lines that can be queried. Increasingly, immunotherapies are being studied or used clinically in combination with other immunotherapeutic agents or with conventional cancer therapies including chemotherapy [7–10]. To assist researchers with the selection of combinations of FDA approved anticancer drugs, NCI provides an online database and analysis interface, called “A Large Matrix of Anti-Neoplastic Agent Combinations” or NCI-ALMANAC (https://dtp.cancer.gov/ ncialmanac). The NCI-ALMANAC [11] presents results of a drug combination screen of pairs of 104 FDA-approved antitumor drugs in the NCI-60 panel. Promising drug combinations identified in the screen were further tested in mouse-derived tumor xenografts. The NCI-ALMANAC online tools allow researchers to mine various drug combinations and evaluate their levels of synergistic activity, to examine how various molecular modifier mechanisms affect drug efficacy, and to identify promising combinations of antitumor agents for further in vitro and in vivo testing and potential clinical use. Another rich dataset which catalogs information about cell line response to drug treatment and various genetic perturbations is the NIH Library of Integrated Network-Based Cellular Signatures (LINCS) project [12, 13]. LINCS contains assay results from human cells treated with bioactive small molecules, growth factors, and cytokines. A variety of molecular assays are used to monitor cellular response to perturbations, to measure transcript and protein expression, and to identify multiple genes signatures that characterize cell response at molecular level. LINCS assays are typically carried out in multiple cell types, time points, and doses. The LINCS project includes several components [12, 14] that use specific core cancer cell lines tested across all available agents, with additional noncancer cell lines screened using specific agents. LINCS data are accessible from the central hub at http://www. lincsproject.org/ and via additional web portals and search engines developed by LINCS Centers and individual subprojects. For example, LINCS L1000 Characteristic Direction Signature Search Engine (L1000CDS2; http://amp.pharm.mssm.edu/ L1000CDS2/) and the LINCS Canvas Browser (LCB; http:// www.maayanlab.net/LINCS/LCB) employ different approaches for finding similarities among gene sets representing each perturbation experiment [12, 15, 16]. The Clue.io platform provides tools to query data against massive datasets of gene expression and proteomic signatures linking them to the disease states in LINCS and the Connectivity Map projects [12, 17]. iLINCS (http:// www.ilincs.org/) is an integrative web portal for analyzing LINCS

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 653 data and gene expression and proteomic signatures which may be of particular relevance to cancer immunotherapy studies, as iLINCS incorporates a number of datasets and a gene expression signatures from studies that explored molecular pathways of cancer immunotherapy. The Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) [18] project (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/ccle) is a collaboration between the Broad Institute and the Novartis Institutes for Biomedical Research. The project conducts a detailed genetic and pharmacologic characterization of a large panel of human cancer models, with the overall goal of developing integrated computational analyses to link distinct pharmacologic vulnerabilities to genomic patterns and to translate cell line genomics into optimal care for patients with cancer. CCLE provides public access to genomic data for over 1100 cell lines as well as analysis and visualization tools to examine associations between genetic mutations and response to drugs. Each gene has associated data including gene expression, copy number, mRNA expression, methylation, and mutations found across the cell lines. Data for individual cell lines is searchable and downloadable. Finally, the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) portal (https://www.cancerrxgene.org) is the result of a collaboration between the Sanger Institute and Massachusetts General Hospital. GDSC provides detailed molecular data on whole-exome DNA sequence variation, copy number changes, DNA methylation, gene expression measurements, and information on response to drug treatments with 255 agents in more than 1000 cancer cell lines [19, 20]. Molecular and cell line drug response data can be downloaded from the portal or explored using graphical and search tools. Most of these publicly available resources with cell line data are active projects, and data are updated on a regular basis. Updates typically involve the integration of additional datasets as well as new computational analysis to empower researchers to query the experimental data and translate this in vitro knowledge to clinical patient care. 3 Data Repositories for Cancer Tissue Specimens and Immunological Research Somatic mutations in cancer can create mutated proteins that are degraded into peptides (called neoepitopes) and presented on the cell surface as neoantigens. With access to large collaborative projects that collect cancer tissue specimen information, researchers can identify putative neoepitopes and assess their immunoprotective properties. In this section, we highlight some of the major projects that share cancer genomic data publicly and that can be used in the pipeline of immunological biomarker discovery.

654 Alida Palmisano et al. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) [21] project was a collaboration between NCI and the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) at the NIH. TCGA’s main goal was to catalogue and discover major cancer-causing genomic alterations and create a comprehensive “atlas” of cancer genomic profiles. TCGA generated comprehensive, multi-dimensional maps of the key genomic changes in more than 30 types of treatmentnaïve tumors. The TCGA dataset (https://cancergenome.nih. gov/ and https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/) contains molecular data on gene expression, DNA sequence variation, copy number changes, and DNA methylation obtained from tumor tissues and matched normal tissues from more than 11,000 patients. The dataset is publicly available and used widely by the biomedical cancer research community. Though TCGA project came to its official conclusion in 2017, new NCI genomics initiatives are continuing to use the same model of collaboration for large-scale genomic analysis and continue to make the genomics data publicly available. The International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) (https://dcc.icgc.org) collects data to systematically study over 25,000 cancer genomes [22]. The ICGC portal (https://dcc.icgc. org) currently integrates data on 84 cancer projects including data on genome variation, transcriptomics, and DNA methylation. These molecular data are linked to clinical outcomes and to chemical characteristics of antitumor drugs. A separate ICGC initiative, Pan Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes (PCAWG), examines whole genomes of over 2800 ICGC tumor specimens. PCAWG data are accessible via the ICGC portal. The American Association of Cancer Research Project Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (AACR Project GENIE) is an international consortium for precision cancer medicine which integrates and provides publicly available clinical- grade data on genomic changes and clinical data [23]. Currently, Project GENIE provides access to over 60,000 de-identified genomic records from patients who were treated at one of the Project GENIE participating institutions. Project GENIE data are available via Sage Bionetworks Synapse Platform (http:// www.synapse.org/genie) and via cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics (http://www.cbioportal.org/genie). The NCI’s Genomic Data Commons (GDC) (https://portal. gdc.cancer.gov/) provides the cancer research community with a unified data repository for data sharing across cancer genomic studies in support of precision medicine [24]. Building upon the experience with the TCGA project, the team behind GDC developed an online platform that allows users to interact with the genomic data to efficiently query and download complete data. The GDC also provides a Data Transfer Tool and an API for programmatic access.

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 655 dbGaP (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gap) was developed to store and provide access to results of studies that investigated the association of genotype and phenotype [25, 26]. The studies belong to a variety of diseases including cancer, and they range from genome-wide association studies (GWAS), molecular diagnostic assays, as well as, associations between genotype and nonclinical traits (e.g., behavioral and personality traits). Data hosted at the dbGaP is distributed through a controlled access system. The information contained in dbGaP includes individual-level molecular and phenotype data, analysis results, medical images, general information about the study, and documents that contextualize phenotypic variables, such as research protocols and questionnaires. Data submitted to this repository undergoes quality control and curation by dbGaP staff before being released to the public. Another repository and web interface developed to connect different sources of genomic data is the NCI’s Cancer Genome Anatomy Project (CGAP) [27] (https://cgap.nci.nih.gov/cgap. html). CGAP’s goal was to determine the gene expression profiles of normal precancerous, and cancer cells, to eventually lead to improved detection, diagnosis, and treatment for patients. Resources generated by the CGAP initiative are available to the cancer community. Interconnected modules at the CGAP website provide access to all CGAP data, bioinformatics analysis tools, and web search tools to other databases of interest (e.g., BioCarta and KEGG) allowing the user to find in silico answers to biological questions of interest. Another widely used resource that collects information on somatic mutations found in cancer cells is the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) [28, 29] (https://cancer.sanger. ac.uk/cosmic). This COSMIC is currently the world’s largest source of manually curated somatic mutation information relating to human cancers. The COSMIC database combines targeted gene-screening panels with information manually curated by experts. The information is extracted from over 25,000 peer reviewed papers and is focused on known and suspected cancer genes and mutations. COSMIC’s compilation of data provides extensive coverage of the cancer genomic landscape from a somatic perspective. Four significant updates to COSMIC data are implemented each year. All COSMIC data are available as downloadable files, ready for researchers to integrate into existing bioinformatics pipelines and tools. GTEx (https://gtexportal.org/) is a comprehensive public resource that provides access to data collected from 53 nondiseased tissue sites across nearly 1000 individuals, primarily for molecular assays including WGS, WES, and RNA-Seq. This resource can be used to study tissue-specific gene expression and regulation thereby helping researchers to understand inherited susceptibility to disease. Additionally, DNA, RNA, and derived cell lines might be available from the GTEx biobank.

656 Alida Palmisano et al. Among publicly available immunological datasets, the 10,000 Immunomes Project (10KIP; http://10kimmunomes.org/) provides data and visualization tools for studying molecular, cellular, and clinical immunological data from healthy individuals [30]. This online portal provides demographic and clinical variables, laboratory measurements, flow cytometry results, ELISA and multiplex ELISA measurements, and gene expression data collected from whole blood and from peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Visualization tools allow researchers to view, plot, and download these data, and to examine molecular measures within different subsets of immune cells such as B cells and T cells, CD4 and CD8 T cells, central memory CD4 and CD8 T cells, effector CD4 and CD8 T cells, effector memory CD4 and CD8 T cells, naïve CD4 and CD8 T cells, regulatory T cells (Treg), γδ T cells, naïve B cells, memory B cells, transitional B cells, lymphocytes, monocytes, CD16+ and CD16− monocytes, NK cells, NKT cells, and plasmablasts. 4 Methods and Resources for Pathway Analysis The core idea behind pathway analysis is that genes and their protein products interact in a complex network to perform some biological processes, and diseases are caused by disruptions in these molecular interactions. The initial effort in this field resulted in the Gene Ontology (GO) project [31] (http://www.geneontology. org), which was a collaborative effort aimed at providing a controlled vocabulary to describe biological processes, cellular components and molecular functions in many different organisms. GO terms are organized in a hierarchical way and each gene product can associate with multiple terms in each ontology. There are a number of different tools that explore the GO database and provide enrichment capabilities that help researcher identify classes of genes or proteins that are overrepresented and may have an association with disease phenotypes or drug response. Some of these tools are web-based, whereas others may require the download of an application in a local environment. These tools differ in the algorithms they use and the statistical tests they offer. A comprehensive list of available tools is provided at the Gene Ontology web site http://www.geneontology.org. Some notable examples are GOrilla and ReViGO. GOrilla (http://cbl-gorilla.cs.technion.ac. il/) [32], which can be used to identify and visualize enriched GO terms in ranked lists of genes. It can either search for enriched GO terms that appear densely at the top of a ranked list of genes; or search for enriched GO terms in a target list of genes compared to a background list of genes. ReViGO (http://revigo.irb.hr/) [33] can take long lists of GO terms and summarize them by removing redundant terms, and then visualize the remaining ones in scatter-

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 657 plots, interactive graphs, or tag clouds where terms that belong to similar biological processes are grouped together. Genomic sequencing data typically results in lists of interesting genes or proteins. Translating this set of genes to insights into the underlying biological mechanism is a fundamental need in biological research. A popular resource that can help to elucidate the mechanism behind a specific set of mutations is the Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) (https://david.ncifcrf.gov/) [34]. The DAVID web-portal provides a comprehensive set of functional annotation tools to understand the biological meaning behind large lists of genes. For any given gene list, the available tools can be used to identify enriched biological themes and functionally related gene groups (with the use of gene ontology GO terms), visualize genes on BioCarta and KEGG pathway maps, search for other functionally related genes not in the original list that may be important targets for further investigations, and highlight protein functional domains and motifs. DAVID results also allow researchers to access related literature and retrieve information about gene-disease associations that may be of interest to help understand the biological mechanisms behind a certain phenotype. Two key resources for understanding high-level functions of biological systems are the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG, https://www.genome.jp/kegg/) [35] and BioCarta (https://cgap.nci.nih.gov/Pathways/BioCarta_ Pathways). KEGG is an integrated database that contains molecularlevel information and large-scale molecular datasets generated by genome sequencing and other high-throughput experimental technologies. Specifically, it contains genomic information, chemical information, as well as drugs and human disease-related information. Recognizing the limitations of the originally developed KEGG pathway modules, the authors introduced a new approach whereby human gene variants are explicitly incorporated into a recently released KEGG NETWORK database [36]. This holds information about disease-related perturbed molecular networks caused not only by genetic mutations but also by viruses and other pathogens, environmental factors and drugs. This more human disease-oriented resource is a reference knowledge-base for the basic understanding of disease mechanisms and drug development. A useful tool that processes information on groups of genes is Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) software (http://software. broadinstitute.org/gsea/index.jsp) [37]. GSEA is a computational method that determines whether a specific set of genes shows statistically significant, concordant differences between two biological states (e.g., healthy vs. tumor cells). GSEA can help to identify the most promising pathways to inform development of treatment selection (predictive) or prognostic biomarkers or signatures. GSEA is distributed as either a standalone desktop application, or as a package for R (R-GSEA).

658 Alida Palmisano et al. For researchers who are familiar with the R scripting language, there are several packages in the Bioconductor platform to support pathway annotation in the data processing pipeline. One example is ReactomePA (http://www.bioconductor.org/packages/ReactomePA) [38], which can be used to perform pathway analysis based on REACTOME [39], which is a manually curated pathway annotation database for discovering high-order biological pathways from high-throughput data. In addition to functional analysis of genomic data, ReactomePA provides several visualization functions to produce highly customizable and effective figures. For researchers who want to assess functional enrichment directly from a web interface, the resource WebGestalt (http:// www.webgestalt.org) [40–42] is in continuous development and has increasing number of functionalities and features. WebGestalt is composed of modules for gene set management, information retrieval, organization/visualization, and statistics. Its interface allows for Boolean operations to generate unions, intersections, or differences between gene sets of interest. The organization/ visualization module organizes and visualizes gene sets in various biological contexts, including Gene Ontology, tissue expression pattern, chromosome distribution, metabolic and signaling pathways, protein domain information, and publications. The statistics module can be used to perform statistical tests and suggest biological areas that are important to a gene set and warrant further investigation. While information at the gene level plays a crucial role in guiding any observed biological phenotype, it is also important to consider the protein to protein interactions, as this may reveal a more actionable target to develop therapeutic interventions. Direct physical associations of proteins, as well as indirect functional connections can be investigated using a database called STRING (https://string-db.org/) [43, 44]. This resource collects data from computational predictions, and it integrates information from multiple organisms. Another resource mostly focused on protein level information is the Protein ANalysis THrough Evolutionary Relationships (PANTHER) Classification System [45, 46]. PANTHER (available from http://www.pantherdb.org/) groups family and subfamily of proteins that evolutionarily have the same function. The tool also allows to explore biological processes in which the proteins are involved to understand the context within the larger network of the cell or the organism. The PANTHER Classifications are the result of human curation as well as bioinformatics algorithm prediction. The tools and resources mentioned so far are publicly available and free, but they are not seamlessly connected; they require the researcher to be familiar with a wide variety of interfaces, file formats, and possibly coding, in order to maximize their utility and

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 659 information gained. However, there has been a need for commercial products providing user-friend interfaces and a variety of computational methods and databases geared toward researchers who need less control and customization of their analysis, but more support in connecting the different steps of the bioinformatic processing pipeline. One widely used commercial product is Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) (https://www.qiagenbioinformatics.com/products/ingenuity-pathway-analysis/) [47]. The process of data analysis and interpretation in IPA builds upon the manually curated content of the Ingenuity Knowledge Base to understand the biological context of expression analysis experiments. The tool allows the user to access many different algorithms to identify the most significant pathways, discover potential novel regulatory networks and causal relationships associated with experimental data. 5 Resources for Linking Variants to Therapeutics Due to the decreasing cost of high-throughput sequencing assays, genomic information is increasingly used in routine clinical settings, and as part of clinical trials. For this reason, there is increasing need for well curated and structured knowledge bases of genetic pathogenicity and clinical relevance. In this section, we outline some public resources that collect this type of information. Somatic mutations in cancer-relevant genes need to be evaluated from multiple partially overlapping perspectives. From a basic and translational research perspective, it is extremely important to determine if a particular variant in a gene of interest is pathogenic or not. Clinical perspective is dominated by diagnostic, prognostic, or therapeutic implications. Therapeutic decisions are heavily based on clinical trial results, FDA approvals, and practice guidelines. Strength of therapeutic relevance and impact on clinical decision making may also depend on context with consideration of additional factors such as co-occurring variants in multiple cancer relevant genes, prior treatment history, morbidities, age, etc. AMP/ ASCO/CAP guidelines for clinical interpretation of somatic variants have been developed based on four tiers of evidence [48]. The four tiers correspond to variants classified as (I) strong clinical significance (II), potential clinical significance, (III) uncertain/ unknown significance, and (IV) benign. Since the AMP/ASCO/ CAP guidelines [48] are relatively recent, most resources linking variants to therapeutics did not have time to adopt them yet; however, increasing adoption is anticipated. Eventual adoption of the AMP/ASCO/CAP approved guidelines for interpretation of clinical relevance and approval/adoption of ACMG/AMP/ASCO guidelines for interpretation of somatic variants pathogenicity

660 Alida Palmisano et al. would pave the way for more accurate, comprehensive, and consistent interpretations of somatic variants. The Jackson Laboratory Clinical Knowledgebase (JAX-CKB) (https://ckb.jax.org/) [49] is a database that can help researchers to interpret complex genomic profiles in the context of cancer therapies and clinical trials. The Jackson Laboratory provides free public access to information about more than 80 genes commonly found in cancer genomic panels. The public resource (CKB CORE) is complemented by larger databases distributed under paid license. The databases are regularly updated with content that reflects the knowledge in the field. One important feature of CKB CORE is that it connects genetic variants to targeted therapies through efficacy evidence annotation and users can query the database by gene, variants, drugs, indications, and clinical trials. Another clinically relevant resource for precision cancer medicine is MyCancerGenome (https://www.mycancergenome.org/) [50]. This public resource is designed for physicians, patients, caregivers, and researchers, and it provides up-to-date information on mutations related to cancer growth as well as related therapeutic implications and available clinical trials. Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center developed and published its own precision oncology knowledge base OncoKB (http:// www.oncokb.org) [51]. OncoKB contains information about the effects and treatment implications of specific cancer gene alterations. Currently it collects data on specific alterations in more than 500 cancer genes. The information is collected and curated from various sources, such as guidelines from the FDA, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), ClinicalTrials.gov, and the scientific literature. For each alteration, OncoKB curates information related to the biological effect, prevalence, and prognostic and treatment implications. Treatment information related to individual genetic mutations is classified using the “Levels of Evidence” of clinical actionability: from standard-of-care to investigational treatments. OncoKB currently contains treatment information for Level 1 (i.e., FDA-recognized biomarkers predictive of response to an FDAapproved drug in a specific indication), Level 2 (i.e., standard-o fcare biomarkers predictive of response to FDA- approved drugs in various indications), Level 3 alterations (i.e., alterations predictive of response based on promising clinical data with targeted agents in ongoing clinical trials), and Level 4 (i.e., alterations considered predictive of response based on compelling biological evidence). Another well-curated resource for clinical interpretation of variants is the CIViC database (https://civicdb.org) [52]. The Clinical Interpretation of Variants in Cancer (CIViC) is an open access, open source, community-driven web resource that is continually updated. Experts serve a critical function in the CIViC community, and they are tasked with maintaining the high quality

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 661 data and interpretations based on literature related to a specific cancer type, gene/pathway, or mutation type. They must approve any new submissions or revisions from other curators in their domain area. The CIViC database is in the process of adapting the four-tier AMP/ASCO guidelines for the interpretation and reporting of sequence variants in cancer [48] and is also working on incorporating variant pathogenicity interpretations. Finally, one of the most extensively used resources that archives reports of the relationships among human variants, phenotypes, and supporting evidence is the National Library of Medicine NCBI’s ClinVar (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/) [53, 54]. ClinVar facilitates exchange of information about the relationships between human variation and observed health status, and the history of that interpretation. A major goal is to support computational (re)evaluation, both of genotypes and assertions, and to enable the ongoing evolution and development of knowledge regarding variations and associated phenotypes. ClinGen (a ClinVar partner) has a comprehensive, rigorous, and well-defined process for domain experts to form and approve expert panels. ClinGen expert panel variant interpretations are a “FDA Recognized Database” resource. ClinVar currently has a relatively small number of somatic variant interpretations, since most ClinVar entries are for germ line variants; however, the number of somatic variant interpretations in ClinVar is expected to grow. Other resources are encouraged to submit their variant interpretations to ClinVar. 6 Visualization Tools for Cancer Genomics Data As is evident from the wide variety of data types, tools, websites, and available resources presented in the previous sections, bioinformatics pipelines need to aggregate a large amount of data in a way that makes it easy for individuals who are not computational experts to interpret underlying patterns and generate biologically actionable hypotheses. Systems to visualize large genomics datasets in compact, but informationally dense graphical displays are powerful tools to discover biologically interpretable patterns. In this section, we highlight a few computational tools that facilitate summarization of large amounts of information from sequencing pipelines and databases and presentation of the results in graphical form. One resource that has been widely used for the interactive exploration of multidimensional cancer genomic data sets is cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics (http://www.cbioportal.org/) [55, 56]. cBioPortal is an open-access, open-source tool that aims at simplifying the interaction of cancer researchers with complex genomic data. The website provides access to molecular information and associated clinical information from many cancer genomics projects.

662 Alida Palmisano et al. The cBioPortal code is available under an open-source license via GitHub and it is maintained by a multi-institutional team. The current online portal supports and stores nonsynonymous mutations, DNA copy-number data, mRNA and microRNA expression data, protein-level and phosphoprotein level data, DNA methylation data, and de-identified clinical datasets from clinical trials and other published biology studies. Note that for many studies, only somatic mutation data and limited clinical data are publicly available. For TCGA studies, other data types are also available. Germ line mutations are supported by cBioPortal but are, with a few exceptions, not available to the public. Currently cBioPortal contains the TCGA provisional datasets imported directly from the original TCGA Data Coordinating Center via the Broad Firehose. The team maintaining cBioPortal also actively imports data from published studies for which those data were made publicly available at time of publication. Mutation calls stored in Mutation Annotation Format (MAF) format are processed through an internal pipeline to annotate the variant effects in a consistent way across studies. The cBioPortal provides a web API, and R/MATLAB interfaces to access different features available in the web interface in a programmatic way, so that this public resource can be seamlessly integrated in a custom bioinformatics pipeline. Finally, to utilize the entire suite of analysis and visualization tools, researchers can install cBioPortal within their own network using the open-source code available on GitHub. While the cBioPortal is a very powerful resource, it may not be easy for people without extensive programming or technical skills to take full advantage of the standalone instance of cBioPortal. One of the most effective visualization approaches used in cBio- Portal is an OncoPrint, which is a variation of a heat map that visually summarizes genomic alterations to reveal correlations in multidimensional genomics data. In this variation of a heat map, individual genes are arranged as rows and individual specimens as columns. Genetic mutations like somatic or copy number changes are visually encoded in different colors. This format can help to visualize trends such as mutual exclusivity or co-occurrence between gene pairs, as these are identified as clusters of cells similarly colored (for cases of mutation co-occurrence) or clusters of cells colored only if other specific cells are not colored (for cases of mutual exclusivity). To support the interactive exploration of genomic datasets on local machines with no programming skills required, D3Oncoprint was recently developed [57]. D3Oncoprint (https://brb.nci.nih. gov/d3oncoprint/) is a standalone software application to visualize and dynamically explore annotated genomic mutation files. D3Oncoprint provides access to curated variant lists from CIViC, My Cancer Genome, and FDA approved drug indication

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 663 lists to facilitate the use of genomic data for biomedical discovery and application. D3Oncoprint also includes curated gene lists to explore commonly investigated biological processes (e.g., BioCarta pathways, FoundationOne cancer panels). D3Oncoprint is a standalone Java application, with a graphical user interface composed of simple buttons and checkboxes, that allows researchers with cohorts of annotated sequencing files (in VCF, MAF or tab-delimited format) to quickly generate an OncoPrint-like heatmap, embedded in a dynamic html page. The researcher can then use filters, search and sorting options to explore the sequencing information, and potentially find patterns of biological interest in the data. A software package that supports the interactive exploration of a wide variety of genomic data types is the Integrated Genomics Viewer (IGV) (http://software.broadinstitute.org/software/ igv/) [58, 59]. IGV is available as a desktop tool for visualizing and interacting with different types of genomic data. IGV has a graphical interface that allows new users to familiarize with the tool, while more experienced users can explore advanced features and customization options. In IGV the supported data types can be integrated and combined with clinical and other specimen metadata to dynamically group, sort and filter data sets. Another distinguishing feature of IGV is the ability to view data in multiple genomic regions simultaneously in adjacent panels, for example to view correlated events in distal regions. While standalone tools that visualize and analyze sequencing data are preferred by some researchers, others prefer to integrate visualization in already ongoing daily pipelines where other data processing and statistical analysis can be also conducted. For these kinds of users, we want to highlight two commonly used types of environments: R and MATLAB. For researchers who are familiar with the R scripting language, the R/BioConductor project (https://www.bioconductor.org/) presents many different analysis tools for processing and visualizing high-throughput genomic data [60, 61]. Bioconductor is open-source and open development. The project is based on userdeveloped packages that cover a vast array of bioinformatics and statistical tools. Some of the most popular packages for visualization, clustering, and network analysis are ggplot2 [62], lattice [63], limma [64], qgraph [65], CancerSubtypes [66], ConsensusClusterPlus [67], ComplexHeatmap [68], GOSim [69], affy [70], VariantAnnotation [71], and fgsea [72]. The main appeal of R/BioConductor is the ability to customize graphics to the users’ own specifications. While a graphic that is made from scratch would require extensive coding knowledge, the packages mentioned above provide many ready-made visualizations and graphical options. The most popular packages come with extensive documentation on how to use them, in the form of reference

664 Alida Palmisano et al. manuals, articles, and books. For example, ggplot2 developers describe how to use the package most effectively in two books [62, 73]. One drawback of R/BioConductor is that because packages are user-contributed, some have not been extensively vetted for bugs and appropriateness of methodology. Finally for researchers who are familiar with the MATLAB environment (https://www.mathworks.com/products/matlab. html) [74], the software provides the Bioinformatics Toolbox (https://www.mathworks.com/products/bioinfo.html) with algorithms for Next Generation Sequencing (NGS), microarray analysis, mass spectrometry, and gene ontology. Researchers can take advantage of functions within this toolbox to read genomic and proteomic data from standard file formats and from online databases such as the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus and GenBank. Sequence browsers, spatial heatmaps, and clustergrams are effective ways to visualize and explore the data. The Toolbox also offers statistical methods for detecting peaks, imputing values for missing data, and selecting features. Researchers can also apply Toolbox methods to data generated from many common assays, like ChIP-Seq, RNA-Seq, microarray, and mass spectrometry. 7 Tools in Genomics, Epigenetics, and Neoantigen Prediction Microarrays experiments measure the gene expression from oligonucleotide or cDNA probes on a genomic scale. These expression data can be used for a variety of purposes such as to identify differentially expressed genes and enrichment analysis using gene sets from Gene Ontology or pathways. However, before the data can be used for any statistical analyses, the data need to be preprocessed and normalized for downstream analyses. For example, the raw Affymetrix data describes probe level expression in a CEL file format. The data are commonly preprocessed and normalized into probe set-level expression values using the Robust Multi-array Average [75] or Frozen Robust Multi-Array method [76] before the data can be used in the next steps of the analysis. Once the data are preprocessed and normalized, different statistical analyses can be carried out depending on the study objectives. Broadly speaking, the analyses can be categorized into three categories: (1) class comparison (2) class discovery, and (3) class prediction. Class comparison aims to identify genes differentially expressed between two or more different tissue types or experimental conditions. Since the class comparison involves simultaneous testing for all genes at a time, a multiple testing problem will arise. The false discovery rate (FDR) method is a commonly used method to control the false discoveries in a set of identified genes. Class discovery is an unsupervised method with the goal of discovering clusters among specimens or among genes. The hierarchical

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 665 clustering algorithm, principal component analysis (PCA), and heatmaps are useful methods to find clusters of specimens or genes with an easy-to-interpret graphical representation. Finally, class prediction methods are used to predict the phenotype of new specimens from gene expression. Some example prediction methods include diagonal linear discriminant analysis, K-nearest neighbors, support vector machine, random forest, and prediction analysis of microarray [77]. There are several software choices for performing gene expression analysis. Users experienced in programming can use the R statistical programming language (https://cran.r-project. org/) together with the Bioconductor repository (https://www. bioconductor.org/) which provides over one thousand packages for the analysis of high-throughput genomic data including gene expression. For users less experienced with coding, more suitable choices may be platform-specific software like Affymetrix Expression Console (for a limited choice of analyses) or a general-purpose software that can handle multiple platforms. For example, BRB- ArrayTools [78–80] is a Windows desktop application with a graphical interface designed for use by researchers who want to use state-of-the-art statistical methods for gene expression analysis. Next generation sequencing (NGS) technology has emerged as an important tool for scientists who conduct biological research. For example, DNA sequencing can be used to discover mutated genes and RNA sequencing can be used to perform gene expression analysis as an alternative to microarrays. Sequencing of nucleic acids generates a tremendous amount of data to be analyzed. This massive amount of data poses challenges for researchers or physicians to handle. Therefore, easy-to-use and powerful software that implements a suitable pipeline for common analysis tasks is critical. Below we provide an overview of a common pipeline for DNA/ RNA sequence analysis and list useful tools to consider. Raw sequence data are commonly saved in the FASTQ format. The FASTQ file must be mapped to a reference genome by using an alignment algorithm. A few examples of alignment tools include TopHat2 [81], STAR [82], Subread [83], and BWA-MEM [84]. After the alignment step, the next step is counting the overlap of reads with genes for expression analysis or variant calling. If the intent is gene expression analysis, the aligned RNA-sequence data need to be summarized by a counting procedure. Both the HTSeq method [85] and featureCounts software [86] can be applied to generate a count of reads mapped to each gene. The count data can be used for gene expression analysis using for example BRB- ArrayTools. However, if the purpose of the study is to discover somatic mutations (or variants), GATK [87] and SAMtools [88] can be applied to the aligned DNA/RNA-sequence data. The output from the variant calling analysis will be Variant Call Format (VCF)

666 Alida Palmisano et al. files containing variant information. These VCF files can be further annotated using tools such as ANNOVAR [89] or SnpEff [90]. The whole DNA/RNA-Seq pipeline analysis should normally be performed by experienced bioinformaticians who have extensive knowledge and experience in programming and big data manipulation. Some free software (Galaxy https://usegalaxy.org/, BRB-SeqTools https://brb.nci.nih.gov/seqtools/) or commercial packages (CLC Genomics Workbench https://www.qiagenbioinformatics.com, Partek Flow http://www.partek.com/ partek-flow/) were developed to ease performance of these tasks. 8 Neoantigen Prediction and Related Databases Studies have shown that there is a strong association between the number of mutations in cancer cells and patients’ responses to immunotherapy. Tumor mutation burden (TMB) has been demonstrated to be a potential biomarker for predicting response to PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 directed therapy across some cancer types [91, 92]. The number of mutations present in a tumor tends to be positively associated with the abundance of tumor neoantigens [93]. Neoantigens are small peptides derived from mutated proteins in cancer cells that can be recognized as foreign by immune cells and trigger immune response. A number of approaches have been used to identify candidate cancer neoantigens from genomic sequencing data [94]. Usually paired tumor and normal tissue WES data would allow directly locating variants in protein [95]. Current studies assume that major histocompatibility complex (MHC) binding is the necessary step for neoantigens to be recognized by T cell receptors. The MHC binding prediction methods can be categorized as binding motifs based [96], position specific score or matrix based [97], and machine learning based such as Artificial Neural Networks [98– 100] or Support Vector Machines [101, 102]. Because of poor sequence similarity between MHC class II and variability in sequence length, the MHC class II binding prediction tools are much less well-developed and less accurate than those for MHC Class I. Several tools available for MHC class II binding prediction are ProPred [103], netMHCII [104], and MHC2Pred [105]. The accuracy of the prediction algorithms varies. In addition, not all MHC binding peptides are immunogenic. Combination approaches have been developed to address this issue. netMHCstabpan [106], which uses a neural network approach based on a dataset of stability values calculated for different peptide–MHC class I complexes, rather than their binding affinity values, since the stability of their interaction has experimentally been shown to be more strongly correlated to T-cell immunogenicity. MHCflurry is an open-source software package for peptide/MHC class I

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 667 binding prediction which also provides prediction models that were trained on affinity measurements and MHC ligands identified by mass spectrometry [107]. MuPeXI, the mutant peptide extractor and informer, is a program to identify tumor-specific peptides and assess their potential to be neoepitopes. The peptides are sorted according to a priority score which is intended to roughly predict immunogenicity [108]. pVACSeq, which was developed by Washington University and now a part of the pVACtools immunotherapy tools suite, provides a flexible, streamlined computational workflow for identification of personalized Variant Antigens by Cancer Sequencing that integrates tumor mutation and expression data [109]. Finally, many existing MHC binding peptides and T cell epitope databases could potentially serve as a training data pool to develop prediction models [110]. For example, The Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) (http://tools.iedb.org/main/datasets), funded by NIAID, provides a comprehensive resource for experimental data on antibody and T cell epitopes studied in multiple diseases [111]. There are still many big challenges in computational methods to identify neoantigens and to predict which ones may serve as optimal targets for development of immunotherapy approaches. Future efforts to improve the accuracy in neoantigen prediction could take advantage of the data from TCR/BCR recognition and tumor microenvironment studies when such data are made available. 9 Copy Number Alternation Unlike changes in gene expression and genetic sequence, copy number alterations generally occur over long regions that encompass multiple genes, chromosomal arms, or even entire chromosomes. A study of 12 cancer types in TCGA revealed that cancers that harbor many copy number alterations in their genomes tend to have less immune involvement and worse response to immune checkpoint blockade immunotherapies [112]. When analyzing copy number data, it is important to approach it in a global way rather than on an individual gene-by-gene basis. Therefore, the first step is to identify a relatively small number of breakpoints that indicate locations of the copy number changes, thus dividing the chromosome into multiple segments. Next, is to assign a copy number call to the segments separated by the breakpoints. This second step can be challenging, because the relationship between tumor copy number and relative DNA concentration depends on the tumor content, which can vary from specimen to specimen. Also, there is the possibility of polyploidy, which may mean that the normalized baseline may not represent a diploid

668 Alida Palmisano et al. copy number. However, these issues can be addressed by making use of the fact that copy numbers are restricted to integer values. Copy number changes can be identified using a number of different assay platforms. Tiling arrays, in which DNA content is measured at many probes spread approximately evenly across the genome, provide a very reliable measure of copy number alterations. Breakpoints are identified at locations where there is a sharp change in signal level. Nontiling SNP arrays can be used in a similar manner but are limited by the SNP locations, so areas with few SNPs may be poorly represented. Additionally, there are algorithms that analyze whole-genome sequence (WGS) data to identify regions that have particularly high and low levels of coverage, which may indicate copy number gains or losses. Since they are not limited by the probe locations, these WGS algorithms can theoretically provide more precise identification of breakpoints. But, due to the difficulty of accurate density estimation, they may be less reliable. The analysis of Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) for copy number identification can be particularly problematic, since there is a lack of even coverage over the genome, and read depth is heavily influenced by the efficiency of the capture, which may vary markedly across the genome. The most popular method for breakpoint identification from array-based data is circular binary segmentation (CBS) as implemented in the DNAcopy Bioconductor package [113]. The field of sequence-based segmentation is rapidly evolving at the time of this publication, with many different methods being proposed. The Varscan2 package [114] is another popular method. The GISTIC2 algorithm [115] estimates copy numbers from segmented data taking into account the possibility of variable tumor content and polyploidy. CNVkit (https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/) is another software toolkit used to infer and visualize copy number from high-throughput DNA sequencing data, which is typically used with hybrid capture, including both whole-exome and custom target panels, and short-read sequencing platforms such as Illumina and Ion Torrent. 10 Bioinformatic Tools for DNA Methylation Analysis Epigenetic alterations including changes in DNA methylation and demethylation, cancer-specific histone modifications, and miRNA dysregulation are widespread in cancer cells and play important roles in malignancy [116, 117]. Epigenetic processes are also highly important in immune response, with epigenetic modulators playing effective regulatory roles in immune evasion [9]. A number of DNA methylation-based biomarkers are established for identification and monitoring of immune cells, including those in Treg, Th17, Tfh, CD4+, CD8+, and CD3+ T cells, B cells, mono-

Bioinformatics Tools and Resources for Cancer Immunotherapy Study 669 cytes, NK cells, and neutrophils [95]. A growing number of clinical trials are combining the use of immunotherapeutic agents such as checkpoint inhibitors with epigenetic drugs (e.g., demethylating agents and histone deacetylase inhibitors) [9, 10]). In addition, the use of bromodomain inhibitors and other categories of epigenetic agents in combination with immunotherapeutic agents to boost the success of immunotherapy is under active investigation [118]. DNA methylation measurements from a large collection of tumor and normal specimens from the Cancer Genome Atlas project can be downloaded from the Genome Data Commons (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/repository). MethHC, the human pan-cancer methylation database (http://methhc.mbc.nctu.edu. tw), provides a web interface of processed data on gene-region based DNA methylation, along with miRNA and gene expression derived from the TCGA dataset. Users can search for strongest correlations between methylation and expression measures, and search for specific genes among specific cancer types [119]. When using user’s own data, ChAMP, COHCAP, DMRcate, EWasher, FastDMA, HOMER, IMA, Lumi, ME-class, MethylAid, Methylumi, Minfi, NIMBL, RefFreeEWAS, RnBeads, shinyMethyl, and wateRmelon, among other packages, allow users to identify differentially methylated regions (DMR); to utilize methylation differences, predictions of regulatory motifs, and findings of lineage- specific DMR regions in order to estimate the proportions of leukocyte lineages and their epigenetic modifications in blood and solid tissues; to determine methylation levels of individual gene regions; and to examine longitudinal changes in DNA methylation [94, 120–137]. These software resources, which have been developed predominantly in R or MATLAB, provide the user with the ability to examine both DNA methylation biomarkers in tumor tissues and to track biomarkers of immune response. ## Chapter 30


680 Vésteinn Thorsson Analyses of these data using methods of immunogenomics have yielded substantial insight into how the immune system responds to cancer. Making use of molecular genomic data from exome sequencing, miRNA sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, protein expression from reverse-phase protein arrays (RPPA), DNA methylation arrays, and SNP arrays, computational methods have been developed and applied to infer multiple aspects of immune response in cancer, including assessment of total lymphocytic infiltrate, the fraction of individual immune cell types, immune gene expression signatures, prediction of neoantigens, T cell and B cell repertoire, expression of viral RNAs, and the relation to germ line mutations and somatic DNA alterations [3–10]. H&E images are available for most TCGA samples, forming a complimentary resource for studying the tumor and stromal environments [11] and lymphocytic infiltrate through image analysis [12, 13]. One aspect of immunogenomic analyses is to increase our understanding of how somatic alterations relate to changes in the tumor microenvironment (TME). This includes identifying overall alterations in cancer cells, such as tumor mutation burden (TMB) or copy number alteration burden that may impact immune response but also identifying somatic alterations in particular cancer driver genes and pathways [10] associated with changes in immune context. With the breadth and depth of data derived from multiple genomics platforms, many relationships of potential relevance to cancer immunology are found by identifying statistical associations, often among data element from disparate measurement platforms. Application of systems biology methodology yields additional insight, for example by prioritizing or supporting derived statistical relationships based on known physical interaction processes and reactions that may underlie observed statistical associations. These methods typically incorporate knowledge and prediction of biological networks of a variety of types, such as intracellular transcriptional networks, signaling networks, and metabolic networks or inter-cellular networks. Depending on the method adopted, this yields networks describing which molecules or other constituents are likely to interact (network connectivity) or networks that are predictive, in which input–output relationships are described by mathematical functions that yield quantitative or semiquantitative predictions of changes when constituents are altered, for example by environmental or genetic perturbations. Importantly, many resources have been developed and made available to researcher to enable access to immunogenomics data, analysis of data, and exploration of immunogenomic results through web portals. In this chapter, we demonstrate aspects of material and workflow adopted for immunogenomic characterization of cancer. Due to the complex nature of these analyses, a complete series of steps cannot be provided. Illustrations of elements of the process are

Multiplatform Integrative Analysis of Immunogenomic Data for Biomarker Discovery 681

given, and pointers to additional resources. Two recent volumes in this series provide helpful expositions of underlying concepts and methods of cancer bioinformatics [14] and of cancer systems biology [15]. Web resources for exploring results from immunogenomics studies are also described. 2 Workflow and Steps in Immunogenomic Analysis Figure 1 provides an overview of some possible steps in a genomics analysis: (2.1) “Establish Data and Analysis Sharing Methods and Obtain Cancer Genomics Data Sets,” (2.2) “Retrieve and Generate Per-Sample Characteristics of Relevance to Immune Response,” (2.3) “Identify Shared Patterns,” (2.4) “Construct a Summary Fig. 1 Anatomy of an integrative analysis of multiple genomic platforms using immunogenomics. The figure gives a broad overview of elements of an immunogenomic analysis, with more details are provided in chapter sections, with corresponding numbering. Step 2.1 Molecular data matrices (each denoted by a rectangle) are obtained from multiple measurement platforms. S indicates a set of sample identifiers, with one row representing each sample. F denotes a set of measured values, such as the expression of individual genes, or amplified copy number regions, as columns in a matrix. S and F typically differ among the platforms (rectangles). In step 2.2 data for individual sample rows Si are scored for immune properties, yielding new per-sample immune-related features Fi. Step 2.3, a commonly applied analysis in cancer genomics, is to identify groups (Fn), or clusters of samples that share similar patterns and is in this case focused on the immune response. Compiling a comprehensive summary data matrix of immune response features and potential covariates (step 2.4, a “feature” matrix) enables many varieties of cancer-immune association studies to be carried out. Step 2.5 Many relationships can be found by looking for associations among a pair of immune features (denoted by linked arrows on two columns) across all samples (rows). Step 2.6 Hypotheses on possible underlying functional and biological mechanisms behind the observed associations can be brought in by systems biology integration of data in the context of biomolecular networks

682 Vésteinn Thorsson Matrix,” (2.5) “Perform Association Studies,” (2.6) “Perform Integrative Network Analysis.” We will describe aspects of individual steps below, in corresponding Subheadings 2.1–2.6. A final section, (Subheading 2.7), will describe web resources available for evaluating evidence for potential biomarkers derived from immunogenomic studies. By way of example, we shall consider a study in which tumor mutation burden (TMB) is being considered as potential biomarker in lung adenocarcinoma. We would like to see if there is evidence for TMB being associated with increased CD8 T cell content in lung cancer. 2.1 Establish Data Sharing data: Most integrative systems biology projects are driven and Analysis Sharing by team science, with teams consisting of a variety of individuals Methods and Obtain with expertise in different fields. Decisions about how data and Cancer Genomics Data results are shared can impact how quickly progress is made during Sets a research project. Platforms for organizing and sharing data become increasingly relevant as a project expands in scope. File sharing services from major software providers, such as Drive (Google), OneDrive (Microsoft), and DropBox are good solutions in terms of ease of use and accessibility. When sharing files, it is of great value to include file format descriptions, how the file was generated, and a name to contact for questions. Synapse by Sage Bionetworks (synapse.org) is designed specifically for sharing data in biological collaborations. Among available features are file versioning and an easily edited wiki format for providing file information. Synapse has been used by multiple research collaborations in cancer including the TCGA and AACR Project GENIE. Sharing computational methods: Code repositories such as github (github.com) are the preferred method for sharing analysis code during the course of a research project. Sharing analysis results: Notebook formats such as those provided by Jupyter (jupyter.org) and RStudio (rstudio.com) are increasingly used as they offer many advantages over more conventional sharing of results files and figures during the course of research. Notebooks allow you interlace written narrative, calculations, and display of results in tabular and graphical form. Notebooks can run code interactively, and in steps, and are easily shared. Obtain cancer genomics data: Primary cancer genomics data can be retrieved from the NCI Genomic Data Commons (gdc. cancer.gov) and the ICGC (dcc.icgc.org) data portals. A recent publication in this series provides an overview of how to access repositories and web resources for these data [16]. To prepare an immunogenomic analysis, data can be retrieved at a variety of levels, as appropriate to the processing that follows. For example, for identifying the repertoire of T cell receptor sequences one would use TCGA exome read-based Level 1 data, while for estimation of

Multiplatform Integrative Analysis of Immunogenomic Data for Biomarker Discovery 683 gene expression signatures one would use the Level 3 gene-level estimates. Some data, particularly lower level data are controlled access, and instructions for applying for and obtaining access to controlled data can be found on the GDC portal. The GDC and ICGC data portals are designed to provide complete and quality-controlled data for all individual samples. In an immunogenomics study, one typically wants to compare across samples, and to do so reliably, additional processing may be needed to correct for any systematic and platform-dependent differences, particularly if the comparisons are wide in scope, such as among multiple cancer studies. It is recommended to make use of efforts where additional harmonization has been performed, such as with consistently applied processing algorithms and with any required batch corrections. These enable more reliable comparison across samples within a study or between studies. In April 2018 the TCGA completed a reprocessing of nearly all data, as part of the final phase of the TCGA, the PanCancer Atlas, which also performed numerous cross-cancer analyses delving into overarching themes on cancer, including cell-of-origin patterns, oncogenic processes, and signaling pathways (https://www.cell.com/pbassets/consortium/pancanceratlas/pancani3/index.html). Data harmonization was performed for all platforms. Notably, expression data for mRNA and miRNA were batch-corrected to adjust for platform differences and sequencing center differences [17], variant calling was performed consistently across exome sequencing data using seven different methods [18], and clinical outcome data was reviewed and endpoints generated consistently [19]. The summarized data is available from the GDC PanCancer Atlas publication page (gdc.cancer.gov/about-data/publications/pancanatlas). A growing number of studies provide immunogenomic data on treatment by with checkpoint inhibitors [20–24]. These data are currently (early 2019) not publicly available in the same harmonized fashion as from the cancer genomic consortia. In order to work with these you must download them from the primary source, or make use of efforts that have combined the data [25]. 2.2 Retrieve To study interactions between tumors and their immune microenand Generate vironment, information is first collected or evaluated for each sam- Per- Sample ple on tumor content, immune content, and the tumor immune Characteristics interface. of Relevance Per-sample characterizations that relate directly to tumor cell to Immune Response content include estimates of somatic alterations of genes, in terms of single nucleotide variations, insertions, deletions, structural variations, and copy number amplifications or deletions, most of which can e.g. be obtained from the GDC and ICGC data portals. Alterations summarized at the level of intracellular oncogenic pathways can also be included [26]. Microsatellite instability calls

684 Vésteinn Thorsson were also generated by the TCGA and potential epigenetic silencing events can be incorporated with the data from DNA methylation arrays. To set up evaluation of associations with changes in the tumor microenvironment, these alterations can be restricted to alterations known to impact immune response [27], or collected in such a way as to enable discovery of potentially new immune-related tumor alterations. Gene expression data yields a wealth of information on tumors and their microenvironment. Some examples of applications are: expression of immunomodulatory genes, evaluation of cancer-related immune signatures, estimation of immune cellular repertoire, evaluation of T cell and B cell receptor repertoire and antigen processing machinery genes.
● Immunomodulatory genes. Cancer genomic data is of great
value for studying the expression of important genes such as checkpoint proteins, which can be compared across tumor types and subtypes.
● Immune signatures. Sets of genes representing functional attri-
butes of the immune response in and relating to response to cancer immunotherapy have been developed in recent years by multiple research teams. These can be used to score gene expression data, for example by using the GSVA R package [28] to perform single sample gene set enrichment.
● Cellular proportion. Gene expression levels from bulk RNA-
seq stem from a mixture of cell types. Cell deconvolution methods estimate the proportion of different cell types present in bulk samples. These methods aim to reconstruct the RNA measurements as a weighted sum of cell signatures of individual cell types (typically based on purified cells), using regression methods. The resulting set of coefficients correspond to estimates of the relative proportion of cell types. To estimate cellular propensities from RNA sequencing data, a number of web apps are available (e.g., CIBERSORT [6, 29] (cibersort. stanford.edu), xCell (xcell.ucsf.edu) [30], and TIMER (cistrome.shinyapps.io/timer) [8]). Information on cellular proportion can also be made from other genomics sources. For example in a recent study [10], the method (ABSOLUTE) [31] that infers tumor purity and malignant cell ploidy directly from analysis of somatic DNA alterations, was used to establish the tumor and nontumor cellular fraction, while DNA methylation arrays were used to assess the overall proportion of immune cells in the tissue.
● T cell and B cell repertoire. One goal of immunogenomic stud-
ies is to characterize the repertoire of B and T cells in patients with cancer, especially before and after immunotherapy-based interventions. Computational methods have been developed

Multiplatform Integrative Analysis of Immunogenomic Data for Biomarker Discovery 685 to directly infer TCR and BCR clonality and complexity from bulk tumor RNaseq data (summarized in [32–34]).
● The most commonly evaluated component of the cancer-
immune interface is the prediction of neoantigens. The predictions are use as input HLA types and observed somatic alterations are performed separately for Class I and Class II MHC and are detailed in recent reviews [32, 35]. As mentioned above, underlying data can be retrieved from files from genomic data portals. However, many of the data files can be very large and cumbersome to download and work with in computer memory. Notably, sequence read-level files can take a long time to download from their source, delaying analysis. In addition, there is often only a small portion of each file that may be needed for an analysis. In order to address these problems, the National Cancer Institute has supported the NCI Cancer Genomics Cloud Resources, which provide secure access to cancer genomic data, and provide support for data access through a web user interface (UI) and an application programming interface (API). In this way, analyses can be performed without transferring the data in bulk to a local resource at a research institution. In Figs. 2 and 3 we illustrate two examples in this regard, using the Institute for Systems Biology Cancer Genomics Cloud Resource (ISB-CGC). Figure 2 shows how the ISB-CGC can be used to obtain all TCGA data on CTLA-4 expression, and Fig. 3 illustrates how to estimate the tumor mutation burden for all lung adenocarcinoma samples, without downloading unrelated data. The queries are performed on the harmonized data of the PanCancer Atlas (see above). Instructions on how to set up access to this resource are at https://isb-cancer-genomics-cloud.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ sections/PanCancer-Atlas-Mirror.html.
