With a 38 Mb estimate of exome size [36], this corresponds to 54 mutations per megabase (2051/(38 Mb) = 2051/(38 × 106 b ) = 5.397 × 10−5/b = 53.97/Mb). 2.3 Identify Shared A very common practice in cancer genomics analysis is to identify Patterns samples that are have similar overall molecular profiles and are thus likely to share similar biology. Most analytical approaches assign each sample to one of a limited set of such patterns, via unsupervised clustering in the high-dimensional space of molecular values. Numerous clustering approaches can be applied, and differ in choices of model assumptions, the way one defines the similarity of two samples (the distance or metric), and in the criterion applied for identification of the optimal number of groups. To ensure that

688 Vésteinn Thorsson results are generalizable, independent testing should ideally be done on a comparable data set. If such a set does not exist, “internal” validation is performed by cross-validation, which involves training on a portion of the data, predicting on remaining portion, and repeating. The R package consensusClusterPlus [37] was used widely in tumor studies by the TCGA, due to relative ease of use, robust statistics, and helpful visualizations for the evaluation of results. In the context of multiple platforms, additional decisions need to be made concerning how to integrate clustering results. Clustering data from multiple molecular platforms offers the possibility of finding shared patterns that are consistent across multiple levels of regulation. Sometimes a decision is used to perform clustering only using a single platform. For example in the recent study [10] we clustered only using gene expression data, as that was thought to provide the most representative picture of the tumor microenvironment. To perform multiplatform clustering one can either derive overall clusters based on patterns found in each platform individually or derive clusters from combined on data from all platforms. Consider two platforms A and B, measuring the levels of nA and nB molecules respectively. Sample j can be represented by a vector of values of length nA + nB Sj = ( Aj, A j,A j,¼,A j,B j,B j,B j,¼.B j) 1 2 3 nA 1 2 3 nB 2.3.1 Derive Clusters We first cluster samples on platform A. Say that kA groups are Based on Patterns Found found. Similarly, clustering samples on platform B, yields kB groups. in Each Platform Sample j can thus be represented by a binary indicator vector, of Individually length kA+kB denoting its clustering membership Ij =(0,0,..,1,0,0,1,0,¼0) The first “1” represents the membership of sample j in among the kA possible clusters, the second “1” the membership of sample j in among the kB possible clusters from platform B, while in the remainder of the slots “0” means the sample does not belong to other clusters. We can now compare the indicator vectors Ij between two samples in terms of how similar they are. Commonly used comparisons employ measures of overlap familiar from twoway contingency tables of association (such as the number of identical clustering assignments over the number of differing cluster assignments). Having a measure of similarity of the indicator vectors, we can cluster them to find groups of samples sharing similar indicator vectors, that is, similarity in terms of patterns derived from each platform.

Multiplatform Integrative Analysis of Immunogenomic Data for Biomarker Discovery 689 2.3.2 Derive Clusters Cluster the vectors Sj to yield similar groups of similar samples, Combined on Data from All using common clustering methods or those designed for multiple Platforms platforms [38]. In either approach considerations or corrections need to be made as to whether all platforms contributed in an equal manner. 2.4 Construct In order to facilitate discovery of how candidate biomarkers relate to a Summary Matrix estimates of tumor response, it is very helpful to gather available per-sample characterizations from multiple sources (Subheadings 2.1–2.3) into a single summary spreadsheet, or matrix. The summary matrix is sometimes called a feature matrix or sample characteristic matrix. In immunogenomics, a feature matrix will typically contain immune-related scores as well as assessed tumor features that might serve roles in correlative studies. A commonly adopted format is that rows represent individuals or samples, each represented by a unique ID (row ID). Each data column comprises measured or estimated values of a given variable, or “feature.” Examples of features include the expression level of an individual checkpoint gene, the estimated Th1/Th2 ratio, TMB, the CD8 T cell fraction, TCR diversity, and tumor stage. In a spreadsheet, such feature names are usually column headers, while the row IDs are the first column. Some practical issues come up when integrating results from disparate analyses into a single feature matrix. For example
● Sometimes multiple values are available for consideration, for a
single one row ID. An example of this is if two samples are available for a given individual, or two assays of the same type are available for single sample. For the summary matrix, it is desirable to report only a single value. Averaging is sometime done over the available values, or a single representative value is adopted if there is a basis for doing so (e.g., external knowledge or internal properties such as signal reliability or strength).
● Two different features may not have data available for the same
samples, particularly if values result from different platforms or differ in how they were derived. If a value is not available for a given feature and sample, it can be reported as an “NA” entry in the spreadsheet, a convention that permits correct handling by many subsequent processing streams. Some researchers prefer to retain rows only if data are “complete” in that data are available for all features, and to remove samples from further processing if not. In our experience with data management in cancer genomics and immunogenomics, we have almost always adopted the approach of retaining summary matrices that include NAs. One reason is that pairwise comparisons (see Subheading 2.5) can be performed with no data losses. Another is that columnar data values and availability are often updated frequently in the course of a research project, and that a completeness needs almost continual reevaluation if it is to be maintained.

690 Vésteinn Thorsson
● Some kinds of data will not be accommodated in useful way in
a summary matrix of this type, for example the repertoire of individual TCR sequences or peptides predicted to be presented by MHCs. 2.5 Perform When many platforms are combined in a study, valuable insight is Association Studies often gained by identifying which pairs of variables are associated among multiple genomics platforms. Relationships are often found by virtue of comparing inherently different types of data. This can happen by direct comparison of features (columns in the feature matrix described in Subheading 2.4), a relatively simple operation which can later be complemented by association studies where multiple variables are used in a multivariate analysis. In cases where direct comparison of hundreds or thousands of variables is performed, multiple hypotheses testing corrections need to be included in the analysis. To assess pairwise associations, one needs to adopt statistical test appropriate to the types of data. These depend on the nature of each of the variables in the pair being tested, which can be organized as follows: Continuous: numerical values not limited to integers; Categorical values, which can be placed into one of a limited number of labeled classes, including dichotomous values (which can be assigned to binary numbers); and Ordinal, numeric variables taking on a limited set of levels that can be ranked into an order. In comparing values, one uses a statistic appropriate to the type of each variable. Table 1 gives a summary of statistics for pairs of variable types. Ordinal values can be treated as continuous values, yielding associations that follow a trend with that variable, or conversely, as discrete variables, which yield relationships with more complex dependence. With a given statistic, a hypothesis test against the null assumption of no association is performed, yielding a p-value. The p-value is used widely, but debates take place both about its validity and how it is applied. Having established the type of test, the tests can be applied over multiple feature pairs, usually by testing each available pair. Table 1 Comparisons of two variables of varying type Variable type 1 Variable type 2 Effect size Statistic or test Continuous Continuous Correlation t statistic Continuous Discrete If discrete is ANOVA; Kruskal–Wallis. If discrete dichotomous: Ratio is dichotomous: t statistic Dichotomous Dichotomous Odd Ratio χ2, Fisher’s exact Each row represents a pair of comparisons between two variables, each of a type (first two columns). Fourth column: an example summary of statistics for pairs of variable types. Tests involving ranked continuous values are often preferred, such as Spearman correlation, over Pearson

One way is to rank the tested pairs by the effect size, the value of the test statistic, or the p-value (Fig. 4a). Results can also be summarized by visualizations, which can be very helpful for understanding the result of such multiple pairwise-tests. These visualizations afford the ability to see relationships between multiple associations, which are not easily seen discerned from a table. For example, “Do two particular variables share multiple associations with another group of variables?” One helpful way to visualize associations using a network, as in Fig. 4b. In this case, top-ranked associations are shown using the Cytoscape network visualization tool (cytoscape.org). For Cytoscape, the association file can be loaded in a simple three col-

692 Vésteinn Thorsson umn format with the two variable labels and the size of the effect. Another very commonly used method for displaying degree of association is a heatmap (Fig. 4c). Here color intensity shows degree of association. P-values can pose a problem in display, and the negative of the logarithm of the p-value is often used a display value to accentuate small values. If an effect size and direction are available (increased or decrease change), they can be combined as follows -sign(effect)∗log(p-value) where sign(effect) is a “+1” or “-1” multiplier capturing an increasing or decrease. This value is large in magnitude for strong associations, positive for correlated values, and negative for anticorrelated values. 2.6 Perform Network analyses go beyond association studies and pairwise asso- Integrative Network ciations and are key component of systems biology. One capability Analysis of such information is to lend support for observed associations through knowledge of physical interactions, that are obtained from auxiliary data. This involves a multifaceted analysis stream of integrating data from multiple platform with assembled networks from databases. Potential network interactions can be obtained with either evidence form molecular or cellular measurements, or if those are not available, by computational inference methods. These representations can describe intracellular networks such as metabolic, signaling and transcriptional networks or describe intercellular networks, such as cytokine networks. Systems biology and biomolecular network methods have been well covered elsewhere, including in other issues in this series [39]. In the work of the TCGA [10] networks based on signaling, transcription, and extra-cellular interactions were derived from the cancer genomics data and auxiliary knowledge of interactions. These networks provide a possible basis in cellular and molecular interactions on how the alteration in tumor cells relate to changes in the tumor microenvironment. 2.7 Evaluate Several excellent resources are available to enable to researchers Biomarkers Using to conduct exploration and evaluation of candidate biomarkers Available Resources based on data from immunogenomics studies. These include The Cancer Immunome Atlas (TCIA, tcia.at), the suite of tools TIMER, TRUST, and TIDE (liulab.dfci.harvard.edu), and CRI iAtlas (www.cri-iatlas.org). TCIA can be queried for the gene expression of specific immune-related gene sets, the cellular composition of immune infiltrates, neoantigens and cancer-germ line antigens, HLA types, and tumor heterogeneity, and can generate Immunophenograms from uploaded gene expression data [5, 40, 41]. TIMER is a comprehensive resource for exploring the clinical relevance of tumor-immune infiltrates, including B cells, CD4 and CD8 T cells, neutrophils, macrophages and

Multiplatform Integrative Analysis of Immunogenomic Data for Biomarker Discovery 693 dendritic cells [8]. TRUST is a toolbox for analyzing T cell receptors in solid tumors using unselected RNA-seq data based on de novo assembly [42]. TIDE is a gene expression biomarker to predict the clinical response to immune checkpoint blockade and further provides gene-wise associations with T-cell dysfunction and immunotherapy resistance [43]. The Cancer Research Institute (CRI) iAtlas is an interactive web-based platform and set of analytic tools for studying interactions between tumors and the immune microenvironment. These tools allow researchers to explore associations among a variety of immune characterizations as well as with genomic and clinical phenotypes. The initial version of iAtlas is based on an analysis performed by the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Research Network on the TCGA data set comprising over 10,000 tumor samples and 33 tumor types [10]. iAtlas is a cloud-based platform for data exploration and discovery, allowing researchers to study TCGA immune response characterizations, and the relationships among them in individual tumor types, tumor subtypes, and immune subtypes. iAtlas supports the adaptive exploration of correlations within the cellularity of the tumor microenvironment, immune expression signatures, tumor mutation burden, cancer driver mutations, adaptive cell clonality, patient survival, expression of key immunomodulators, and lymphocyte spatial maps. Figure 5 shows an example workflow in iAtlas for studying the potential association between tumor mutation burden and CD8 T cell content in lung adenocarcinoma. Note that in step g of Fig. 5, the workflow reproduces the (manually generated) heatmap visualization of the multiple pairwise comparison seen in Fig. 4c. Multiplatform Integrative Analysis of Immunogenomic Data for Biomarker Discovery 695 Fig. 5 (continued) 3 Conclusions Processing and integrating cancer genomics data to derive signatures of immune response in tissue has yielded substantial insight

into how cancer cells and the immune system interact. Analyses of this type are based on detailed characterizations of multiple aspects of immune response in tissue, such as the estimation of neoantigen load, adaptive receptor complexity, overall immune cell content, proportion of particular immune cell types, and immune activation signatures. These estimates typically derive from a variety of

696 Vésteinn Thorsson genomics platforms, and the computational methods for estimating each are in an active state of development. A great deal of insight is gained by subsequently relating these estimates among different tumor samples. Relatively simple direct comparisons of these heterogeneous measures have been very informative. Further analyses by multivariate statistics, and by systems biology methods providing additional context in terms of network biology lead to additional hypotheses on functional relationships. Several web portals are now available that make it easier to explore results from immunogenomics studies. It is anticipated that technological and methodological improvements are likely to further the importance of immunogenomics for both understanding the underlying biology of the tumor immune microenvironment and for furthering advances in cancer immunotherapy. # Part IX

Regulatory Perspective

## Chapter 31


702 You Li et al. therapies remains one of the major unmet needs for the oncology community. The translation of robust predictive biomarkers to effective diagnostic tests may maximize clinical benefits from novel immuno-therapeutic agents. Translation of predictive biomarkers to in vitro diagnostic tests require appropriate analytical and clinical validation so that tests accurately identify the populations most likely to benefit from current and emerging immunotherapeutic agents. This chapter is designed to give an overview of considerations for the analytical and clinical validation of in vitro diagnostic tests in immuno-oncology. 1.2 Biomarkers Biomarkers are defined as characteristics that are measured as an and Diagnostics indicator of normal biological processes, pathogenic processes, or for Precision Medicine responses to an exposure or intervention, including therapeutic interventions [2]. Molecular, histologic, radiographic, or physiologic characteristics are types of biomarkers. This chapter will be restricted to development of in vitro diagnostics for molecular biomarkers including detection of protein, DNA and RNA signatures associated with response to immunotherapy. Biomarkers can be classified as predictive or prognostic. Predictive biomarker is a single trait or signature of traits that separates a population with respect to the outcome of interest in response to a particular treatment. Prognostic biomarkers can identify patient subgroups with underlying difference in clinical outcomes irrespective of treatment [4, 5]. Predictive and prognostic biomarkers are valuable for clinical decision-making when detected by a validated in vitro diagnostic test designed to identify biomarker status in patient populations to enable precision therapy. A biomarker is a biological measure associated with disease state, whereas an in vitro diagnostic (IVD) test is a well-defined system with a defined performance that is used to measure a biomarker status in the patient population. An IVD test identifies the system for measuring the biomarker that includes the specimen, the analyte, the instruments, the protocol and type of test (i.e., quantitative or qualitative), and the clinical decision point, (i.e., clinical cutoff) for the test system. The critical features of diagnostic tests include definition of the biological matrices (tumor tissue, blood, urine, etc.); the analyte of interest, (i.e., protein(s), DNA or RNA(s)); the test platform (i.e., immunohistochemistry, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), quantitative-PCR (q-PCR), or next-generation sequencing (NGS)); the output (i.e., qualitative or quantitative tests); and the clinical decision point. 1.3 FDA Regulatory IVD tests are medical devices and are subject to FDA regulation Framework for IVD (21 CFR § 809.3). FDA regulates medical devices based on the Tests risk to patients. This is in turn based on intended use (how the test is used) and the indication of use (what condition and why the test is used). FDA defines three risk classes in its regulation of d iagnostic

Translating Immuno-oncology Biomarkers to Diagnostic Tests: A Regulatory Perspective 703 tests: low (Class I), moderate (Class II) and high (Class III). The risk associated with a diagnostic test is based on the intended and indication of use and the consequence of a false test result to patient health. An FDA premarket review of diagnostic devices depends on the risk class. Generally, most class I devices do not require premarket review, most class II devices are reviewed under the 510(k) program, and most class III devices are reviewed under the pre market approval (PMA) program. Diagnostic tests can select a patient population for whom a therapeutic product is indicated or identify biomarker-defined patient subgroups with varying clinical outcomes. Diagnostic tests that are essential for safe and effective use of associated therapeutic product are referred to as companion diagnostic tests [6]. Most pharmaceutical manufacturers use tests to select a clinical trial that is limited to a marker-defined subgroup, the companion diagnostic is indication is limited to a patient “selection” claim [7]. Since companion diagnostic test results are used to make specific treatment decisions, an incorrect test result could lead to significant risks to the patient. A patient with a false-negative test result would not receive effective therapy and those with a false positive result may not benefit from the therapeutic and would be exposed to the associated toxicity. These patients could potentially miss out on or delay alternate effective treatments potentially resulting in poorer health outcomes. Most companion diagnostics are currently regulated as Class III devices and require manufacturer to submit a PMA application to the Agency for review and approval. The FDA approves a medical device based on its determination of the safety and effectiveness of the device. FDA evaluates information provided by the device manufacturer (or sponsor of the premarket submission) to determine if there is a reasonable assurance that the probable benefits of using the device outweigh any probable risks [860.7 (d)(1)] and a reasonable assurance that the use of the device will provide clinically significant results [860.7 (e) (1)]. This evidence is determined for diagnostic tests by assessing the analytical validation (assurance of test performance) and clinical validation (correlation between test result and clinical condition) [7]. 2 Considerations for IVD Validation Precise definition of biomarkers during test development and validation is essential for identification of the patient population for whom the therapeutic may be effective. Biomarkers may be a simple measure of a single analyte (e.g., protein expression status or mutation status for a gene) or complex such as an aggregate measure of multiple analytes/markers that is combined to read out a phenotype or genotype (e.g., gene expression profile, MSI or TMB

704 You Li et al. status). Test systems may measure a biomarker in quantitative metrics (e.g., number of mRNA copies or copy number for a gene) or can identify a qualitative state (e.g., gene mutation state or presence of a protein). Validation of an IVD test for a biomarker should address the underlying complexity of the measurement as well as consider the nature of the measurement (quantitative or qualitative). Therefore, it is critical to define the biomarker and the underlying analyte being measured during validation. This is of special importance for complex biomarkers, such as genomic signatures, or panels for phenotypic measurement. In such cases, the components of the panel should be well defined and the algorithm for final diagnostic result be fully specified prior to analytical and clinical validation of the device. Critical analytical performance parameters for a diagnostic test include specificity, sensitivity and precision of biomarker measurement. The types of studies required to establish these performance metrics are dependent on the analyte(s) and the platform used. The following section uses examples of validated biomarkers in immuno-oncology to delineate the types of studies that are useful for analytical validation of a diagnostic test. The clinical validation of a diagnostic test for a predictive claim or selection claim associated with a therapeutic product usually comes from clinical trials establishing the efficacy of the therapeutic product. The intended use and indications of use for the diagnostic device for the predictive claim or selection claim are determined by the clinical trial design for patient selection or stratification. Immuno-therapeutic agents have demonstrated clinical activity in a wide range of tumor indications. This chapter will use the current biomarker landscape in immuno-oncology as a case study for developing diagnostic tests for either selection of patients for therapy or to differentiate clinical outcomes in biomarker identified patient subgroups. 3 Clinically Validated Immuno-oncology Biomarkers Clinical trials for ICIs (anti PD-1 and PD-L1 therapeutics) have explored the role of multiple biomarkers, including programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) protein expression in the tumor and tumor micro environment, microsatellite instability (MSI) as a marker for selection of patients for treatment [8], and tumor mutational burden (TMB), which has been suggested to be associated with clinical outcomes for patients treated with checkpoint inhibitors in retrospective studies [9]. The following sections details considerations for analytical and clinical validation of in vitro diagnostic tests for the various immuno-oncology biomarkers. These sections cover the types of validation for PD-L1 IHC tests as well as for NGS based assessment of MSI and TMB.

Translating Immuno-oncology Biomarkers to Diagnostic Tests: A Regulatory Perspective 705 3.1  PD-L1 IHC Expression of the programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) protein on tumor cells is hypothesized to induce immune tolerance and an ability to evade innate immune response against tumor cells [10]. For ICIs targeting PD-1 and PD-L1, it is hypothesized that expression of PD-L1 on tumor cells may be predictive of an immune suppressed state and inhibition of the PD-1/PD-L1 interaction can accelerate the native anti-tumor activity. This hypothesis was supported in early phase studies that indicated that PD-L1 expression was potentially associated with response to checkpoint inhibitor treatment [10]. With emerging evidence of potential difference in clinical outcomes, early development of checkpoint inhibitors such as Opdivo® (nivolumab) and Keytruda® (pembrolizumab) was accompanied by exploration of PD-L1 protein in tumor cells as a potential predictive/selection biomarker in various indication. The various anti PD-1 and PD-L1 therapeutic programs employed unique PD-L1 IHC tests for either selection or stratification of clinical trial population to assess outcomes (response rate, progression free survival (PFS) or overall survival) based on PD-L1 expression status. Starting in 2014, rapid approvals of the various ICIs for a wide range tumor indication were accompanied by approval of four distinct PD-L1 IHC tests developed with partnerships between various drug and device makers. 706 You Li et al. two of the four tests, Dako PD-L1 IHC 22C3 and Ventana PD-L1 SP142 assay, are companion diagnostic tests that are required for safe and effective use of the Keytruda and Tecentriq in specified indications. Dako PD-L1 IHC 28-8 pharmDx test and the Ventana PD-L1 SP263 are diagnostic tests for associated indications where the test identifies a patient subgroup with a different benefit risk profile than the broader population for which the therapeutic is indicated and is beneficial for clinical decision-making. However, the clinical evidence did not indicate that the test would be required for safe and effective use of the associated therapeutic product. 3.2 Defining Tumor The four FDA approved PD-L1 IHC tests are qualitative tests that PD-L1 Status determine patient tumor as PD-L1 positive or negative, and each and Challenges of these tests use varying definitions for PD-L1 positivity including with PD-L1 IHC Tests employing indication specific clinical cutoffs and or biomarker definitions. The factors accounting for this variation are the unique scoring algorithm for the four tests that displays variously defined PD-L1 expression status using either tumor cell expression (Dako PD-L1 IHC 22C3 with Keytruda® and PD-L1 IHC 28-8 pharmDx with Opdivo®), or tumor associated immune cells expression (Ventana PD-L1 SP142 assay with Tecentriq®), or a combination of tumor and immune cells expression of the protein (Ventana PD-L1 SP263 with Imfinzi® and PD-L1 IHC 22C3pharmDx with Keytruda) [11–13]. Consequently, each of these tests identifies a unique biomarker defined patient population for whom clinical outcomes with associated drugs have been characterized. One of the central questions for the PD-L1 IHC tests is the comparability of PD-L1 assessment across tests and the underlying measure of analyte. In 2015, FDA in collaboration with AACR and ASCO hosted a public workshop to discuss the comparability of the various PD-L1 IHC devices [14]. As a result of this discussion an academic and industry partnership initiated the Blueprint study to compare the assay performance in archival samples tested with four IHC assays. The Blueprint study results provided an outline for the comparability of test performance with respect to assessing tumor PD-L1 staining in non small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with an associated companion diagnostic test [15, 16]. Results from initial Blueprint studies conducted with limited sample sets suggests that three of the four IHC tests show comparable performance for measurement of PD-L1 expression in tumor tissue. However, the same studies also identified that assessment of immune cell PD-L1 expression to be inherently difficult and more variable. While initial data on harmonization of the PD-L1 IHC tests is promising with respect to comparability of analytical performance, these tests were designed to identify unique population based on scoring criteria specified in clinical trials and are therefore not interchangeable. Thus, clinical comparability of assay performance with differing PD-L1 definition may require head to head studies that assess all factors that contribute assay variation.

Translating Immuno-oncology Biomarkers to Diagnostic Tests: A Regulatory Perspective 707 3.3 Considerations As summarized in Table 1, four FDA approved PD-L1 IHC devices for Validation of PD-L1 are available on the market and most of these devices have been IHC Tests validated in more than one tumor indication. PD-L1 IHC device reviews included assessment of all factors that contributed to variation in device performance in indication specific validation with attention to the predefined clinical cutoff. All validation studies included sufficient marker positive and negative specimens as well as challenging around cutoff specimens. A summary of the types of studies that were performed and reviewed is given below.
1. Preanalytical variables: Analytical validation studies that address
preanalytical variables generally explore device performance with test variables that are indication independent as they address device components and protocols that impact performance of the test systems. For the FDA approved PD-L1 IHC tests these factors included specificity of the primary antibody, cross reactivity to isoforms and protein family members, antigen characterization and retrieval conditions that would remain unchanged across indication. System level controls—negative reagent control tissue controls (positive and negative) as mitigation to ascertain proper performance of the device. Preanalytical variables that can impact device performance include fixation type and time, ischemia, tissue preprocessing such as decalcification, and tissue thickness can be examined in indication independent studies. The specimen type (i.e., tumor resection, biopsy, fine needle aspirates, etc.) is an important variable that is validated by indication as different indications may require different specimen types. For a given indication, the specimen types used in patient enrollment in clinical studies validates its claim for a device (e.g., core needle biopsies for gastric indication for PD-L1 IHC 22C3 pharmDx). Additional preanalytical variables considered as indication specific factors included specimen age and specimen stability especially as cut slides were independently assessed for each indication. For a clear understating of the impact of the preanalytical factors impacting the test outcomes, clinical studies collected data on the specimen type and age (resection, biopsy, block, or slides and age of block or slides) to support device specific claims.
2. Clinical cutoff: A variety of biomarker strategies for ICI have
been employed to identify patient populations that respond to treatment. Among them has been employing indication specific clinical cutoffs and or biomarker definitions. Analytical validation and clinical validation for qualitative tests—such as the PD-L1 IHC—are performed with attention to the clinical decision point (clinical cutoff) for a given intended and indication of use. With growing research of biomarker and evolving understanding of the role of tumor and immune cells in the tumor microenvironment to checkpoint inhibition, the algorithms

708 You Li et al. used to define PD-L1 positivity has evolved across tumor types. Evolving definition for determination of PD-L1 expression status has required tumor type specific validation of the various PD-L1 IHC tests to support their intended use. These tumor type specific device validations were performed with studies designed to the clinical cut point for each clinical indication and accounting for all sources of variance to accurately determine device performance.
3. Analytical validation
• Sensitivity/prevalence: Sensitivity studies are intended to address the range of analyte detection and examined PD-L1 expression in a case series to ascertain the staining characteristics in intended use population. Additional studies in intended use population included assessment of tumor heterogeneity (primary to metastatic and within and between block). • Specificity: Tissue specificity intended to assess cross reactivity across normal tissue and antigen expression across tumor types. These studies include both normal tissues and tissue specimens representing a range of tumors to assess specific and background staining for the antibody in its use context. • Robustness studies: The robustness studies are intended to assess protocol variables and the tolerance in minor variations in testing condition, and these include antigen retrieval time, temperature, and pH. Primary antibody incubation time may be another variable to assess in robustness studies. • Analytical precision: Precision of assessment included testing assay variables such as day, instrument, lot, and run. Site-to-site reproducibility in at least three sites was provided for distributed test kits. Since IHC tests were assessed manually by the pathologist, reader reproducibility measures were essential part of performance characterization.
4. Clinical validation: As indicated in the preceding section the
types of claims for diagnostic tests depend on the types of clinical studies with associated therapeutic products. Typically, marker selected clinical trials that characterize drug activity in a biomarker defined population requires a diagnostic test for safe and effective use of drug and require a contemporaneous review of a companion diagnostic device. For example, approval of Keytruda in NSCLC was for patients whose tumors expressed PD-L1 in tumor cells, assessed as tumor proportion score (TPS) >=1, with a concurrent approval of the Dako PD-L1 IHC 22C3 pahrmDx test as a companion diagnostic based on a marker selected trail Keynote010 [10]. However, when clinical studies that enroll

Translating Immuno-oncology Biomarkers to Diagnostic Tests: A Regulatory Perspective 709 patients irrespective of the biomarker status but stratify patients into treatment arms on basis of biomarker status, the diagnostic test claim is based on the efficacy outcomes in biomarker defined subgroups. For example, Dako PD-L1 IHC 22C3 was approved as a companion diagnostic test for selection of Gastric cancer patients for treatment with Keytruda based on efficacy observations in the PD-L1 positive patient population [16], while Dako PD-L1 IHC 28-8 pharmDx was not required to determine patient eligibility for treatment with Opdivo in HNSCC based on drug efficacy in overall population; however the test identified patient populations with differential overall survival outcomes in the PD-L1 defined subgroups & was approved for that indication. Typically, the diagnostic claim is based on the clinical trial design, such as all comer or biomarker selected, and the clinical efficacy outcomes in the study. Clinical outcomes in biomarker defined subgroups for therapeutics determine the claims associated with a diagnostic test. Thus, device claims can remain uncertain until late in the development program for both the therapeutic and the diagnostic test. Therefore, careful consideration to biomarker hypothesis and the device use early in clinical trial design phase is essential for successful diagnostic device validation. Clinical trial design should prespecify appropriate statistical analysis plans for efficacy assessment in biomarker defined subgroups. 3.4 Mismatch Repair FDA’s approval in May 2017 of PD-1 blockade therapy Keytruda Deficiency/ (pembrolizumab) for treating adult and pediatric patients with Microsatellite unresectable or metastatic solid tumors with microsatellite Instability (MSI) instability- high (MSI-H) or mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) regardless of cancer origin is one of the major breakthroughs in cancer immunotherapy [18] (Lemery et al. 2017). This is the first time the agency has approved a cancer treatment based on a common biomarker for tissue-agnostic indication rather than the location in the body where the tumor originated. The drug approval stipulated a post marketing commitment by the drug company for developing companion diagnostic tests- a dMMR test as well as a MSI test- to enable availability of well characterized diagnostic test for safe and effective use of the drug in this setting. Mismatch repair (MMR) proteins MLH1, PMS2, MSH2 and MSH6 are critical part of DNA repair pathway responsible for correcting base pair mismatches that occur during DNA replication [19]. Mutations or epigenetic events resulting in loss of MMR protein expression are oncogenic drivers and results in increased DNA replication error rates in cells [19]. The phenotypic consequence of loss of MMR protein expression is impaired DNA repair of single base mismatches resulting short insertion and deletions readily measured in short DNA repeats (up to six base pairs) or microsatellite sites [20]. Changes to microsatellite length in tumor tissue is termed as microsatellite instability (MSI) and is a molecular phenotype

710 You Li et al. marked by the spontaneous gain or loss of nucleotides from within repetitive microsatellite tracts, which results in the production of novel microsatellite MSI is most prevalent in MMR-related cancerprone syndrome Lynch Syndrome, with over 90% of Lynch syndrome patients manifest MSI [21, 22]. MSI also occurs sporadically in nonhereditary cancers, the prevalence for MSI-H vary significantly across different tumor types, with colorectal, endometrial, and gastric cancers among those with highest prevalence for MSI [22]. Diagnosis of MSI often has important clinical implications, such as informing therapeutic options, cancer prognosis, and familial cancer risk. Mismatch repair status for a tumor can be determined by IHC test for the four MMR proteins with assessment of expression in tumor cells as either proficient (pMMR) or deficient (dMMR) when one of the four MMR proteins is absent in the tumor tissue. dMMR tumors have been shown to exhibit MSI and the two biomarkers are considered to identify a patient population with the same underlying biology [20]. The MSI status of MSI- high (MSI-H) or microsatellite stable (MSS) is determined by molecular tests for repeat regions such as PCR or NGS. Genotyping of informative microsatellite markers by PCR (MSI-PCR) is the standard DNA-based method for detection of MSI in current clinical practice. Select microsatellites are PCR amplified using fluorescently labeled primers, and fragment length polymorphisms are identified through capillary electrophoresis. Current guidelines for MSI- PCR recommend the use of relatively small, standardized panels of microsatellites that include highly unstable mononucleotide or dinucleotide repeat loci [21, 22]. 3.5 MMR IHC Test The MMR IHC tests are a case of simple panel tests and comprised of four MMR proteins whose expression in patient tumors is assessed independently. Further, a simple algorithm assesses the dMMR vs. pMMR status whereby loss of any one of the four proteins is sufficient to determine dMMR status. FDA has authorized the Ventana MMR Lynch syndrome panel indicated in patients with confirmed colorectal cancer diagnoses who would benefit from additional test for lynch syndrome [23]. The validation data supported its use as an aid for differential diagnosis between sporadic CRC and probable Lynch syndrome. Importantly, this test is not validated to select patients for any immunotherapy treatment. The analytical validation challenges for panel-based biomarkers include identifying sufficient cases that represent the range of possible test results and assessing the variability in the panel performance both comprehensively and of individual analyte for adequate understanding of all sources of variation. The clinical studies that formed the basis of approval for tissue agnostic biomarker defined indication of Keytruda included patients with a variety of tumor types and defined dMMR as loss of one or more MMR proteins by IHC tests or MSI as measured by PCR. Clinical validation of MMR/MSI as compan-

Translating Immuno-oncology Biomarkers to Diagnostic Tests: A Regulatory Perspective 711 ion diagnostic should come from the tissue agnostic clinical trials and analytical validation of a tissue agnostic MMR IHC test should include sufficient specimens across multiple tumor indications. 3.6 MSI Detection The MSI status of MSI- high MSI-H or microsatellite stable (MSS) is determined by molecular tests for repeat regions such as PCR or NGS. The advance and maturation of next-generation sequencing (NGS) technology has revolutionized the field of genomic research and precision medicine. NGS-based oncology panels have been widely used in the clinical settings, which not only generate comprehensive tumor mutation profiling data, but can also simultaneously provide genotypic data on microsatellite loci across the targeted genomic regions. Several NGS-MSI algorithms have been developed to conduct MSI analysis with NGS data, such as MSIsensor, MANTis, and mSING [24–26]. Studies have shown that the NGS-MSI results may have high concordance with clinically established PCR-based MSI results [20, 25, 27, 28]. One major benefit of NGS testing is its lack of specificity to tumor type. The PCR-MSI had the highest clinical relevance in Lynch syndrome-related cancers, such as CRC, endometrial cancer, and gastric cancer. The sensitivity and specificity of these small PCR-MSI panels have been shown reliable in these cancer types through decades of research. However, these MSI loci were predominately selected based on markers from CRC, potentially excluding loci that would predict other cancer types. It is likely beneficial to establish pantumor MSI using a large number of microsatellite loci, regardless of their associations to a specific cancer type, across the genome using NGS technology. Recent studies suggested that NGS-MSI may have higher sensitivity and specificity than the five-marker Bethesda panel (MSI-PCR) in colorectal cancer and had higher sensitivity and similar specificity in prostate cancer, although the clinical validity of NGS-MSI as a tumoragnostic predictor for immunotherapy response remains to be further studied across cancer types [27, 28]. 3.7 Case Study: There is currently no FDA-approved MSI companion diagnostic Considerations test for any specific therapeutic. However, the agency has authofor Analytical rized the first comprehensive NGS tumor profiling test MSK- Validation of NGS- IMPACT in November 2017 through the De Novo process. Based MSI Test MSK-IMPACT is a 468-gene NGS oncopanel with the ability to for Tumor Profiling also detect and report MSI findings. Using MSK-IMPACT decision summary [29] as a case study, below is a summary of some Claim major considerations for the analytical validation and reporting of NGS-MSI findings.
1. Analytical concordance: Given the microsatellite loci included
on each panel and the underlying algorithm for MSI analysis may vary dramatically across different NGS panels, the MSK-

712 You Li et al. IMPACT validation study was designed to establish concordance with clinically established PCR-MSI and dMMR-IHC methods. For the MSK-IMPACT MSI accuracy study, the MSI cutoff (i.e., MSIsensor score ≥10 indicates MSI-H) was first established using a training dataset of 138 colorectal cancer (CRC) samples and 40 endometrial carcinoma (EC) samples with matched normal with known MSI status determined by from a validated MSI-PCR or MMR IHC test, then the analytical accuracy was demonstrated using two independent validation cohorts: first cohort includes 66 CRC/EC samples (13 MSI-H) and the second cohort includes 119 samples from other non-CRC/non-EC cancer types (59 MSI-H from 25 cancer types).
2. Detection sensitivity: Several factors may significantly impact the
detection sensitivity of NGS-MSI, such as tumor purity and sequence depth. Using MSK-IMPACT assay established minimal requirements of 25% tumor content and average target coverage above 200× in order to maintain high detection sensitivity for somatic MSI.
3. Precision: Both interrun and intrarun precision of the MSK-
IMPACT MSI results were established using both MSI-H and MSS specimens. The MSI-H samples validated covered the range of the underlying MSI score expected in the clinical setting, including challenging samples near the assay cutoff. Precision analysis was not only performed with the qualitative MSI findings but also performed with the quantitative underlying scores used to determine the categorical MSI results.
4. Tumor type comparability: To validate a pantumor MSI test,
MSK-IMPACT assay performance was demonstrated across different tumor types. Potential interference substance associated with specific tumor type was assessed to ensure it did not lead to any significant increase in assay invalid rate or inaccurate results for a specific tumor type.
5. Report of NGS-MSI findings: The MSK-IMPACT test report
clearly indicates MSI-H by MSK-IMPACT is defined by a different set of unstable microsatellite loci from those in a standard PCR-MSI panel. Additionally, since the current authorization for the test is for a tumor profiling claim and not for a “Prediction” claim or a “selection” claim, the report form also indicates that the clinical validity of the NGS-based MSI-H findings has not been well established, the results are not conclusive or prescriptive for labeled use of any specific therapeutic.

Translating Immuno-oncology Biomarkers to Diagnostic Tests: A Regulatory Perspective 713 4 Emerging Immunotherapy Biomarker and Analytical Validation Challenges 4.1 Panel Based IHC The combined experience across indications and drug products for Biomarkers checkpoint inhibitors suggest that PD-L1 status is useful but by itself maybe insufficient to predict outcomes for immunotherapy agents. Recent research exploring markers in tumor microenvironment with the use of panel of proteins in multi-marker immunofluorescences tests show promise in improving sensitivity and specificity in predicting response to immunotherapy agents. Such immune signature panels can be comprised of immune cell markers such as CD8, CD4 and CD62 and use a complex scoring system that not only accounts for their abundance but uses complex image analysis algorithms that can assess interaction of the immune and tumor cells to measure [30]. While single analyte IHC test validations are relatively straight forward, robust validation of biomarker panels presents unique challenges in accurate assessment of assay performance and requires careful consideration of all factors that can contribute to assay variation. Of critical importance is the scoring system used to define the biomarker population and the contribution of each of the panel members to the final score. Once a scoring system is locked down, it is important to consider whether specimens representing the range of possible biomarker status are included in the validation specimen set, and to assess performance including variability for each component in the test system. Such assessments provide for better understanding of the contribution of each panel member to assay variability and help identify challenges in accurate measurement of complex panels [31]. 4.2 Tumor Tumor mutational burden (TMB) is another emerging biomarker Mutational Burden for cancer immunotherapy response. TMB is a measure of somatic (TMB) mutation load in the tumor genome. It is often reported by the number of mutations per megabase (mut/Mb), determined by 4.2.1 Introduction whole-exome sequencing or targeted NGS-oncopanel. It has long been hypothesized that cancers with a greater number of somatic mutations may provoke a stronger antitumor immune response. The rationale behind this hypothesis relates to neoantigens—protein peptides expressed on the surface of cancer cells that are encoded by mutated genes. Neoantigens are unique to cancer cells and have the potential to be recognized as foreign pathogen by the immune system. A greater number of neoantigens might lead to increased stimulation of the immune cells and a stronger antitumor immune response. TMB has recently been intensively studied in various types of cancer, especially in non-small cell lung cancer. Results from retrospective clinical studies have suggested that TMB is a very promising biomarker for ICI response [32–35]. These studies suggest that cancer patients with high TMB (TMB-H) may have better

714 You Li et al. response to ICI therapy. Additionally, the data from recent studies also suggested that TMB may be an independent biomarker from PD-L1 expression, although patients with both high TMB and high PD-L1 expression (i.e., TMB/PD-L1 double positive) may have even more profound response to ICI. 4.2.2 Challenges TMB is a very promising biomarker predictive of immunotherapy for TMB Assay Analytical response. However, there are significant challenges to universally Validation define and evaluate TMB as a predictive biomarker. The lack of standards on panel TMB definition and calculation, as well as the lack of reference material and standardized reference methods are major challenges for the validation and assessment of TMB assay performance. There is currently no consensus on how TMB is measured and reported. Differences in the underlying variant detection and the TMB score calculation algorithm across different NGS oncology panels make it extremely challenging to interpret and compare TMB findings from different assays. Various analytical characteristics of the NGS panel will have a significant impact on the TMB results. The following factors should be considered for development of a TMB assay and comparison of TMB results across different TMB assays: panel genomic context and panel size; variant types to be included for TMB calculation; analytical sensitivity (i.e., lower limit of detection of the underlying somatic variants); germline variant filtering approach; TMB score cut-offs to differentiate categorical TMB findings (e.g., TMB-high vs. TMB-low). Whole-exome based TMB is generally considered the gold-standard for TMB measurement, as it provides an objective assessment of somatic mutation load across the cancer genome. However, due to its high cost and longer turnaround time, it has not been widely used in the clinical settings. In addition, a standardized WES- TMB workflow and assay specification still remains to be developed. To address these challenges, FDA has been actively engaged in the Friends of Cancer Research (FoCR) TMB Harmonization working group (https://www.focr.org/tmb). Through collaborative efforts, the working group is aimed to develop reference standards for validating and reporting TMB findings, which will help improve patient care through consistent TMB reporting in a clinical setting despite differences in the testing panel used. 5 Conclusion With rapid development of therapeutic options for patients in the immuno-oncology space, biomarkers promise to enable personalization of treatments and improve clinical outcomes. However, this promise requires the translation of biomarkers from experimental space to the clinical space as validated diagnostic tests. The

Translating Immuno-oncology Biomarkers to Diagnostic Tests: A Regulatory Perspective 715 critical factors in successful translation to diagnostic test is the very definition of the biomarker, the means (i.e., the appropriate technology) to measure the biomarker with precision and clinical validation of the fully defined diagnostic test for a clear understanding of the clinical outcomes in the biomarker defined population. A well-considered approach is required for effective translation of a biomarker assay to a diagnostic test. FDA has been actively engaged in several collaborative initiatives aimed to facilitate and expedite the development of new biomarkers for cancer immunotherapy [36]. Rapid innovations in test development promises to usher a new era in personalized immunotherapy with improved clinical outcomes for patients. References
